docs.title: iqmq
docs.text:
One small, capability-honest, bytes-first Go API for publishing and consuming messages across Kafka, NATS/JetStream, NSQ, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Redis Streams and Pulsar, plus a deterministic in-process memory engine.

Under construction

The project is being built increment by increment against the specification. See Status. No performance, delivery-guarantee or compatibility claim is made until the reproducible evidence described there exists.

docs.title: Is this ready to use?
docs.text: No. It is pre-alpha and under construction against the specification. Status is the honest list of what works, what is measured and what is open, including the parts of the specification the implementation does not yet meet.

docs.title: Does it give me exactly-once processing?
docs.text:
No, and nothing can give you that at the messaging layer alone. The specification recognises broker-scoped exactly-once delivery — Pub/Sub exactly-once subscriptions, Kafka transactions with read_committed, Pulsar transactions, JetStream dedup — and each of those deduplicates the broker's own record, within its own scope and window.

Your side effects are a different problem, and the answer is an idempotent handler or an inbox table. See duplicates and idempotency and inbox and outbox.

docs.title: Why one Go module per driver?
docs.text:
So that depending on this library costs you one broker SDK — the one you chose — rather than eleven. The root module and the memory driver depend on the standard library only, and make stdlib-check holds them to it.

It is a security property as much as a build-time one: your program's attack surface is the client you actually use.

docs.title: Why is the API so large?
docs.text:
Because a portable messaging API has two honest designs and both are bad. The intersection of what every broker does is small and useless. The union is large and requires lying about the brokers that cannot do it.

This library takes the union and pays for it with the capability model: everything is guarded by a level the driver either advertises or refuses, and asking for something a broker cannot do fails at construction or before any I/O. Capability negotiation is the mechanism.

docs.title: Why does Publish block?
docs.text: Because mq.BackpressureBlock is the default, and blocking is the reliable answer: the caller is either served or told. If you would rather shed load, put a deadline on the context or ask for mq.BackpressureReject. The two drop modes exist and are never defaults, because they lose a publication without telling the caller. Backpressure.

docs.title: Why won't it retry my ambiguous publish?
docs.text: Because a library that silently retries an ambiguous publication silently duplicates whatever that publication caused. The specification forbids the core from auto-retrying unless native idempotent publication makes it safe within its documented scope, or you asked for it explicitly. Ambiguous publishes.

docs.title: The same message keeps arriving and never gets dead-lettered. Why?
docs.text: Almost certainly because your broker does not keep a delivery count, so Delivery.Attempt is 0, and under the default mq.OrderingRelaxed the runner has no count to compare with mq.WithMaxAttempts. Use mq.OrderingStrict — which holds the message in the process and counts exactly — or a broker with a native count. The matrix says which have one. Ordering.

docs.title: Why did throughput collapse after one failure?
docs.text: mq.OrderingStrict at the default mq.WithConcurrency(1). A strict retry holds the lane in the process for the whole backoff, so one worker is parked for up to the configured 30-second cap — and at concurrency 1 that is the whole runner. Raise the concurrency, or lower mq.ExponentialBackoff.Max.

docs.title: What does (N) mean in the capability matrix?
docs.text: The driver advertises that level and no probe verified it. A bare N means a probe verified it in both directions. There are also — (not offered, and the refusal was observed), · (a denied guarantee no run contradicted), ? (nothing established it either way), ! (a scenario FAILED), and ◐ (the evidence is an emulator's). Capability negotiation has the whole table.

docs.title: Can I use the memory driver as a mock?
docs.text:
Use it as a driver. It implements the same mq.Backend as Kafka, so a test against it exercises the real runner and the real settlement state machine. memory.NewForTest(t) adds a fake clock, AutoCreate, and a leak check.

It is never persistent and never advertises durable storage, so it cannot stand in for a durability test. The memory driver.

docs.title: How do I test a 30-second backoff?
docs.text: broker.Advance(30 * time.Second) — never time.Sleep. Inside a testing/synctest bubble you can go further and assert the schedule, which is what catches a runner that stopped waiting between attempts. synctest.

docs.title: How do I assess performance?
docs.text: Run the benchmarks against the revision, broker and workload you plan to deploy. See the performance guide and methodology. Budget thresholds describe targets; they are not measurements or evidence that a target was met.

docs.title: Which driver should I use?
docs.text: The one your broker is. The selection guide compares them, and where there are two clients for one broker — Kafka, Redis — the choice is which module you import, with the bake-off's recommendation on the driver page.

docs.title: How do I write a driver for a broker you do not support?
docs.text: The driver author guide. The short version: implement Backend, Sink and Source; add the optional interfaces your broker can support; build errors with driverkit.ErrorMapper or an mq.OpError; and run testkit.RunConformance against it. The kit uses only the portable API, so it works from outside this repository — examples/custom-driver is a worked example, with a test proving it imports no internal package.

docs.title: Where do I report a bug?
docs.text: A GitHub issue, with the iqmq doctor dump for a driver bug — that is what the issue form asks for. A security issue goes through private vulnerability reporting and never a public issue.

docs.title: The iqmq command
docs.text:
iqmq is the command-line tool: publish, consume, watch, generate load, and ask a broker what it can actually do.

go install github.com/iqhive/iqmq/cmd/iqmq@latest

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
The library is the product. The CLI exists for the things you cannot do from a library:

  • iqmq doctor — point it at a DSN and it tells you which driver answered, what that driver advertises about itself, what limits it declares, and which variant kinds are in force. It is the first thing to run when a deployment behaves unlike the documentation, and its output is what a driver bug report should carry.
  • iqmq pub / iqmq sub — put a message in, take a message out, with settlement and confirmation stated rather than implied.
  • iqmq tail — watch a topic, and be told plainly when watching it costs somebody else their messages.
  • iqmq bench — see roughly how fast this machine talks to that broker.
  • iqmq topology plan / apply — declare the topics and subscriptions a deployment needs, see what would change, and then make it so. Open never creates production topology ((../concepts/index.md)), so something has to, explicitly; this is it.
  • iqmq bridge — move messages from one broker to another, with what the seam guarantees stated on every run rather than left to be assumed.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
A script branches on these, so they are a contract.

Code Meaning 0 success 1 the operation ran and did not succeed — the broker refused, a publication was not confirmed, a deadline passed with the work unfinished 2 the invocation could not be acted on — bad flags, a DSN that does not parse, a scheme no driver claims 3 the driver does not have a capability the command needs ((../concepts/capabilities.md))

Exit 3 is separate from exit 1 on purpose: nothing a caller retries will change it. iqmq tail against a work queue exits 3, and the message names the feature and the level it read.

docs.title: Flags may follow positional arguments
docs.text:
$ iqmq pub memory://?autocreate=true orders --header trace=abc 'hello'

Go's flag package stops parsing at the first non-flag argument, which would make that invocation report "a DSN and a topic are required" — true of nothing you typed. The CLI moves flags ahead of positionals before parsing, so a flag works wherever you put it.

The one consequence: a positional that begins with - has to come after a -- terminator. In practice that is a pub body:

$ iqmq pub memory://?autocreate=true orders -- '-starts-with-a-dash'

docs.title: Credentials never reach the terminal
docs.text:
This is a security property, not a convenience, and it is built in two layers because neither is enough alone.

Nothing in the CLI renders a DSN parameter or a configuration field itself. A target is rendered as scheme, user, endpoints and path — the password becomes redacted and every query parameter is dropped, because the CLI cannot know which of a driver's parameters is a credential and a list it maintained would be wrong the moment a driver added one. A resolved configuration is rendered by the driver's own Config.String, which (../security/index.md) makes the driver's obligation and which each driver proves in its own tests.

Everything the CLI prints then passes through a scrub holding each credential it can identify — the DSN's password, the value of every credential-named parameter, the value of every credential-named environment variable. That layer exists because the output also carries driver error strings, native client messages and broker replies, none of which the CLI wrote.

So:

$ iqmq doctor 'sqs://AKIAEXAMPLE:wJalrXUtnFEMI@127.0.0.1:9324?region=elasticmq&sessiontoken=FQoGZ'
target
  dsn                   sqs://AKIAEXAMPLE:redacted@127.0.0.1:9324?<2 parameters, not shown>
  parameters            region sessiontoken=<redacted>

The environment is reported by name and set/unset only. There is nowhere in the report for a variable's value to go.

A credential that is also an ordinary word is replaced wherever it appears, which can over-redact: a broker whose password is artemis and whose profile is also called artemis produces profile=redacted. That is the right trade — a scrub that skipped short or dictionary-word secrets would be a hole with a threshold on it — so the CLI says when it happened, counting the occurrences it replaced and printing a note under the report.

Message bodies and headers are a separate question. sub and tail print the body by default, because showing you the message is what you invoked them for, and they do not print headers unless you pass --headers — a bearer token in an authorization header is exactly what the specification is about.

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
$ iqmq doctor memory://?autocreate=true

doctor reports four different kinds of fact, and keeps them apart:

  1. The build — this binary's version, platform, registered drivers and schemes, and the driver modules it cannot register with the reason. "The CLI cannot open it" and "iqmq has no such driver" are different facts.
  2. The target — the redacted DSN, the driver that claimed the scheme, the configuration the driver parsed it into, and whether a connection and a ping succeeded.
  3. What the driver advertises — every feature of the inventory with the level and scope the driver claims. This is not probe evidence. A conformance run verifying a claim is a separate fact, and the capability matrix renders six distinct states to keep advertised apart from verified. Nine features have no behavioural probe in any conformance run at all, so a driver advertising one cannot be held to it; doctor marks those rows [never probed] and names all nine in its own output rather than leaving them to be looked up.
  4. The variant kinds — two lists, because they are two facts. The build list is every family's Auto binding, a generated constant chosen by a bake-off, with the provisional flag that says the campaign was not authoritative. The target list is the kind actually in force for this DSN, and says whether it came from the DSN or from the Auto binding.

--no-connect reports everything that needs no I/O. -o json is the form a bug report should attach. --drivers reports the driver table alone.

docs.title: pub
docs.text:
$ iqmq pub memory://?autocreate=true orders '{"id":1}'
$ iqmq pub kafka://localhost:9092 orders -H trace=abc -k customer-7 --file events.ndjson
$ iqmq pub sqs://key:secret@aws?region=eu-west-1 orders --confirm durable --receipt

Bodies come from positional arguments, or one per line of --file (--file - for stdin), or as one whole message with --no-lines. --batch sends the lot through PublishBatch, and a partly failed batch is reported per message: (../drivers/author-guide.md)'s index alignment is what makes that possible, and a batch result aligned with anything else is how a batch publish loses a message silently.

Confirmation is explicit and the exit status honours it. --confirm durable asks for a durable boundary and fails at construction where the profile cannot define one. A publication whose acceptance the broker never reported is not a success: it is counted as NOT CONFIRMED (acceptance unknown) and the command exits 1.

--delay requires FeatureScheduledPublish and --receipt requires FeatureReceipts; both are checked before the publisher is constructed, so the refusal names the feature rather than arriving at the first message. The publication controls are folded and validated before a connection is opened too, so --priority 999 tells you about the priority and not about the dial.

docs.title: sub
docs.text:
$ iqmq sub memory://?autocreate=true orders billing --max 10
$ iqmq sub kafka://localhost:9092 orders workers --settle nack --nack-action dead-letter
$ iqmq sub nats://localhost:4222 orders workers --idle 5s --concurrency 4 -o json

Settlement is never implicit:

  • --settle ack|nack|reject|none is what a handled delivery is settled with.
  • --on-stop ack|nack|reject|none is what a delivery still in flight when the run ends is settled with, and it defaults to nack. --max 1 against a batch of ten gives one delivery back to you and returns nine, rather than holding them until their leases expire with nothing in the output saying so.
  • Every disposition is counted and printed, and abandoned is not spelled the same as acked.

The settlement flags are capability requirements, checked before the consumer is opened: --settle nack needs FeatureNack, --settle reject needs FeatureDeadLetter (it is Nack(NackActionDeadLetter) — the specification makes "destroy this" explicit, so Reject is the dead-letter route and not a drop), --nack-delay needs FeatureDelayedRedelivery, and --start earliest needs FeatureReplay. A settlement the driver refuses as unsupported at run time exits 3, not 1, and says that no retry will change it.

Note that naming a dead-letter destination is not the same as having one: a driver may refuse reject because the destination does not exist, and the reference driver deliberately will not create it for you.

--settle none leaves everything unsettled, which makes sub a read-only probe on a driver whose unsettled deliveries are redelivered. It is not free: an unsettled delivery holds a prefetch slot, so such a run stops when it has filled the window, and says so.

docs.title: tail
docs.text:
$ iqmq tail nats://localhost:4222 'orders.>'

tail starts at the latest message, takes a subscription of its own, and settles nothing where the driver permits it.

Whether a topic can be tailed at all is a fact about the broker. tail reads two capabilities before it opens anything:

Capability What it decides FeatureFanOut whether a subscription of tail's own receives a copy. Without it, every message tail takes is one a competing consumer does not get — so tail refuses with exit 3 unless --consume says that is wanted. FeatureAtLeastOnce whether an unsettled delivery comes back. Without it, and with explicit acknowledgement, a delivery tail does not settle is lost; tail says so and carries on.

Several drivers cannot be tailed without consuming. That is a capability fact and not a limitation of this tool, and the refusal quotes the feature and the level it read so you can check it against the driver's page.

docs.title: bench
docs.text:
$ iqmq bench memory://?autocreate=true orders --messages 2000
$ iqmq bench memory://?autocreate=true orders --variants
$ iqmq bench kafka://localhost:9092 orders --trace /tmp/iqmq.trace

These figures are operational, not iqmq's budgets

iqmq bench measures this machine talking to that broker at the moment you ran it, alongside whatever else the host is doing. It prints that notice every time, and the JSON form carries "source": "cli-operational" and "authoritative": false.

(../performance/methodology.md)'s budgets come from the benchmarks module, under hack/benchguard.sh on a quiet host, with contention recorded and a run discarded when another benchmark touched the machine. make gate is what holds a change to them. Do not quote a bench number as iqmq's performance, and do not read two runs of it as a regression gate.

The output carries GOMAXPROCS, the CPU count and the host load average for exactly that reason: a reader who cannot see the load cannot judge the number.

--trace PATH turns on runtime/trace's flight recorder for the whole run and writes the window it still holds when the run ends. Read it with go tool trace. It is the tool for "the first two hundred publications were fast and then something stalled", which a summary line cannot show you.

--variants runs one arm per kind of every variant family the target selects through its DSN, and prints a row per arm; -- sweeps one family alone. iqmq doctor lists which families a target selects; a target that selects none says so rather than running one arm and calling it a sweep.

A kind of a runtime-selectable family is not automatically reachable from a connection string, and a sweep says which ones it could not measure. Family the specification's custom nack strategy needs a Go callback (Config.Decide), so nack=custom is refused by both Kafka drivers: the family has four kinds and a DSN can select three. bench prints the excluded kind with its reason before the first arm runs, because three arms presented as a family comparison would be a lie about what was measured. The memory driver is the special case: its DSN selects kinds only in bulk — engine=safe pins every family at once to its mutex-backed reference kind — so its sweep has two arms that each move nine families, and it is labelled engine rather than a family id, because calling it The specification would be a lie about what was measured.

docs.title: topology
docs.text:
$ iqmq topology plan  memory://?autocreate=true --topic orders --subscription orders=billing
$ iqmq topology apply kafka://localhost:9092 -f topology.json

Open never creates production topology, which is why every other command in this tool fails against a topic that does not exist. topology apply is the explicit route (../concepts/index.md) keeps for that, over the portable Admin surface — Ensure operations only. DeleteTopic, DeleteSubscription and Purge are the destructive operations and no spec this tool reads can reach them; TestApplyNeverReachesADestructiveOperation counts the calls through a fake to prove it.

plan performs no mutation. It reads what exists and prints what apply would do. --no-connect plans without opening anything, and then says so on every row rather than presenting a guess as a reading.

The desired topology comes from flags, from a JSON file, or from both:

{"version": 1,
 "topics": [{"name": "orders"}, {"name": "orders/dead"}],
 "subscriptions": [{"topic": "orders", "name": "billing"}]}

"version" is required — a format that accepts an unversioned file can never introduce a version later without guessing which grammar an old file was written in — and an unknown field is refused, applying the same strictness as DSN parsing: a misspelled key that is silently ignored is a deployment that quietly does not provision what its author wrote down.

A subscription on the command line is written TOPIC=SUB, because = is the one byte a portable topic name cannot contain (the grammar is segments of ALPHA/DIGIT/./_/- joined by /), so the split is unambiguous for every name this tool accepts.

docs.title: Three things it reports that nothing else does
docs.text:
apply ensures and then RE-READS. EnsureTopic returns nil whether it created the topic or found one, so the call's own success is not evidence that anything is there. Asking again is. An object that was ensured and is still absent is reported as ENSURED BUT NOT VISIBLE and fails the run, because that is a defect in the driver and not in the spec.

A state nothing could read is unknown, not absent. the specification's Admin has no ListSubscriptions, so the only read-only question there is about a subscription is Stats. A CodeNotFound answer is evidence of absence; ErrUnsupported is evidence of nothing, and a plan that rendered the second as the first would promise a creation it had no reason to believe was needed.

The two Admin facts are kept apart, the way doctor keeps advertised apart from verified: the level the driver claims for FeatureAdmin, and whether Client.Admin() actually answered one. doctor can only ever report the first; this command produces the second, so it can compare them — and a disagreement either way round is a defect in the driver, printed as one.

An unregistrable target is reported with its reason rather than as absent:

$ iqmq topology plan amqp10://host --topic orders
iqmq topology plan: amqp10://host: the scheme "amqp10" is claimed by
  github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/amqp10, which this binary cannot register:
    the generic AMQP 1.0 core ships no Profile value, and its Register takes one; …

"No driver claims that scheme" and "a shipped module claims it and this binary cannot register it" read the same to a user and mean entirely different things. A scheme two modules claim — nats:// and natsjs://, which drivers/natsunified claims as well — reports which driver answered.

docs.title: bridge
docs.text:
$ iqmq bridge natsjs://localhost:4222 orders bridge kafka://localhost:9092 mirror
$ iqmq bridge --dry-run memory://?autocreate=true orders bridge memory:// mirror

A bridge settles on two brokers that know nothing about each other, so nothing can make the destination's acceptance and the source's acknowledgement one atomic step. The order is fixed and it is the whole design:

receive -> publish -> flush (CONFIRMED, not merely admitted) -> settle the source

so the guarantee is at-least-once, with duplicates possible on the destination, and the command prints that sentence on every run. A crash, a cancelled context or a broker that stops answering between the confirmation and the source settlement leaves the source delivery unsettled: the source redelivers a message the destination already has. The reverse order — settle, then publish — loses messages instead, and that is the trade: a duplicate is something a destination can be built to tolerate, a lost message is not. There is no third order without a transaction spanning both brokers, which the specification does not offer.

Two details of that order are easy to get wrong and both are load-bearing:

  • Flush, not just Publish. Publish returning nil means the message was admitted to the driver, which for a buffering driver is not the same as accepted by the broker ((../concepts/confirmation.md)). Settling the source against an admission is the same lost message as settling before publishing.
  • Nack on every failure path. A message the destination refused is a message the source still owes. bridge refuses to start against a source that cannot nack (FeatureNack, exit 3), because there the refusal of a publication would become a lost message.

The run counts what the guarantee cost, and the counters are the point:

Counter What it means moved confirmed on the destination and settled on the source: nothing outstanding publish-failed the destination did not take it; the source delivery was returned, so nothing is lost ambiguous the publication failed with the destination's acceptance unknown — every Flush failure is one, and so is a Publish failure the driver marked ambiguous. The destination may hold a message the source is about to redeliver duplicate-risk the destination confirmed and the source would not settle. That message moved and will come again returned handled and handed back with --on-stop (every delivery of a --dry-run)

--max N receives at most N deliveries, so the run takes nothing from the source that it would only hand back. --dry-run takes --on-stop nack or none and refuses ack and reject, because a dry run must leave the source as it was.

--dedup-from id asks the destination to suppress the duplicates by carrying each source message's id as the publication's de-duplication key ((../concepts/idempotency.md)). It requires FeatureDeduplication and refuses without it — and it does not change the guarantee: the de-duplication window belongs to the destination broker, so a redelivery that arrives after the window has closed is a duplicate the destination accepts. A source delivery with no message id gets no key, and those are counted as unkeyed rather than passed over in silence.

The bridge is single-flight by design: one message is confirmed before the next is received, so the destination sees the source's order wherever the source delivers in order. A concurrent bridge would be faster and would reorder, and a flag that silently reordered a stream somebody bridged for its order is not a default worth offering.

examples/bridge is the same pattern as a program, and it produces the duplicate rather than describing it.

docs.title: doctor against a harness
docs.text:
hack/doctor-harness.sh runs doctor against the brokers conformance/suites.json names, one container at a time, from the digests conformance/harness/images.lock pins:

$ hack/doctor-harness.sh list          # what can be reached, and what cannot
$ hack/doctor-harness.sh run nats      # start the broker, run doctor, remove it

The suite list is the single source of truth for which harnesses exist, so the script has no list of its own. A suite entry carries a doctor recipe only once somebody has run doctor against that broker and recorded what worked -- make suites-check refuses a recipe with no verification date -- and list reports a suite without one as unreachable rather than guessing, so the absence is visible instead of silent.

Seventeen of the twenty-two suites have a verified recipe and all seventeen pass. The five that do not each have a different reason, and none of them is the CLI's:

Suite Why doctor has no recipe memory in-process. There is no container and memory:// needs no address; iqmq doctor memory:// works and is covered by the unit tests. natsunified its schemes are nats:// and natsjs://, which the two profile drivers already claim, so this binary does not register it at all. doctor --drivers says so with the reason. goredis exports no Register by design: it is the second client library behind one capability table, and a connection string cannot choose between two client libraries. rabbitmq-delayed its image is built from hack/images/rabbitmq-delayed/, not pulled, so conformance/harness/images.lock pins no digest for it and the script will not start an image it cannot pin.

The seventeen that pass cover sixteen distinct driver profiles: NATS Core, Kafka (franz-go and kafka-go), NSQ, Pub/Sub (emulator), SQS standard, SQS FIFO, SQS on LocalStack, SNS+SQS, Redis Streams, RabbitMQ over AMQP 0-9-1 and over AMQP 1.0, ActiveMQ Artemis and Classic over AMQP 1.0, and both of them over STOMP, plus Pulsar. Each one reports its own profile, its client library's version and, where the broker tells it, the broker version.

docs.title: What the CLI could not express
docs.text:
The CLI is the first consumer of the DSN layer, the driver registry and the capability model from outside the library's own tests, and a few things it wanted are not there. They are recorded rather than worked around silently:

  • Not every shipped driver can be registered at once. drivers/natsunified claims nats:// and natsjs://, which drivers/nats and drivers/jetstream already claim, and dsn.Registry.Register treats a second claim as a conflict rather than a replacement — deliberately, since resolving it by import order is a decision nobody reading the program can see. The CLI registers the two profile drivers, so that doctor can name the profile that answered.
  • drivers/amqp10's generic amqp10:// scheme is not registrable from outside. Its Register takes a Profile, and the module ships no generic Profile value, so a caller must author one in Go.
  • drivers/gcppubsub/v1compat and drivers/redis/goredis export no Register, by design: each is the second client-library arm of a variant family behind one capability table, and one scheme cannot select between two client libraries.
  • memory.Config implements neither String nor LogValue, the two renderings the specification asks a configuration for. It carries no credential, so nothing leaks; it does mean the CLI cannot render a memory configuration the uniform way it renders every other driver's, and reports the resolved engine kinds instead.

doctor reports the first three as unregistered with the reason, so the gap is visible in the tool rather than only in this page.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The semantic model of specification, one page per concept. Read them in this order the first time: each one assumes the ones above it.

Page The question it answers Architecture Where does the code I call sit, and what holds the policy? Delivery guarantees What does an ack mean, and what does it not mean? Duplicates and idempotency Why will I see the same message twice, and what do I do about it? Ordering When is order guaranteed, and what breaks it? Acks and leases What happens between "received" and "settled"? Groups and subscriptions Who gets which message? Backpressure What happens when a producer outruns a broker? Confirmation boundaries When Publish returns nil, what has actually happened? Ambiguous publishes What if nobody knows whether it was accepted? Metadata modes How do headers survive a broker that has none? Capability negotiation How do I find out what this broker can do, before I depend on it?

docs.title: The one idea underneath all of them
docs.text:
A portable messaging API has exactly two honest designs. It can offer the intersection of what every broker does, which is small and useless; or it can offer the union and lie about the brokers that cannot do it.

This library takes a third route and pays for it in surface area: the API is the union, and every member of it is guarded by a capability the driver either advertises or refuses. Asking for something a broker cannot do fails at construction or before any I/O, with ErrUnsupported and a message that names the feature — never silently, and never with an emulation you did not ask for.

That choice is why these pages keep saying "which the driver page states". A concept page here tells you what the word means; the driver page tells you what your broker does about it, and the capability matrix tells you which of those statements a probe has actually verified.

Pre-alpha, and the docs say where the gaps are

This is not a finished library, and these pages are not marketing. Where a guarantee is unproven, unprobed or breached, the page says so and links the evidence. Status is the list of what is open.

docs.title: Acks and leases
docs.text:
What happens between "your handler received this" and "the broker will not send it again".

That diagram is the runner's actual control flow — run.go's settle, fail, retry, exhaust and deadLetter — rather than the obvious version, and four of its details are worth reading twice.

docs.title: A lease is a deadline, not a lock
docs.text:
When a broker hands you a message it usually hands you a deadline with it: visibility timeout (SQS), ack deadline (Pub/Sub, JetStream), in-flight timeout (NSQ). Past that instant the broker considers the delivery abandoned and gives the message to somebody else — while your handler is still running.

Delivery.LeaseExpires is when that happens, where the driver knows. Delivery.Extend(by) pushes it out. mq.WithLeaseExtension(d) asks the runner to do it for you while a handler is slow, and mq.WithLeaseDeadline() narrows the handler's own context to the lease so that a handler cannot keep working past the point at which its work no longer counts.

WithLeaseExtension takes a lead — how long before the deadline to ask — and there is one scheduler and one timer for the whole runner, never a timer per delivery. What it asks the broker for is the lease's own length, and the lead decides when: an extension is requested a lead before the deadline it is renewing.

A lead longer than the lease cannot be honoured, and the runner extends more often instead of asking for more time. Nothing can buy 30 seconds of notice out of a 10-second visibility timeout, and asking the broker for 30 seconds would be refused outright on the three drivers that cap an extension (drivers/sqs, drivers/gcppubsub, drivers/nsq) — so the runner keeps the delivery alive on shorter notice rather than losing it altogether. The floor is half the lease: the deadline is never less than half a lease away, and the lead is honoured exactly whenever it is under that.

A refused extension is not retried. The lease is either gone — in which case the broker has the message and the settlement that follows says so — or the driver refused, and asking again on the same interval turns one broken delivery into a busy loop. Your handler is not cancelled either: it finds out at its own settlement, and the OnSettle hook fires for the failed extension with kind SettleExtend if you want to know sooner.

Two honest limits. A driver with no DeadlineExtender cannot extend at all, and Extend returns ErrUnsupported — the matrix's ExtendLease row says which. And extension is a race you can lose: the broker may have already redelivered, in which case the settlement that follows returns ErrLeaseLost rather than quietly settling somebody else's delivery.

docs.title: The generation token is why a stale handle is safe
docs.text: Every delivery carries a generation. A *Delivery you captured in a closure and settle after the message has been redelivered settles nothing and returns ErrLeaseLost — it cannot reach the new delivery, even though the runner has pooled and reused the struct underneath. This is the invariant that makes buffer reuse safe to have at all.

docs.title: The dead-letter order is the whole point
docs.text:
Publish to the dead-letter destination, confirm it, and only then ack the original. A publication that is refused or ambiguous leaves the original unacked and requeues it, and increments a counter of its own.

A runner that acked first would destroy the message in exactly the case the dead-letter topic exists for. A runner that acked after a publication it could not confirm would do the same, less often and less reproducibly.

The five provenance headers a dead-lettered message carries:

Header Content iqmq-origin-topic the topic it was consumed from iqmq-origin-subscription the subscription that consumed it iqmq-attempts the failed attempt, in decimal; absent where the broker counts none iqmq-failure the error the handler reported, rendered by its own Error iqmq-first-delivered-at when it was first delivered — written only when this delivery is the first

The last row is a deliberate absence. A redelivery may reach a different process entirely and nothing in the SPI carries a first-delivery time back, so a missing header says "not known" and a header holding this attempt's receive time would say something false.

On a driver whose broker moves the message itself — mq.WithNativeDeadLetter() over Delivery.Nack(mq.NackDeadLetter()) — there is no publication, no confirmation over d.Nack(mq.NackDeadLetter()) — there is no publication, no confirmationwindow, and no provenance headers, because nothing on that path writes a over d.Nack(mq.NackDeadLetter()) — there is no publication, no confirmation window, and no provenance headers, because nothing on that path writes amessage. What the destination receives is what the broker put there.

docs.title: Who settles
docs.text: mq.WithSettlement(mq.SettlementManual) hands settlement to your handler entirely: the runner dispatches and then leaves the delivery alone, whatever the handler returns. Under the default mq.SettlementAuto the handler may still settle for itself, and is not overruled — the runner checks, and every settlement it performs tolerates ErrAlreadySettled, because the handler may settle on another goroutine and win the race with that check.

docs.title: Where the specification is not met yet
Ambiguous publishes
docs.text: An ambiguous publication is one whose outcome nobody knows: the connection dropped after the bytes went out and before the confirmation came back, or the context was cancelled while the broker was accepting. Specification the specification makes this a first-class outcome rather than an error to be lumped in with the others, and the specification also calls misclassifying it a disqualifying correctness defect — the strongest thing the specification says about any bug.

docs.title: Detecting it
docs.text:
if err := pub.Publish(ctx, msg); err != nil {
    switch {
    case mq.IsAmbiguous(err):
        // Nobody knows. See below.
    case mq.IsRetryable(err):
        // Definitely rejected, and the operation may be repeated.
    default:
        // Definitely rejected, and repeating it will not help.
    }
}

mq.IsAmbiguous and mq.IsRetryable are the two questions, and ambiguity wins: IsRetryable answers "safe to repeat", and an unknown outcome never is, because repeating it is what produces the duplicate. The specification attaches "may be retryable" to the definitely rejected outcome and to nothing else, so an error that is both is not retryable here.

The error can still carry both flags — a driver reports a connection that died after the publication left the socket as mq.CodeUnavailable, Retryable and Ambiguous — and the precedence between them is applied once, inside IsRetryable, rather than by every caller. The switch above therefore reads correctly in any order; it is written ambiguity-first because that is the case you must handle, not because the order changes the answer.

The driver's own judgement is not lost, and a caller who can de-duplicate needs it — the specification allows an ambiguous retry only when native idempotent publication, a DedupKey inside the broker's dedup window, or an explicit application decision makes it safe. Read the flag where it lives:

var e *mq.OpError
if errors.As(err, &e) && e.Retryable {
    // The driver's transport judgement, ambiguity aside. Repeating this is
    // YOUR decision, and it duplicates unless your broker deduplicates it.
}

middleware.Retry's default predicate, Transient, never retries anything ambiguous whatever its code.

IsAmbiguous is true when the error's Ambiguous flag is set or its code is mq.CodeAmbiguous or mq.CodeSettlementUnknown: those two codes mean an unknown outcome, so an error carrying either is ambiguous whatever its flag says.

A batch error is ambiguous when any of its items is: IsAmbiguous reads every entry of an *mq.BatchError and every branch of an errors.Join, and a batch none of which was accepted, but whose items were partly refused and partly ambiguous, is reported per item rather than as its first error.

A batch is therefore not retryable when any of its items is ambiguous, even when the first item in it was definitely refused: republishing such a batch duplicates the item nobody knows the fate of.

Only an *mq.OpError answers IsRetryable, deliberately: retryability is a property of the operation and not of the code. mq.CodeUnavailable on a publish may be safe to repeat; the same code on an ack may mean the lease is already somebody else's.

docs.title: What the library does about it: nothing
docs.text:
The core must not auto-retry an ambiguous publication. The three exceptions The specification allows are all explicit:

  1. native idempotent publication makes the retry safe within its documented scope — Kafka's producer idempotence, a DedupKey inside the broker's dedup window;
  2. you enabled ambiguous retry yourself;
  3. a retry middleware you installed distinguishes rejected from ambiguous and decides.

A library that silently retried would silently duplicate, and on a payment path that is not a trade-off anybody should be making on your behalf in a default.

docs.title: What you do about it
docs.text:
Three answers, in order of how much they cost you:

Make the publication idempotent at the broker. mq.DedupKey("order-42") where the broker has publication dedup — Nats-Msg-Id on JetStream, SQS FIFO's MessageDeduplicationId, Pulsar's dedup. Then a retry is safe inside the window, and the window is the broker's and is documented on the driver page. ErrUnsupported before any I/O where there is none.

Make the consumer idempotent. Then a duplicate costs nothing and you can retry freely. This is the answer that works on every broker and it is the one the duplicates page argues for.

docs.title: The library's own ambiguous publication
docs.text:
The runner meets this problem itself, once, and its answer is worth knowing because it is the same trade-off: when it dead-letters a message it publishes to the dead-letter destination and waits for the confirmation, and if that outcome is ambiguous it requeues the original rather than acking it. So the message may be dead-lettered twice.

It chooses the duplicate over the loss, and counts the event — ConsumerStats.DeadLetterFailures — so that an operator can see how often the choice is being made. Acks and leases has the sequence.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Five facts about that picture are worth stating in words, because they are the ones that decide how the library behaves when something goes wrong.

docs.title: The core holds every policy, and the drivers hold none
docs.text:
Retries, backoff, attempt counting, dead-lettering, ordering mode, publisher backpressure, lease extension, panic recovery and drain are all in the root package. The specification puts it as a prohibition on drivers: a driver MUST NOT implement worker pools, retries or dead-letter logic.

The reason is not tidiness. A retry loop in a driver is a second owner of redelivery accounting, and two owners produce a message that is retried 25 times when you asked for 5, or dead-lettered by one layer and requeued by the other. The specification requires exactly one owner, and the way to have exactly one is for the layer that the caller configures to be the only layer that decides.

Where a broker has its own retry and dead-letter policy — SQS redrive, Pub/Sub dead-letter topics, RabbitMQ DLX, Pulsar's DLQPolicy — the driver maps the configuration onto it rather than adding a loop beside it, and the runner's own policy stands down. mq.WithNativeDeadLetter() is how you ask for that explicitly; the driver page says whether it exists.

docs.title: The SPI is three methods, and everything else is optional
docs.text:
A driver must implement Backend (open, ping, describe, close), Sink (publish) and Source (fetch). That is the whole obligation.

Everything a broker does differently is an optional interface: BatchSink, AsyncSink, OwnedSink, FlushSink, Settler, BatchSettler, DeadlineExtender, AdminBackend, HealthReporter. The core type-asserts each one once, when it opens the sink or the source, and compiles the answer into a boolean. Nothing on a message's path performs a type assertion, which is the rule 4 and the reason the abstraction can be thin enough to have a measured overhead budget at all.

docs.title: The root module depends on the standard library only
docs.text:
So does the memory driver, which lives inside it. Every driver that needs a third-party SDK is its own Go module under drivers/, integrations/ or codec/. Depending on this library therefore costs you one client library — the one you chose — and not eleven.

make stdlib-check holds that property; it is not a convention.

docs.title: memory is a driver, not a mock
docs.text:
The in-process engine implements the same Backend as Kafka does, and it is the reference target for the state-machine, linearizability and differential tests. A test written against memory.NewForTest exercises the same runner, the same settlement state machine and the same capability guards as production. See the memory driver.

It is not persistent and never advertises durable storage.

docs.title: Internal implementations
docs.text: The variant families under internal/ contain alternative implementations for queues, wait strategies, timers, hashes, pools and dispatch. Use the benchmark tools to compare candidates on your intended workload. The public API does not expose these internal choices.

docs.title: What the diagram does not show
docs.text: The picture has no arrows back from the driver to the core, and that is accurate: a Source never consults the core, because every parameter it needs is in the SourceConfig it was opened with. It also has no callback path — the core pulls with a bounded Fetch and never registers a handler with a client library, so a push-delivering client (NSQ, Pub/Sub streaming pull, Pulsar) is adapted to a pull by driverkit.PushAdapter inside the driver rather than turning the core inside out.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text: Specification. There are two independent bounded buffers in a publishing path and they fail differently, so this page separates them before it says anything else.

docs.title: The two places a publication can be held
docs.text:
The broker's, or rather the client library's. This is the one you cannot see: franz-go's producer buffer, rueidis's pipeline, the Pub/Sub publisher's batch. Every one of them has a bound and every one of them has its own policy, and the driver page states it.

The publisher's own, which is this library's and which you configure. mq.PublisherConfig.MaxPendingMessages and MaxPendingBytes bound the asynchronous path — PublishAsync and the batching publisher — and PublisherConfig.Backpressure, an mq.BackpressureMode, says what happens when a bound is reached:

Zero for MaxPendingMessages selects mq.DefaultMaxPendingMessages rather than "unbounded": the specification requires the buffer to be bounded by default, so there is no value of the field that turns the bound off.

Mode When the buffer is full Reliable? mq.BackpressureBlock the caller waits until there is room or the context ends yes — the default mq.BackpressureReject the call returns ErrBufferFull immediately yes mq.BackpressureDropNewest this publication is discarded no mq.BackpressureDropOldest an earlier, unsent publication is discarded no

BackpressureMode.Reliable() is that last column, in code. Blocking and rejecting are reliable because the caller is either served or told; the two drop modes lose a publication the caller was not told about, which is why they are never a default and why iqmq_dropped_total{policy} exists.

docs.title: Blocking is the default, and blocking means blocking
docs.text: A Publish on a full buffer with mq.BackpressureBlock waits. It waits until there is room, or until the context you passed is done — which is the whole reason every call takes a context. A service with no deadline on its publish context and a broker that has stopped accepting will stop serving; that is not a defect, it is the reliable choice propagating. Put a timeout on the context if you would rather shed load, or ask for mq.BackpressureReject and decide what to do with the error.

docs.title: The consumer side is a bound, not a policy
docs.text:
A consumer does not need a drop policy, because the broker is already holding the messages: mq.ConsumerConfig.Prefetch bounds how many unsettled deliveries the runner will hold, and when it is reached the runner simply stops fetching. That is backpressure in the direction that costs nothing — the messages stay at the broker, redeliverable, rather than in your heap.

mq.WithMaxInFlight(n) bounds the same thing from the runner's side. A prefetch far above your concurrency buys latency and costs duplicates after a crash, because every unsettled delivery is a delivery that comes back.

docs.title: Inside the memory engine
docs.text:
memory.TopologyConfig.Overflow is the same question for the in-process engine, where the publication really does have nowhere else to go: memory.OverflowBlock (the default), OverflowReject, OverflowDropNewest, OverflowDropOldest. And memory.TopologyConfig.Fanout decides what a slow subscription does to a fast one: Atomic reserves capacity in every target before it enqueues to any, so a full subscription blocks the publication rather than silently getting fewer messages than its siblings.

That atomic default is why the memory engine is a faithful stand-in rather than a fast approximation: the failure mode you would meet on a real broker with an overfull consumer is the failure mode you meet in a test.

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text: The publisher's backpressure path is measured and gated — benchmarks/budgets.yaml holds its allocation and latency budgets — but the overhead budgets against the raw clients are breached on the batched path on every broker family measured, by 7 % to 46 %. Driver overhead has the figures and the methodology. Nothing here is widened to make that look better.

docs.title: Capability negotiation
docs.text: Specification. This is the mechanism the whole library is built around, so it is worth understanding before anything else: you find out what a broker can do by asking, at construction, and a claim that no probe has verified is rendered differently from one that has.

docs.title: Five levels, not a boolean
docs.text:
const (
    mq.Unsupported      // absent
    mq.Conditional      // only with a profile or an option, and the condition is stated
    mq.EmulatedVolatile // emulated in process; lost on a crash; NEVER satisfies a durability requirement
    mq.EmulatedDurable  // emulated by iqmq using durable broker features, e.g. a dead-letter topic publish
    mq.Native           // the broker does it itself
)

The two emulated levels are the reason a boolean would not do. "This driver supports delayed redelivery" is true of JetStream (Native, a Nak with a delay), true of Redis Streams (Conditional, a Lua mover whose durability depends on the server's persistence settings), and true of a broker where the core just holds the message in the process (EmulatedVolatile, and a crash redelivers it immediately). Those are three different promises, and Level.Durable() is the one line of code that separates them.

mq.Conditional carries its condition in Support.Note, because a conditional support that does not say what the condition is cannot be planned against.

docs.title: Asking
docs.text:
caps := client.Capabilities()
if caps.Has(mq.FeatureDelayedRedelivery) { … }
switch caps.Support(mq.FeatureDeadLetter).Level {
case mq.Native, mq.EmulatedDurable: …
}

Has is a bounds check and a load — the representation is an array indexed by mq.Feature — so asking is free and you can ask on a path you care about. Capabilities are constant for the life of a Client: the driver builds them at open from its profile plus a cheap probe, and nothing mutates them afterwards. That constancy is what lets the core compile them into booleans once instead of consulting them per message.

docs.title: Requiring
docs.text:
Asking is for code that adapts. Requiring is for code that does not, and it is the better default:

pub, err := client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{
    Topic: "orders",
    Requirements: []mq.Requirement{
        mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureNativeHeaders, mq.Native),
        mq.RequireAny(mq.FeatureScheduledPublish, mq.Native, mq.EmulatedDurable),
    },
})

An unmet requirement fails at construction, with an error that names the feature and the level it found. Not on the first publish, and not by quietly emulating. RequireAtLeast uses Level.Rank()'s documented ordinal; RequireAny is for the acceptance sets that are not ordinal — "native or durably emulated, but not volatile" is exactly the case RequireAtLeast cannot express, because the ranks do not line up with what you mean.

docs.title: Limits are Limit[T], and unknown is not zero
docs.text:
type Limit[T any] struct{ Value T; Known bool }

caps.Limit(mq.LimitMaxMessageBytes) returns that, and Known == false means the driver has not said — not "the limit is zero". This is a small type with a large purpose: an unadvertised limit read as a limit of zero refuses every message, and an unadvertised limit read as "unbounded" accepts one the broker will reject. The zero Capabilities advertises nothing and every limit is unknown, which is the honest answer for a driver that has not spoken.

Limits are enforced before I/O: MaxHeaderCount, MaxHeaderBytes, MaxMessageBytes and the batch bounds are checked in the core, so a message that cannot fit is refused locally rather than round-tripped to be rejected.

docs.title: Truthfulness is a gate, not a promise
docs.text:
The matrix and capabilities.json are generated from conformance runs — conformance/cmd/confgen, held by make generate-check — and the conformance kit asserts both directions for each claim:

  • advertised support actually works;
  • unsupported returns ErrUnsupported;
  • volatile emulation cannot satisfy a durable requirement;
  • conditional support names and tests its condition.

Which is why the matrix has two notations for "supported":

Glyph Meaning N C ED EV the level, verified by a probe in both directions (N) (C) (ED) (EV) the driver advertises the level and no probe verified it — not offered, and a probe observed the refusal · a denied guarantee that no run contradicted — one run cannot observe an absence ? not offered, and nothing established that either ! a scenario for the claim FAILED ◐ the evidence is an emulator's, never presented as the managed service's

docs.title: What is not verified, and why that is in the docs
docs.text: A claim in parentheses is not a lie. It is a claim, marked as a claim.

docs.title: Confirmation boundaries
docs.text:
When Publish returns nil, what has actually happened? Specification.

The answer is whatever mq.ConfirmationMode you asked for, on the broker you are talking to — and the second half is why every driver page has to state its own boundary in words.

docs.title: The four modes
docs.text:
Mode Boundary Fails at construction when mq.ConfirmDefault resolves to ConfirmAccepted never mq.ConfirmNone the native client admitted it locally. May be lossy. never mq.ConfirmAccepted the strongest ordinary acknowledgement the profile offers without extra round trips never mq.ConfirmDurable the broker has it durably the profile cannot define a meaningful durable boundary

ConfirmDurable failing at construction is the important row. On NATS Core and on the memory engine there is no durable boundary that could be honoured — NATS Core's publish confirmation is a flush, and the memory engine is never persistent — so asking for one is a config error rather than a promise nobody keeps. That is the whole design in one behaviour: the library would rather not compile your intent than pretend to satisfy it.

docs.title: What ConfirmAccepted means, per broker
docs.text:
These are the boundaries the driver pages state. They are not equivalent, and the differences are exactly the differences in your loss window:

Driver ConfirmAccepted is kafka acks=all with idempotence jetstream the PubAck nats (core) a flush — never durable rabbitmq a publisher confirm sqs / snssqs the API response gcppubsub the API response pulsar the send callback nsq the OK redis the XADD reply, with no WAIT memory the record is visible as ready or delayed

A flush and a PubAck are both "accepted", and one of them survives a broker restart. This is why a portable API cannot have one word for it and why ConfirmNone, ConfirmAccepted and ConfirmDurable are three modes rather than a boolean.

docs.title: What nil never means
docs.text: It never means the message was consumed, and it never means a side effect happened. The specification says so in one line and it is worth repeating: a publication's outcome is about the broker's custody of bytes, not about anything downstream.

docs.title: The three outcomes
docs.text:
Every publish resolves to exactly one of three states, and the API keeps them distinguishable:

  • accepted — nil. The configured boundary was reached.
  • definitely rejected — an error whose outcome is rejected. It may be retryable; mq.IsRetryable(err) reads the operation's own judgement, and only an *mq.OpError answers, because retryability is operation-specific rather than a property of a code. IsRetryable means safe to repeat, so ambiguity wins: a driver reports a connection that died after the write as Retryable and Ambiguous, and IsRetryable answers false for it. The driver's flag is still on the error (errors.As to *mq.OpError) for a caller who can de-duplicate and decides to repeat it deliberately.
  • ambiguous — mq.IsAmbiguous(err) is true. Nobody knows. See ambiguous publishes.

There is no hidden retry between those. Native SDK retries may stay on where they are part of documented confirmation behaviour, their ambiguity implications are documented, and they are configurable — but nothing in this library retries a publication you did not ask it to retry.

docs.title: Batches are not atomic
docs.text:
Not unless the driver advertises FeatureAtomicBatchPublish, which today no driver in the matrix does — the row is ? everywhere, meaning nothing established it either way.

A partially failed batch returns an *mq.BatchError whose Errs is index-aligned with the input, so item 3's error is Errs[3]. That alignment is the whole contract: a batch error that told you "four failed" without saying which four would be unusable. BatchError carries mq.CodePartial, so errors.Is(err, mq.ErrPartial) is true, and Unwrap returns the entries so errors.Is and errors.As reach a single item's cause.

A batch none of which was accepted returns the single error when every item has the same outcome — all refused, or all ambiguous — so a whole call refused for one reason reads like a single publication's refusal. When the items' outcomes differ — some refused, some that may already be in the broker — it returns the index-aligned *mq.BatchError instead, because no one error can say both. mq.IsAmbiguous(err) is true of a batch error when any item is ambiguous, so check it before republishing anything, and then republish only the items whose own error is a definite refusal.

When an error the sink cannot continue past — a closed sink, a cancelled context, a deadline — stops a batch part-way, the items after it were never offered to the driver. Their errors carry that same code, so errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) still holds, but they are definite: they are not in the broker, even when the error that stopped the batch was itself ambiguous.

Large batches are split into bounded native sub-batches. Splitting is not atomicity and the library does not present it as such.

docs.title: Receipts
docs.text: mq.PublisherConfig.Receipts asks the driver to fill Message.Receipt with what the broker returned — partition and offset on Kafka, sequence on JetStream. It is a capability (FeatureReceipts) and it costs something on some drivers, which is why it is opt-in rather than always populated.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
Specification. Four guarantees are recognised, and one of the four is not something this library provides.

Guarantee What it means here Who provides it At-most-once the message may be lost and will not be delivered twice a driver that acknowledges before the handler runs, or a broker with no settlement at all (NATS Core) At-least-once the message is delivered until it is settled; a crash between handler and ack produces a duplicate the default, on every driver that has explicit acknowledgement Broker-scoped exactly-once delivery the broker suppresses a duplicate within a documented scope and window Pub/Sub exactly-once subscriptions, Kafka transactions with read_committed, Pulsar transactions, JetStream dedup Exactly-once processing your side effects happen once not provided. x/idempotency and x/inbox are helpers for building it

The third row is the one that gets misread, so the specification states it and so does this page: a broker dedup or transaction feature does not make an arbitrary side effect exactly-once. A payment charged inside a Kafka transaction is still charged twice if the process dies after the charge and before the commit. What the broker deduplicates is its own record, within its own window, on its own key.

docs.title: What an ack means
docs.text:
An ack means two things at once, and no more:

  1. your handler completed — it returned nil, or called Ack itself; and
  2. the driver accepted the strongest configured native settlement action.

What that means is broker-specific, and every driver page states which of these it is: recorded in the local client, written to the connection, confirmed by the broker, or included in a broker exactly-once acknowledgement mode. They are four different durability stories, and the difference is your duplicate rate after a crash.

Under the at-least-once default the ack happens after the handler returns nil. The window between those two events is real and cannot be closed by any API: a process that dies in it produces a duplicate. That is the cost of not losing the message, and it is why the duplicates page is not optional reading.

docs.title: Settlement is a state machine, not a boolean
docs.text:
active ──► settling ──► settled
              ├─► active              (definite rejection; retry allowed)
              └─► settlement-unknown  (ambiguous native result)

The rules the core enforces, all of them observable through errors rather than through logs:

  • exactly one concurrent terminal attempt wins. The loser gets ErrSettlementInProgress while the winner is in flight.
  • a second terminal action after a success returns ErrAlreadySettled and is not silently ignored — that is how a double-settle bug in your handler becomes visible. The runner treats it as non-fatal.
  • a stale delivery returns ErrLeaseLost. Every delivery carries a generation token, so a handle you kept past a redelivery cannot settle the new one — including after the delivery struct has been pooled and reused.
  • settlement after the consumer closed returns ErrClosed.
  • an ambiguous native result stays explicitly unknown rather than being guessed either way.

docs.title: Non-settleable deliveries
docs.text: On NATS Core there is nothing to acknowledge: the protocol has no settlement. Ack, Nack and Extend return ErrNotSettleable, and the runner treats a handler that returned nil as locally complete without pretending to have acknowledged anything. A driver that cannot settle never advertises FeatureExplicitAck, so the capability check catches this before your code depends on it rather than at three in the morning.

docs.title: What is verified, and what is asserted
docs.text: FeatureAtLeastOnce and FeatureExplicitAck are probed in both directions on every driver with a conformance report, and the matrix renders the result. FeatureAtMostOnce, FeatureExactlyOnceDelivery and FeatureDurableStorage are among the claims The specification has no portable probe for: a guarantee's absence is not observable in one run, and a durability claim needs a broker restart the kit does not perform. Those render as advertised-and-unverified, in parentheses, and the matrix says so.

docs.title: Duplicates and idempotency
docs.text: You will see the same message twice. This page is about where the duplicates come from, which of them this library can remove, and what to do about the rest.

docs.title: Where a duplicate comes from
docs.text: Source Why Can the library remove it? the crash window between your handler returning and the ack landing at-least-once, by construction no — removing it would mean losing messages instead a retried publication after an ambiguous outcome nobody knows whether the first one landed only where the broker has native idempotent publication, within its documented scope a lease that expired while your handler was still running the broker gave the message to somebody else no, but mq.WithLeaseExtension narrows it — see acks and leases a rebalance that revoked a partition mid-flight the new owner starts from the last committed offset no; ConsumerStats.Redelivered counts it an ambiguous dead-letter publication the runner requeues rather than acking, deliberately no, and the direction is chosen: see below a broker's own redelivery after a nack you asked for it no

docs.title: The one the library chooses to create
docs.text:
When the runner dead-letters a message it publishes to the dead-letter destination, waits for the confirmation, and only then acks the original. A publication whose outcome is ambiguous therefore leaves the original unacked — so the message comes back, is tried again, and may be dead-lettered a second time, producing a duplicate in the dead-letter topic.

That is the deliberate direction, and it is worth understanding why: the specification already makes a duplicate something a consumer has to handle, and a poison message that was destroyed because its dead-letter publication could not be confirmed is something nobody can recover. A duplicate in a dead-letter topic is an inconvenience; a lost one is a bug report you cannot answer.

docs.title: What to do about the rest
docs.text:
Make the handler idempotent. This is the only answer that works on every broker, and everything below is an optimisation of it. A handler is idempotent when running it twice with the same message has the same effect as running it once — usually because it writes with a natural key, or checks before it acts.

Use the message's identity, not its content. Delivery.ID is the broker's own identifier where the broker has one. Delivery.Attempt is the broker's delivery count, and is 0 on a broker that keeps none — a distinction that matters more than it looks; see the ordering page.

Deduplicate at the edge where the broker can. mq.DedupKey(s) maps to Nats-Msg-Id, SQS FIFO's MessageDeduplicationId, and the equivalents; it fails with ErrUnsupported before any I/O where there is none. What it gives you is publication dedup within the broker's window, not processing dedup.

Keep a processed-message set when you need cross-broker dedup. x/idempotency provides memory and Redis stores for this purpose.

docs.title: What the library will never do
docs.text:
It will not retry an ambiguous publication behind your back. The specification forbids it unless native idempotent publication makes the retry safe within its documented scope, or you asked for it explicitly. A library that quietly retries an ambiguous publish is a library that quietly duplicates payments.

It will not report an ambiguous outcome as rejected or accepted. Misclassifying ambiguity is called out as a disqualifying correctness defect, which is the strongest thing the specification says about any bug.

docs.title: Metadata modes
docs.text:
Specification. Some brokers have no headers at all (NSQ), some restrict values to strings (SQS attributes, Pub/Sub attributes), some cap the count (SQS: ten). Your mq.Headers do not change shape because of that, so something has to give, and the answer is that you choose which.

mq.PublisherConfig.Metadata selects it:

Mode What it does when the broker cannot carry the metadata mq.MetadataNativeStrict refuses, with ErrUnsupported or ErrMessageTooLarge, before any I/O. The zero value. mq.MetadataPortableEnvelope always wraps: body and headers go into a self-describing envelope in the broker's payload field mq.MetadataAdaptive uses native fields where they fit, and wraps only the messages that do not

docs.title: Why strict is the default
docs.text:
Because the alternative is a driver that silently changes your wire format. An envelope is bytes in the body: a non-iqmq consumer reading that topic sees a framed blob instead of your JSON. That may be exactly what you want, and it must never be what you get by accident — so the mode that can do it is opt-in and the mode that refuses is the zero value.

This is the same principle as ConfirmDurable failing at construction: a refusal you can see beats an emulation you cannot.

docs.title: What the envelope is
docs.text:
A small, deterministic, versioned framing in wire: a magic prefix, a version, the headers in their portable encoding, and the body. It round-trips headers exactly — order, duplicates, binary values, the lot — through a broker that has none.

Two things about it are worth knowing before you turn it on:

It is visible to everyone else on that topic. A consumer that is not this library sees the framing. If the topic has other readers, the envelope is a breaking change to them.

Adaptive mode has to sniff. A message arrives and the driver has to decide whether its body is an envelope or a native payload that happens to begin with the same bytes. The magic prefix makes that cheap and not free: a native body that starts with the envelope's magic was once mis-decoded, which is a fixed defect with a committed regression input and a fuzz target — see fuzzing. If your bodies are arbitrary binary and you need certainty rather than a very good guess, MetadataPortableEnvelope removes the question by never sniffing.

docs.title: Which drivers need it
docs.text: drivers/nsq has no headers at all, so portable metadata means the envelope there and the driver says so. The attribute-limited brokers — drivers/sqs, drivers/snssqs, drivers/gcppubsub — need it for binary values, for repeated keys, and for values over the broker's per-value cap.

docs.title: Headers themselves
docs.text:
mq.Headers is ordered, duplicate-preserving, binary-capable and case-sensitive with a lowercase-kebab convention. Set replaces (last-write-wins, which is the portable contract); Add and Values are the multi-valued path and need FeatureDuplicateHeaders — a driver that cannot represent duplicates rejects at publish rather than dropping one.

iqmq- is reserved (mq.ReservedHeaderPrefix) and a conflict is rejected. The runner is the only writer of that prefix, and it writes exactly the five dead-letter provenance headers.

Received binary values are surfaced zero-copy, because received headers are read-only. That is the specification's ownership contract: the storage is borrowed until the delivery is settled, and Delivery.CloneMessage is how you keep something past that point.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Specification. No global ordering is implied by anything. Order is a capability with a scope, and the scope is part of the claim.

docs.title: The four conditions
docs.text:
Order holds for a set of messages only when all four of these are true. Three of them are yours.

  1. the profile supports the requested scope. FeatureOrderedByKey, FeatureOrderedByPartition and FeatureOrderedGlobally are separate features and a driver advertises each one separately; the matrix has a row for each.
  2. the messages share a non-empty Key — or the scope you asked for is partition or global.
  3. the runner is configured to order. mq.WithOrderingByKey() is the request. The routing it implies — every delivery of one key to one lane, one lane at a time — is the runner's default with or without the option, so raising the concurrency does not by itself reorder a key.
  4. exactly one active handler per lane. The runner guarantees this; a handler that starts a goroutine of its own and returns breaks it, and the library cannot tell.

docs.title: What ordering does to a failure
docs.text:
This is the part that surprises people, because it is a semantic choice rather than an implementation detail, and the three answers have very different throughput.

Two options, and they are different questions. mq.WithOrdering(o) takes an mq.Ordering and decides what shares a lane — mq.OrderingByKey (the zero value), mq.OrderingUnordered, mq.OrderingByPartition. mq.WithOrderingByKey(mode...) asks for order and carries the mq.OrderingMode that decides what a failure does to the lane:

mq.OrderingStrict — the default once ordering is enabled. A failed delivery blocks its lane until it is settled or terminally routed. The runner holds the message in the process, waits out the backoff, and calls the handler again. Nothing behind it on that lane moves.

Two consequences, one good and one expensive. The good one: because the message never left the process, the attempt count is exact even on a broker that keeps none. The expensive one: a worker is parked for the length of the backoff, and at the default mq.WithConcurrency(1) that is the whole runner stopped for up to the configured 30-second cap. If you ask for order, raise the concurrency.

mq.OrderingRelaxed — what a runner that was never asked for order keeps. The failed message goes back to the broker with the delay, and the deliveries behind it carry on. Order is lost for that key from that moment.

mq.OrderingStopOnFailure — stop the consumer and let the broker's own redelivery decide what happens next. The right answer when your ordering requirement is stronger than your availability requirement.

docs.title: The attempt bound can be unreachable
docs.text:
mq.WithMaxAttempts(5) is a bound on a count, and the count has to come from somewhere.

Delivery.Attempt is the broker's delivery count, and it is 0 on a broker that does not keep one. A message the runner gave back under relaxed ordering carries nothing else — so on such a broker the runner can never conclude that the attempts are exhausted, the failure policy is never reached, and the message is retried for as long as it keeps failing.

Two things make the bound real: strict ordering, which counts in-process because the message never leaves; or a broker with a native count. The matrix says which drivers have one, and the driver pages state it under Attempt counting. It is recorded as a known limitation rather than a surprise — the runner cannot invent a count that no layer kept.

docs.title: What else reorders
docs.text:
Concurrency, retries, rebalances, dead-lettering and delayed delivery all can, and each driver page says how. Three worth naming:

  • a rebalance moves a partition to another process, which starts from the last committed position. Kafka's offset tracker commits only the highest contiguous completed offset, so a gap blocks the commit rather than skipping it — see rebalance.
  • dead-lettering removes a message from the middle of a key's sequence. Every message behind it then proceeds, in order, without it.
  • a delayed nack moves a message to the future. Under strict ordering it takes its lane with it; under relaxed it does not, and the key is reordered.

docs.title: Batches
docs.text: RunBatch groups deliveries before it calls you, and the grouping respects the ordering mode: under mq.OrderingByKey a batch holds the deliveries of one key hash, and under an unordered mode a whole fetch is one batch. So a batch handler under ordering sees fewer, smaller batches — the grouping is a correctness constraint, not a tuning knob.

docs.title: Groups and subscriptions
docs.text: Who gets which message. Specification the specification maps three words onto eleven brokers, and this page is that map plus the two places it leaks.

docs.title: The vocabulary
docs.text:
iqmq means Kafka JetStream SQS Pub/Sub RabbitMQ NSQ Redis Streams Pulsar topic where a message is published topic subject in a stream queue name/URL topic exchange (or queue) topic stream key persistent://t/ns/topic subscription a named, independent consuming position consumer group durable pull consumer (empty — SQS has no fan-out) subscription durable quorum queue bound to the exchange channel consumer group subscription lane one unit of ordered work inside a subscription partition — — — — — shard partition

mq.ConsumerConfig{Topic: "orders", Subscription: "billing"} is therefore "consume the orders topic under the billing group's own position". Two processes with the same Subscription compete; two with different ones each get everything.

docs.title: Where it leaks: SQS has no fan-out
docs.text:
drivers/sqs maps a topic to one queue, and a queue has exactly one set of competing consumers. There is no second independent position to give a second Subscription, so the driver leaves Subscription empty and does not advertise FeatureFanOut. Asking two SQS consumers for two subscriptions of one topic does not give you two copies; it gives you a config error, before any I/O.

drivers/snssqs is the composite that fixes it: the topic is an SNS topic, the subscription is an SQS queue subscribed to it, and fan-out is the broker's. That is a different driver rather than a flag, because it is a different topology with different failure modes and a different cost.

docs.title: Where it leaks: not every subscription is durable
docs.text: FeatureDurableSubscriptions means a subscription's position survives every consumer disconnecting. On the memory driver it does not — the engine is never persistent, so the claim renders as emulated-volatile rather than as support. On NATS Core there is no position at all. The matrix's DurableSubscriptions row is the authority, and ? in it means nothing established the answer either way rather than "no".

docs.title: Where a subscription starts
docs.text:
mq.ConsumerConfig.Start decides what a subscription with no committed position does. It has four kinds, and three of them need a capability:

mq.StartPosition Needs Meaning mq.StartLatest — only messages published after the subscription exists. The safe default. mq.StartEarliest FeatureReplay the oldest message the broker still retains mq.StartAt(t) FeatureSeekByTime the first message at or after t mq.StartAtSequence(n) FeatureSeekBySequence the broker sequence n

A start position the driver cannot honour fails when the consumer is constructed, not on the first fetch. It is also ignored once a position exists: a restart resumes, it does not re-read, and a Start that surprises you on a second run is almost always a subscription that already had a position.

docs.title: Fan-out inside the memory engine
docs.text: The memory driver has three topology kinds — memory.TopologyQueue, memory.TopologyTopic and memory.TopologyStream — and they are genuinely different data structures rather than one with flags, because the specification requires the queue fast path not to pay for stream bookkeeping. Which you get decides whether a new subscription sees history, whether a slow subscription blocks a fast one, and whether the log is retained at all. See the memory driver page.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository root is the normative version — developer setup, the seven rules, and the review checklist. This page is the map, plus the things that are easier to learn from a page than from a failed CI run.
