  • ::, /, ,, :, whitespace and control characters are refused in any name, and 255 bytes is the ceiling. Each is a character that means something to a destination parser: :: is Artemis's FQQN separator, :// and a leading / are Classic's scheme and path forms, , separates the parts of a Classic composite destination, and : separates a STOMP header's name from its value.

docs.title: Reading a JMS queue by name
docs.text:
The mapping above names its own queues, so it cannot reach a queue that some other application created and named, such as an ORDERS.IN a JMS producer writes to. Set Config.Addressing to activemq.AddressQueue (or addressing=queue in the DSN) and the topic becomes the queue's name, for publishing and for consuming:

cl, err := activemq.Open(ctx, activemq.Config{
    Broker:     activemq.Artemis,
    Addrs:      []string{"broker:5672"},
    Addressing: activemq.AddressQueue,
})
// ...
con, err := cl.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{Topic: "ORDERS.IN", Subscription: "billing"})
Artemis Classic publish to and consume from <prefix><topic>, with the AMQP queue capability on both links so that an address carrying both routing types resolves to its ANYCAST queue queue://<prefix><topic> what Admin creates an ANYCAST address and a durable ANYCAST queue, both called <prefix><topic> nothing: Classic has no Admin where DeadLetterTopic sends a dead letter another queue, named the same way, and the dead-letter link asks for the queue capability too another queue, named the same way

In this mode:

  • ConsumerConfig still requires a subscription, and the driver ignores it. Every consumer of the queue competes for its messages, so FeatureFanOut is withdrawn from the capability table. A second client in the default mode is how one program gets fan-out and a JMS queue at once.
  • Prefix goes in front of the queue's name. Leave it empty to read a queue that another application named.
  • The name rules above apply to the queue's name, so a queue whose name contains /, : or :: cannot be addressed this way.
  • Admin.DeleteSubscription removes nothing and succeeds, because the queue it would resolve to is shared by every consumer and producer. DeleteTopic removes the queue and its messages.
  • Admin.ListTopics reports every queue whose name starts with the prefix. With no prefix that includes the broker's own DLQ and ExpiryQueue, because they are JMS queues too.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
A publication is one transfer on a sending link attached to the topic's destination. The boundary is the shared core's, narrowed by what these brokers do:

Mode Boundary ConfirmNone the transfer is sent pre-settled: the frame leaves, no disposition is coming, the call costs no round trip. Local admission, which the specification says may be lossy ConfirmAccepted the peer's accepted disposition for this transfer ConfirmDurable the same accepted disposition for a message published with AMQP's durable flag set. Conditional, and the condition is the deployment's: Artemis writes its journal entry before it accepts and Classic writes its store before it acknowledges a persistent send, so the acceptance is the durability — provided the destination is one the broker's address settings persist. It is withdrawn for a client configured NonDurable, which clears the flag the whole argument rests on

Two publication outcomes deserve naming because a caller acts on them differently from an ordinary failure.

  • Unroutable. A released disposition on a publication means the broker took the transfer and routed it nowhere: on Artemis a multicast address with no queues bound to it, and on Classic a virtual topic nobody has a consumer queue for. That is the specification's "the topology is not there" rather than a retryable failure, so this profile adds one rule to the table and it is the only one it adds: on OpPublish, released is CodeNotFound. Reporting it as Unavailable would have a publisher retry for ever into a destination that will never take the message. The rule is registered for OpPublish only: a released on the consume side is this driver's own release path and never reaches the mapper as a failure.
  • Ambiguous. A transfer that has left the socket and whose disposition never arrived may have been accepted. The specification makes reporting that as a definite failure a disqualifier, so it is ambiguous — mq.IsAmbiguous(err) is true — and TestCriticalSenderLinkDetachIsAmbiguousAndRecovers is what holds it. A peer's own rejected or released disposition stays definite, which is the half a driver that marked everything ambiguous would destroy.

A target whose address does not exist is a third thing again, and only on a broker configured to say so: Artemis with auto-creation off refuses the attach with amqp:not-found ("AMQ119002: target address … does not exist" for a sender, "AMQ119010: source address does not exist" for a receiver), which the core's condition table turns into mq.CodeNotFound.

A batch is N transfers on one link. There is no batch frame in AMQP 1.0 at all, so a batch is never atomic: the link's credit makes it cheap and does not make it one operation.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
A source is a receiving link attached to the subscription's destination — an FQQN on Artemis, the consumer queue on Classic — with a credit window. No link is attached when the source is opened: the first fetch attaches one, so a broker that is down at that instant is a retryable fetch failure rather than a consumer that could not be constructed.

Config.Credit is the ceiling on the link credit one source may hold, and it is the prefetch. It is the only window this protocol has, because AMQP 1.0 grants no lease at all: an unsettled delivery is this receiver's for as long as the link lives, so DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires is the zero time, FeatureExtendLease is unsupported, and there is no extender anywhere in the module.

DeliveryInfo.Attempt comes from the AMQP header section's delivery-count, which counts previous attempts — so Attempt is 1 on a first delivery and rises across a nack. That it is a protocol field of the header section rather than a broker header extension is one of the four rows this protocol wins over STOMP, where there is no count at all.

On Classic the consumer queue must exist BEFORE the first publication. A virtual topic copies a publication into the consumer queues that exist at that moment, so a queue created afterwards gets nothing — measured against the pinned image, a scenario that published first and subscribed second received nothing at all. FeatureFanOut is therefore conditional on Classic and native on Artemis, and the condition is stated: it is the broker's default virtual-destination configuration, and a deployment that changed the prefix would take the fan-out away with no error anywhere.

A delivery this driver cannot decode is not handed over and not acknowledged: acknowledging it would destroy it, so it stays unsettled and the broker gets it back.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
The four AMQP dispositions carry the verbs, and the mapping is the shared core's:

action AMQP 1.0 outcome Notes Ack accepted final when the disposition frame is written under the default receiversettle=first Nack(NackRequeue()) modified{delivery-failed} the delivery comes back and the attempt count rises Nack(NackRequeue(), NackDelay(d)) — ErrUnsupported, and settles nothing. Measured; see below Nack(NackDrop()) rejected AMQP 1.0 has no destroy outcome, so on a destination with a dead-letter address a dropped message reaches it rather than being destroyed. The safe direction, stated rather than hidden Nack(NackDeadLetter()) rejected, which reaches the broker's dead-letter address or a publication to Config.DeadLetterTopic, when one is set Reject rejected Extend — there is no lease and no frame; FeatureExtendLease is unsupported a closing consumer's unsettled deliveries released, with delivery-failed clear the driver is giving back what it never handed out, not reporting a failure, so the attempt must not count

released is deliberately NOT the requeue, and the reason is measured rather than argued. On both brokers a released delivery comes back with delivery-count unchanged — three rounds at 0, 0, 0 — while modified{delivery-failed} comes back at 0, 1, 2. Attempt has to rise across a nack or the specification's MaxAttempts is compared against a number that never moves and a poison message is retried for ever.

modified's undeliverable-here flag is NOT set, and that too is measured. On Artemis a delivery modified with undeliverable-here is never redelivered to the consumer that modified it — so a subscription with one consumer loses the message entirely. A requeue that lost the message on a single-consumer subscription would be a silent data defect, so the flag stays clear.

There is no delayed redelivery, and the absence is measured rather than assumed. A publication's delay works (see "Delays"); the same annotation on a modified disposition does not: on Artemis a modified carrying x-opt-delivery-delay: 3000 was redelivered immediately, with delivery-count 1. The annotation is honoured on a publication and ignored on a disposition, and each product's redelivery delay is an address setting (Artemis's redelivery-delay) rather than a per-nack value. So there is no protocol spelling for the delayed requeue and it is refused before any I/O, settling nothing — the delivery stays the broker's, and a caller told "unsupported" can still do something else with it.

A settlement the driver cannot perform is refused before the delivery's slot moves, which is the specification's "returns ErrUnsupported and settles nothing": a driver that took the slot first and then discovered it could not honour the action would leave the delivery unsettleable for ever.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Ordering by key is native, at key scope, and the mechanism was measured. the specification's JMSXGroupID is AMQP 1.0's group-id message property, and both products read it as the JMS message group and dispatch one group exclusively to one consumer of a subscription. Measured on Artemis with two competing consumers on one queue: every k0 message went to the first consumer and every k1 message to the second, in publication order within each group.

That is the only ordering claim this driver makes beyond one queue's FIFO order. FeatureOrderedByPartition is claimed at group scope — a queue is FIFO, so one subscription's messages arrive in the order the broker routed them — and FeatureOrderedGlobally is not claimed: a multicast address fans a publication into several queues and each is consumed independently. A nack returns a message to its queue and the core makes no promise about where in it.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
A scheduled publication is supported on both products, spelled differently on each, and this is the one capability a deployment can take away:

Classic's scheduler is off by default and its absence is silent. With schedulerSupport unset the broker accepts the property, delivers the message immediately, and passes the property through to the consumer untouched. A driver that wrote the key anyway would report success for a delay that did not happen — so Config.Scheduler is how a deployment says the scheduler is on, and without it the profile's delay rule is the zero rule, which the core reads as "this broker has no way to express that" and answers with ErrUnsupported before any I/O. FeatureScheduledPublish is withdrawn to match. On Artemis the field is ignored.

Limits.MaxDelay is left unknown rather than advertised: neither product documents a ceiling on a scheduled delivery and neither refused one in testing, and the rule is that an unknown limit is never an overloaded zero.

A delayed redelivery does not exist on either product over either protocol; the measurement is under "Ack / nack / extend mapping" and FeatureDelayedRedelivery is withdrawn.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
There are two routes and a caller chooses which by configuration, because the two have different failure modes and the specification will not let one stand for the other.

DeadLetter and NoDeadLetter both set is a construction error, because the driver cannot ask the broker which is true.

What reaches either route is a rejected disposition. Measured on Artemis: one rejection raised DLQ's countMessages from 0 to 1 and the message was not redelivered.

With no DeadLetterTopic the profile supplies no DeadLetterAddress to the shared core, deliberately: supplying one would make the core publish a copy itself and then reject the original — one more copy, one more window, and a second dead-letter mechanism for a broker that already has one. The conformance run records the consequence honestly, skipping dlq/failed-publish-never-acks with the note "this configuration publishes no dead letter: a rejected delivery reaches the broker's own dead-letter address … and there is no publication of the driver's to fail. Set Config.DeadLetterTopic for the route this scenario is about".

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
A portable header is an AMQP application property, and the values are typed: a header value that is not valid UTF-8 travels as an AMQP binary and comes back byte for byte, so FeatureBinaryHeaders is native. That is the second row this protocol wins over STOMP, where every header is text.

A repeated key cannot travel at all, because application-properties is a map and a second value under one key replaces the first; MetadataPortableEnvelope and MetadataAdaptive carry one in the envelope and MetadataNativeStrict refuses it.

Under MetadataAdaptive a message is also enveloped when its body begins with the envelope's own magic (IQMQ and a version byte), even if the native fields could carry everything else: the adaptive read side decides from the body, so a native body that looks like an envelope would be claimed as one and refused. A non-iqmq consumer therefore reads such a body wrapped.

Config's annotation prefix is x-opt-, which is the prefix of Artemis's own message annotations: a caller's header under it belongs in the message-annotations section rather than in application-properties. The reserved x-iqmq- prefix is the driver's own, and a caller's header under it is refused rather than shadowed.

The limits, and why only one is advertised:

Limit Advertised Why MaxHeaderBytes 255 both products really impose a name ceiling, and the mapping enforces it before any I/O: an oversized header name is refused by the mapper rather than by the broker with a link detach. 255 is the smallest ceiling any broker in this repository's harness imposes, so it is the one a portable driver can advertise without claiming a limit it cannot check MaxMessageBytes unknown the only place AMQP 1.0 carries a message-size ceiling is a link's attach performative, and the facts are read at open, before any link exists. A number here would be this driver's assertion rather than the broker's answer. (The pinned images' acceptors carry 100 MiB frames; that is the deployment's, not the protocol's) MaxDelay, MaxLease unknown there is no lease at all, and neither product documents a delay ceiling. Advertising zero would read as "every lease expires immediately", which the specification makes a different answer

A delayed publication costs one more allocation on Artemis than on Classic, and no amount of work in this driver can remove it. An AMQP 1.0 message-annotations map is keyed by any (amqp.Annotations is map[any]any), so an annotation boxes its key as well as its value, while application-properties is map[string]any and boxes only the value. Artemis reads the delay from the annotation section and Classic from the properties section, so the exact counts this profile adds over an undelayed publication are:

Control Artemis Classic a bare payload with a TTL and a priority 0 0 (both are AMQP header fields; this profile's rules touch neither) PublishOptions.Delay 2 (key + value, boxed into a map[any]any) 1 (value only, into a map[string]any) PublishOptions.DedupKey 1 (the key is already a string; boxing it is the one allocation) — (refused: Classic has no de-duplication)

The asymmetry does not compound: the annotation section's extra boxing is paid once per annotation and the scheduled delivery is the only annotation either product's rules write, so the same whole publication differs by exactly one allocation between the products. allocs_test.go pins every one of these counts exactly, so a rule whose value function built a string would be a diff in that file rather than a number drifting upwards.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The shared core owns the dial loop, which the specification requires of this driver family: go-amqp does not reconnect, so the core's supervisor notices the connection's death, bumps the connection generation before anything else happens, invalidates every delivery token, and re-dials with jittered backoff. Config.Backoff names the policy explicitly rather than leaving it to the variant family's Auto, whose provisional winner is none — meaning no delay at all, which the specification forbids.

Config.Addrs is a failover set tried round-robin across reconnect attempts: Artemis's failover pair, Classic's network of brokers. What it is not is a cluster the driver follows — AMQP 1.0's connection-redirect is classified as a retryable transport failure by the core and is not followed, so a redirect costs one reconnect interval rather than being honoured. Config.ReconnectAttempts bounds the reconnector's whole life rather than one outage, which is how the helper defines it; NoReconnect makes a lost connection terminal, and a borrowed connection (OpenWithClient with ClientBorrowed) is never redialled at all — dialling would replace a connection the caller still holds — so such a client goes Degraded and stays there.

There is no topology to restore, which is the one way a reconnection here is simpler than on a driver that declares: this driver declared nothing, so a reconnection re-dials and re-attaches links and nothing else.

A link detach is a different event from a connection loss, and the difference is load-bearing. A broker detaches a link without closing the connection when the destination is deleted, when a link is stolen by another client of the same name, or when an address's settings change under it — Artemis does all three. The connection is alive afterwards, so the reconnect loop never runs: the link is dropped and re-attached by the next fetch, the connection generation does not move (bumping it would invalidate every other link's deliveries as well), and one fetch surfaces the failure once rather than every fetch failing for ever. Two of the six critical tests are about exactly this.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
From the transfer that delivered the message until the disposition the broker acted on. A process that stops inside it — a crash, a link that detached, a connection that died — leaves the delivery unsettled, and detaching an AMQP 1.0 link returns everything unsettled on it to the queue, where the broker hands it to whichever consumer of that queue is next. So a handler may run twice for one message and the application has to absorb the duplicate; DeliveryInfo.Attempt is the header's delivery-count plus one, so the second delivery says so.

Under the default receiversettle=first a settlement is final when the disposition frame is written, so an Ack costs no round trip and a link that died immediately afterwards leaves the message redeliverable — at-least-once behaving as advertised.

ReceiverSettleSecond is refused on Artemis, and that is measured rather than assumed. Artemis answers an attach requesting receiver-settle-mode second with first, and go-amqp refuses the negotiation outright (amqp: receiver settlement mode "second" requested, received "first" from server). So Config.Validate refuses the combination at construction rather than letting every source fail at attach with a message about settlement modes instead of about configuration.

A settlement whose link belongs to an older link or an older connection is refused with ErrLeaseLost and never written to the wire. That is the specification's disqualifier in AMQP 1.0's clothing: delivery ids start again from zero on a new link, so a disposition built for the old link's delivery 0 would name the new link's delivery 0 — settling somebody else's message, redelivering the caller's own, and reporting nothing. TestCriticalStaleDispositionIsRefusedOnAReattachedLink holds it, and asserts that the reattached link received no disposition at all.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
Config is ActiveMQ's vocabulary, translated into the shared core's configuration by Config.CoreConfig rather than embedding it: a caller configuring an ActiveMQ driver should be reading about addresses, queues and virtual topics, and the protocol's own fields are passed through because they are the protocol's rather than because they are interesting here.

Field What it is Broker required, no default: activemq.Artemis or activemq.Classic Addrs amqp://host:port, amqps://host:port or bare host[:port]; a failover set tried round-robin across reconnect attempts Username, Password SASL credentials. Password is a dsn.Secret, so no rendering can carry it. Artemis requires a user by default; Classic's pinned image allows anonymous connection HostName, ContainerID, Properties the OPEN frame's hostname, this client's container id and extra connection properties. The container id is worth setting on Artemis: it is what the broker shows in its connection list, and a fleet whose clients all report the same generated id is a fleet nobody can debug SASL, InsecurePlainSASL, TLS, InsecureSkipVerify the security surface; the default refuses PLAIN over a plaintext connection Prefix prepended to every address and queue name. Inside VirtualTopic. on Classic — see "Topic / subscription mapping" Addressing activemq.AddressFanOut (the default) or activemq.AddressQueue, which reads from and publishes to a JMS queue by its own name; see "Reading a JMS queue by name" BrokerAutoCreates reports that the broker still creates a destination from an attach. It changes no behaviour — the driver creates nothing either way — it changes what Profile.AutoCreates and this page's capability output report, so that a deployment reading its own output is not told a refusal it will not get. Forced true on Classic by the profile Scheduler reports that the broker's message scheduler is enabled. Ignored on Artemis; required on Classic for FeatureScheduledPublish Prioritised reports that the broker's destination policy reorders by priority. Ignored on Artemis, whose queues are priority-ordered; required on Classic for FeaturePriority, for the same reason and with the same silence as Scheduler DeadLetter, NoDeadLetter, DeadLetterTopic the dead-letter route; see "Dead-letter queue" Credit the link credit ceiling of one source: this protocol's basic.qos and its only window MaxPending how many asynchronous publications one sink may have outstanding NonDurable publish with the AMQP durable flag clear. Inverted so that the zero Config publishes durable ReceiverSettle first (default) or second. second is refused on Artemis; see "At-least-once window" SenderSettle the sender's settlement mode IdleTimeout, MaxFrameSize, MaxSessions, DialTimeout, OperationTimeout, WriteTimeout the connection and operation bounds Backoff, Reconnect*, NoReconnect the dial loop Publisher, Consumer the core's per-link option sets — link name, properties, capabilities, source filters — which is this profile's escape hatch Clock, Hooks the injected clock and the callbacks

The DSN scheme is activemq, and the product is a required parameter:

activemq://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672?broker=artemis&prefix=iqmq.
activemq://localhost:5672?broker=classic&scheduler=true

One scheme for two products is the opposite of the obvious design and it is the same decision Config.Broker documents: a scheme per product would let a deployment move from one to the other by editing four characters of a connection string, and the two products' topic mappings name nothing in common. Making it a parameter means a DSN that does not say is refused rather than guessed at. The scheme is not amqp10, which the shared core's generic profile claims, and it is not shared with drivers/activemq/stomp, which registers activemq+stomp — a registry in which one scheme could open either protocol would make a connection string ambiguous about which capability table the caller gets, and the two tables really differ: no nack at all over STOMP, no selector over AMQP 1.0. Registering both modules with one registry is the supported arrangement.

This driver's parameters are broker (required), addressing (fanout or queue), prefix, scheduler, prioritised, autocreate, deadletter, deadlettertopic and credit; the shared core's — containerid, hostname, sasl, tls, insecureskipverify, insecureplainsasl, sendersettle, receiversettle, idletimeout, maxframesize, maxsessions, maxcredit, maxpending, nondurable, dialtimeout, operationtimeout, writetimeout, backoff, reconnectbase, reconnectmax, reconnectgrowth, reconnectattempts and noreconnect — pass through unchanged. Anything else is a construction error naming it, which is how a copied parameter is caught rather than ignored.

A DSN has no path. Neither ActiveMQ has virtual hosts and AMQP 1.0 has no virtual-host field, so a path could only be a caller's mistaken expectation and it is refused rather than ignored. Config.DSN() renders the configuration with the credential replaced by the redaction marker and everything else intact, and the result parses back.

docs.title: Artemis's management protocol, as measured
docs.text:
Client.Admin() exists on Artemis only, and it is the broker's own management address reached over the very connection the client already has. It is not the AMQP management specification, and the encoding took three tries against the container:

A request is a message sent to the activemq.management address with _AMQ_ResourceName ("broker", "queue.<name>", "address.<name>") and _AMQ_OperationName ("createAddress", "createQueue", …) in its application properties and an AMQP value body holding the operation's arguments as a JSON array string. Two other encodings were tried first and both fail with "Error reading in simpleString", because the broker decodes the body with its own SimpleString codec:

Body encoding Result a data section carrying the JSON bytes fails: "Error reading in simpleString" an AMQP value holding a real list fails: "Error reading in simpleString" an AMQP value holding the JSON array as a string works

The reply arrives on a dynamic receiver named by the request's reply-to and carries _AMQ_OperationSucceeded and a JSON array body of its own. A refused operation arrives as a successful delivery whose _AMQ_OperationSucceeded is false and whose body is the reason, which is why reading the reply is a separate step from receiving it: a caller that only checked for a transport error would read "Queue X already exists" as success. AMQ229019 becomes CodeConflict and AMQ229204 becomes CodeNotFound; AMQ229017/AMQ229203 ("does not exist") are what make a Delete idempotent, and the already-exists codes are what make an Ensure idempotent, which requires.

Every request opens its own session, sender and dynamic receiver and closes them again — three frames per operation, and the right price: a long-lived management link would be a fourth handle the reconnect supervisor has to invalidate, and the operations are rare by construction.

Each request is bounded by the caller's deadline or, when it has none, by OperationTimeout. Closing the session gets a fresh OperationTimeout of its own, because the request's deadline may be what ended it. A broker that never answers the close costs the caller that much more time, not a call that never returns.

EnsureSubscription states every field of the queue rather than leaving any to the broker's default, because Artemis's default for an auto-created topic subscriber's queue is the opposite of what the specification asks for: routing-type: MULTICAST, durable: true, max-consumers: -1 (the "two consumers of one subscription compete" half), purge-on-no-consumers: false (true would make it a non-durable subscription, so the queue and everything in it would go when the last consumer left), auto-create-address: false (a create that made its own address would be the implicit topology this driver refuses) and auto-delete: false.

Stats reports countMessages as the depth and getDeliveringCount as the in-flight count, and leaves lag unknown rather than computed: a broker with no log has no position to be behind, and reporting the depth twice would make two different questions look answered. ListTopics reports the topics with at least one subscription rather than every address on the broker — a broker's address list holds activemq.management, DLQ, ExpiryQueue, every MQTT session store and every temporary reply address, and a driver that reported those as topics would be reporting the broker's furniture.

docs.title: This driver creates no topology, and only one deployment can prove it
docs.text:
The specification makes implicit topology creation a defect, and on Artemis it is a defect with teeth: a typo in a topic name becomes an address, the publications go into it, and nothing anywhere reports a problem. So a sink or a source attaches and never creates, and topology is Client.Admin()'s.

The consequence a deployment has to know is that this driver's guarantee is only as good as the broker's configuration:

Artemis Classic does the broker create a destination from an attach? by default, yes — and it can be told not to: artemis create --no-autocreate, or <auto-create-queues>false and <auto-create-addresses>false in the address settings yes, and it cannot be told not to without an authorization plugin with creation off, an attach to a destination that does not exist is refused with amqp:not-found — "AMQ119010: source address does not exist" for a receiver, "AMQ119002: target address … does not exist" for a sender — which the core turns into CodeNotFound. This is what makes the claim provable not applicable so the "creates no topology" claim is observable, and the shipped conformance evidence is taken with auto-creation off the driver's own code rather than an observable refusal

Run Artemis with auto-creation disabled. With it on — which is the image's default — the same attach silently creates the address and this driver cannot tell.

docs.title: What a caller who chooses this driver over the STOMP one loses
docs.text:
Nothing, on Artemis, except a selector. The AMQP 1.0 arm supports 19 of the features natively on Artemis against STOMP's 15, and the four rows it wins are the ones that matter: a real negative settlement, a real attempt count, a binary header value, and a receive window that is the protocol's own credit rather than a broker-specific subscribe header. What it gives up is FeatureServerFilter: a JMS selector is an AMQP 1.0 link source filter and go-amqp exposes no way to set one, so a selector is unavailable over this protocol whatever the broker supports. See Choosing between the four combinations.

The specification marks two things about this driver (verify), and both are the delay mechanisms. Both were verified against containers, and one of them turned out to have a condition the specification does not mention:

the claim Status What was found delay via x-opt-delivery-delay (Artemis (verify)) verified against apache/activemq-artemis:2.44.0-alpine a 2000 ms annotation delayed delivery by 2.0 s, with a plain string key and with an amqp.Symbol key alike. x-opt-delivery-time works as the absolute form. AMQ_SCHEDULED_DELAY sent as an annotation delayed nothing delay via AMQ_SCHEDULED_DELAY (Classic STOMP (verify)) verified, and understates it the header is not STOMP-only: over AMQP 1.0 Classic reads it as an application property and delayed delivery by 2.2 s. The x-opt-delivery-delay annotation Artemis reads delayed nothing here. And the scheduler is off in the pinned image: with schedulerSupport unset the broker delivers immediately and passes the property through, so the capability is withdrawn unless Config.Scheduler says the broker has it

Everything else on this page that says "measured" was measured against one of those two images; where a fact is documented rather than measured the page says so. One fact is documented rather than measured and is called out here so that nobody reads it as container evidence: Classic's "creates no topology" claim, above, which is the driver's own code rather than an observable refusal because Classic cannot be told not to auto-create.

docs.title: Smaller ones
docs.text:
• Classic does not reorder by priority unless its policy says so, and the absence is silent — exactly like the scheduler's. Classic carries the AMQP header's priority and dispatches in FIFO order unless the destination's policy sets prioritizedMessages="true", which the pinned image does not do for queues at all. Measured with it off, a high-priority publication arrives after a low-priority one — so FeaturePriority is withdrawn on Classic unless Config.Prioritised says the policy is there, and the driver cannot read the policy to check it. Artemis's queues are priority-ordered and the field is ignored there.
  • Config.DeadLetter is true by default, because both pinned images configure a dead-letter address for every address. It is an assertion about the broker that the driver cannot check: neither product reports a queue's dead-letter address over AMQP 1.0.
  • A de-duplication key is refused on Classic rather than sent and ignored: Classic has no broker-side duplicate detection at all. FeatureIdempotentPublish is withdrawn on both products, and that withdrawal matters more than it looks — neither has a producer epoch or a sequence number, so a retried publication is a second message unless the caller supplied a de-duplication key for it. A caller who read an idempotent- publish claim would retry an ambiguous publication and get two messages.
  • The conformance suite needs the topology created first. This driver declares nothing, so a run against an empty broker fails at the first attach. ConformanceHarness provisions it — on Artemis through this driver's own Admin, and on Classic by attaching a receiver to each consumer queue and letting go again, which is not a workaround but the whole of Classic's topology API over AMQP 1.0.
  • Two scenarios must not share a topic on Artemis, because the derived queue name is <topic>.<subscription> and an Artemis queue name is unique across the whole broker — the second scenario would consume the first's messages. The harness's topic names carry a nonce for that reason, and a . is mapped out of a generated name because ParseQueue takes the queue apart at the last one.
  • Client.Admin() on Classic reports ErrUnsupported rather than returning a surface that refuses every call. The profile supplies no Admin, so the backend does not satisfy mq.AdminBackend at all — which is what the specification asks of a driver that does not have the feature.
  • FeatureAdmin on Artemis is Conditional, not Native. The management address is a destination like any other, and it needs the connecting user to hold the broker's management permissions — which the driver cannot check before the surface is used. A deployment that secured or disabled it would leave the surface present and every call refused.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
the list for this driver is "ActiveMQ link detach, failover, protocol-specific redelivery metadata". All six tests below run against the shared core's scripted peer and none needs a container, which is the point: three of the behaviours this driver has to get right cannot be provoked from a broker at all — a disposition sent on a link that has since detached, a consumer cancelled while a fetch is parked, and a publication whose disposition never arrives.

  • TestCriticalStaleDispositionIsRefusedOnAReattachedLink — the specification's disqualifier. A receiving link that detaches and re-attaches starts its delivery ids again from zero, so a disposition built for the old link's delivery 0 would settle the new link's delivery 0: somebody else's message acknowledged, the caller's own redelivered, and nothing reporting an error. It would catch a driver that sent the settlement anyway — and it checks the other half too, that refusing the stale one did not poison the live one.
  • TestCriticalLinkDetachIsRecovered — a broker detaches a link without closing the connection (a deleted destination, a stolen link, changed address settings; Artemis does all three). It would catch a source that keys re-attachment on the connection generation alone and therefore holds a dead link for ever, failing every fetch with a retryable error the engine then retries for ever. It also asserts the generation does not move, which would catch a fix that invalidated every other link's deliveries as well.
  • TestCriticalSenderLinkDetachIsAmbiguousAndRecovers — the publish side. It would catch a publication whose disposition never arrived being reported as a definite failure (the ambiguous window), which makes a caller republish and the broker hold two copies — and a sink that never recovers afterwards.
  • TestCriticalConsumerCancelUnblocksAParkedFetch —. A fetch parked on a link with no messages has nothing to interrupt it: the peer will not send and the context is not done, so only the close can wake it. It would catch a driver that waited for the context, which hangs for as long as the caller's deadline — or for ever, for a caller with none. It also asserts a second Close is a no-op.
  • TestCriticalConsumerCancelReleasesUnsettledDeliveries — a consumer that goes away holding unsettled deliveries must give them back, or they sit in the broker's delivering set until the link times out and the next consumer waits for them. It would catch a close that dropped them — and, specifically, one that released them with delivery-failed set, which would make MaxAttempts fire on a message nobody tried.
  • TestCriticalLinkDetachWhileAFetchIsParkedIsRecovered — the state in which the link-loss guard on the read is the only thing that can recover. A source whose whole credit is already with the peer issues no more, so a top-up cannot fail and cannot discover the death. It would catch a driver that dropped a dead link only when a flow frame failed, which holds this one for ever with every fetch failing on a link the window thinks is fine.

Two fuzz targets guard the parts a stranger's input reaches: FuzzActiveMQAnnotations (the annotation and application-property mapping) and FuzzActiveMQDestinations (the destination derivation for all four combinations). allocs_test.go pins this profile's own hot-path allocation counts exactly, so a change to the delay or de-duplication rules is a diff in a test file rather than a number that drifted.

docs.title: Choosing between the four combinations
docs.text:
the expected answer is "feature completeness on Artemis, then perf → AMQP 1.0 default; STOMP kept for Classic", and the measurements bear it out — with one qualification the row does not mention.

The coverage score is how many of the 39 features each combination supports natively, computed from the protocol's own support table (internal/activemq/protocol) rather than guessed:

So: AMQP 1.0 is the default, on both products. STOMP is kept for Classic, and specifically for a caller who needs a server-side filter, because that is the only thing in the family that the default cannot do.

The qualification is the nack, and it is sharper than a coverage score suggests. A STOMP NACK frame returns no message on either broker — measured, on Artemis it is treated as an acknowledgement — so the STOMP arm's requeue is a subscription reset whose cost falls on every delivery the consumer was holding. A caller who nacks often, or who holds a deep prefetch, wants this driver and not that one. activemq-stomp.md states the whole finding first, because it is the one a reader most needs.

What criterion does not decide from a benchmark is the second term, perf. The benchmark measures the cost of the property mapping each protocol's message model demands, which is on the hot path of every publication and every delivery; the two protocols' throughput against the real brokers needs two brokers and two client libraries, and records that as the criterion's gap. A warning about reading the mapping's ns/op: the two arms do not do the same amount of work, because the STOMP arm validates every header value as UTF-8 and checks every header name against the frame's own while this arm's typed sections need neither — so a faster STOMP row would be evidence that it checked less, which is exactly why the row puts feature completeness first.

docs.title: amqp10 (shared AMQP 1.0 core)
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Module: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/amqp10

The split is the point. AMQP 1.0 is a wire protocol with a settlement model, and almost everything in this page is the protocol's rather than a broker's: links, sessions, credit, dispositions, the message model, the error conditions and the reconnection. What is not the protocol's — what an address means, how a durable subscription is named, where a delay goes, which field counts attempts, what is dead-lettered and how, and which broker versions work at all — is a Profile, which is a struct of function fields a broker module fills in. The core refuses to guess at any of it: every optional field's zero value means "this broker cannot express that", and the answer a caller gets is ErrUnsupported before any I/O rather than a guess that reaches the wire.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
Client Pinned version What it gives github.com/Azure/go-amqp see drivers/amqp10/go.mod connection, session, sender and receiver links, dispositions, manual credit

The native baseline for AMQP 1.0 lives with the profile that has a broker to measure against; this module measures the protocol mapping, which is variant the subject.

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
• credit is the flow control, and the driver issues it. go-amqp issues credit itself unless ReceiverOptions.Credit is -1, and this core always sets -1. The reason is the sticky unknown: a delivery whose settlement outcome is unknown never becomes settled, and under automatic credit the library re-issues credit when it considers a delivery settled — which for an unknown outcome is never. The window would shrink by one for every ambiguous settlement, permanently, and nothing could report it. With manual credit the drift is a counter a deployment reads (Source.CreditStats). Verified against: go-amqp ReceiverOptions.Credit; drivers/amqp10/credit.go; the specification.
  • a session is the flow-control scope, so each link gets one. The incoming and outgoing windows belong to the session and every link on it shares them, so a sink and a source on one session would make a stalled consumer throttle an unrelated publisher. A session costs one BEGIN frame and one channel number, of which there are 65,536. Verified against: AMQP 1.0 §2.5.6; drivers/amqp10/links.go; the specification.
  • released does not count a delivery attempt and modified{delivery-failed} does. This is the difference between a driver whose MaxAttempts policy works and one whose attempt count never rises. Nack means "I tried and failed", so it is modified; a delivery the driver gives back — a closing source's unhanded-out deliveries — is released. Verified against: AMQP 1.0 §3.4.4–3.4.5; conformance nack/immediate-redelivery against RabbitMQ 4.3.5; the specification.
  • a message with no body section is legal and several brokers refuse it. So a nil body is an explicit amqp-value of null rather than an omitted section, and an empty non-nil body is one data section of zero bytes. That is how the nil-versus-empty distinction survives the protocol. Verified against: AMQP 1.0 §3.2; drivers/amqp10/mapping.go; the specification.
  • group-id is a string, and a key is bytes. The specification makes Message.Key bytes and AMQP 1.0's group identity a string, so a key that is not valid UTF-8 travels as a binary application property instead. A textual key stays in group-id, where a broker that orders a message group can see it. Verified against: AMQP 1.0 §3.2.4; TestABinaryKeyTravelsAsABinaryProperty; the specification.
  • go-amqp exposes no range disposition. A disposition frame can cover a range of delivery ids and the library offers only the per-message wrappers, so FeatureBatchSettle is unsupported rather than a loop wearing a name that promises a saving. Verified against: go-amqp Receiver.AcceptMessage and friends; drivers/amqp10/capabilities.go.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
There is none in this module, and that is deliberate. An AMQP 1.0 address is opaque to the protocol: /exchanges/orders/orders and topic://orders and queue:orders are all legal and mean whatever the broker says. So Profile.SinkAddress and Profile.SourceAddress are functions a broker module supplies, and the core calls them with the topic and the subscription and attaches to what comes back.

A profile that returns an error refuses the topology, and the core turns the refusal into ErrUnsupported before any frame — which is how a wildcard topic, a partition count a broker has no lanes for, and a retained topic on a broker with no log are all answered without a socket.

Profile.AutoCreates says whether attaching to an address the broker does not have creates it. It is a fact about the broker and not a choice: RabbitMQ 4's AMQP 1.0 endpoint creates nothing and answers amqp:not-found, and Artemis creates an address by default. The rule about creating production topology behind a caller's back therefore falls to whoever runs the broker, and the profile's job is to say which it is so the capability table is honest.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
One sending link per sink, on a session of its own. A publication is one transfer; the boundary is the disposition.

ConfirmationMode Boundary Mechanism ConfirmNone the socket write a pre-settled transfer: the sender settles as it sends and the peer answers nothing ConfirmAccepted the peer's accepted disposition an unsettled transfer, awaited ConfirmDurable accepted plus the profile's own statement that acceptance means durable Profile.Durable; refused at construction by a profile that does not claim one

ConfirmDurable is the one a profile has to earn. AMQP 1.0's accepted says the peer took responsibility and says nothing about disks, so the core refuses a durable-confirmation publisher unless the profile states the boundary — which is the rule that a driver either states the boundary or fails at construction, applied to a protocol that cannot state it itself.

PublishAsync is bounded by Config.MaxPending and the message is borrowed until the callback runs. A synchronous publication's body is not copied; an asynchronous one's is, because the library holds the message until its disposition.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
One receiving link per source, on a session of its own, attached by the first Fetch and not by the open.

The lateness is deliberate and is the same decision drivers/rabbitmq makes for basic.consume: an attach tells the peer it may send, and everything it sends is unsettled and counts against the prefetch whether or not anybody has asked for a delivery. The generation bump and the token invalidation after a reconnection are eager, because those are the correctness half — a settlement must be refused from the instant the connection died — and the attach is lazy because it cannot be done well eagerly: a supervisor re-attaching thirty links has no caller's context and no good answer to "the fourth attach was refused".

The observable consequence is one failed fetch per reconnection, which is what a caller of an at-least-once driver already handles. The observable consequence for a test is that Quiesce has to warm the links first, which is what WarmForTest is for.

Credit is issued manually, exactly the prefetch, and Source.CreditStats reports the window: the prefetch, the credit the peer holds, the deliveries held unsettled, and how many of those have an outcome nobody knows. The last number is the one to watch: it never falls, and a source whose whole prefetch is unknown has to be reopened.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
iqmq AMQP 1.0 disposition Ack accepted Nack(requeue) modified{delivery-failed=true} Nack(requeue, delay) modified with the profile's delay annotation; delivery-failed is the profile's choice Nack(deadletter) the profile's dead-letter route, or rejected with a condition Nack(drop) rejected with amqp:not-allowed ExtendLease unsupported: a delivery is this receiver's for as long as the link lives, so there is no deadline to extend

A message the mapper cannot represent is answered with modified — the attempt counted and the link marked as one not to redeliver to — rather than released or rejected: releasing it would have the broker hand it straight back for ever, and rejecting it would destroy or dead-letter a message whose only fault is a body shape iqmq has no field for. Source.Undecodable counts them.

NackOptions.Reason is transported on a rejection only, in the condition's description, because a dead-lettered message with no reason in it is a message somebody has to guess about.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
A link delivers in order. Beyond that the protocol promises nothing, and this core claims nothing: FeatureOrderedByPartition is the link's own order and FeatureOrderedGlobally is not claimed at all.

FeatureOrderedByKey is a profile's claim, and it rests on the message GROUP: Message.Key is the group-id property, which is what Artemis orders as JMSXGroupID. A profile whose broker does not order groups must not claim it, and a key that is not valid UTF-8 is not a group at all (it travels as a property), so the claim's note has to say that the ordering is for a textual key.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
The protocol has none. A delayed publication and a delayed redelivery are both annotations a broker reads, and the key differs per broker — Artemis reads x-opt-delivery-delay, ActiveMQ Classic reads AMQ_SCHEDULED_DELAY, and no verified spelling exists for RabbitMQ 4.

So Profile.Delay and Profile.NackDelay are the seam, and their zero value refuses: a core that guessed a key would publish a message the broker delivers immediately, which is the worst kind of unsupported — the publication succeeds and the delay does not happen. A profile that names no rule gets ErrUnsupported before any I/O, and the capability table says so.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Two shapes, and a profile picks one.

  • Profile.DeadLetterAddress is nil. The broker's own policy routes a rejected delivery, which is what a queue argument or an address setting does. Nothing is published and nothing can fail.
  • Profile.DeadLetterAddress is set. The core publishes a copy to that address and only then settles the original — publish, await the disposition, then reject — so a crash between them duplicates rather than loses, and a failed or ambiguous publish settles nothing.

The first shape is the better one wherever the broker has a policy, because the second costs one more copy and one more ambiguity window.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
Message.Headers become application properties, typed: a value that is valid UTF-8 travels as an AMQP string and one that is not travels as binary and comes back byte for byte. A duplicate key cannot exist, because application-properties is a map — MetadataPortableEnvelope and MetadataAdaptive carry a repeated key in the envelope instead.

Under MetadataAdaptive a message is also enveloped when its body begins with the envelope's own magic (IQMQ and a version byte), even if the native fields could carry everything else: the adaptive read side decides from the body, so a native body that looks like an envelope would be claimed as one and refused. A non-iqmq consumer therefore reads such a body wrapped.

The AMQP properties iqmq has no field for are reachable under the reserved x-iqmq- prefix: x-iqmq-amqp-to, -amqp-subject, -amqp-user-id, -amqp-absolute-expiry-time, -amqp-group-sequence, -amqp-reply-to-group-id and -amqp-first-acquirer, plus x-iqmq-causation-id and x-iqmq-key, which the protocol has no home for. Every other name under the prefix is refused in every metadata mode: a header the mapping does not consume would be published as an application property whose name claims to be iqmq's.

Profile.AnnotationPrefix decides whether a header may become a message annotation instead. It is empty for RabbitMQ, because that broker converts between its two protocols through application properties and an annotated header would be in a different place on the other profile.

Limits: Limits.MaxMessageBytes is the peer's own max-message-size, read off the sender link at the first attach — a limit read from the broker rather than configured. Profile.Limits may add what only the broker knows. Everything a profile does not know stays unknown rather than zero, which is the rule.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The core owns the dial loop (driverkit.Reconnector), with Config.Backoff defaulting to full jitter and not to the specification's Auto — whose current winner is none, i.e. no delay at all, which the specification forbids outright. Since ReconnectConfig.Policy's own zero value is jittered too, so this default agrees with the helper's rather than working around it.

  1. the connection generation is bumped and every source's token table is invalidated, so a settlement for a delivery handed out before now is refused with ErrLeaseLost from that instant;
  2. every sink's outstanding publication is resolved ambiguous, because the peer may have taken it;
  3. the dial loop runs with its backoff;
  4. links re-attach lazily, on the next operation.

Config.NoReconnect leaves supervision to a caller who brought their own connection. A borrowed connection is never closed by the driver (driverkit.Ownership).

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
A delivery is unsettled until the receiver disposes of it, and the window is the link's lifetime rather than a lease: there is no deadline, so DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires is the zero time and FeatureExtendLease is unsupported.

What that buys is a handler that may take as long as it likes. What it costs is that a link which dies takes every unsettled delivery back to the broker, so the redelivery count after a reconnection is the prefetch. Profile.Attempt says where the count comes from — delivery-count plus one, by default — and a profile whose broker does not maintain it must say so in the claim's note, or the specification's MaxAttempts is compared against a number that never moves.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
Config is the transport and the protocol: addresses, SASL, TLS, the settle modes, the idle timeout, the reconnect bounds, the pending bound and the link options. Profile is the broker. Open(ctx, profile, cfg) needs both.

The DSN scheme is amqp10 for the generic profile a broker module registers its own — rabbitmq+amqp10, activemq — with Register(registry, scheme, profile), which is one line rather than a second copy of the DSN table. One scheme opening two profiles would make a DSN ambiguous about which capability table the caller gets, decided by registration order.

amqp10://user:password@host:5672,host2:5672?sasl=plain&tls=true&sendersettle=mixed

Config.DSN() renders a configuration back, with the credentials redacted and the host percent-escaped. The escaping is not decoration: a rendering that its own parser refuses makes the function useless for the one thing it exists for, which the DSN fuzzer proved in fourteen seconds.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
In this module (TestCritical*, run by make ci against the scripted peer):

  • TestCriticalStaleDispositionAfterDetach and TestCriticalStaleDeliveryGenerationIsRefused — the disqualifier, from both sides: a disposition for a delivery taken before a detach must never settle whatever holds that delivery id afterwards, and a settlement carrying a token from before a reconnection is refused with ErrLeaseLost rather than applied. They discriminate as well as assert — an ack for a delivery that was never handed out is not reported as a lost lease — so neither check is vacuously true.
  • TestCriticalAmbiguousPublishWhenDispositionNeverArrives and TestCriticalDefinitePublishFailureIsNotAmbiguous — the two halves of The specification. A transfer whose disposition never comes is ambiguous, because the peer may have taken it; a transfer the peer REFUSED is definite, because it answered. Reporting either as the other is what the specification names a settlement disqualifier.
  • TestCriticalCloseWhileSendInFlight — the close against a publication in the socket: every outstanding transfer resolves exactly once, and the message a caller owned is released exactly once.
  • TestCriticalCreditExhaustionDoesNotDeadlockFetch — the failure mode manual credit invites: a source whose every slot holds an unknown settlement can issue no credit, and it must say so (ResourceExhausted) rather than park a Fetch for ever.
  • TestCriticalCloseUnblocksAParkedFetch — the specification's "Close unblocks a parked operation", with ErrClosed and not the link error the close caused.

The RabbitMQ profile adds three of its own. Each test here was watched failing under a one-line mutation before it passed; the campaign's log is in the increment's own record.

docs.title: Driver author guide
docs.text:
How to write an iqmq driver for a broker this repository does not support, from outside this repository. Specification.

examples/custom-driver is the worked example: a complete backend implemented in a module of its own, held to the same conformance suite the memory driver is held to, with a test — TestNoInternalImports — proving it imports no internal/ package and uses exactly four iqmq packages. "Written from outside the repository" is a fact there rather than an assertion.

docs.title: The obligation is three interfaces
docs.text:
type Backend interface {
    Info() DriverInfo
    Capabilities() Capabilities
    OpenSink(ctx context.Context, cfg SinkConfig) (Sink, error)
    OpenSource(ctx context.Context, cfg SourceConfig) (Source, error)
    Ping(ctx context.Context) error
    Native() any
    Close() error
}

Plus Sink (publish) and Source (fetch). That is all a driver must implement. Info, Capabilities and Native are answered without I/O and must be safe to call concurrently.

Everything a broker does differently is an optional interface, and the core type-asserts each one once, when it opens the sink or source:

Interface For a broker that BatchSink publishes a batch in one call AsyncSink has an asynchronous publish with a completion callback OwnedSink can take ownership of the caller's buffers FlushSink has a flush distinct from a publish Settler settles a delivery (ack, nack) BatchSettler settles several at once DeadlineExtender can extend a lease AdminBackend has a topology surface HealthReporter knows more about its health than the core can infer

Implement the ones your broker has. Leave out the ones it does not: the core's answer to a missing interface is ErrUnsupported, which is the correct and honest behaviour, and the conformance kit will check that it happens.

docs.title: What a driver must NOT do
docs.text:
The specification is explicit, and it is the rule that keeps the semantics consistent across eleven brokers: a driver must not implement worker pools, retries or dead-letter logic. Those belong to the runner, which is what the caller configures. Two owners of redelivery accounting produce a message retried 25 times when the caller asked for 5.

A Source also never consults the core: every parameter it needs is in the SourceConfig it was opened with.

And Open must not create production topology. The specification. A driver may offer an explicit AutoCreate or an Admin surface; it may not quietly create a topic because somebody published to it.

docs.title: Errors: the one question with a definite answer
docs.text:
Do not reach for internal/errcode. drivers/nats imports it — it is inside this repository and can — and a driver at github.com/acme/mq-foo cannot. A driver author's first instinct is to look for errcode.New, find it in the source, import it, and be unable to explain later why their driver cannot be built outside this repository.

There are two public answers and both carry the codes:

driverkit.ErrorMapper — native sentinels plus an ordered rule set. This is the shape a driver over a real client wants, and it is what the toy driver uses:

var mapper = driverkit.ErrorMapper{
    Driver: "myq",
    Rules: map[string][]driverkit.Rule{
        mq.OpPublish: {
            {Match: driverkit.MatchIs(myq.ErrTooBig), Code: mq.CodeMessageTooLarge},
            {Match: driverkit.MatchContains("quota"), Code: mq.CodeThrottled, Retryable: true},
        },
    },
    Fallback: []driverkit.Rule{ /* … */ },
}

err = mapper.Map(mq.OpPublish, topic, "", nativeErr)
err = mapper.MapNet(mq.OpPublish, topic, "", nativeErr, sentAlready)

Rules are ordered and the first match wins, so write the specific rules before the general ones. The mapper never throws the native error away: the result wraps it, so errors.As still reaches your client library's own type.

Rules are per operation because retryability is. A connection reset on a publish that has already left the socket is ambiguous; the same reset on a fetch is a plain retry. MapNet's sentAlready is how you say which, and driverkit.ClassifyNet is the underlying helper.

An mq.OpError literal — for the cases a rule set does not cover. Fill the fields you know. Note Address is a field and is never rendered by Error(): the specification forbids addresses and credentials in error strings.

docs.title: What else driverkit gives you
docs.text:
Optional, all of it. Nothing in the core depends on driverkit, and a driver that uses none of it is a perfectly good driver.

Envelope, EnvelopeConfig portable metadata over a broker with no headers, or with limited attributes. wire's framing, with the sniffing decision made for you. TokenTable lease tokens with generations, so a stale settlement cannot settle a newer delivery Reconnector, ReconnectConfig bounded redial with topology restoration PushAdapter, PushConfig adapt a push-delivering client library to the core's bounded Fetch BatchSettler, BatchConfig coalesce settlements, with the batching strategy as a typed choice offset the Kafka-shaped contiguous-watermark offset tracker nack, flush the nack-strategy and flush-strategy shapes CapabilityBuilder build a Capabilities without getting the levels wrong BaseBackend, BaseConfig the boilerplate an Open needs

docs.title: Capabilities: claim only what you can prove
docs.text:
Capabilities is an array of Support indexed by Feature. Three rules:

  • the zero value advertises nothing, and that is the right answer for a feature you have not thought about. An unadvertised limit is Known: false, never zero.
  • Conditional must state its condition in Support.Note. A conditional claim with no condition cannot be planned against.
  • EmulatedVolatile never satisfies a durability requirement. If your emulation is lost on a crash, say so with the level rather than in prose.

Then prove it. The conformance kit checks both directions: the feature works when you claim it, and the unsupported path returns ErrUnsupported when you do not.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
// conformance_test.go, in package mydriver_test — NOT in the driver's package.
func TestConformance(t *testing.T) {
    testkit.RunConformance(t, testkit.Harness{
        Driver:    "myq",
        Open:      open,
        TopicName: func(p string) string { return "conformance." + p },
        Timeout:   30 * time.Second,
        Evidence:  testkit.EvidenceContainer,
    })
}

package mydriver_test, not the driver's own package. drivers/nats/conformance_test.go and the toy driver's package toydriver_test are the models. A harness that reaches unexported helpers works for its own driver and is useless as an example for anybody else's — which is the state memory/conformance_test.go is in, and it is recorded as such rather than defended.

Set Evidence honestly: EvidenceContainer for a real broker, EvidenceEmulator for a vendor emulator, EvidenceInProcess for a fake, EvidenceManaged for the real service. An emulator's answer is never presented as the managed service's.

testkit has the rest, including what the kit cannot probe.

docs.title: The page you owe
docs.text:
The specification fixes fifteen sections for a driver page, docs/drivers/_template.md is the template, and make docs-check holds every driver page in this repository to them in order — reading the list out of the template itself, so the list has one home and a page and the template cannot disagree about it:

client & version policy · topic/subscription mapping · publish path & confirmation boundary · consume path · ack/nack/extend mapping · ordering · delays · dead-letter queue · headers & limits · reconnect · at-least-once window · config & DSN · known gotchas · maturity & tier · driver-specific critical tests

Two of them are the ones readers actually need and the ones authors skip. Publish path & confirmation boundary must say in words what mq.ConfirmAccepted means on your broker — a flush and a durable write are both "accepted" and only one survives a restart. At-least-once window must say where the duplicate comes from. Both of those are the honest content; everything else is reference.

Line 5 is your maturity declaration, and it is the only one. The template fixes the shape — **Maturity:** <level> · **Tier:** <n> · … — and make docs-check reads it: the level has to be one of the four (Experimental, Beta, Stable, Deprecated, read out of the specification rather than hard-coded here), the tier has to be 1, 2 or 3, there has to be exactly one such line, and it has to be on line 5. A new driver starts Experimental and nothing objects. Two further rules bite only when you claim more:

Do not restate the level anywhere else. docs/drivers/index.md's Maturity column is held to line 5 by the same check; a driver module's README should link the page rather than repeat it, because the one that repeated it drifted.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text: A driver exposes Register(dsn.Registrar) and never reaches for a global registry, so a program composing two brokers owns the registry both are registered with. There is no process-wide registry: a program builds one with dsn.NewRegistry() in main and passes it to whatever opens clients.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Backend, Sink, Source; the optional interfaces your broker has
  • [ ] no worker pool, no retry loop, no dead-letter logic
  • [ ] Open creates no production topology
  • [ ] errors through driverkit.ErrorMapper or mq.OpError — not internal/errcode
  • [ ] Config redacts in String, GoString, LogValue and DSN, with a test that pushes it through a real log/slog handler
  • [ ] capabilities claim only what a probe can prove; Conditional states its condition
  • [ ] testkit.RunConformance in package <driver>_test, with an honest Evidence
  • [ ] critical tests for the things only your broker does
  • [ ] fuzz targets for your native mapping and any parser
  • [ ] a driver page with the fifteen sections, and one **Maturity:** line on line 5 — Experimental until you can cite the evidence for more
  • [ ] Register(dsn.Registrar), no global

docs.title: gcppubsub
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's pubsub image (make bench-native CLIENTS="pubsub"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary pubsub cloud.google.com/go/pubsub/v2 cloud.google.com/go/pubsub/v2@v2.7.0 PublishResult.Get: server-assigned message ID (emulator, not evidence for managed Pub/Sub)

The driver itself is built on the same pin. drivers/gcppubsub/v1compat is the second arm, over the deprecated cloud.google.com/go/pubsub@v1.51.1; DriverInfo.Profile is the client generation (v2 or v1compat) so a report or a log line always names the library that answered, and the two arms share one capability table (TestBothArmsAnswerOneCapabilityTable).

Family Arms Where it is measured Decision v2 · v1compat drivers/gcppubsub/v1compat, both arms against one in-process pstest service over one gRPC connection Fixed on v2. The row's criterion is correctness (a gate, not a metric), maintenance (the v1 module is deprecated upstream) and a native comparison (the driver against the raw client, which is benchmarks/native-baselines/pubsub against the container). The measurement reports what each generation costs and does not choose.

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • client generation. cloud.google.com/go/pubsub/v2 replaces the v1 Topic and Subscription types with Publisher and Subscriber handles obtained from the client, and exposes the generated admin surface as client.TopicAdminClient and client.SubscriptionAdminClient. Verified against: pubsub/v2 v2.7.0 doc.go, publisher.go:146, subscriber.go:58, pubsub.go:51-59.
  • settlement. Ack and Nack must be called inside the Receive callback or flow control is not respected, and the exactly-once path is AckWithResult/NackWithResult, which return an AckResult carrying an AcknowledgeStatus instead of failing silently. Verified against: pubsub/v2 v2.7.0 doc.go and message.go:29-44,102-120.
  • delivery attempts and ordering. Message.DeliveryAttempt is only populated when the subscription has a dead-letter policy, and publishing with an ordering key fails unless Publisher.EnableMessageOrdering is set. Verified against: pubsub/v2 v2.7.0 message.go:84-95 and publisher.go:74-75,194,218.
  • emulator evidence. The emulator is not evidence for managed Pub/Sub: it does not implement exactly-once delivery, and its latency and quota behaviour are unrelated to the service, so emulator-based claims are marked as such and managed numbers are measured separately. Verified against: conformance/harness/brokers.go PubSub; the performance budgets layer 4.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
A topic maps to a topic ID by a pure function, and a (topic, subscription) pair maps to a subscription ID by another. Both mappings are injective, which the SQS driver's is not and documents as a gotcha: ~ is in the service's identifier grammar and is not in mq.ValidateTopic's, so no two portable names can collide.

Portable Pub/Sub topic orders topic <TopicPrefix>orders topic orders/eu topic <TopicPrefix>orders~eu topic that is already a resource name (projects/p/topics/t) used verbatim (topic orders, subscription workers) subscription <SubscriptionPrefix>orders~workers (topic, subscription) named in Config.SubscriptionIDs that identifier, verbatim

The subscription identifier carries both halves and it has to. A Pub/Sub subscription names exactly one topic and has its own acknowledgement state, so two topics sharing one subscription identifier would be one resource attached to whichever topic created it first — and a consumer of the second topic would silently read the first topic's messages. Config.SubscriptionIDs, keyed by "<topic>/<subscription>", is the escape hatch for a deployment whose subscriptions are named by Terraform or by a naming policy.

An identifier the service's grammar would refuse, or one over its 255 characters, is a construction failure and not a surprise at the first message. A topic that is already a fully qualified resource name is passed through, which is reachable only through the SPI: mq.ValidateTopic refuses a name with a / and a scheme in it, so a portable caller uses Config.TopicPrefix. Both arms address such a name in the project it names. The v1 library can only create a topic or subscription in the client's own project, so v1compat refuses to create one qualified with another project.

Nothing is created unless Config.AutoCreate is set. The specification makes provisioning opt-in, and a driver that created a subscription for a typo would leave a backlog nobody reads and a bill nobody expects.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
Publisher.Publish hands the message to the client library's bundler and returns a pending result; PublishResult.Get is the confirmation.

Mode What it means here Extra round trips ConfirmNone the same boundary as the two below — there is no fire-and-forget publication in the client library, so there is nothing weaker to offer none ConfirmAccepted PublishResult.Get returned a message identifier none ConfirmDurable the same call: the service stores a message in at least two zones before it answers none

The receipt says which boundary the publication actually reached, and it is always ConfirmDurable — the specification's "a driver that had to fall back says so here", read in the direction where the driver did better than it was asked. PublishReceipt.MessageID is the server-assigned identifier; Partition, Offset and Sequence stay zero, because this broker has none and an invented value is worse than an absent one.

Publish waits on the calling goroutine. PublishAsync waits in a fixed completion-worker pool. The obvious implementation of the asynchronous path on this library is go func() { res.Get(ctx); done(err) }(), which is a goroutine per message — rule 3's prohibition, verbatim. So completions nobody is waiting on go through Config.CompletionWorkers goroutines with a queue bounded by Config.CompletionQueue, and a submission blocks when the queue is full. A synchronous publication is not routed through the pool, because the caller is already blocked: adding a hand-off, a channel and a wake-up to a path that has a goroutine of its own by definition buys nothing.

PublishBatch hands every message to the bundler first and waits for every result afterwards, so a batch is as few publish requests as the bundler decides rather than len(ms) of them. A message the driver refuses before any I/O fails at its own index and the rest of the batch is still published, which is why the encoding happens in a first pass.

Flush waits for what the publisher holds. The library's Flush takes no context, so the wait happens on one goroutine per flush — not per message — and the caller's context bounds the call rather than the flush.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
Subscriber.Receive delivers by callback and the SPI asks the driver to be called instead. driverkit.PushAdapter is what makes the two meet:

  • the callback pushes each delivery into a bounded ring and blocks while the ring is full;
  • the library releases a message's flow-control slot when the callback returns, so a blocked callback is a stream that stops asking for more. That is the only backpressure a streaming pull has;
  • MaxOutstandingMessages is the prefetch and so is the ring's capacity;
  • NumGoroutines is one, always. A second stream is a second source of out-of-order delivery for an ordering key, and the ring behind the callback is what bounds concurrency instead.

Both bounds being the prefetch means the driver holds at most twice it: prefetch deliveries in the ring and up to prefetch callbacks parked on the push. That is stated rather than hidden, because it is the number an operator sizing memory needs. The alternative — making the callback wait for the settlement — would hold one library goroutine per unsettled message for as long as a handler runs.

Fetch drops a delivery the ring still holds that a later delivery of the same message has superseded, or whose lease has run out while it waited. It is not an optimisation: handing out a delivery whose settlement is certain to be refused gives the caller work it cannot complete, while the message itself is either one slot along in the ring or back at the service with a full deadline.

A message the driver cannot decode is nacked, not acknowledged: the subscription's own dead-letter policy is what takes a corrupt record away after MaxDeliveryAttempts deliveries, and the failure is reported through Health because there is no delivery to attach it to.

Config.Filter becomes the subscription's server-side filter. The service evaluates it and acknowledges what it does not match, so a filtered message is never delivered and never counted against the backlog. The grammar is the service's and this driver does not parse it.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text: Portable Pub/Sub Notes Ack Message.Ack fire-and-forget: the library queues the acknowledgement identifier into a batched Acknowledge Ack with Config.ExactlyOnce Message.AckWithResult the settlement has an outcome and Ack returns it AckBatch a loop the library coalesces the identifiers itself, so there is no flush policy to choose (belongs to a driver whose settlement is its own round trip) Nack Message.Nack (a ModifyAckDeadline of zero) the message is deliverable again at once Nack with a delay an in-process hold emulated; see below Reject (NackActionDeadLetter) publish to Config.DeadLetterTopic, then acknowledge the original see "Dead-letter queue" NackActionDrop refused with ErrUnsupported a negative settlement cannot destroy a message on this broker Reject with a delay refused with InvalidArgument a delay asks for a redelivery held back and a dead-letter settlement produces none: the message goes to another topic and the original is acknowledged. The specification refuses an option a driver cannot honour rather than ignoring it Extend nothing is sent emulated; see below DeliveryAttempt DeliveryInfo.Attempt zero without a dead-letter policy, because the service counts nothing and the specification forbids reading an unknown as a value

docs.title: Why Extend sends nothing
docs.text:
The client library extends a held message's acknowledgement deadline automatically, so a handler that needs longer than the deadline gets it without asking. The driver tells the library to extend for the delivery's whole lease: the longer of the acknowledgement deadline and Config.MaxExtension, capped at 60 minutes. It has to, because streaming pull sets its own deadline on each stream, which overrides the subscription's, and the library lets a message go once its extension budget has passed. Extend(by) checks that by fits inside what is left of that lease and moves the driver's own view of it.

It sends no ModifyAckDeadline of its own, and it cannot: the acknowledgement identifier that request needs is private to the client library's message type and there is no accessor for it.
