The specification says "Extend via ModifyAckDeadline" for this driver and that is not reachable through Subscriber.Receive; the capability is therefore advertised as EmulatedVolatile with the emulation named, rather than as a native call that does nothing. An extension beyond the budget is refused with ErrUnsupported: a handler told its lease runs for another minute, whose message is redelivered in ten seconds, is worse off than one told the extension is not available.

docs.title: The local lease check
docs.text:
The service accepts an acknowledgement for an identifier whose message another consumer now holds. There is no API that asks "do I still hold this?", the acknowledgement does not fail, and the message is gone from the other consumer's backlog. So the refusal happens in the driver, before the call: every settlement compares the delivery's lease — as the driver recorded it at the delivery, on the injected clock — against now, and answers ErrLeaseLost when the lease has run out.

It is a local view and the driver says so. It cannot see a deadline the service moved for its own reasons, and it deliberately refuses on a lease this process believes has passed even when the service would still have accepted the acknowledgement. Both directions of that trade are the safe one: the cost is a redelivery, and the alternative is acknowledging somebody else's work.

A second, sharper case is the same message delivered twice to one source, because its deadline expired. Both acknowledgement identifiers are valid at the service. The source marks the earlier delivery superseded the moment the later one arrives, so a settlement for the earlier one reports ErrLeaseLost rather than acknowledging the message the later delivery owns.

docs.title: Close settles before it waits
docs.text: Close ends every hold, wakes every parked callback, nacks what the ring still holds and nacks what was handed out and never settled — and only then cancels the receiver and waits for it. The order is not a preference: the client library's shutdown waits for every message it has handed to the callback to be settled (messageIterator.stop blocks on exactly that), so a Close that waited for Receive first would deadlock for the whole automatic-extension budget. Ten minutes on the default configuration.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Conditional on Config.Ordering, and the condition is the client library's: EnableMessageOrdering is a flag on the publisher, not on a publication, so a publisher built without it refuses every message that carries an ordering key.

With it, Message.Key becomes the ordering key — verbatim when it is valid UTF-8 of at most 1024 bytes, and base64 otherwise — and the service delivers one key's messages in publication order to one subscriber. A subscription this driver creates gets enableMessageOrdering too, which the service needs before it will deliver an ordered key in order.

Base64 rather than a refusal, because a Pub/Sub ordering key is a string and a binary key cannot be one verbatim. The three answers were refusing the publication, publishing it unordered, and encoding the key: refusing costs a core round-trip scenario that is not about ordering at all, publishing it unordered is the silent downgrade the specification forbids, and encoding keeps the guarantee because base64 is injective. What encoding costs is that a text key which happens to spell the base64 of some binary key shares that key's ordering group, which can only merge two groups and never split one — the same argument the SQS driver makes for hashing a key into a FIFO message group.

Without Config.Ordering the key is still carried (in the iqmq-k attribute, so it round-trips) and publications are simply not ordered by it.

Nothing else is ordered. There are no partitions, so OrderedByPartition is not a claim, and a topic has no global order: messages with different ordering keys, or none, arrive in whatever order the service finds them in.

docs.title: The publisher that silently stops
docs.text:
When an ordered publication fails, the client library puts that key into a permanently failed state and refuses every later publication of the same key for the life of the publisher — reporting the pause only to those later publications, never to the one that caused it. A driver that does not call ResumePublish therefore has a publisher that has silently stopped carrying one key while every other key still works, which is the message loss in slow motion rather than an error anybody sees.

This driver resumes the key on every failure of an ordered publication, on the synchronous path and in the completion pool, and it does so unconditionally rather than only on the library's paused-key error — because the first failure is a plain service error and by the time a paused-key error arrives, every publication of that key since has already been refused.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
There are none, in either direction, natively.

  • No scheduled publication. A message is deliverable as soon as the service has stored it. Delay and DeliverAt are refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O rather than silently ignored, and FeatureScheduledPublish is not claimed.
  • No nack delay. A nack is a ModifyAckDeadline of zero and the message becomes deliverable at once. A delayed negative settlement is therefore an in-process hold: the driver keeps the delivery unacknowledged while the library goes on extending its deadline, and nacks it when the delay elapses.

The hold is advertised as EmulatedVolatile and three things follow, which is why it must be declared an emulation rather than claimed as native:

  1. it does not survive a process death — a hold interrupted by a crash becomes a redelivery when the acknowledgement deadline expires, which is sooner than the delay asked for;
  2. it is bounded by what is left of the delivery's lease, and a longer delay is refused before anything is held, because a hold that outlives the lease is a redelivery at a time nobody chose. That bound is what Limits.MaxDelay advertises;
  3. it costs a timer and a goroutine per held delivery — bounded, because a source holds at most its prefetch, and the price of a delay on a broker that has none.

Close ends every hold at once. A hold that outlived its source would be a goroutine and a timer nobody can stop, and a message held unacknowledged by a source that no longer exists until its deadline expires — a three-hundred-millisecond delay silently becoming the acknowledgement deadline.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Two routes, both needing Config.DeadLetterTopic.

The subscription's own dead-letter policy is native and needs no settlement at all: the service moves a message it has delivered Config.MaxDeliveryAttempts times to the dead-letter topic. The service's own minimum for that number is five, which is why Config.Validate refuses a policy below it.

An explicit Reject cannot wait for five deliveries, so it publishes the message to the dead-letter topic and acknowledges the original only once that publication is confirmed. The order is what makes it safe: a failure anywhere in between leaves the original unacknowledged and the message is redelivered, which is at-least-once with a possible duplicate in the dead-letter topic. A route that acknowledged first and then failed to publish would destroy the message.

A Reject on a client with no dead-letter topic configured is refused with ErrUnsupported rather than destroying the message or requeuing it for ever, and the delivery stays settleable.

The message is republished unchanged. The five provenance headers are the runner's route (mq.WithDeadLetter) and not the topology's, so a driver that stamped its own would put two different provenance schemes on one message.

The dead-letter policy is also what makes DeliveryAttempt present at all: without one, DeliveryInfo.Attempt is zero and Redelivered is false, because the service counts nothing.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
A Pub/Sub attribute value is a string. The question for this driver is what happens to a binary header value, a repeated header key, a key the service's attribute-name grammar refuses, and the hundred-and-first attribute.

Portable Pub/Sub Message.Body Message.Data, verbatim — there is no binary-body policy on this driver a nil or empty body Data empty plus iqmq-enc = nil / empty; protobuf cannot tell an absent bytes field from a present empty one, and the specification can Message.Key iqmq-k (and iqmq-kenc = b64 when the key is not text, empty when it is empty) Message.ID iqmq-id Properties.ContentType … CreatedAt iqmq-ct, iqmq-ce, iqmq-cid, iqmq-cause, iqmq-reply, iqmq-ts one header one attribute of the same name an enveloped message the whole message in Data, plus iqmq-env = 1

The specification reserves the iqmq- prefix and the service reserves goog for itself, so a caller's header may be in neither. A collision is refused in every metadata mode, because an envelope would carry it and the decoder would then hand it back as a header the driver wrote.

docs.title: What each mode does
docs.text:
Trigger NativeStrict Adaptive PortableEnvelope LenientDrop a binary header value refused enveloped enveloped dropped a repeated header key refused enveloped enveloped dropped a header value over 1024 bytes refused enveloped enveloped dropped more than 100 attributes refused enveloped enveloped dropped a header key over 256 bytes refused refused refused dropped a header key that is not valid UTF-8 refused refused refused dropped a non-UTF-8 identifier or property refused refused refused refused

The three bold rows are the interesting ones, and they are why the admission bound asks driverkit.Envelope.Check rather than reproducing the decoder's numbers. The service's attribute-name limit and the envelope decoder's MaxHeaderKey are the same 256 bytes, so a longer key has no representation in either half — and a driver that enveloped it anyway would publish a record its own Unwrap refuses for ever: undeliverable, therefore unsettleable, which is the disqualifier reached through a record the driver made out of a publication it accepted. FuzzPubSubAttributes found the identifier case in a third of a second.

docs.title: The limits this driver advertises
docs.text:
Read from the pinned client library and from the service's published quotas at that version, and recorded here rather than in the portable API — which is what The specification asks. Re-verified when the client pin moves.

Limit Value Source MaxMessageBytes 10,000,000 pubsub.MaxPublishRequestBytes MaxBatchMessages 1,000 pubsub.MaxPublishRequestCount MaxBatchBytes 10,000,000 the same publish-request limit MaxHeaderCount 100 − 11 reserved = 89 the service's attribute count, less what this driver spends MaxHeaderBytes 1,024 the service's attribute-value limit MaxDelay Config.MaxExtension (10 minutes by default) what the in-process hold can keep the lease alive for MaxLease 600 s the service's ackDeadlineSeconds ceiling

What the mapping costs, measured by TestAllocsMappingIsBoundedPerPublication and logged on every run: 1 allocation for a body-only publication (the attribute map), 4 with a key and an identifier, and 10 with eight sixteen-byte headers — an attribute value IS a string and the SPI's header value is a []byte, so the per-header conversion is the boundary's and not this driver's to remove. A refused publication allocates nothing beyond that map: the refusals are preallocated errcode values rather than formatted strings.

Not advertised, because the driver does not know them: nothing else in the specification's table. Two more numbers bound resource names rather than messages — an identifier is 3 to 255 characters and an ordering key is 1024 bytes — and both are checked before any I/O.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The client library owns it. Pub/Sub is a gRPC service and the library re-establishes its streaming pull and its publish channel on its own, with its own backoff, so there is no dial loop here and no driverkit.Reconnector.

What the driver adds is the part the library does not do:

  • a streaming pull that returns a non-retryable error is restarted after receiveBackoff (500 ms), so a subscription that has been deleted or a credential that has expired costs one attempt per interval rather than a spin, and a stream the service tears down by design is simply reopened;
  • every such failure moves Health to Degraded and the next success moves it back to Ready. The specification makes that the only place a background failure can surface, because there is no call to return it from;
  • the ordering-key resume, without which a reconnection that failed one ordered publication would silently stop that key for ever.

Health is deliberately weaker than a driver that owns its connection, and it says so: a client that has never been asked to do anything reports Ready because nothing has failed, not because anything has been proved. Ping is the call that proves it — one ListTopics bounded to a single result, which consumes no message and creates no topology.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
From the delivery to the acknowledgement.

A delivery is invisible to other consumers of its subscription for its acknowledgement deadline, and the client library extends that automatically while a handler holds the message. The driver asks the library to extend for the longer of the deadline and Config.MaxExtension, capped at 60 minutes, and that window is what DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires reports. Up to v1.0.8 the driver reported a deadline longer than Config.MaxExtension without asking the library for it, so the library let the message go at Config.MaxExtension while the delivery still claimed it.

Past it, the service delivers the message again to somebody else — and the first delivery's acknowledgement would then acknowledge a message another consumer is working on, which is why the local lease check refuses it before the call.

Nothing here makes a delivery exactly-once. Config.ExactlyOnce creates a subscription with the service's enableExactlyOnceDelivery and settles through AckWithResult, which means:

  • an acknowledged message is never redelivered, and the acknowledgement has an outcome the driver reports rather than swallows;
  • an unacknowledged message whose deadline expires is redelivered exactly as on any other subscription.

the specification's ExactlyOnceDelivery is a guarantee about delivery multiplicity, which is the second thing, so this driver does not claim it however the subscription is configured. Setting Config.ExactlyOnce is still worth it, for the settlement outcome.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
client, err := gcppubsub.Open(ctx, gcppubsub.Config{
    ProjectID:   "my-project",
    Ordering:    true,
    AckDeadline: 30 * time.Second,
})

gcppubsub://my-project?ordering=true&ackdeadline=30s
gcppubsub://127.0.0.1:8085/my-project?insecuretransport=true&autocreate=true

The authority is the endpoint when the DSN names one and the project when it does not, which is the one shape that makes both forms readable: a DSN with an endpoint puts the project in the path (how the emulator is reached), and a DSN with no endpoint puts the project in the host, because a client with no endpoint talks to the service's own and the only thing left to name is the project.

The authority names one thing. A second host is refused, a project has no port (gcppubsub://my-project:8085 is refused; an endpoint names its project in the path), and a project is read as written: gcppubsub://[example.com:my-project] and gcppubsub://example.com%3Amy-project are both the domain-scoped project example.com:my-project. An endpoint host that decodes to @, /, ?, #, a backslash, a space or a control character is refused, because gRPC would dial somewhere else (a%3Fb:8085 becomes dns:///a). The project and endpoint parameters are the other spelling of those two settings, and a DSN that names one in both places is refused rather than resolved: gcppubsub://emulator-host?project=p used to keep the parameter, drop the emulator and dial the managed service.

Config.DSN() renders a configuration so that it parses back to itself, and uses two more shapes when the two above cannot carry a value: a project the authority would have to escape goes in the path of an empty authority, and an endpoint that is not host[:port] goes in the endpoint parameter.

gcppubsub:///example.com:my-project
gcppubsub://my-project?endpoint=https://pubsub.example:443

The credential is not in the DSN. A Pub/Sub credential is a service-account key — a JSON document with a private key in it — and a DSN is a string that ends up in logs, environment listings and process tables. credentialsfile names a path, which is what a deployment has; Config.CredentialsJSON is reachable only from Go, and OpenWithClient is the way in for everything else — workload identity federation, an impersonated service account, a token source of the deployment's own.

Both credential fields are service-account keys and only that. The client library's untyped options (option.WithCredentialsJSON, option.WithCredentialsFile) accept any credential configuration, including an externally-sourced one whose URLs decide where a token is fetched from, and are deprecated for exactly that reason; this driver uses the typed form with the type pinned to ServiceAccount, so a configuration from an untrusted source is refused rather than dialled.

Parameter Field project, endpoint, credentialsfile the same insecuretransport InsecureTransport — plaintext gRPC and no credentials, which is what an emulator needs and a real endpoint must never be given ordering, exactlyonce, retainacked, autocreate, strictackdeadline, compression the same flags ackdeadline, maxextension, retention, apitimeout, publishdelay, publishtimeout the same durations prefetch, maxoutstandingbytes, publishcount, publishbytes, completionworkers, completionqueue, maxdeliveryattempts the same counts topicprefix, subscriptionprefix, filter, deadlettertopic the same

Every parameter is read exactly once and anything left over is an error, so a typo is a refusal rather than a setting that silently did nothing. Config.Validate is pure — no clock, no environment, no network — and Config.String, GoString, LogValue and DSN all redact.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
The managed service's acknowledgement deadline is 10 to 600 seconds; the emulator accepts one. Config.StrictAckDeadline refuses a deadline outside the managed range before any I/O, and it is off by default: several scenarios ask for five hundred milliseconds and the emulator grants it, so a driver that refused locally would report "unsupported" for a topology the broker under test builds happily. On the managed service the range is enforced by the service, with an InvalidArgument this driver maps and reports. Turn the flag on to find out at construction instead. A conformance report made against the emulator therefore proves the lease scenarios in a configuration the managed service would refuse, which is what EvidenceEmulator means.

A handler may hold a delivery for the longer of the acknowledgement deadline and Config.MaxExtension, whose default is ten minutes. The library keeps extending for that long, so a handler that hangs holds its message for the whole of it and no other consumer can take it. Lower both for a consumer whose handlers should be fast.

A subscription created after a publication never sees that publication. A Pub/Sub backlog begins at the subscription's own creation, however long the retention is. That is why Replay is conditional and why the conformance harness provisions every subscription a scenario names before the scenario publishes: several scenarios publish before they open a consumer, and on this broker every one of them would otherwise look like a driver that drops publications.

Deleting a topic leaves its subscriptions. They are detached, with the backlog they already had. Admin.DeleteTopic does not delete subscriptions it did not create, and the specification's "everything in it" is therefore not quite what happens.

Admin.Stats returns ErrUnsupported. Pub/Sub does not answer the question through its own API: the undelivered-message count and the oldest-unacknowledged-message age are Cloud Monitoring metrics, which is a different service, a different credential scope and a sampling delay of minutes. the rule that an unknown is never an overloaded zero makes the refusal the honest answer, because a caller cannot tell an empty subscription from one nobody can measure.

Admin.Purge is a seek forward. It needs no retained messages — seeking forward is always available — which is why it is native while seeking backwards is conditional on Config.RetainAcked.

A topic that is already a resource name reaches the driver only through the SPI. mq.ValidateTopic refuses a name with a / and a scheme in it, so Client.Publisher(… Topic: "projects/p/topics/t") fails in the core. Config.TopicPrefix and Config.SubscriptionIDs are the reachable forms. This is the recorded finding shared with drivers/sqs and drivers/snssqs.

The client library's stream keep-alive handler outlives a closed source by up to ten seconds. It exits on its own tickers rather than on the iterator's stop signal. It is a shutdown lag rather than a leak — one goroutine per closed source, bounded, and it does exit — and this repository's goleak configurations ignore it by name.

Tracing is not wired. The client library can emit OpenTelemetry spans and this driver turns them off (option.WithTelemetryDisabled on an insecure endpoint, and no tracer provider otherwise): integrations/otel owns the semantic conventions and the span names.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
drivers/gcppubsub/critical_test.go, each watched failing against a deliberate mutation of the production code before it was trusted:

Test The failure mode TestCriticalOrderingKeyIsResumedAfterAFailedPublication the real client library over pstest, with a PermissionDenied injected into the publish-response queue: a publisher that is not resumed silently stops carrying one key TestCriticalOrderingKeyPauseIsRealInTheFake the scripted fake's own pause contract, so it is usable as an oracle TestCriticalDelayedNackIsAnInProcessHold both directions of the hold: not deliverable during it, deliverable after it TestCriticalDelayedNackHoldEndsOnClose the hold racing Close for three thousand rounds under -race TestCriticalCloseWithUnsettledDeliveriesDoesNotHang the library's shutdown waits for settlement, so Close must settle before it waits TestCriticalStaleSettlementAfterRedeliveryIsRefused the local lease check TestCriticalCompletionsDoNotCostAGoroutinePerMessage the fixed completion pool against a goroutine per message, with the fake's results gated so a thousand publications are outstanding at once TestCriticalRejectReachesTheDeadLetterTopicBeforeAcknowledging republish before acknowledge, proved by making the republication fail TestCriticalRejectWithNoDestinationIsRefused the refusal with nowhere to send the message TestCriticalRejectRefusesADelay on the one combination whose halves are both supported and whose combination means nothing

drivers/gcppubsub/ambiguity_test.go covers the and the boundary: a publication that fails with a transient code is ambiguous (the service answers after it has read the request), a settlement that fails is not (the message is still unacknowledged, so it comes back and the delivery is settleable again), and a settlement past the lease is refused before the call — proved by the message still being outstanding at the service afterwards.

TestConformance in the driver's own module runs the suite against an endpoint named by IQMQ_PUBSUB_ADDR, for somebody who has one and does not want the conformance module, its testcontainers dependency or Docker. Set IQMQ_PUBSUB_MANAGED for a run against a real project: it reads the evidence as managed, which drops the emulator-only skips and makes limits/advertised strict.

drivers/gcppubsub/v1compat adds the specification's TestModel (one scripted sequence through both arms), TestBothArmsAnswerOneCapabilityTable and TestTheArmsAreWireCompatible (publish through each generation, consume through the other).

FuzzPubSubAttributes and FuzzPubSubErrorMapping carry committed regression inputs; testdata/fuzz/FuzzPubSubAttributes.README says what each one reaches.

docs.title: goredis
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Module: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/redis/goredis · Profile: goredis

This is the same driver as redis over a different client library. The specification asks for two Redis drivers "both implement[ing] a small internal command interface", and that interface is internal/streams.Commander: one method that sends a command and returns a reply. Everything that decides whether a message is lost or duplicated — the key naming, the entry field layout, the commands, the reply semantics, the reclaim accounting, the nack strategies, the capability table, the error table, the Config type and the DSN parser — is shared code, and this module is the adapter plus its entry points.

So every section below that is not about the client library says "as redis" and points at it. That is not a gap in this page: two copies of the same prose is two copies to drift, and the half that drifted would be the half nobody reads. What this page carries in full is what the client library changes, and the evidence that it changes nothing else.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text: Client library github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 Pinned version v9.23.0 Interface taken redis.UniversalClient (so *redis.Client, *redis.ClusterClient, *redis.Ring and a Sentinel failover client all fit) Minimum server Redis 6.2, as redis — the reclaim loop is XAUTOCLAIM Protocol RESP3 (go-redis's default); RESP2 is exercised by internal/streams/respsrv's own tests

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building this driver; re-verify when the pin moves.

  • go-redis retries a command it has already written. Options.MaxRetries defaults to 3 and shouldRetry returns true for a write error and for a read timeout, both of which happen after the command may have reached the server. On this broker a retried XADD is a second copy of the message, reported to the caller as one successful publication. This driver sets MaxRetries: -1. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 options.go (MaxRetries default), redis.go (_process's retry loop, shouldRetry).
  • go-redis cannot find the key in a command sent through Do. cmdFirstKeyPos reads the position from the server's own command table, which knows nothing about an arbitrary Do, and cmdSlot falls back to hashtag.RandomSlot() — a random node. SetFirstKeyPos is how a caller states it, and this driver states it from streams.Cmd's key span. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 command.go (SetFirstKeyPos), cluster.go/ring.go (cmdSlot); TestKeyRoutingIsDecidedByTheCommandsKeyAndNotAtRandom.
  • A per-command read timeout is not reachable from outside go-redis. Cmder.readTimeout() and baseCmd.setReadTimeout are unexported, so the only lever for a blocking command is the connection's ReadTimeout. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 command.go:553, command.go:557.
  • go-redis's default ReadTimeout is five seconds, and so is this driver's default Block. They raced: every idle fetch came back as read tcp …: i/o timeout. ReadTimeout is now the block plus the dial timeout. A client you pass to OpenWithClient keeps its own ReadTimeout: a Block left at its default is shortened to fit inside it, and a Block you set that does not fit is refused as invalid configuration. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 options.go (ReadTimeout default); drivers/redis.DefaultBlock; TestABlockingReadWaitsOutTheBlockRatherThanTimingOut.
  • redis.Nil is a CONSTANT of a string type. So var x = redis.Nil gives a string-typed variable that is boxed into an error interface on every use — one allocation per call, charged to whatever called it. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 redis.go:28, internal/proto/reader.go:44.
  • go-redis reports a null reply as an ERROR (redis.Nil), not as a value. An XREADGROUP that timed out and one that failed are different answers, so the adapter turns redis.Nil into streams.Nil and everything else into a failure. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 internal/proto/reader.go (ReadReply).
  • go-redis decodes a reply into any: string, int64, float64, bool, *big.Int, []any (array, set and push), map[any]any (RESP3 map), and a nested error reply as a proto.RedisError VALUE inside the slice. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 internal/proto/reader.go:338 (ReadReply), readSlice; TestConvertRendersEveryReplyGoRedisCanProduce.
  • go-redis does NOT strip the ERR prefix from an error reply and rueidis DOES (a kvrocks compatibility workaround in RedisMessage.Error). The shared error table therefore matches the distinctive phrase rather than the prefix. Verified against: rueidis v1.0.77 message.go:751; go-redis v9.22.0 proto.RedisError; TestBothClientsMapOneServerReplyToOneCode.
  • Pipeline.Exec returns the FIRST error among its commands, and sets a transport failure on every command it holds while leaving a server's error reply on the command that got it. Verified against: go-redis v9.22.0 pipeline.go:104, redis.go:1607 (generalProcessPipeline, setCmdsErr).

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
As redis, including the entry field layout (b, k, t, h:<n>, p:<n>), the hash-tagged {topic} / {topic}:<i> shard keys and the XGROUP CREATE … MKSTREAM subscription. The key naming is internal/streams.Keys and is shared character for character.

One thing is this module's own: go-redis is told the first key's position in every command, from streams.Cmd's key span. Without it a cluster or a ring routes every command this driver sends to a random node — correct by accident on a standalone server and wrong everywhere else. Only the first key's position is stated because that is all go-redis's routing reads, and it is enough: every key of a topic carries the topic's hash tag, so all of a command's keys are on one slot and the first one names it.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
As redis: XADD with MAXLEN ~ N when configured, ConfirmAccepted at the server's reply, ConfirmDurable via WAITAOF and conditional on Redis ≥ 7.0 with an append-only file, and the admission bound applied before any I/O in every metadata mode.

What differs is what a publication costs and what it may not do:

  • Batching. A batch is Pipeline → Process per command → Exec, one write and one read, with one reply per command. DoMulti returns a result per command index-aligned with its input, and treats Exec's own error as the batch's only when no command carries one of its own — because Exec returns the first command's error, and reading that as the batch's would report one message's outcome for another.
  • No retries. MaxRetries is -1. The retry policy is the core, applied where a caller can see it, and a publication whose reply never arrived is reported Ambiguous rather than silently sent again.
  • Allocations. go-redis takes a command as ...any, so every token of every command is boxed: a nine-token XADD costs ten allocations before it reaches the socket. TestAllocsAdapting pins the adapter's own share, and The specification measures the difference.
  • The message body is not copied here, and is on redis. go-redis writes and reads in the calling goroutine, so a []byte argument is on the wire before Publish returns; the body therefore goes out as the caller's own slice. rueidis queues a command for a background writer and can return from a cancelled Do with the command still queued, so the same trick there would put the caller's LATER bytes on the wire, and that arm copies. It is a statement rather than a performance note, and it is part of why the batched budget reads differently on the two profiles.

One obligation follows for you. A redis.Hook installed through OpenWithClient that STORES the Cmder and reads its arguments after its own call returns must copy what it stores: the body argument is the publisher's buffer, and the specification has already given it back.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
As redis: XREADGROUP COUNT prefetch BLOCK, a delivery buffer holding at most one delivery per entry, and the generation re-check in the drain.

streams.Cmd.Blocking is honoured as far as this library allows: rueidis routes a blocking command to a connection pool of its own, and go-redis has no per-command lever at all (setReadTimeout is unexported), so the connection's bound is what carries it. go-redis takes a connection per command from a pool, so a blocking read occupies one connection rather than stalling the others — the head-of-line problem Blocking exists for on a multiplexed client does not arise here.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
As redis, including both halves of the guarded acknowledgement — the per-source generation table that refuses a superseded settlement with no command sent, and the Lua script that checks the pending row's consumer atomically with the XACK — and the XCLAIM … JUSTID extension behind the same ownership check. Both are re-proved over this client (TestAckOfAStolenDeliveryIsRefused, TestExtendDoesNotStealTheEntry, TestSweepRedeliversAnUnsettledDelivery), because both travel over the client library: the generation table decides without a command and the Lua check is an EVALSHA whose reply this adapter parses.

Negative settlement is the four strategies, unchanged and shared.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: As redis: per shard, and a topic with several shards has no total order. The key-to-shard mapping is FNV-1a over the key bytes (redis.ShardOf) and is the same function, so a key published through one client and consumed through the other lands in the same shard.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text: As redis: only the zsetmover nack strategy honours an arbitrary redelivery delay; the other three refuse a delay they cannot honour rather than redelivering early. A delayed publication is unsupported on this broker under either client.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text: As redis: a destination is configuration (Config.DeadLetterTopic or Config.DeadLetterSuffix) and is empty by default, so a Reject on a subscription that has none reports ErrUnsupported and settles nothing. The suffix form is one atomic Lua move (the keys share the topic's hash tag); the topic form is two commands with a documented duplicate window.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
As redis: native, ordered, binary-safe and duplicate-preserving, because a stream entry is a field-value list of binary-safe strings; bounded by the portable envelope's decode limits in every metadata mode.

The client library is where binary safety could be lost, so it is proved here rather than assumed: TestTheFieldLayoutRoundTripsEveryMessageThisClientAccepts round-trips a body carrying \r\n, a NUL and high bytes, header values carrying the protocol's own terminator, sixteen headers, the identifier at the limit, and a message with nothing in it at all. The capability table's limits are identical under both clients (TestCapabilitiesAreTheSameUnderBothClients).

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
As redis in shape: the client library owns its reconnection and reports nothing back, so a lost link shows as the failure of whatever command met it and as a Degraded health transition, not as a transition of its own. driverkit.Reconnector is not used because there is no dial loop for it to run.

go-redis's own behaviour: a pool connection that fails is discarded and redialled on the next command, with DialerRetries (5) attempts and DialerRetryTimeout (100 ms) between them. Command retries are off , so a failure reaches the driver's error mapper rather than being absorbed — which is what lets MapNet classify a post-write failure as Ambiguous.

Maintenance-notification handling (CLIENT MAINT_NOTIFICATIONS) is left at go-redis's default (auto): on a server without it the library disables the feature on the error, and its background worker stops with the client.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text: As redis. The lease is this driver's, not the broker's: Redis grants none, nothing expires and nothing redelivers, so the mandatory XAUTOCLAIM sweep is the only thing that hands a dead consumer's entries to another. Close's latency is bounded by Config.Block and not by Close: neither client aborts an in-flight blocking read, so the fetch loop returns ErrClosed when the block expires and it looks again.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
goredis.Config is redis.Config — a type alias, not a copy — and goredis.ParseDSN is redis.ParseDSN. A program that already configures the Redis driver changes one import and one call.

This module registers no DSN scheme. A DSN naming redis has to mean one thing, and which client library serves it is a build-time choice a connection string has no business making; that is redis.Scheme's own documented decision and this is the other half of it. TestTheSchemeBelongsToTheBrokerAndNotToTheClient holds it.

goredis.UniversalOptions(cfg) is the configuration translated into go-redis's options, exported so that a caller building its own client starts from the driver's answer rather than guessing. Three fields in it are decisions:

Field Value Why MaxRetries -1 a retried XADD is a duplicate the caller is told is one publication ReadTimeout Block + DialTimeout a blocking read legitimately takes the whole block PoolSize go-redis's default the connection model IS what the specification measures; pinning it would measure a pool this driver invented

Anything the typed configuration cannot carry — a Sentinel or Ring topology, a pool size, a custom dialler, a hook, instrumentation — goes through OpenWithClient, with driverkit.ClientBorrowed or ClientOwned saying who closes it.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
Beyond the shared suite, this module holds the two clients to each other. That is the whole reason a second implementation of one contract is worth having.

Test What it holds TestBothClientsMapOneServerReplyToOneCode one server reply, two clients, one mq.ErrorCode — the divergence that found TestBothClientsRenderOneReplyAsOneValue a script of every reply shape a stream command produces, rendered identically, and the two servers' own state equal afterwards FuzzRedisClientReplyEquivalence an arbitrary reply written on the wire by internal/streams/respsrv and read by both shipped adapters (1.06M executions clean) TestCapabilitiesAreTheSameUnderBothClients every claim and every limit, under both TestKeyRoutingIsDecidedByTheCommandsKeyAndNotAtRandom a redis.Ring over two servers: one stream's commands must all land on one shard, and the read must reach the shard the writes did TestABlockingReadWaitsOutTheBlockRatherThanTimingOut a 6-second BLOCK over go-redis's 5-second default read timeout TestPipelinedResultsAreIndexAligned a pipeline with a refusal in the middle: the commands behind it still ran and their results are where they belong TestTheFieldLayoutRoundTripsEveryMessageThisClientAccepts binary safety through this library, message by message TestAckOfAStolenDeliveryIsRefused, TestExtendDoesNotStealTheEntry the disqualifier and, over this client TestConvertRendersEveryReplyGoRedisCanProduce every Go type proto.Reader.ReadReply can return, including the ones no command in this driver produces

internal/streams/respsrv is what makes all of that possible with no container: a real TCP server speaking real RESP whose command semantics are internal/streams/fakestreams, with the fake's settable clock and inspectable pending list still underneath.

docs.title: jetstream
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Module: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/jetstream · Profile: JetStream

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's nats image (make bench-native CLIENTS="jetstream"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary jetstream github.com/nats-io/nats.go github.com/nats-io/nats.go@v1.54.0 JetStream PubAck from a file-backed stream (R1)

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • per-message TTL and schedules. The client exposes per-message TTL as the Nats-TTL header (jetstream.MsgTTLHeader) and message schedules as a schedule header taking an @at timestamp, an @every duration or a cron expression, gated by StreamConfig.AllowMsgSchedules; TTL needs a 2.11+ server and schedules a 2.12+ server, and the harness pins nats 2.14.6. Verified against: nats.go v1.53.1 jetstream/message.go:210,220-232 and jetstream/stream_config.go:211; conformance/harness/images.go.
  • deduplication and progress. Publish deduplication uses the Nats-Msg-Id header (jetstream.MsgIDHeader) against the stream's duplicate window, and a consumer extends its ack wait with Msg.InProgress rather than a lease API. Verified against: nats.go v1.53.1 jetstream/message.go:169,378.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq JetStream Notes Topic subject inside Config.Stream / becomes .; Config.SubjectPrefix is prepended as a token ConsumerConfig.Subscription durable pull consumer two consumers of one subscription compete; two subscriptions each receive everything ConsumerConfig.Topic (pattern) the consumer's FilterSubjects * matches one token, a trailing > matches the rest ConsumerConfig.Prefetch MaxAckPending and the client's PullMaxMessages the same number, which is what makes the prefetch a real bound ConsumerConfig.AckDeadline AckWait Config.AckWait (30s) when the consumer names none Message.Key iqmq-key header base64, because a NATS header value is a text line Properties.ReplyTo Msg.Reply the native reply subject DeliveryInfo.Attempt NumDelivered the server's own count, which starts at 1 DeliveryInfo.Sequence the stream sequence always set; it is also what the stale-ack guard is keyed on DeliveryInfo.Source the stream name

The subject alphabet this driver will build or accept is letters, digits, _, - and $, with . as the separator — the image of the portable topic grammar under the separator swap, plus the $ that NATS system subjects use. Anything else is refused before any I/O, because a malformed subject does not produce a rejected publication on this protocol: it produces a malformed frame on a connection every other publisher and subscriber in the process is sharing.

The mapping is not injective. orders/created and orders.created are one subject, so DeliveryInfo.Topic reports the subject the message really arrived on with the prefix stripped. A deployment that needs the two to stay distinct uses one spelling.

A publication's topic may never be a pattern. A consumer's topic may be one, and that is what FeatureWildcardSubscribe means here.

docs.title: The stream, and who creates it
docs.text:
Config.Stream is the one piece of topology JetStream really has, and Config.ManageStream is off by default: the specification forbids a driver from provisioning topology behind the caller's back, so a client whose stream does not exist fails at Open with CodeNotFound. A deployment that wants the driver to own the stream says so, and then gets the stream the configuration describes (StreamSubjects, Storage, Replicas, MaxAge, MaxMsgs, MaxBytes, MaxMsgSize, DuplicateWindow).

ManageStream needs either a SubjectPrefix or an explicit StreamSubjects. The guess that suggests itself — >, every subject — is not merely broad: JetStream refuses a stream that captures every subject unless it is also created with NoAck, which would discard every acknowledgement this profile exists for.

A publication to a subject the bound stream does not capture is refused with ErrTopicNotFound when the publisher is opened. That is not fussiness: under ConfirmNone the publication is a core publish with no reply subject, so the server drops it and tells nobody. The subject list is read at Open; a stream reconfigured underneath a running client is not noticed until the next one.

docs.title: Durable consumer names
docs.text:
A subscription maps to a durable named Config.ConsumerPrefix + the sanitised subscription + a short hash of the filter — iqmq-billing-1f3k9z. The hash is not decoration: a JetStream durable is per (stream, filter), so the same subscription name used on two topics has to be two durables, or the second would inherit the first's ack floor and skip messages. Every byte JetStream refuses in a name is mapped to -, and the hash keeps two names that map alike apart.

An existing durable's own configuration wins. CreateOrUpdateConsumer cannot change a consumer's DeliverPolicy, and a second consumer of one subscription asking for a different start position must not be the reason the subscription stops working, so an update the server refuses becomes a lookup — which is what a durable subscription means.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
Mode What it waits for ConfirmNone nothing: a core publish to a stream-bound subject, with no reply subject asked for ConfirmDefault / ConfirmAccepted the stream's PubAck ConfirmDurable the stream's PubAck — the same round trip

On this broker "accepted" and "durable" are the same boundary, because the PubAck is sent after the message is committed to the stream's storage. That is why ConfirmDurable is not refused here — the Core driver refuses it at construction — and why FeatureDurableConfirm is a native claim. It is withdrawn, with FeatureDurableStorage, when the bound stream is memory-backed: a stream that loses everything on the next restart cannot support a durability claim, and a program that requires one fails at construction instead.

ConfirmNone costs no round trip and reports nothing. The message still reaches the stream — the subject is bound to it — but a failure is invisible, which is what the mode means.

Per-call controls:

Control Answer DedupKey Nats-Msg-Id, de-duplicated inside the stream's Duplicates window TTL Nats-TTL — conditional: a 2.11+ server and a stream created with AllowMsgTTL Delay / PublishOptions.DeliverAt a Nats-Schedule control message — conditional: a 2.12+ server and AllowMsgSchedules Priority ErrUnsupported before any I/O Partition ErrUnsupported — a subject is the only partition there is

The controls are written as the server's own headers rather than through the client library's PublishOpt functions, so that all three publication paths carry them identically: a ConfirmNone publication is a core publish and never sees a PublishOpt, and a caller who asked for de-duplication has no way to tell which path its message took.

PublishBatch publishes every message asynchronously — bounded by Config.PublishAsyncMaxPending — and waits for every PubAck, so each message of a batch is exactly as durable as a single publication and the result is index-aligned with the batch. It is not atomic: JetStream's atomic batch is a stream flag this driver does not set, which is why FeatureBatchPublish is EmulatedDurable rather than Native.

PublishAsync costs no goroutine per message, which the specification forbids outright. The JetStream client reports every asynchronous publication through two connection-wide callbacks that carry the *nats.Msg the publication was made with, so the backend keeps a map from that pointer to the publication and resolves each one from the client's own reply goroutine. A publication still outstanding when the publisher closes reports CodeSettlementUnknown, which is the truth: the message had left and its PubAck had not arrived.

Every asynchronous path copies the payload. nats.go appends the payload to its own write buffer inside PublishMsg, so the first attempt never aliases the caller's slice — but the JetStream client retains the *nats.Msg and republishes it on a "no responders" retry and after a reconnection, and a retry that read the caller's slice would put whatever the caller wrote next on the wire. Backend.AsyncBodyCopies counts them. A synchronous publication retains nothing and copies nothing.

FeatureReceipts is native: a receipt carries the stream sequence, the confirmation boundary (always ConfirmDurable, because that is what a PubAck is here), the confirmation time and <stream>:<sequence> as the identifier.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
OpenSource creates or binds the subscription's durable pull consumer and starts the client library's Consume loop, whose callback pushes into a driverkit.PushAdapter sized at the consumer's prefetch.

The prefetch is a real bound on this broker rather than a client-side buffer, because it is three numbers at once: the ring's capacity, the client's PullMaxMessages, and the consumer's MaxAckPending. Blocking in the callback therefore stops the server, not just the client.

Fetch is one blocking wait, then a non-blocking take of everything the ring holds — which is what makes FeatureBatchReceive true — and then one filter. The filter is not optional. MaxAckPending counts unacknowledged messages, so a record whose lease keeps expiring while nobody settles it is delivered again and again and every copy lands in the ring behind the first. Handing the caller the oldest would be handing it a delivery the driver already knows is dead: its settlement is refused with ErrLeaseLost and the handler's work is thrown away. A delivery whose token went stale while it waited is dropped here, and Backend.SupersededDeliveries counts them. A deployment that sees that counter climb raises AckWait.

All four start positions exist: StartLatest is DeliverNew, StartEarliest is DeliverAll, StartAt is DeliverByStartTime and StartAtSequence is DeliverByStartSequence. A start sequence of zero is refused — JetStream stream sequences begin at 1. The policy only decides where a consumer with no committed position begins; a durable that already has an ack floor resumes from it.

A consumer whose pattern also matches Config.ScheduleSubject's tree is refused. A JetStream consumer has no negative filter, so the alternative is handing the caller the driver's own schedule control messages as though the application had published them.

Close does four things in an order where each depends on the one before: it sets the closing flag, closes the ring (which wakes a parked callback), drains the client library's own buffer so that what it had already fetched reaches the callback and is naked, and then naks every delivery the token table still calls active — which is the ring's leftovers and everything the source handed the core that was never settled. Abandoning instead would lose nothing, because the server redelivers after AckWait, but on a thirty-second default it is the difference between a restart that resumes and one that appears to hang.

One window a Close cannot reach. A pull consumer's request is outstanding for a whole batch, and nats.go drops what arrives after it unsubscribes, so messages the server had already put on the wire towards the dying subscription are never seen by the driver and cannot be naked. They wait out their lease: at most one batch per close, stalled for at most one AckWait, never lost — at-least-once is the server's. nats-server then advances the consumer's ack floor over such messages once its pending set empties, so a handful can be accounted for at the broker without this client settling them at all. A deployment that closes consumers often and cannot afford the stall lowers AckWait.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
iqmq JetStream Delivery.Ack +ACK — a publish to the delivery's reply subject, or a request/reply round trip under Config.DoubleAck Delivery.Nack() / Nack(NackRequeue()) -NAK Nack(NackDelay(d)) -NAK {"delay":<d>} — the server holds the message; nothing is held in this process Nack(NackDrop()) +TERM — destructive, which is why the specification makes it something a caller has to write Delivery.Reject() / Nack(NackDeadLetter()) a durable publication to Config.DeadLetterTopic, then +TERM Delivery.Extend(by) +WPI — the server resets the redelivery timer

Config.DoubleAck decides the positive boundary. Without it the ack is a publish and the call returns as soon as it is in the write buffer, so a link that dies immediately afterwards leaves the message redeliverable — which is at-least-once behaving as advertised. With it the ack is a request and the call returns only once the server has recorded it, at the cost of one round trip per message.

docs.title: A stale ack must not settle a redelivery
docs.text:
This is the part worth reading the source for, and the specification makes the unguarded behaviour a disqualifier.

JetStream acknowledges by reply subject, and nats-server's AckExplicit path deletes its pending entry for the message's stream sequence without looking at which delivery the reply subject came from. So the reply subject of a delivery whose lease expired still works: acking it acknowledges the record that a later delivery now owns, the holder of that later delivery never sees a redelivery, and nothing in the client or the server reports the loss.

This driver refuses that ack. Every delivery takes a slot in a driverkit.TokenTable, and the source keeps an index from stream sequence to token: when a record is delivered again, the previous delivery's slot is released — which bumps its generation — and a settlement carrying the old token reports ErrLeaseLost before anything reaches the wire. Backend.StaleSettlements counts the refusals.

TestStaleAckWouldOtherwiseSettleTheRedelivery reaches past iqmq through Delivery.Native() and makes the ack the guard refuses, so that the guard has something to be measured against; FuzzNATSStaleAck holds the invariant over every interleaving with a model beside it; and the broker-version matrix checks the guard on 2.10, 2.11, 2.12 and 2.14, because it is the server's behaviour that makes the guard necessary.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
JetStream stores one subject's messages in the order the stream accepted them, and a single consumer of a subscription sees them in that order. That is the whole guarantee, and the three ordering features are three names for it:

Feature Level Condition OrderedGlobally conditional one publisher, one subject, one consumer of the subscription OrderedByKey conditional there is no message key; a key orders only in so far as its messages share a subject OrderedByPartition conditional there are no partitions; a subject is the only partition there is

Three things break it and all three are ordinary: two publishers are not ordered against each other, a subscription with two consumers interleaves across them, and a nack puts a message behind the messages that followed it. A deployment that needs order keeps one publisher per subject and one consumer per subscription — the same trade every broker makes, stated here rather than implied.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
Two different things, and only one of them is version-gated.

Delayed redelivery is native and unconditional: Nack(NackDelay(d)) is -NAK {"delay":<d>}, the server makes the message deliverable again when the delay is up, and nothing is held in this process. This is the one a retry policy uses.

Scheduled publication is conditional. Delay and PublishOptions.DeliverAt are written as a Nats-Schedule: @at <timestamp> control message on Config.ScheduleSubject's tree, with the topic's subject as the Nats-Schedule-Target; the server generates the application's message on that subject when the schedule fires. It needs a 2.12+ server and a stream created with AllowMsgSchedules, and the claim is read off the stream this client is bound to rather than off a version string.

The schedule tree is a sibling of the topic tree and not a child of it — iqmqsched.<stream>.> — so a wildcard subscription under SubjectPrefix cannot receive the control messages, and the stream's name is part of the root because JetStream refuses two streams in one account whose subjects overlap. When the driver manages the stream it adds the tree itself; when the caller supplies StreamSubjects, a schedule root the stream does not capture withdraws the claim, because a control message the stream does not hold is a schedule that never fires.

A schedule in the past is refused with CodeInvalidArgument: a caller who asked for a delay and got none has been told something untrue about when its message becomes visible.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Reject() publishes the message to Config.DeadLetterTopic and then terminates the original. The order is the whole of it:

  1. js.PublishMsg to the dead-letter subject — a durable publication that returns after the stream has committed the copy, not a core publish that returns from the write buffer;
  2. only once that PubAck is in hand, +TERM on the original.

A backend with no dead-letter subject configured answers Reject with ErrUnsupported and settles nothing, which is the rule. FeatureDeadLetter is therefore conditional on every client, and the note says which side of the condition this one is on.

The copy carries the original's payload and caller headers unchanged, minus the server's own Nats- headers, plus three reserved ones: iqmq-dead-letter-from (the subject it was rejected from), iqmq-dead-letter-attempt (the delivery count) and iqmq-dead-letter-reason (NackOptions.Reason). The specification makes Reason local diagnostics "unless the driver documents that it transports it"; this driver documents that it does, on this route only, because a dead-letter queue with no reason in it is the one place the diagnosis is worth the bytes.

A message the consumer cannot decode is the one message the driver dead-letters on its own. That is a plain body arriving at a MetadataPortableEnvelope consumer, or an envelope a MetadataAdaptive consumer refuses, and the application never sees it. With Config.DeadLetterTopic set, the driver publishes a raw copy there in Reject's order (the PubAck first, then +TERM), with iqmq-dead-letter-reason set to undecodable: and the decode error, so the original does not come back and the messages behind it keep arriving. Health stays as it was and Backend.DeadLettered counts it. With no dead-letter topic, or when the copy cannot be stored, the driver sends -NAK with a delay of one lease (the consumer's AckDeadline, or Config.AckWait) and reports the failure to health and Backend.ConsumeErrors. MaxDeliver is unlimited by default, so the message then comes back once per lease for ever unless you set Config.MaxDeliver. JetStream keeps a naked message in the consumer's pending set while it waits, so it also holds one slot of the prefetch: under Prefetch: 1 nothing behind it is delivered. Set DeadLetterTopic if your producers can write messages this consumer cannot read.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
NATS headers are an HTTP-like block, Name: value per CRLF-terminated line. That decides what can be carried, and the rules are about framing rather than taste:

Rule Why a name may not be empty, carry a colon, a space, a control byte or a byte above ASCII the reader truncates at the colon and a CR or LF forges a second header a name may not be in the Nats- namespace the server owns it: Nats-Msg-Id is de-duplication, Nats-TTL is expiry, Nats-Schedule is a schedule, so a caller header there would change the broker's behaviour rather than travel with the message a value must be valid UTF-8 the block is a text line and the reader is net/textproto's a value may carry no control byte CR and LF forge a header; the rest do not survive a value may not begin with a space or a tab the reader eats those after the colon, so the value comes back shorter

The Nats- rule is this profile's own and the Core driver does not need it. It runs in both directions: a caller header there is refused under MetadataNativeStrict and dropped under MetadataLenientDrop, and a header the server wrote is never decoded back as a caller header — a message the scheduler generated carries Nats-Scheduler and Nats-Schedule-Next, and handing those to the application would be inventing metadata it never published.

A header that breaks one of the other rules is refused with ErrUnsupported under MetadataNativeStrict, dropped under MetadataLenientDrop (and counted by Backend.DroppedMetadata), and carried in the portable envelope under MetadataAdaptive and MetadataPortableEnvelope. FeatureBinaryHeaders is therefore unsupported and FeatureNativeHeaders and FeatureDuplicateHeaders are native.

Header order is not preserved. nats.Header is a Go map, so the publisher's ordering is gone by the time the client hands the message over; this driver decodes the names sorted, which is deterministic where a bare map iteration would give one message a different order on every delivery. Duplicate values of one name keep their order.

Everything the specification names that has no native field travels under the reserved iqmq- prefix, and the names are identical to the Core driver's so that a message published by one profile is readable by the other: iqmq-key, iqmq-id, iqmq-content-type, iqmq-content-encoding, iqmq-correlation-id, iqmq-causation-id, iqmq-created-at, iqmq-empty-body, iqmq-env, and the three dead-letter headers above.

Upgrade producers before consumers

A message enveloped by a version of this driver that predates the marker carries none, so a MetadataAdaptive consumer on the NEW code delivers it natively — the envelope's own bytes as the payload — rather than decoding it. The pairing that breaks is narrow: a producer that enveloped (either MetadataPortableEnvelope, or MetadataAdaptive with metadata NATS cannot carry) read by a MetadataAdaptive consumer, for messages published before the producers are upgraded. A MetadataPortableEnvelope consumer is unaffected in either direction, and an upgraded producer is read correctly by an OLD consumer, because the old code sniffs the body and the extra header is invisible to it. So: producers first, then consumers.

iqmq-empty-body is the driver's own: nats.go builds every payload with make([]byte, n), so a zero-length payload always arrives as an empty non-nil slice and the nil-versus-empty distinction would be lost in one direction.

Limits. Limits.MaxMessageBytes is the smaller of the server's max_payload and the stream's own MaxMsgSize, which is the only answer that cannot lie in the dangerous direction; a publication past it is refused with ErrMessageTooLarge before any I/O. Every other limit is left unadvertised — The specification forbids reading an unadvertised limit as zero, so "we do not know" is a Limit whose Known is false. The driver's own bounds are a 1 KiB subject, 64 subject tokens, a 255-byte stream or consumer name, a 256-byte header name and an 8 KiB header value.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The client library owns the dial loop, and this driver owns what it means:

  • a lost link makes health Degraded with the reason (DisconnectErrHandler);
  • a re-established link makes it Ready again and fires Hooks.OnReconnect with the attempt number (ReconnectHandler);
  • a connection the server closed for good makes it Closed, which is terminal in driverkit.Health, so a late callback cannot report Ready afterwards;
  • a slow consumer makes it Degraded and increments Backend.SlowConsumers;
  • the JetStream consume loop has an error channel of its own — a deleted consumer, a leadership change, a missing heartbeat, a refused pull request — and every one of those reaches health and Backend.ConsumeErrors. Nothing on the fetch path reports them, and the symptom is a consumer that simply stops receiving.

A reconnection does not invalidate the delivery generations, and that is a decision rather than an omission. An acknowledgement here is a message to a delivery's own $JS.ACK.… reply subject, and that subject survives a reconnection: the consumer, its pending state and its ack floor are the server's, not the connection's. A driver that bumped the generation on reconnect would answer ErrLeaseLost to a caller whose ack would have worked. What does make a token stale on this broker is a redelivery of the same record.

Nothing is buffered across a reconnection beyond the client's own reconnect buffer, whose overflow is reported as CodeBackpressure. Asynchronous publications outstanding across a reconnection are reported as ambiguous: the message had left and the PubAck had not arrived.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
From the first delivery until the ack the server recorded. Three ordinary things widen it and each produces a redelivery the application has to absorb:

  • a handler that takes longer than AckWait (use Delivery.Extend, or raise the deadline);
  • a process that dies mid-handler;
  • a link that drops after Ack returned but before the ack reached the server — which is what Config.DoubleAck closes, at one round trip per message.

DeliveryInfo.Attempt is the server's NumDelivered, so the second delivery of a record says so, and DeliveryInfo.Redelivered is Attempt > 1.

Publication has an ambiguous window too: a PubAck that times out, a link that drops with a publication outstanding, or a publisher closed before its PubAck arrived, are all reported with OpError.Ambiguous or CodeSettlementUnknown, because the stream may hold the message. A retry may duplicate — which is what DedupKey and the stream's Duplicates window exist for.

What this driver does not have is exactly-once delivery. Publication de-duplication is real and advertised; a delivery whose lease expires is still redelivered, so a handler may run twice, and FeatureExactlyOnceDelivery is unsupported.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
client, err := jetstream.Open(ctx, jetstream.Config{
        Addrs:           []string{"nats://broker-1:4222", "nats://broker-2:4222"},
        Stream:          "ORDERS",
        SubjectPrefix:   "acme",
        ManageStream:    true,
        AckWait:         30 * time.Second,
        DeadLetterTopic: "orders/dlq",
        DoubleAck:       true,
})

or from a DSN, once the driver is registered with a dsn.Registry:

natsjs://user:password@host-1:4222,host-2:4222/acme?stream=ORDERS&managestream=true&ackwait=30s&doubleack=true&deadlettertopic=orders%2Fdlq
Parameter Meaning path SubjectPrefix stream, streamsubjects, managestream the stream and whether the driver owns it (; separates subjects, because , separates the endpoints) storage, replicas, maxage, maxmsgs, maxbytes, maxmsgsize, duplicatewindow the stream's own settings consumerprefix, ackwait, maxdeliver, inactivethreshold the durable consumer's deadlettertopic where Reject routes before it terminates schedulesubject, disableschedules the schedule tree, or no schedules at all doubleack make Ack a request/reply round trip publishasyncmaxpending, publishtimeout the asynchronous bound and the round-trip bound apiprefix, domain a JetStream API prefix or a leaf-node domain (exclusive) name, creds, token, userinfo, tls, insecureskipverify the connection and its credential pendingmessages, pendingbytes, connecttimeout, reconnectwait, maxreconnects, pinginterval, maxpingsout, draintimeout the client library's own bounds

An unknown parameter is a construction error naming it, and every credential is a dsn.Secret: Config.String(), Config.LogValue() and Config.DSN() all render the redaction. Config.Validate() is pure — no I/O, no dial — so a typo is an immediate refusal rather than a five-second timeout.

Authentication that needs a signing callback (NKey, a custom JWT handler), a custom dialler or a websocket URL is reached through OpenWithClient: build the *nats.Conn however the deployment needs and hand it over with an explicit driverkit.Ownership.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
1. Config.ManageStream is off. Without it, Open fails with CodeNotFound unless somebody has already created the stream. That is, not an oversight.
  2. A stream that captures > needs NoAck, which would discard every acknowledgement, so ManageStream requires a SubjectPrefix or an explicit StreamSubjects.
  3. A short AckWait wastes handler work. A record whose lease keeps expiring is delivered again and again; the driver drops the superseded copies rather than handing them out, but each one was a message the broker sent for nothing. Watch Backend.SupersededDeliveries and Backend.StaleSettlements.
  4. Ack is not a round trip unless you ask. Set Config.DoubleAck when a redelivery after a lost link is unacceptable.
  5. Reject is ErrUnsupported without Config.DeadLetterTopic, and the delivery stays settleable. That is deliberate: the alternative destroys the message.
  6. Nack(NackDrop()) destroys the message. It is +TERM, and nothing brings it back.
  7. A per-message TTL and a scheduled publication depend on the STREAM, not on the driver. An older server ignores the flags, the stream comes back without them, and the claim is withdrawn — so check Capabilities().Has(FeatureMessageTTL) rather than the broker's version string, and remember that a stream created before an upgrade still lacks the flag.
  8. A consumer whose pattern reaches the schedule tree is refused. Narrow the pattern, or set Config.DisableSchedules.
  9. a/b and a.b are the same subject. Pick one spelling per deployment.
  10. Header order is sorted, not published order, and a binary header value is refused outright unless you choose an enveloping metadata mode. A caller header in the Nats- namespace is refused too.
  11. A memory-backed stream withdraws the durability claims. That is the point — but a program that did not require them will run happily on one and lose everything on the next restart.
  12. Durable consumers are not cleaned up unless Config.ConsumerInactiveThreshold is set. A test suite that opens a subscription per run leaves a durable per run behind.
