docs.title: kafka (franz-go)
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's redpanda image (make bench-native CLIENTS="franzgo kafkago sarama"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary franzgo github.com/twmb/franz-go github.com/twmb/franz-go@v1.22.2 acks=all on an idempotent producer (client default), ProduceSync kafkago github.com/segmentio/kafka-go github.com/segmentio/kafka-go@v0.4.51 RequiredAcks=RequireAll set explicitly, synchronous WriteMessages sarama github.com/IBM/sarama github.com/IBM/sarama@v1.61.1 Producer.RequiredAcks=WaitForAll with Idempotent=true, SyncProducer

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • franz-go defaults. franz-go produces with acks=all and an idempotent producer by default; idempotency is only turned off by DisableIdempotentWrite, and its default partitioner (UniformBytesPartitioner) hashes keys with murmur2, so partition assignment matches the Java client. Verified against: franz-go v1.21.6 pkg/kgo/config.go:663,672 and pkg/kgo/partitioner.go:254,278.
  • Sarama defaults. Sarama's NewConfig defaults are weaker than franz-go's: Producer.RequiredAcks is WaitForLocal (acks=1) and Producer.MaxMessageBytes is 1 MiB; an idempotent producer additionally requires RequiredAcks=WaitForAll, Net.MaxOpenRequests=1 and Retry.Max>=1. Verified against: Sarama v1.60.2 config.go:569-570,811-824.
  • Sarama partitioner compatibility. Sarama's default hash partitioner uses FNV-1a, not Kafka's murmur2, and NewReferenceHashPartitioner only fixes the sign handling; matching the Java client exactly needs NewCustomPartitioner with a murmur2 hash function. Verified against: Sarama v1.60.2 partitioner.go:170-195,250-264; franz-go pkg/kgo/partitioner.go:540-560.
  • kafka-go maintenance and acks. segmentio/kafka-go carries no maintenance-mode or deprecation notice for the project, but kafka.NewWriter and kafka.WriterConfig are deprecated in favour of the Writer struct — and a zero-valued Writer.RequiredAcks means RequireNone, because only the deprecated constructor rewrites 0 to RequireAll. Verified against: kafka-go v0.4.51 README.md and writer.go:499-511.
  • message size. The broker's default message.max.bytes is 1 MiB, so a 100-message batch of 64 KiB payloads must be split; Sarama splits a produce set when a partition's buffer would reach Producer.MaxMessageBytes, and franz-go splits at ProducerBatchMaxBytes. Verified against: Sarama v1.60.2 produce_set.go:316-336; Kafka broker default.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq Kafka topic topic, prefixed with Config.TopicPrefix verbatim subscription consumer group Message.Key record key (murmur2 partitioner, Kafka-compatible) Message.Headers record headers, binary and duplicate-preserving, in order Message.Body record value (nil is a tombstone and stays nil) DeliveryInfo.Partition / .Offset partition and offset, always populated ordering lane partition

The mapping is the identity plus the prefix, and a topic Kafka cannot carry is refused rather than transformed. Kafka's grammar — [a-zA-Z0-9._-], at most 249 bytes, never . or .. — is a subset of what the specification allows, so:

  • a name outside it is CodeInvalidArgument before any I/O;
  • a name carrying a regular-expression metacharacter is ErrUnsupported, on the assumption that somebody is asking for a pattern subscription (see Known gotchas);
  • Config.TopicPrefix is used verbatim, separator included. acme. gives acme.orders. The driver does not insert a separator of its own, because Kafka has none and inventing one would make the deployment's own tooling — kafka-acls, a Grafana query — point at a topic nobody configured.

A subscription is required: Kafka has no anonymous group, and a driver that invented one would give two processes the same durable position by accident.

Everything the specification names that Kafka has no native field for travels as a header under the reserved iqmq- prefix, and a caller's own header under that prefix is refused: iqmq-id, iqmq-content-type, iqmq-content-encoding, iqmq-correlation-id, iqmq-causation-id, iqmq-reply-to. Properties.CreatedAt uses the record's native timestamp, marked by an empty iqmq-created header — because Kafka stamps every record whether the publisher set a time or not, so a decoder that read the timestamp unconditionally would invent a creation time for every message that carried none. The creation time therefore round-trips at millisecond resolution, which is Kafka's.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
acks=all with an idempotent producer, which is franz-go's own default and is not turned off unless Config.DisableIdempotency says so. A record's promise fires when every in-sync replica has the record in its log.

mode boundary ConfirmNone the record is in the producer's buffer. Flush is what waits for it. ConfirmAccepted every in-sync replica has the record in its log. ConfirmDurable the same boundary. Kafka's strongest ordinary acknowledgement is already a durable one, so ConfirmDurable costs no extra round trip and is never refused.

All four optional publication surfaces are implemented:

  • BatchSink — every record is handed to the producer and the call waits for all of their promises. The result is index-aligned with the input, which is the whole contract: franz-go's promises fire in whatever order the partitions resolve, so a driver that collected results in completion order would report message seven's failure against message two.
  • AsyncSink — franz-go's produce is asynchronous, so the promise is the callback. No goroutine per message.
  • OwnedSink — the release happens in the promise, which is the earliest moment it can: nothing is copied.
  • FlushSink — for what ConfirmNone left in the buffer.

ConfirmNone copies the key, body and header values into a pooled buffer, because lets the caller reuse its buffers the instant Publish returns and franz-go is still reading them. The pool means the steady state allocates nothing; the other modes wait for the promise and copy nothing.

docs.title: The ambiguity, which is the part to read
docs.text:
Everything that goes wrong after the record has entered the producer's buffer is reported as the specification's ErrSettlementUnknown with OpError.Ambiguous set, and the native cause is still reachable through errors.Is/errors.As:

condition why it is unknown REQUEST_TIMED_OUT the broker ran out of time; the append may have happened NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS_AFTER_APPEND by its own name, the record was appended kgo.ErrRecordTimeout, kgo.ErrRecordRetries franz-go gave up after several attempts; one may have landed OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER, UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID the idempotent sequence is broken; the client no longer knows what the broker has a context cancellation or deadline after buffering the client has the record and the connection is open

Reporting any of them as a definite failure is how a caller retries and publishes twice while believing it published once. The other direction matters as much: MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE, TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, INVALID_REQUIRED_ACKS and INVALID_RECORD are definite refusals, and marking those ambiguous would make every caller reconcile a publication that certainly did not happen.

NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS is a definite refusal as an error and reaches a caller as an ambiguous one as an outcome, because franz-go retries it: by the time the record is failed there have been several attempts and the client cannot know whether one of them landed. The rule table says the first and the behaviour says the second; both are right.

Config.UnboundedDelivery is the knob behind this. franz-go refuses by default to let a delivery timeout or the caller's own cancellation fail an in-flight idempotent record, so a Publish against a cluster answering REQUEST_TIMED_OUT never returns — which the specification forbids. The driver therefore sets AllowIdempotentProduceCancellation and bounds the record with Config.DeliveryTimeout (2 minutes, Kafka's own delivery.timeout.ms default), reporting the outcome as unknown. Setting UnboundedDelivery restores franz-go's behaviour for a caller who would rather wait for ever than reconcile. It has no effect on a transactional producer, where franz-go refuses the option.

Config.Linger is zero by default, which is Kafka's own linger.ms default. A non-zero default looks attractive and is wrong for a synchronous publisher: Publish waits for the promise, so every publication pays the linger before its record is even sent.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
One *kgo.Client per source, with a consumer group, because a franz-go client consumes at most one group. Fetch is the poll:

That order is what keeps a partition's records in order — a fetch that went to the broker first would hand out a later offset before the earlier one it is already holding.

  • cooperative-sticky balancer, so a rebalance does not stop the world for partitions nobody is taking away.
  • auto-commit off. The commit is the acknowledgement; a client committing on a timer would acknowledge records the application has not finished.
  • BlockRebalanceOnPoll, so the rebalance callbacks never run while a fetch is filling the driver's tables. AllowRebalance is deferred, because a member that forgot it would hold the group's rebalance until the coordinator's timeout and then be removed from the group.
  • PollFetches, not PollRecords. franz-go buffers each fetch response separately and PollRecords serves one at a time; a Kafka fetch returns as soon as one byte is available, so the first response of a burst routinely holds a single record. A driver built on PollRecords fills one slot of a caller's batch and looks as though it cannot batch at all.

Start positions. All four work, and they are made durable at OpenSource: the resolved offset is committed for every partition the group has no position for, so a subscription that was opened and closed without consuming anything still remembers where it was asked to start. Every position is clamped into the log's own range — a sequence beyond the end resolves to the end, one below the start to the start, and a time no record is at or after to the end — because an out-of-range fetch offset is an error the caller cannot act on, and Kafka's own auto.offset.reset exists for the same reason. StartAtSequence(n) is the Kafka offset n, and a Kafka offset is zero-based.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
iqmq Kafka Ack the offset completes in driverkit/offset's tracker; the watermark is committed on the ticker, at a revoke and at Close AckBatch the same, and the commit is one round trip whatever the batch size — the acknowledgement is cumulative Nack Config.Nack's strategy; see below Reject NackActionDeadLetter: published to Config.NackConfig.DeadLetterTopic, then the offset completes Extend ErrUnsupported. Kafka grants no per-record lease

An Ack means this offset has completed, not this offset is committed. The tracker computes the offset after the highest record whose completion can no longer lose work, and a failed or unresolved offset below it blocks the commit — which is what makes the committed offset safe rather than merely recent. Acknowledging therefore costs no round trip, and the price is the at-least-once window (below).

Backend.Commit(ctx) commits every open source's watermark synchronously, for a caller that wants the window closed at a point of its own choosing.

docs.title: Nack strategies
docs.text:
Kafka has no per-record negative acknowledgement, so what a Nack does is a policy, and the specification requires all four to exist and none to be selected silently — because two of them reorder a partition and one halts a subscription.

Config.Nack what it does ordering throughput nack.BlockPartition (default) holds the record in process, pauses the partition and hands out nothing later of it until the record is redelivered after the delay; the offset stays uncommitted preserved, in the order records are handed out (below) the partition stops while a record is retried nack.RetryTopic publishes to <topic>.retry.<n> with the attempt in a header, then commits the original offset broken for the moved record unaffected nack.Stop stops the consumer; nothing after the refused record is consumed and the record is not acknowledged preserved zero until somebody restarts it nack.Custom the caller's own function, whose plan is validated its own its own

While block-partition holds a record, the topic's other partitions keep flowing. The block ends when the record is redelivered, not when it is acknowledged, so the records behind it can arrive in the same Receive as the redelivery. A record already handed out is not called back: one that was out before the nack, such as the rest of the same batch, can be handled before the redelivery, and one that arrived with the redelivery can be handled before the next attempt if the redelivery fails again. A custom plan that sets Pause gets the same block.

Auto resolves to BlockPartition by specification and not by measurement: the specification fixes the default independently of any number, so a campaign that finds retry topics faster records the margin a caller pays for ordering rather than moving the default.

When a record's attempts are exhausted (NackConfig.MaxAttempts) or its retry levels run out (NackConfig.Retries), the configured failure policy applies: the dead-letter topic when one is configured, and a halt when one is not. The halt surfaces from Receive as CodePoisonMessage.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
A partition is the ordering lane, and the core serialises a lane, so per-key ordering holds end to end.

  • FeatureOrderedByKey — native. The key is hashed with Kafka's own murmur2 partitioner ((murmur2(key) & 0x7fffffff) % partitions), so one key's records share a partition with the records the rest of the fleet produced. A Go producer that hashed differently would split one key's order across two partitions — silently, and only in a mixed-language deployment.
  • FeatureOrderedByPartition — native.
  • FeatureOrderedGlobally — conditional: only on a topic with a single partition. Kafka orders within a partition and never across partitions.

A keyless record is sticky: it goes to one partition until the producer starts a new batch. Round-robin across sixteen partitions would make sixteen batches of a sixteenth the size, which is sixteen produce requests instead of one.

Publish(..., mq.Partition(n)) routes explicitly. The request travels in the record's enrichment context rather than in Record.Partition, because franz-go writes the partition it picked into that field before buffering — so the field cannot carry what the caller asked for.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
Kafka has none, in either direction:

  • a scheduled publication (mq.Delay, mq.PublishOptions.DeliverAt) is ErrUnsupported before any I/O, in every metadata mode. A delay is not metadata an envelope could carry, it is behaviour the broker does not have.
  • a delayed redelivery (d.Nack(mq.NackDelay(d))) is emulated: the block-partition strategy holds the record in this process with its offset uncommitted and redelivers it after the delay. The claim is therefore EmulatedVolatile: if the process dies, the delay is lost and the record is redelivered immediately by whoever takes the partition. Under nack.Stop there is no delayed redelivery at all and the claim is withdrawn.

mq.TTL is ErrUnsupported: Kafka has topic retention, not a per-message time to live. mq.Priority is ErrUnsupported: a partition is a queue, not a heap. mq.DedupKey is ErrUnsupported: the idempotent producer de-duplicates a producer's own retries and nothing an application would call a key.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
EmulatedDurable, advertised unconditionally, with the condition in its note:

  • with Config.NackConfig.DeadLetterTopic set, Reject publishes the record there with its provenance and commits the original offset only after that publication is confirmed. The destination is a durable Kafka topic, so the route survives a restart.
  • with none set, Reject is refused with ErrUnsupported rather than destroying the message.

Both are the same behaviour described from two sides, which is why the claim is constant: the specification makes a capability table constant for the life of a client, and a table that answered differently depending on a field left the claim provable in neither direction.

The dead-letter topic is not created by the driver. The specification forbids a driver provisioning behind a caller's back, and a dead-letter destination created by a produce would have the cluster's default partition count and retention.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
Kafka's record headers are ordered, duplicate-preserving and binary, so the specification's three promises are all native and no envelope is needed. MetadataNativeStrict refuses nothing here except a caller's header under the reserved prefix, and MetadataAdaptive and MetadataLenientDrop therefore behave identically to it; only MetadataPortableEnvelope changes the bytes on the wire, and a caller asks for it when a non-iqmq consumer must not have to understand the header mapping.

Upgrade producers before consumers

A record enveloped by a version of this driver that predates the marker carries none, so a MetadataAdaptive consumer on the NEW code delivers it natively — the envelope's own bytes as the payload — rather than decoding it. The pairing that breaks is narrow: a MetadataPortableEnvelope producer read by a MetadataAdaptive consumer, for records already on the topic when the consumers are upgraded. A MetadataPortableEnvelope consumer is unaffected in either direction (the mode says every value is an envelope and it never consults the marker), and an upgraded producer is read correctly by an OLD consumer, because the old code sniffs the body and the extra header is invisible to it. So: producers first, then consumers, or drain the topic across the change.

limit value MaxMessageBytes the cluster's own message.max.bytes, read once at open with DescribeConfigs; unknown when the cluster will not say MaxBatchBytes the same number: the broker bounds a batch by it too everything else unknown. Kafka bounds headers and batch counts only by the message size, and it has no delay and no lease, so the specification forbids advertising a number for any of them

The size limit is enforced by the driver before any I/O, which is what makes the advertised number worth reading.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
• a lost connection is HealthDegraded with the reason;
  • a re-established one is HealthReady, and fires Config.Hooks.OnReconnect — the first connection of the client's life is not reported as a reconnection;
  • Close is terminal, so a late callback cannot report a closed client ready.

The counters a deployment samples are Backend.Reconnects, DegradedTransitions, Rebalances, LostPartitions, Commits and AmbiguousPublications. The last two are the ones to alert on.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
"Everything completed since the last commit."

A delivery is acknowledged when its offset has completed in the tracker and the resulting watermark has been committed. The two are not simultaneous, because a commit is a round trip:

  • on the ticker, every Config.CommitInterval (250 ms by default);
  • synchronously in OnPartitionsRevoked;
  • synchronously on Close;
  • whenever Backend.Commit is called.

A process that dies between a completion and the commit that would have carried it redelivers those records. That is a configuration choice — a commit per record would cost a round trip per record — and Backend.Commit narrows it to zero at a point of the caller's choosing.

A rebalance closes the window; a loss opens it. OnPartitionsRevoked stops dispatch for the revoked partitions, waits a bounded Config.RevokeWait for their in-flight deliveries to settle, commits the safe boundary synchronously, and then invalidates the generation — so a settlement arriving afterwards reports ErrLeaseLost instead of acknowledging a record another member is now processing. OnPartitionsLost does the same without the commit, because a lost partition is one the coordinator has already taken away and a commit for it would overwrite the position of the member that now owns it. Those records are redelivered, and Backend.LostPartitions is what says it happened.

The bounded wait is not optional. A callback that overran the group's rebalance timeout would take the member out of the group, and its partitions would be taken rather than handed over — which is the OnPartitionsLost path, where the boundary cannot be committed at all. Overrunning the wait is therefore strictly worse than giving up on it.

Attempt is 1 on a first delivery, rises on an in-place retry, and comes from the iqmq-attempts header on a retry topic. A record redelivered because its offset was never committed arrives looking exactly like a first delivery, which is honest: Kafka does not count attempts.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
kafka://user:password@broker1:9092,broker2:9092/prefix?sasl=scram-sha-512&tls=true

The typed Config is what a production program writes; the DSN parses into exactly it. Every credential is a dsn.Secret, so neither Config.String nor a slog record nor an error built from one can carry it. A parameter nothing read is a construction error naming it.

parameter field clientid ClientID sasl=plain\|scram-sha-256\|scram-sha-512 SASL tls, insecureskipverify TLS, InsecureSkipVerify disableidempotency DisableIdempotency unboundeddelivery UnboundedDelivery autocreatetopics AutoCreateTopics readcommitted ReadCommitted instanceid, transactionalid static membership, transactions linger, batchmaxbytes, maxbufferedrecords the producer fetchmaxwait, fetchmaxbytes the consumer sessiontimeout, rebalancetimeout, heartbeatinterval the group commitinterval, revokewait the commit and the revoke requesttimeout, deliverytimeout the two bounds partitions, replicationfactor what the typed Admin creates with tracker=<kind> the offset tracker nack=<kind>, deadlettertopic, maxattempts, retries, nackdelay

Everything a typed Config cannot carry — an OAUTHBEARER token source, GSSAPI, a custom dialler, a compression codec, franz-go's own metrics hooks — is reached through OpenWithClient, which takes a *kgo.Client the caller built and an explicit driverkit.Ownership. That client is the producer: every source opens a client of its own.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
test what it proves TestCriticalRebalanceWithDeliveriesInFlight one member holds an unsettled delivery from each of two partitions; a second joins, so cooperative-sticky must hand one over. The delivery from the partition that moved is refused with ErrLeaseLost; the one from the partition that stayed is acknowledged. TestCriticalRevokedDeliveryReportsLeaseLost a partition lost rather than revoked, forced by fencing the member's heartbeat with UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID. Ack and Nack both report ErrLeaseLost, and the record is redelivered because its boundary could not be committed. TestCriticalOutOfOrderCompletion twelve records settled from the top down; the committed offset does not move until the lowest completes, and then it passes all twelve. TestCriticalLeaderChange every partition re-elected mid-stream; nothing lost. TestCriticalRetryTopicPublicationFails the republication to <topic>.retry.1 is refused; the settlement fails, the original offset is not committed, and exactly one copy reaches the retry topic once the fault is removed. TestCriticalDeadLetterPublicationFails the same on the dead-letter route, which is the one the specification names.

And the ambiguous publication, which the conformance kit skips because the portable API cannot reach it: TestAmbiguousPublishAfterRetries, TestAmbiguousPublishOnBrokenIdempotence, TestAmbiguousPublishOnCancellationAfterBuffering, TestAmbiguousBatchIsIndexAligned, TestAmbiguousRepublicationNeverAcks — and TestDefinitePublishFailures, which proves the other direction, because a driver that marked everything ambiguous would pass the first six.

docs.title: kafka (kafka-go)
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

This driver uses github.com/segmentio/kafka-go; drivers/kafka uses franz-go. Both are available. Choose according to the capabilities and client APIs your application needs.

No generated conformance reports are tracked here. Run the suites for both profiles on the intended source revision and broker when comparing behaviour. The cross-driver tests in drivers/kafka/kafkago/crossdriver_test.go check reserved headers, topic validation, partition hashing and portable error codes.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The scheme is separate deliberately. The two drivers have different producer guarantees, different rebalance behaviour and different capability tables, so one connection string must not be able to mean either — a caller reading a DSN could not tell which client it got. A program that wants both registers both, which is possible precisely because the schemes differ.

The native baselines for both clients live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ (make bench-native CLIENTS="franzgo kafkago sarama") and are the denominator for any overhead claim; the shared pin table and the verified facts are on the franz-go page, which is the kafka driver's page for both profiles.

docs.title: Six defaults this driver sets that kafka-go does not
docs.text:
Each one is a correctness requirement rather than tuning, and each is listed because a caller building its own kafka.Writer for OpenWithWriter has to set them too.

Field kafka-go's default This driver Why Writer.RequiredAcks RequireNone (acks=0, fire and forget) RequireAll every confirmation mode would otherwise be a lie Writer.BatchSize 100 1 kafka-go has no immediate flush, so a batch above one makes a synchronous publish wait out the timer Writer.BatchTimeout 1 s 10 ms at kafka-go's default a synchronous publisher manages one message a second Transport.MetadataTTL 6 s 1 s kafka-go refreshes metadata on a timer and on nothing else, so this is the window in which a leader election fails publications Writer.WriteBackoffMin/Max 100 ms / 1 s 250 ms / 1 s so that MaxAttempts attempts SPAN the metadata TTL and the retry can find the new leader ConsumerGroupConfig.JoinGroupBackoff 5 s 1 s a transient coordinator error would otherwise be a five-second outage for the subscription ReaderConfig.MaxWait 10 s 500 ms a cancelled Fetch cannot return until the read in flight does

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq Kafka topic topic, prefixed with Config.TopicPrefix verbatim subscription consumer group Message.Key record key (murmur2, the same formula the franz-go driver and the Java client use) Message.Headers record headers, binary and duplicate-preserving, in order Message.Body record value — see the gotcha below: this client cannot READ BACK the difference between a null value and an empty one Message.ID iqmq-id header Properties.CreatedAt record timestamp, with an iqmq-created marker so that a record the publisher did not stamp does not acquire a creation time lane partition DeliveryInfo.Offset record offset (Kafka's sequence IS the offset, so Sequence stays unset)

The topic mapping is the identity plus the prefix. Kafka's grammar — [a-zA-Z0-9._-], at most 249 characters, never . or .. — is a subset of what the specification allows, so a name the broker would refuse is refused here rather than transformed: a Kafka topic name is something operators type into kafka-acls and Grafana queries, and a driver that silently renamed it would point the deployment's own tooling at a topic nobody configured.

A consumer group name is required. kafka-go refuses an empty ConsumerGroupConfig.ID, Kafka has no anonymous group, and a driver that invented one would give two processes the same durable position by accident.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
acks=all. A record's reply arrives when every in-sync replica has it in the log, so ConfirmAccepted and ConfirmDurable are the same boundary and neither costs an extra round trip or is refused. ConfirmNone returns as soon as the record is in the writer's batch, and the message's storage is copied first (lets a caller reuse its buffers the instant Publish returns).

There is no idempotent producer. kafka-go's writer sends no producer id and no sequence numbers, so the broker cannot de-duplicate the writer's own retries: a retried produce whose predecessor was written and whose response was lost leaves TWO copies in the log, and Config.MaxAttempts (3 by default) bounds how many. FeatureIdempotentPublish is therefore unsupported here and native on the franz-go driver, and Backend.DuplicablePublications() counts the publications that may have duplicated.

The driver owns two writers because Async is a field of a kafka.Writer and not of a call: one with Async false for the publications that wait, one with Async true for PublishAsync, PublishOwned and a sink configured ConfirmNone. They share one transport, so the second costs no connections.

Batching. kafka-go produces a batch when it is FULL or when its timer fires; there is no "the caller has stopped publishing, send what you have". So Config.BatchMaxRecords defaults to one — a synchronous publisher pays no linger — and a caller that publishes in batches raises it and pays Config.BatchTimeout on any partially filled batch. With a batch size of one a PublishBatch of a hundred costs a hundred produce requests; raise the batch size to batch.

Flush is the driver's own. kafka.Writer has no flush: its only flush is Close, which is terminal and would end every other sink on the backend. So the driver counts the publications it has admitted and not yet had a reply for, and Flush waits for that count to reach zero — which is exact rather than a timer.

docs.title: Ambiguity
docs.text:
Everything that fails after the record entered the writer is ambiguous, not failed: ErrSettlementUnknown (CodeSettlementUnknown) with IsAmbiguous true and the native cause underneath. The window is wider here than on franz-go and kafka-go says so itself: when WriteMessages returns early because the caller's context is done, "there are no guarantees made on whether messages were written to kafka, they might also still be written after this method has already returned". The caller's context ends the WAIT, not the WRITE.

Outcome Portable code Ambiguous NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS_AFTER_APPEND CodeSettlementUnknown yes — by its own name, an append that happened REQUEST_TIMED_OUT CodeSettlementUnknown yes — the append may have happened the caller's deadline or cancellation, after submission CodeSettlementUnknown yes — the write continues NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS CodeUnavailable, retryable no — refused before appending MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE, RECORD_LIST_TOO_LARGE CodeMessageTooLarge no a protocol code this driver's table does not name CodeUnavailable + retryable if Kafka calls it retriable, else CodeUnknown no

That last row is a defect this increment fixed twice, and both times the cause was the same: kafka.Error is an integer type with Error, Timeout AND Temporary methods, so it satisfies net.Error, and driverkit's transport classification reads a net.Error on a send path as ambiguous. First, every one of the 55 protocol codes the table did not name came out of a publish as "the broker may have written it" for answers the broker gave INSTEAD of writing anything. Then the same thing happened to the codes the table DOES name, when MapNet began OR-ing the transport classification's ambiguity into a matching rule's : the driver now routes a protocol code through Map, which honours the rule table alone, and only a cancellation, a deadline, an EOF or a genuine net.Error through MapNet. driverkit cannot know that this client's protocol error type is not a transport error; the driver can.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
kafka.ConsumerGroup for membership and kafka.Client.Fetch for reading — neither of kafka-go's two convenient consumer surfaces whole, and both choices are requirements rather than preferences.

Membership is ConsumerGroup and not Reader because a Reader owns group membership and never tells its caller that a rebalance happened, so a driver built on it cannot refuse a settlement for a partition it no longer owns — it would acknowledge a record another member is processing.

Reading is Client.Fetch and not a per-partition Reader because of The specification: a Kafka record value is a nullable byte string, and a Reader reads records through kafka-go's legacy Conn/Batch path, whose readNewBytes returns nil for any length at or below zero — so it collapses an empty body and an absent one into the same nil Body, and the same for an empty key. The modern protocol path keeps them apart. This driver failed the specification's publish/roundtrip-bodies until the read path moved. Fetching directly also puts the consume path on the same Transport as the producer and the administrative client, so the connection pool, the metadata cache and the credential are one thing rather than two — and it replaces the Reader's buffering with the source's own bounded record queue (Config.QueueCapacity), its read backoff with one fetch wait, and its opaque offset-out-of-range behaviour with an explicit re-resolve to the log's earliest offset.

A generation is the assignment. The driver starts one function per generation through Generation.Start — not one per partition — because kafka-go ends a generation as soon as any started function returns and waits for all of them before it rejoins, so one function is the only place the specification's sequence can run. That function spawns a reader goroutine per assigned partition, waits for the generation's context, and then performs the sequence below.

Fetch is one blocking receive from the fetch loops' shared bounded channel followed by a non-blocking drain, which is the specification's "one blocking wait then a non-blocking drain". The drain is what makes a batch a batch: one fetch returns a record batch and the loops hand its records to the channel one at a time, so a driver that returned after its first receive would fill one slot of a caller's batch whatever the backlog.

Pausing. kafka-go offers no per-partition pause on either consumer surface. A partition whose tracking window is full is held back by the source's own backlog and by the bounded channel the fetch loops write into, which is back-pressure by construction rather than a client-side pause.

docs.title: The rebalance sequence
docs.text:
1. Stop dispatch. Nothing more is handed out and the redeliveries the partitions were holding are dropped: they belong to whoever takes the partition next.
  2. Stop the readers and discard what they had read. Every queued record carries the generation it was read under, so a record left over from an ending generation is dropped rather than re-basing the next generation's tracker.
  3. Wait, bounded (Config.RevokeWait, 5 s), for the in-flight deliveries to settle. Bounded because kafka-go will not rejoin until this returns, and a member that overruns the group's rebalance timeout is removed from the group — which is strictly worse, because a removed member cannot commit.
  4. Commit the safe boundary synchronously, through the ENDING generation. The safe boundary is each tracker's watermark and never the highest offset seen.
  5. Invalidate the generations, so a settlement that arrives afterwards reports ErrLeaseLost.

Every rebalance is eager. kafka-go's assignors are range and round-robin and there is no cooperative one, so a generation revokes the WHOLE assignment and hands it back: a member that gains one partition reports ErrLeaseLost for every delivery it was holding, where the franz-go driver keeps the ones whose partitions did not move. That is the difference TestCriticalRebalanceWithDeliveriesInFlight asserts in both drivers, with opposite expected outcomes.

There is no revoked-versus-lost distinction. franz-go calls OnPartitionsRevoked for a cooperative handover and OnPartitionsLost when the coordinator has already taken the partitions away, and commits only in the first case. kafka-go ends a generation the same way whichever it was and does not report why, so this driver ALWAYS attempts the safe-boundary commit and reads the answer: a commit the coordinator refuses IS the lost case, and Backend.LostPartitions() counts it. Attempting it is safe because a refused commit changes nothing; not attempting it would turn every cooperative handover into redelivery.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
Portable Kafka Ack the offset completes in driverkit/offset's tracker; the watermark is committed by the ticker, by Backend.Commit or when the generation ends AckBatch one cumulative OffsetCommit whatever the batch's size Nack Config.Nack's strategy Reject the dead-letter route, or ErrUnsupported when none is configured Extend not implemented, and that is a decision: Kafka grants no per-record lease, so there is nothing an Extend could move

A settlement is resolved through a token (the partition's slot, stable for the life of the source) and a generation (the tracker's, which rises on every rebalance). A settlement whose generation has been superseded reports ErrLeaseLost — in both directions, positive and negative, because neither may reach a partition somebody else owns.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
A partition is the unit and a key maps to a partition by murmur2, which is what makes per-key order hold across a mixed-client fleet: a Go producer that hashed differently would split one key's order across two partitions, silently and only in a mixed-language deployment. The implementation is the specification's internal/hash.KafkaPartition, the same one the franz-go driver uses, and TestCrossDriverPartitioning plus FuzzCrossDriverPartitioning hold the two drivers to the same answer.

A keyless record rotates every Config.BatchMaxRecords records rather than sticking to one partition per batch. franz-go's partitioner is told when a batch ends (TopicPartitionerOnNewBatch) and re-rolls then; kafka-go's Balancer interface has no such notification, so the run length is the only thing stickiness can be keyed on here and the writer's own batch size is the honest choice. At the default batch size of one this is plain round-robin, which is kafka-go's own default.

Global order holds only for a single-partition topic, which is a topology the deployment chooses, so FeatureOrderedGlobally is conditional with the condition stated.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text: Kafka has none. A publication cannot be delayed or scheduled and PublishOptions.Delay/DeliverAt are refused with ErrUnsupported before anything is written. A redelivery delay is the consumer's business and reaches it through the nack strategy: block-partition holds the record in this process and redelivers it after the delay, so the delay is volatile — it is lost if the process dies, and the record is redelivered immediately by whoever takes the partition. FeatureDelayedRedelivery is advertised only when Config.Nack resolves to block-partition or custom.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Config.NackConfig.DeadLetterTopic, and the route is iqmq's own: the driver publishes the record there with the provenance headers (iqmq-origin-topic, iqmq-origin-subscription, iqmq-origin-partition, iqmq-origin-offset, iqmq-attempts, iqmq-failure, iqmq-first-delivered-at) and commits the original offset only after that publication is confirmed. A failed or ambiguous move never acknowledges the original, which is the rule and what TestCriticalDeadLetterPublicationFails and TestAmbiguousRepublishNeverAcksTheOriginal prove.

A Reject on a client with no destination configured is refused with ErrUnsupported rather than destroying the message.

Note what happens after an ambiguous move: the core refuses a second settlement of that delivery with ErrSettlementUnknown, because iqmq cannot tell whether the record reached the destination. What the driver owes is that the original offset was not committed, so the record returns to whoever reopens the subscription.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
Kafka's record headers are ordered, binary and duplicate-preserving, and its key and value are nullable byte strings, so three of the four metadata modes behave identically: strict refuses nothing, adaptive envelopes nothing and lenient drops nothing. Backend.DroppedMetadata() is always zero and exists to say so. Only MetadataPortableEnvelope changes the bytes on the wire.

A caller's header under the iqmq- prefix is refused, not renamed.

Upgrade producers before consumers

A record enveloped by a version of this driver that predates the marker carries none, so a MetadataAdaptive consumer on the NEW code delivers it natively — the envelope's own bytes as the payload — rather than decoding it. The pairing that breaks is narrow: a MetadataPortableEnvelope producer read by a MetadataAdaptive consumer, for records already on the topic when the consumers are upgraded. A MetadataPortableEnvelope consumer is unaffected in either direction (the mode says every value is an envelope and it never consults the marker), and an upgraded producer is read correctly by an OLD consumer, because the old code sniffs the body and the extra header is invisible to it. So: producers first, then consumers, or drain the topic across the change.

Limit Value MaxMessageBytes the cluster's own message.max.bytes, read at open through DescribeConfigs MaxBatchBytes the same figure: the broker bounds a batch by it too MaxHeaderCount, MaxHeaderBytes, MaxBatchMessages, MaxDelay, MaxLease unknown — Kafka bounds none of them on its own, and the specification forbids reading an unadvertised limit as zero

Reading message.max.bytes takes two round trips: kafka-go's DescribeConfigs takes a resource NAME, so a broker's configuration can only be asked for by broker id, and the id comes from the metadata. franz-go's kadm can be called with no id at all — and that is exactly what made the specification's driver advertise no limit, because the resource an absent id names is the cluster-level one, which apache/kafka:4.3.1 answers with the DYNAMICALLY set broker configuration and nothing else. message.max.bytes has source DEFAULT_CONFIG, so it is not in that answer; it is in a named broker's effective configuration. Both drivers now name the broker.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
kafka-go offers no connection hook of any kind: neither Writer nor Transport nor Dialer reports a dial, a dial failure or a disconnection, and driverkit.Reconnector cannot be used either because the client owns its own dial loop. So the events this driver reports are the ones it drives itself :

  • a generation established is Ready, and every generation after the first is counted by Backend.Reconnects() and fires Hooks.OnReconnect;
  • a generation ended is Degraded, because the subscription is not consuming until the next one is established;
  • a fetch error, a commit failure or an undecodable record is Degraded with the mapped reason.

Reconnects() is therefore not a count of sockets: a group rejoins for a rebalance as well as for a broken link. A caller that needs socket-level health polls Ping, which is a metadata round trip.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
A delivery is acknowledged when its offset has completed in the tracker AND the resulting watermark has been committed. The two are not simultaneous, so the window is "everything completed since the last commit":

Closed by When the commit ticker every Config.CommitInterval (250 ms) the end of a generation synchronously, through the ending generation, before kafka-go rejoins Close by closing the consumer group, which ends the generation and runs the sequence above while the coordinator connection is still open Backend.Commit(ctx) at a point of the caller's own choosing, one round trip per source

A source with no live generation commits nothing, and that is not a shortcoming to work around: kafka-go's OffsetCommit carries the generation and the member id, so an offset committed between generations would be refused by the coordinator — or, worse, accepted for a generation this member no longer holds.

The window opens wider than CommitInterval when a generation ends before the boundary can be committed, which Backend.LostPartitions() counts. A non-zero value means duplicates reached the application.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
kafkago://user:password@broker1:9092,broker2:9092/prefix?sasl=scram-sha-512&tls=true

The path is Config.TopicPrefix, used verbatim, separator included. Every parameter is in ParseDSN's doc comment; dsn.Params.Strict turns a parameter this driver does not have into a construction error naming it, rather than a setting nobody notices was ignored.

Three of the franz-go driver's parameters are absent rather than ignored, and asking for one is an error naming it: disableidempotency (there is no idempotent producer to disable), transactionalid (there is no transactional producer) and instanceid (kafka-go has no static group membership). linger is batchtimeout here and unboundeddelivery has no analogue.

Config.Validate is pure: no I/O, no dial. It refuses one thing kafka-go would otherwise PANIC on — FetchMinBytes above FetchMaxBytes, which kafka.NewReader panics on, from a goroutine this driver started, long after the configuration was accepted.

Every credential is a dsn.Secret, so neither String, nor LogValue, nor an error built from a configuration can carry it.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
1. Do not build your own reader with kafka.NewReader and expect an empty body back. A Reader collapses a null record value and a zero-length one into the same nil Body (readNewBytes returns nil for any length at or below zero), and the same for the key. This driver does not use one for exactly that reason ; a caller reaching past the driver through Backend.Client() should fetch, not read.
  2. A publication may leave two copies in the log. There is no producer id, so Config.MaxAttempts is the number of duplicates one publication may produce. Set it to 1 and reconcile the ambiguous outcome yourself if you cannot tolerate that.
  3. Every rebalance costs the whole assignment. Eager assignors only. A scale-up is a burst of ErrLeaseLost for every in-flight delivery, not just the moved partitions'.
  4. A batch size above one makes a synchronous publish wait. There is no immediate-flush path, so Publish pays BatchTimeout per message when BatchMaxRecords > 1. The default is 1 for that reason.
  5. A PublishBatch at the default batch size is one request per message. Raise BatchMaxRecords to the batch you publish.
  6. Purge does not destroy records. It commits the end offsets for the group, so the subscription resumes at the end and the backlog is skipped. The records stay in the log for whoever else is reading it.
  7. Reconnects() counts generations, not sockets.
  8. A commit's context does not bound it. Generation.CommitOffsets takes no context: the round trip is bounded by the coordinator connection's own timeout, which is Config.RequestTimeout.
  9. WatchPartitionChanges is off by default. A rebalance is eager here, so a poll that notices a new partition stops every member's consumption.
  10. Every delivery copies its key, value and headers once. A fetched record points into the fetch response's page buffers, which kafka-go documents as valid only until the record set is closed, and a delivery outlives the fetch it came from. MessageFrom is where that copy is made, and it is what preserves the nil-versus-empty distinction as well.
  11. A cancelled Publish does not cancel the produce, so the record's storage is still being read after Publish has returned. The driver reference-counts the pooled buffer for that reason ; a caller reusing its own key or body buffer immediately after an AMBIGUOUS Publish is writing storage kafka-go may still be serialising, so a caller that pools its own payloads should treat an ambiguous outcome as "still in flight" rather than "done".
  12. There is no pattern subscription at all, where franz-go has one this repository does not wire. CheckTopic refuses a name carrying a regular-expression metacharacter with ErrUnsupported rather than "invalid topic", so the difference is visible.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
Every one of these needs control over the broker that the portable API does not have, so they run against kfake — franz-go's in-process Kafka broker, which is a real protocol server on a real socket and a test-only dependency of this module. GOWORK=off go build ./... links neither kfake nor franz-go.

Test What it would catch TestCriticalRebalanceWithDeliveriesInFlight a settlement landing on a partition another member now owns. Its outcome is the OPPOSITE of the franz-go driver's, because the assignors are eager TestCriticalRevokedDeliveryReportsLeaseLost a fenced member acknowledging a record it no longer owns, and a record not coming back when its boundary could not be committed TestCriticalOutOfOrderCompletion a commit passing an offset that has not completed, which loses every record still in flight below it TestCriticalLeaderChange a leader election reported as a definite publication failure. This one FOUND the metadata-staleness defect above TestCriticalRetryTopicPublicationFails a record acknowledged on its source topic and written nowhere TestCriticalDeadLetterPublicationFails the same on the dead-letter route, which the specification names TestCloseRacesSettlement, TestCloseRacesPublication 2,000 crossings each under -race: a settlement or a pooled buffer landing after Close has drained TestCancelledPublishDoesNotRecycleALiveBuffer a pooled buffer recycled while the writer is still serialising the record it holds. This one FOUND the buffer-lifetime defect: -race reports a write in Encode against a read in kafka-go's RecordSet.writeToVersion2 TestCrossDriverNullAndEmptyBodiesSurvive the nil-versus-empty body, over all four crossings between the two Kafka drivers. This one FOUND the read-surface defect: a kafka.Reader collapses them and Client.Fetch does not TestCrossDriver*, FuzzCrossDriver* the two Kafka drivers drifting apart on the reserved headers, the topic grammar, the partition formula or the portable error codes

docs.title: memory
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

the driver documentation delegates this page, and the specification describes the engine. What follows is the driver over that engine: what a caller of the public API sees, and where this driver's answer differs from a network broker's.

A memory:// DSN names a broker inside one process, and two processes that open the same DSN do not meet. The scheme looks like every other driver's, so it is worth saying plainly: there is no socket, no port and no address, and the string after memory:// selects a broker within this program rather than a place to reach. Two goroutines share one; two processes -- a producer and a consumer started separately, or a test binary and the program under test -- each get their own and neither sees the other's messages.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
There is no client library and no broker. The driver is a github.com/iqhive/iqmq.Backend over internal/engine, in the same module as the root package, so it is always available and always the same version as the core. Client.Info() reports Name: "memory", a ClientName naming the engine it wraps, and an empty BrokerVersion — the specification makes an empty string "the driver did not say" rather than a claim, and there is no broker here to report one.

Nothing is persistent. The specification forbids this driver from advertising durable storage and it does not: FeatureDurableStorage and FeatureDurableConfirm are unsupported, and the two guarantees that are real but die with the process — a subscription outliving its consumers, and deduplication inside a window — are advertised as EmulatedVolatile, the one level the specification forbids from satisfying a durability requirement.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
A topic is a topic and a subscription is a subscription; nothing is mapped onto anything.

iqmq memory topic engine.Topic, one per name, created through the admin surface or by AutoCreate subscription engine.Subscription, one independent consumer group per name consumer engine.Consumer, attached to a subscription; consumers of one subscription compete partition one lane per subscription-partition, TopologyConfig.Partitions of them

AutoCreate is false by default, which is what every network driver does and what the specification requires of Open: a publisher or a consumer naming an unknown topic fails with ErrTopicNotFound. NewForTest turns it on, and Admin.EnsureTopic is the explicit route.

Topic names are held to the portable grammar mq.ValidateTopic defines. The driver adds no restriction of its own.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
Publish validates, copies the caller's storage once, hashes the key to a lane, reserves capacity in every target subscription in a stable order and enqueues. It returns when the record is in every lane the fan-out policy made it wait for.

That is the whole of the confirmation this driver can offer, and it is what each mode means here:

Mode Boundary ConfirmNone the same as ConfirmAccepted: there is no local admission step separate from the lane ConfirmAccepted (default) the record is in every target lane and a consumer can claim it ConfirmDurable fails at construction with ErrUnsupported

ConfirmDurable fails when the publisher is opened, not when it publishes: there is no durable boundary to define, and the specification requires the refusal to be at construction.

PublishBatch reaches the engine's own batch call. The result is index-aligned with the caller's slice: the engine's batch stops at the first element it refuses and names its index, and the driver records that element's outcome and offers the rest, so a refusal is never reported against the messages behind it.

Three ownership modes ship:

Surface Contract Sink.Publish (default) safe copy: the message is cloned on admission and the caller may reuse its Key, Body and header storage the instant Publish returns OwnedSink.PublishOwned the storage transfers to the engine and Release runs exactly once — on settlement, on rejection, on a refused option and on close AsyncSink.PublishAsync the storage is borrowed: it stays the caller's and must stay valid and unmutated until the completion callback runs, which is when the last subscription that was admitted settles the record

FlushSink.Flush is implemented and has nothing to do: the engine admits synchronously, so a flush is a barrier that has already passed. It is implemented rather than omitted so that the boundary is stated here instead of inferred from a missing method.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
Source.Fetch fills the caller's slice from the consumer's assigned lanes, rotating the start index so that no lane starves. It blocks only when nothing is available, and it allocates nothing per fetch and nothing per message: the claims come out of a buffer allocated once when the source opens, and the engine handle a settlement needs later is a pointer in DriverDelivery.Ref's interface word rather than a boxed value.

Source.Close unblocks a parked Fetch (the obligation), which is why the core never has to merge the caller's context with a cancellation of its own — a merge costs two or three allocations on the one path that may not have them.

DeliveryInfo is filled as follows. The Has flags matter: the specification forbids "the broker did not say" from being the same answer as zero.

Field Memory Topic the resolved topic; on a wildcard topic the publication's subject rather than the pattern Source always empty: there is no broker-side origin behind a memory topic Subscription the subscription the source was opened on ReceivedAt the broker clock at the fetch LeaseExpires ReceivedAt plus the lease; the zero time when the topology's AckDeadline is negative, which is "leases never expire" Attempt the delivery count, 1 on a first delivery Redelivered Attempt > 1 Partition / HasPartition the lane; always set Sequence / HasSequence the record's publication sequence within its topic; always set Offset / HasOffset never set: the engine has no per-partition offset distinct from the sequence

Delivery.Native() is nil. The engine's envelope is opaque by contract and a caller could not name its type, so surfacing it would be an escape hatch that escapes to nothing. Client.Native() returns the *memory.Broker, which is the escape hatch that is worth having.

A received Body, Key and header value alias the engine's own storage and are valid until the delivery is settled, which is the safe receive mode. Nothing is recycled unless ConsumerConfig.BufferReuse is set. With ZeroOnRelease the engine overwrites the payload as it releases the record, so a delivery read after it was settled sees zeros rather than its data.

The source implements DeadlineExtender and deliberately not BatchSettler: the engine settles one delivery at a time under one lane mutex, so a batch method would be the loop the core already writes, and a driver that offers one makes the core skip its own adapter for no saving.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
Verb Native action Ack terminal: the record leaves the subscription and its payload is released once every subscription has settled it Nack (requeue) the record returns to its lane, immediately or through the delayed structure when a delay is named; the attempt count survives and the next delivery increments it Nack(NackDrop()) the engine's terminal settlement — the same native action an acknowledgement takes Reject / Nack(NackDeadLetter()) publish to the topology's DeadLetterTopic, then acknowledge Extend the lease deadline moves to at least by from now, through the broker's shared lease scheduler

Two of those need a sentence each.

Drop is an acknowledgement to the engine. The engine has one terminal settlement, so a dropped record is counted in Snapshot.Acked rather than in Snapshot.Dropped, and Snapshot.Dropped keeps its own meaning: a record discarded without a settlement. Most brokers are the same — a delete or an offset commit serves both verbs — and the distinction iqmq keeps is the consumer's own: ConsumerHandle.Stats() counts a drop as a negative settlement.

A settlement carries the generation the delivery was claimed under, so a stale one is answered rather than applied to the redelivery that took its place: a lease that expired or was rebalanced away reports ErrLeaseLost, and a consumer that closed reports ErrClosed.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
This is the sentence delegates to each driver page.

The memory driver delivers one ordered lane per subscription-partition, in publication sequence. With the default Partitions: 1 that is one ordered lane per subscription, which is the guarantee without the caller asking for it. A topic with more than one partition orders each lane and not the topic; a key always hashes to the same lane, so one key's records are ordered with respect to each other.

What may overtake is a redelivery. Under the default OrderingRelaxed a record that comes back from a negative acknowledgement, a lease expiry or a consumer close is placed by the retry-lane kind (pushfront by default), which serves it before the records still waiting — the redelivery-first order real brokers use. OrderingStrict stops it: the redelivery blocks its lane, and nothing published behind it is delivered until it has been settled or routed to a dead-letter topic.

Three things carry a caveat of their own, and all three are control operations rather than delivery:

Reorder (the fault) never fires on a lane whose topic asked for strict ordering, nor on an engine whose kinds order what they hold.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
Native, both forms. Delay and DeliverAt hold a publication back; a negative acknowledgement with NackDelay holds a redelivery back; TTL discards a record that has still not been delivered that long after it became due.

All three are driven by one scheduler per broker, which sleeps until the next non-empty slot: there is no timer and no goroutine per message. The granularity is the selected EngineConfig.Timer kind's: Broker.SchedulerResolution() reports it, the wheels quantise to a millisecond and the heaps fire at the exact due time. A Config.SchedulerResolution finer than the selected kind provides is refused at construction rather than silently approximated.

Time moves by itself on the wall clock and only on demand under a TestClock: Broker.Advance moves the clock and runs the sweeps the move implies, which is why TestClock has no Advance of its own. Inside a testing/synctest bubble the wall clock follows the bubble clock, so a test needs neither.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
There is no implicit dead-letter topic: TopologyConfig.DeadLetterTopic names one and it must already exist, because the engine never creates a topic behind the operator's back. A record whose attempts run out with no usable destination is discarded and counted in Snapshot.Dropped.

Two routes reach it, and they are accounted differently:

  • The attempt budget. A failed delivery past MaxAttempts is published to the dead-letter topic by the engine and counted in Snapshot.DeadLettered. A publication that fails returns the record to its lane and is counted in Snapshot.DeadLetterFailures — it never acknowledges.
  • An explicit Reject. The driver publishes and then acknowledges, so the record is counted in Snapshot.Acked on the source subscription. See "Ack / nack / extend mapping".

A rebalance never dead-letters: a revoked delivery is not a failed one, so it does not consume an attempt.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
Every piece of metadata is native. The engine stores the *mq.Message itself, so binary header values, duplicate keys, insertion order, the identifier and every typed property travel unchanged, and nothing is ever unsupported metadata. Three of the four modes therefore come out identical here: MetadataNativeStrict has nothing to reject, MetadataAdaptive never needs the envelope, and MetadataLenientDrop never drops anything.

MetadataPortableEnvelope is honoured as written, because the whole point is that the envelope is never applied by accident and never skipped when it was asked for. A sink in that mode wraps the message in the iqmq/wire envelope and publishes the envelope as the whole body; a source in the same mode decodes it. A source in native mode on the same topic sees the envelope bytes, exactly as a consumer written against a broker's own client would, which is the body-interoperability change the specification requires the mode to be explicit about. A source in envelope mode reading a body that is not an envelope reports CodeCorruptMessage rather than handing over nonsense.

Limits: only what the broker really knows is advertised, because the specification forbids an unadvertised limit from being read as a limit of zero.

Limit Memory MaxMessageBytes the default topology's MaxMessageSize, when it has one MaxLease not advertised. This broker has no longest lease: Extend sets the deadline to now + d for any d, and the lane's scheduler is a list move rather than a timer per delivery. The topology's AckDeadline is the lease a delivery STARTS with, which the specification's Limits has no field for MaxBatchMessages, MaxBatchBytes, MaxHeaderCount, MaxHeaderBytes, MaxDelay not advertised: there is no limit

Capabilities is constant per backend and cannot describe one topic, so a topic created with a different MaxMessageSize through the admin surface is enforced by the engine rather than by the core's pre-flight check.

Byte accounting counts the key and the body, not the header storage: counting headers means walking the header set on every publication, and mq.Headers exposes no allocation-free size accessor. Snapshot.Bytes and the capacity bounds are therefore key-plus-body figures.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
There is nothing to reconnect to, so there is no reconnect loop, no backoff and no Hooks.OnReconnect event from this driver. Client.Health() is Ready until the broker closes and then Closed; it is never Degraded.

Faults.Reconnect() simulates what a reconnect does to a subscription: the assignment generation increments and every lease outstanding under the old one is revoked, so a settlement holding one reports ErrLeaseLost. The deliveries it revokes are not failures and do not consume an attempt.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
At-least-once is the default and the only delivery model this driver ships. The window in which a message can be delivered twice is the ordinary one: a delivery that was processed and whose acknowledgement did not reach the engine — because the lease expired first, because a rebalance revoked it, or because the consumer closed — is redelivered. Faults.DuplicateDelivery reproduces it deterministically (and is a documented no-op under a shared partition log, which hands each slot to each cursor exactly once by construction; Faults.Duplicates() reports which happened).

FeatureExactlyOnceDelivery is not advertised, and it used to be. The root API defines it as "de-duplicated at-least-once delivery" — a consumer never sees one publication twice — and the paragraph above says plainly that this broker redelivers a delivery whose lease expired, so a consumer can. What the claim described was publication de-duplication: a publication carrying a dedup key is discarded if the topic has seen that key inside DedupWindow, in this process, and a restart forgets the window. That is FeatureDeduplication, which is still advertised as Conditional on TopologyConfig.DedupWindow.

ConfirmAccepted means the record is in every target lane. A process that dies after a publication returned loses the record: there is no durable boundary, and ConfirmDurable says so by failing.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
memory.Config is the struct. The zero value is usable and is the bounded, ordered configuration: one partition per subscription, 65,536 records per lane, a 30-second lease, the blocking overflow policy, the real clock, and the configured variant-family defaults.

Two fields are deliberately asymmetric, so that "I did not set it" and "I want no limit" cannot be the same value:

Field Zero Negative TopologyConfig.CapacityMessages 65,536 records per lane unbounded, which selects the chunked ready queue TopologyConfig.Partitions 1 lane, and therefore strict order GOMAXPROCS lanes TopologyConfig.AckDeadline 30 seconds leases never expire

TopologyConfig.MaxInFlight and MaxDelayed are fields the engine does not have: it bounds the ready, in-flight and delayed records of a lane together through CapacityMessages. A non-zero value is refused at construction rather than ignored.

EngineConfig pins one kind of every variant family: the ready queue, the fan-out architecture, the wait strategy, the scheduler, the key hash, the pools, the topic registry, the counters and the retry placement. The zero value is each family's Auto; Safe forces the mutex-backed reference kind of every family at once, which is the configuration that contains no lock-free data structure at all. The single-producer and single-consumer ready queues are refused: a lane is fed by any number of publishers and drained by any number of consumers.

DSN, under memory:// and the alias mem://. A memory DSN names no host, user, path or fragment — there is nothing to connect to — and an unknown parameter is an error rather than a warning.

memory://?partitions=8&capacity=100000&overflow=block&wildcards=true&autocreate=true
Parameter Values autocreate true | false partitions a positive integer, or auto for GOMAXPROCS capacity a positive integer, or unbounded capacitybytes, maxmessagesize, maxtotalmessages, maxtotalbytes positive integers kind queue | topic | stream overflow block | reject | dropnew | dropold fanout atomic | independent | besteffort | dropslow ordering relaxed | strict ackdeadline a Go duration, or never maxattempts a positive integer deadletter a topic name dedupwindow, retentionage Go durations retentionmessages, retentionbytes positive integers priority, wildcards, zeroonrelease true | false engine safe

memory.Register(reg) registers both schemes with a DSN registry. A driver exposes Register and never reaches for a global registry of its own.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
• Admin.DeleteTopic answers ErrUnsupported. The engine's registry has no removal: a topic exists for the life of the broker. A caller that wants a fresh one builds a fresh broker, which in process costs nothing. Closing every subscription and leaving the topic in the registry would be neither a delete nor a no-op, so it is not done.
  • Admin.Purge is an emulation and does not reach everything. A temporary consumer claims and settles every record the subscription has ready. It does not discard a record another consumer holds in flight — that record is not the subscription's to throw away while a lease is outstanding — nor one still waiting for its due time. What it discards is counted in Snapshot.Acked, for the same reason a drop is.
  • FeatureWildcardSubscribe is unsupported even though the engine has subject routing. SourceConfig carries no filter, so a wildcard subscription cannot be opened through the SPI; a topic may still be created with wildcards, and a delivery from one reports the resolved subject as its topic.
  • A delivery is borrowed until it is settled. Reading d.Body after d.Ack() is reading storage the engine may have released — and, with ZeroOnRelease, storage it has overwritten. d.Message.Clone() is the independent copy.
  • Publishing to a topic with no subscription is not an error. The record is discarded and released, which is an admission of nothing to nobody; Broker.Totals() reports it as discarded.
  • The default overflow policy blocks. A publisher that finds a full lane parks until room appears or its context ends. That is the default and it is the right one for a test double, but it means a publication into a lane nobody is draining hangs rather than failing. OverflowReject is the fail-fast policy.
  • Broker.Advance needs a clock the broker owns. It answers ErrUnsupported on a broker built with no Config.Clock or with a clock of the caller's own, because a fault that silently did nothing would make a test that relies on it pass for the wrong reason. NewTestClock is the clock it needs and NewForTest installs one.
  • Faults is broker-wide. A fault armed for "the next n" is armed for the next n of anything, on any topic.
