docs.title: nats
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Module: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/nats · Profile: core

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's nats image (make bench-native CLIENTS="nats"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary nats github.com/nats-io/nats.go github.com/nats-io/nats.go@v1.54.0 core NATS at-most-once: server round-trip via Flush, no store

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • delivery guarantee. Core NATS is at-most-once with no store and no per-message acknowledgement: a publish is only known to have reached the server after a round trip (Conn.Flush), and a subscription that is not connected when a message is published never sees it. Verified against: nats.go v1.53.1 nats.go Conn.Flush; NATS core documentation.
  • max payload. The server advertises its max_payload in the INFO it sends on connect and the client rejects larger publishes locally with ErrMaxPayload; the default is 1 MiB, so payload limits are a server setting, not a client constant. Verified against: nats.go v1.53.1 nats.go (Conn.MaxPayload, ErrMaxPayload); nats-server default.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq NATS Core Notes Topic subject / becomes .; Config.SubjectPrefix is prepended as a token ConsumerConfig.Subscription queue group two consumers of one subscription compete; two subscriptions each receive everything ConsumerConfig.Topic (pattern) subject wildcard * matches one token, a trailing > matches the rest Message.Key iqmq-key header base64, because a NATS header value is a text line Properties.ReplyTo Msg.Reply the native reply subject, which is what makes request/reply work

The subject alphabet this driver will build or accept is letters, digits, _, - and $, with . as the separator. That is the image of the portable topic grammar under the separator swap, plus the $ that NATS system subjects use. Anything else — a space, a control byte, a quote, a byte above ASCII — is refused before any I/O, because a malformed subject does not produce a rejected publication on this protocol: it produces a malformed frame on a connection every other publisher and subscriber in the process is sharing.

The mapping is not injective. orders/created and orders.created are one subject, and no reverse can tell which one was published, so DeliveryInfo.Topic reports the subject the message really arrived on with the prefix stripped and the separator left as .. A deployment that needs the two to stay distinct uses one spelling.

A publication's topic may never be a pattern: orders.* and orders.> are refused when the publisher is constructed. A consumer's topic may be one, and that is what FeatureWildcardSubscribe means here — ConsumerConfig.Topic documents that a driver supporting it accepts its pattern syntax there.

There is no topology to create and none to delete. A subject exists because somebody published to it, which is why this driver implements no AdminBackend and Client.Admin answers ErrUnsupported, and why topology/no-hidden-creation is reported as inapplicable rather than passed.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
Publish maps the message, writes it into the connection's write buffer with PublishMsg, and then applies the confirmation boundary:

Mode What it waits for ConfirmNone the publication is in the client's write buffer; nothing has left the process ConfirmDefault / ConfirmAccepted FlushWithContext — a PING/PONG round trip, so the server has parsed every byte written before it ConfirmDurable refused when the publisher is constructed

That is the whole of the confirmation this profile can offer: the server has seen the message and has already forgotten it. ConfirmDurable fails at construction rather than at the first message, which is the rule, because a publisher that discovered it later would already have told the application it was safe to forget the data.

The default therefore costs one round trip per publication. A caller who wants throughput asks for ConfirmNone, or publishes a batch: PublishBatch writes every message and confirms all of them with a single flush, so a batch of a hundred costs one round trip instead of a hundred. That batch is the driver's own and is not atomic — NATS has no batch verb — which is why FeatureBatchPublish is advertised as EmulatedVolatile and not Native. Its result is index-aligned with the batch.

FlushWithContext requires a deadline. When the caller's context has none, Config.FlushTimeout (10s by default) supplies one; when the caller has a deadline, the caller's is used unchanged.

Per-call publication controls this broker cannot honour are refused before any I/O with ErrUnsupported: Delay, DeliverAt, TTL, Priority, DedupKey and Partition. Ignoring them is the dangerous alternative — a caller who asked for a delay and got none has no way to find out, and the message is already delivered.

Message is not retained past Publish: header names and values are copied into the nats.Header and the payload is serialised into the write buffer by the call, so a caller may reuse its buffers the instant it returns.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
OpenSource opens one QueueSubscribe on the mapped subject with the subscription name as the queue group, and wires the callback into a driverkit.PushAdapter whose capacity is the consumer's prefetch.

NATS delivers by calling the driver and the SPI asks the driver to be called, so the bounded ring between them is the whole adapter. Fetch is one blocking wait and then a non-blocking drain of everything the ring holds, which is what makes FeatureBatchReceive true; it allocates nothing per fetch.

Blocking in the callback is the backpressure, and on this broker it has a consequence worth stating plainly: while the callback is parked, nats.go keeps delivering into the subscription's pending queue, and once that queue passes SetPendingLimits the client drops what it cannot deliver and reports a slow consumer. On an at-most-once broker that is the contract — there is nowhere to push back to — and it is why the health transition below matters more here than it would on a broker with flow control.

Config.PendingMessages (64Ki) and Config.PendingBytes (64Mi) are the limits every subscription is opened with.

Only StartLatest exists. The broker retains nothing, so StartEarliest, StartAt and StartAtSequence are refused with ErrUnsupported when the consumer is constructed rather than silently answered with StartLatest.

Close unsubscribes, wakes a parked Fetch with ErrClosed and drops whatever the ring still held. There is nothing to requeue: a message this source holds is one the server has already forgotten, so the specification's "requeue or abandon" can only be abandon.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
There is none. Source.Settler() returns nil, which is how AckNone model is declared: the core answers every Ack, Nack, Reject and Extend with ErrNotSettleable and never calls the driver.

iqmq NATS Core Delivery.Ack ErrNotSettleable Delivery.Nack ErrNotSettleable Delivery.Reject ErrNotSettleable Delivery.Extend ErrNotSettleable DeliveryInfo.Attempt 0 — the specification's "the broker does not count attempts" DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires the zero time — the specification's "the broker grants no lease"

A delivery is complete the moment the handler has it. A settler whose Ack silently succeeded would be the worse lie of the two available: the caller would believe a message was safely processed by a broker that had already forgotten it, and nothing anywhere could tell the difference.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
NATS Core delivers one subject's messages to one subscriber in the order one publisher connection wrote them. That is the entire guarantee, and the three ordering features are three names for it :

Feature Level Condition OrderedGlobally conditional one publisher connection to one subject, delivered to a single subscriber OrderedByKey conditional there is no key; a key orders only in so far as its messages share a subject OrderedByPartition conditional there are no partitions; a subject is the only partition there is

Two things break it and both are ordinary: a queue group with more than one member interleaves across its members, and two publisher connections are not ordered against each other. A deployment that needs order keeps one publisher connection per subject and one member per queue group — which is the same trade every broker makes, stated here rather than implied.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
None. Delay, DeliverAt and TTL are refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O, and FeatureScheduledPublish, FeatureMessageTTL and FeatureDelayedRedelivery are all advertised as unsupported.

Delayed redelivery would need a redelivery, and there is none. A caller who needs any of the three uses drivers/jetstream.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
None. There is no settlement, so there is no Reject to route and no attempt count to exhaust; FeatureDeadLetter is unsupported.

The core's own dead-letter route (WithDeadLetter on a runner) works, and it needs one thing said about it. It is a publish to another topic followed by a settlement, and the settlement is a no-op here — so a dead-lettered message is published to the destination and the original is neither redelivered nor acknowledged, because it was never redeliverable in the first place.

What is not obvious is how the route is reached. Nack answers mq.ErrNotSettleable and this broker keeps no attempt counter, so under the default OrderingRelaxed the runner requeues by nack, the nack fails, and the message is never declared exhausted: nothing is ever dead-lettered. Ask for mq.WithOrderingByKey(mq.OrderingStrict), which holds the retry in process and makes the attempt count exact whatever the broker does.

Until the route did not work here at all: this driver's Representable refused every header under mq.ReservedHeaderPrefix, which is all five of the provenance headers the route stamps, and Encode dropped them.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
NATS headers are an HTTP-like block: Name: value per CRLF-terminated line. That decides what can be carried, and the rules are about framing rather than taste.

Rule Why a name may not be empty, carry a colon, a space, a control byte or a byte above ASCII the reader truncates at the colon and a CR or LF forges a second header a value must be valid UTF-8 the block is a text line and the reader is net/textproto's a value may carry no control byte CR and LF forge a header; the rest do not survive a value may not begin with a space or a tab the reader eats those after the colon, so the value comes back shorter

A header that breaks one of them is refused with ErrUnsupported under MetadataNativeStrict, dropped under MetadataLenientDrop (and counted by Backend.DroppedMetadata), and carried in the portable envelope under MetadataAdaptive and MetadataPortableEnvelope. FeatureBinaryHeaders is therefore unsupported and FeatureNativeHeaders and FeatureDuplicateHeaders are native.

Header order is not preserved. nats.Header is a Go map, so the publisher's ordering is gone by the time the client hands the message over; this driver decodes the names sorted, which is deterministic where a bare map iteration would give the same message a different order on every delivery. Duplicate values of one name keep their order.

Everything the specification names that has no native field travels under the reserved iqmq- prefix, which Headers.Validate keeps a caller out of and this driver refuses independently :

iqmq-key, iqmq-id, iqmq-content-type, iqmq-content-encoding, iqmq-correlation-id, iqmq-causation-id, iqmq-created-at, iqmq-empty-body, and iqmq-env.

Upgrade producers before consumers

A message enveloped by a version of this driver that predates the marker carries none, so a MetadataAdaptive consumer on the NEW code delivers it natively — the envelope's own bytes as the payload — rather than decoding it. The pairing that breaks is narrow: a producer that enveloped (either MetadataPortableEnvelope, or MetadataAdaptive with metadata NATS cannot carry) read by a MetadataAdaptive consumer, for messages published before the producers are upgraded. A MetadataPortableEnvelope consumer is unaffected in either direction, and an upgraded producer is read correctly by an OLD consumer, because the old code sniffs the body and the extra header is invisible to it. So: producers first, then consumers.

The last is the driver's own: nats.go builds every payload with make([]byte, n), so a zero-length payload always arrives as an empty non-nil slice and the nil-versus-empty distinction would be lost in one direction. Marking the rarer half keeps both, and means a message from a non-iqmq publisher with no payload decodes as a nil body.

Limits. The only limit this driver knows is the server's own max_payload, taken from the INFO on connect, and it is advertised as Limits.MaxMessageBytes; a publication past it is refused with ErrMessageTooLarge before any I/O. Every other limit is left unadvertised — The specification forbids reading an unadvertised limit as zero, so "we do not know" is a Limit whose Known is false. The driver's own bounds are a 1 KiB subject, 64 subject tokens, a 256-byte header name and an 8 KiB header value.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The client library owns the dial loop, and this driver owns what it means:

  • a lost link makes health Degraded with the reason (DisconnectErrHandler);
  • a re-established link makes it Ready again and fires Hooks.OnReconnect with the attempt number (ReconnectHandler);
  • a connection the server closed for good makes it Closed, which is terminal in driverkit.Health, so a late callback cannot report Ready afterwards;
  • a slow consumer makes it Degraded with the subscription's subject and queue group in the error (ErrorHandler), and increments Backend.SlowConsumers.

That last one is the only place a dropped message surfaces at all: a slow consumer is invisible to the consuming path, which simply stops seeing messages. the specification's "background failures surface via hooks and health, not only logs" is not a formality on this driver.

Config.ReconnectWait, Config.MaxReconnects, Config.PingInterval and Config.MaxPingsOut configure the loop. Nothing is buffered across a reconnection beyond the client's own reconnect buffer, whose overflow is reported as CodeBackpressure.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
There is none, because there is no at-least-once. NATS Core is at-most-once: a message is routed to whatever is subscribed at the instant it arrives and is then gone.

The failure mode of this driver is loss, not duplication:

  • a subscriber that is not connected when a message is published never sees it;
  • a subscriber that falls behind its pending limits has messages dropped by its own client;
  • a handler that panics loses the message it was holding;
  • a publication under ConfirmNone that was in the write buffer when the link went away was never sent.

A publication under ConfirmAccepted whose flush fails is ambiguous — the bytes had already left, so the server may have taken them — and is reported that way (OpError.Ambiguous), which is the rule and is the one place this driver can duplicate: a retry of an ambiguous publication may deliver twice.

Anything that needs at-least-once uses drivers/jetstream.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
client, err := nats.Open(ctx, nats.Config{
        Addrs:           []string{"nats://broker-1:4222", "nats://broker-2:4222"},
        Name:            "orders-service",
        SubjectPrefix:   "acme",
        PendingMessages: 64 << 10,
        FlushTimeout:    10 * time.Second,
})

or from a DSN, once the driver is registered with a dsn.Registry:

nats://user:password@host-1:4222,host-2:4222/acme?creds=/etc/nats.creds&tls=true&pendingmessages=8192
Parameter Meaning path SubjectPrefix name connection name the server reports creds NATS credentials file token, userinfo token or user/password authentication tls, insecureskipverify TLS with the platform roots; skipping verification needs tls=true pendingmessages, pendingbytes per-subscription SetPendingLimits connecttimeout, flushtimeout, reconnectwait, maxreconnects the dial and confirmation bounds pinginterval, maxpingsout, draintimeout the connection's own liveness and drain noecho do not deliver a connection its own publications

An unknown parameter is a construction error naming it, and every credential is a dsn.Secret: Config.String(), Config.LogValue() and Config.DSN() all render the redaction. Config.Validate() is pure — it performs no I/O and never dials — so a typo is an immediate refusal rather than a five-second timeout.

Authentication that needs a signing callback (NKey, a custom JWT handler), a custom dialler or a websocket URL is reached through OpenWithClient: build the *nats.Conn however the deployment needs and hand it over with an explicit driverkit.Ownership, which says who closes it.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
1. Settler() is nil. Every Ack returns ErrNotSettleable. Code written against an at-least-once driver compiles and runs and silently stops acknowledging. Check Capabilities().Has(FeatureExplicitAck), or require it: Requirements: []mq.Requirement{mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureExplicitAck, mq.Native)} fails at construction here, which is the point.
  2. MaxInFlight stalls a runner. Nothing is ever settled, so the in-flight count only rises. Leave it unset on this driver until the core's accounting treats a non-settleable delivery as terminal.
  3. The default confirmation costs a round trip per message. ConfirmNone or PublishBatch is what a throughput path wants.
  4. a/b and a.b are the same subject. Pick one spelling per deployment.
  5. Header order is sorted, not published order, and a binary header value is refused outright unless you choose an enveloping metadata mode.
  6. A slow consumer loses messages and nothing on the consuming path says so. Watch Client.Health() and Backend.SlowConsumers(); size PendingMessages/PendingBytes and the consumer prefetch together.
  7. A publisher bound to a wildcard is refused, and a consumer subscribed to > receives the whole prefix. Both are deliberate.
  8. The reply subject of a Request is the request's own inbox, so a Properties.ReplyTo set on a request message is ignored rather than honoured.

docs.text: Test What it holds TestAckNoneSettlementIsRefused every settlement verb reports ErrNotSettleable, and Settled() stays false TestSourceHasNoSettler the SPI half: the source declares it, rather than the core inferring it TestQueueGroupsCompete / TestFanOutAcrossSubscriptions one subscription competes, two subscriptions each receive TestWildcardSubscription / TestWildcardPublishRefused a pattern subscribes and reports the resolved subject; a pattern never publishes TestRequestReply / TestRequestWithNoResponderIsNotFound native correlation, and the immediate CodeNotFound that is its whole advantage TestRequestOverridesTheCallersReplyTo an answer never goes where the requester is not listening TestSlowConsumerDegradesHealth the only place a dropped message surfaces TestSourceFetchIsBoundedByPrefetch the ring is a bound, checked at the driver's own seam rather than through the core's TestBackendCloseUnblocksAFetchNobodyClosed the specification's "a backend closes what it opened" TestKeyAndBodyRoundTrip / TestNilVersusEmptyBody the observable distinctions over a protocol that has neither TestUnsupportedPublishControlsRefusedBeforeIO five controls refused, and nothing published TestBorrowedConnectionSurvivesClose explicit ownership, both ways TestDecodeIsDeterministic one message decodes to one header order, every time FuzzNATSSubjectMapping no input produces a subject that breaks the protocol or becomes a wildcard FuzzNATSHeaders everything Representable accepts survives nats.go's own header decoder byte for byte FuzzNATSDSN a DSN the parser accepted is a configuration Validate accepts and renders without its credential

docs.title: natsunified
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 1 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/natsunified is one entry point to both NATS profiles: Core (drivers/nats) and JetStream (drivers/jetstream). It is a facade over two drivers and not a third driver: it dials nothing, publishes nothing, settles nothing and maps no subject.

Every section below has two columns, because the facade has two profiles and they disagree about nearly everything a queue is judged on. Where a row says "the profile's", the page it belongs to is nats.md or jetstream.md and nothing here changes it.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
Core profile JetStream profile Driver module drivers/nats drivers/jetstream Client.Info().Name nats jetstream Native client github.com/nats-io/nats.go v1.53.1 the same, plus its jetstream package Server tested against nats:2.14.6-alpine (pinned by digest in conformance/harness/images.lock) the same image, --jetstream

The facade adds no client library of its own and pins no version: it requires the two driver modules, and they pin nats.go. natsunified.Version is empty until the module is tagged, which the specification makes "the driver did not say" rather than a claim.

Client.Info().Name is deliberately not natsunified. The facade returns the profile driver's own client, so Info() is that driver's answer, and a caller reading a log line can tell which driver is serving it. natsunified.ProfileOf(client.Info()) maps it back to a Profile.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
Entirely the selected profile's. The facade passes Config.Core or Config.JetStream through untouched, including SubjectPrefix, so the subject a topic maps to and the consumer or queue group a subscription becomes are exactly what the profile's own page documents.

What the facade adds is the mapping from a DSN scheme to a profile, and it is the whole of its dispatch table:

DSN Profile Driver nats://user:pw@host:4222,host2:4222/prefix?… ProfileCore drivers/nats natsjs://user:pw@host:4222/prefix?stream=S&… ProfileJetStream drivers/jetstream anything else — ErrDriverNotRegistered

There is no profile= parameter and there will not be one: two spellings for which broker you are talking to is one too many, and the second would have to be refused whenever it contradicted the scheme. The refusal a caller actually meets is better than that. Each scheme carries its profile's own strict parameter table, so nats://host?stream=ORDERS is refused naming stream, and natsjs://host?noecho=true naming noecho.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
The selected profile's, unchanged — including the refusal.

Mode Core profile JetStream profile ConfirmNone the message is in the write buffer the asynchronous publication is admitted ConfirmAccepted PING/PONG: the server has parsed it and stored nothing the stream's PubAck, sent after the message is committed to storage ConfirmDurable refused at Client.Publisher the same PubAck as ConfirmAccepted

ConfirmDurable is the question a facade is most likely to get wrong, and the answer is structural rather than defensive: Open resolves the profile, so by the time there is a publisher there is no longer a choice to defer. The sink is drivers/nats's own sink and the refusal is its own errNoDurableConfirm, at publisher construction, before a single message exists. A facade that deferred the profile choice to the first publication would have turned the fail-fast into a per-message failure; this one cannot.

One refusal earlier still is the facade's own. Config.Require carries requirements and is evaluated inside Open, against the table the connected broker really produced:

cfg, err := natsunified.ParseDSN(os.Getenv("QUEUE_DSN"))
cfg.Require = []mq.Requirement{
        mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureDurableConfirm, mq.Native),
        mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureExplicitAck, mq.Native),
}
client, err := natsunified.Open(ctx, cfg)   // refused on nats://, at the Open

It costs the dial, which is unavoidable — JetStream's table is read off the bound stream, so there is no honest answer before the connection exists — and a client it refuses is closed before the error is returned. A DSN cannot carry a requirement, so this is a two-step and it is the recommended shape for any program whose profile comes from configuration.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text: The selected profile's. Core is a subscription with SetPendingLimits and a driver-side ring; JetStream is a durable pull consumer with MaxAckPending. The facade opens no source of its own.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
Core profile JetStream profile Ack ErrNotSettleable — Settler() is nil (AckNone) +ACK, or a request/reply round trip with doubleack=true Nack ErrNotSettleable -NAK, with {"delay":n} for a delayed requeue Reject ErrNotSettleable publish to DeadLetterTopic, await its PubAck, then +TERM Extend ErrNotSettleable +WPI

This is the difference the facade cannot smooth over and does not try to. A program that selects its profile at run time and calls Ack gets a no-op success on one profile and an error on the other, from identical portable code. It is held by TestSettlementDiffersByProfile on both profiles so that nobody has to find out in production.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: The selected profile's, and the two happen to agree in shape: neither broker has partitions or message keys, so all three ordering features are conditional on both profiles and all three conditions reduce to "one publisher's messages on one subject, delivered to a single consumer". A queue group with more than one member interleaves on Core; a subscription with two consumers interleaves on JetStream; on JetStream a nack additionally puts a message behind the messages that followed it.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text: Core profile JetStream profile PublishOption Delay / DeliverAt ErrUnsupported a Nats-Schedule control message, conditional on a 2.12+ server and AllowMsgSchedules Delayed nack ErrNotSettleable native, -NAK {"delay":n}

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Core profile JetStream profile Destination none; Reject is ErrNotSettleable Config.DeadLetterTopic, conditional support Route — publish, await PubAck, then +TERM — never +TERM first

The facade sets neither. deadlettertopic= in a natsjs:// DSN reaches drivers/jetstream; the same parameter in a nats:// DSN is refused by name.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text: The selected profile's. NATS headers are text lines on both, so binary headers are unsupported on both and duplicate headers are native on both. The message ceiling is the server's max_payload on Core, and the smaller of that and the stream's MaxMsgSize on JetStream. The facade advertises no limits of its own and Capabilities().Limits() is the profile's, compared field for field by TestCapabilitiesAreTheProfilesOwn.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text: The selected profile's nats.go reconnect loop and the selected profile's driverkit.Health state machine. The facade wires no handlers and holds no health state.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
Core profile JetStream profile Window none — there is no redelivery, so the failure mode is loss from the PubAck until the delivery is acknowledged; a lease that expires redelivers Duplicates never yes, on lease expiry, reconnection or Close

A caller that selects a profile at run time must be written for the JetStream column and must additionally tolerate loss on the Core one. Common() does not contain FeatureAtLeastOnce, and that is the machine-readable form of this paragraph.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
natsunified.Config is four fields:

type Config struct {
        Profile   Profile            // ProfileCore or ProfileJetStream; there is NO default
        Core      nats.Config        // read when Profile is ProfileCore
        JetStream jetstream.Config   // read when Profile is ProfileJetStream
        Require   []mq.Requirement   // requirements, checked inside Open
}

There is no default profile. A Config with ProfileUnset is a construction error carrying CodeInvalidConfig, and the DSN scheme is the only other way to set one. The two profiles disagree about at-most-once versus at-least-once delivery — the most consequential property a queue has — so a zero value that resolved to either would decide it by omission, which is the reasoning that already gave memory.Open its AutoCreate: false.

Both profile configurations may be filled in at once and only the selected one is read or validated. That is the shape a facade is genuinely good for: an application deployed against Core in development and JetStream in production writes both and flips Profile. Config.Validate() is pure, checks that a profile was named and delegates the rest to the selected profile's own Validate; the unselected half is not validated, because refusing a program for a typo in configuration this deployment never reads would make that shape unusable.

Why it is not one merged field set. The two driver configurations share 19 connection fields — Addrs, Name, Username, Password, Token, CredentialsFile, TLS, InsecureSkipVerify, SubjectPrefix, PendingMessages, PendingBytes, ConnectTimeout, ReconnectWait, MaxReconnects, PingInterval, MaxPingsOut, DrainTimeout, Clock, Hooks — and disagree about 24 more: 2 Core-only (FlushTimeout, NoEcho) and 22 JetStream-only. A single field set would therefore be 19 retyped fields plus two profile-only groups, 38 assignments and two validation paths, all of which have to be kept in step with two other modules by hand, with nothing able to notice when one of them grows a field. Carrying the two typed configurations costs none of that. TestSharedConfigurationFields recomputes the partition by reflection and fails when either driver changes, so the figures in this paragraph are a measurement rather than a count taken once.

DSN. Every parameter is the selected profile's own; see nats.md and jetstream.md for the two tables. ParseDSN reads the scheme and hands the whole string to that profile's parser, which costs one extra pass over the string and buys the thing that matters: neither parameter table is duplicated here to go stale.

nats://user:password@host:4222,host2:4222/prefix?creds=/path.creds&tls=true
natsjs://user:password@host:4222/prefix?stream=ORDERS&managestream=true&doubleack=true

Config.DSN(), String() and LogValue() are the selected profile's redacted rendering, so the scheme in the result is the one that would select the same profile again. A Config with no profile renders as natsunified://?profile=unset: there is no connection string for "the caller did not say which broker".

Naming and auto-create. The facade creates no topology.

Core profile JetStream profile Topology none: a subject exists because somebody published to it a stream Default nothing to create ManageStream: false A name that does not exist works immediately Open fails with CodeNotFound, naming the stream Explicit creation — managestream=true, in the connection string where it is reviewable

Naming the stream in that failure is new in this increment: the client library's own message is nats: API error: code=404 err_code=10059 description=stream not found, which says everything except which stream, and a deployment with five of them cannot act on it. drivers/jetstream now wraps it.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
• Info().Name is not natsunified. It is nats or jetstream, on purpose. If your logging or metrics key on the driver name, a profile switch changes the key — which is the honest signal, and natsunified.ProfileOf(info) is how to recover the profile.
  • OpenBackend returns the interface, not a concrete type. A function that dispatches between two backend types cannot name both in its signature, so *nats.Backend.Conn(), *jetstream.Backend.Stream() and Facts() are behind a type assertion. CoreBackend and JetStreamBackend are that assertion under a findable name; the profile driver's own OpenBackend avoids it entirely, and a program that already knows its profile should use that.
  • A feature in Common() can still mean two different things. FeaturePublisherConfirm is native on both profiles and is the socket on one and the disk on the other. FeatureBatchPublish is EmulatedVolatile on Core and EmulatedDurable on JetStream, so RequireAtLeast(FeatureBatchPublish, EmulatedDurable) passes on one profile and fails on the other — from a feature both "have". Read Capabilities().Support(f).Note, not just Has(f).
  • A DSN cannot carry a requirement. OpenDSN is one call and checks nothing beyond the profile's own validation. The two-step — ParseDSN, set Require, Open — is the form that fails fast, and it is the one to use whenever the DSN is not yours.
  • One *nats.Conn serves both profiles. NATS Core and JetStream are the same protocol on the same socket, so OpenWithClient with driverkit.ClientBorrowed can back a Core client and a JetStream client on one connection. This is the facade's clearest technical win and the one place where a single entry point is not merely cosmetic.
  • ManageStream is never turned on for you, even when the stream the DSN names does not exist. See the table above.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
The module's own tests run against two embedded nats-server instances, one plain and one with JetStream, and need no container. The ones that are about the facade rather than about either driver:

Test What it holds TestCapabilitiesAreTheProfilesOwn the facade's table is the profile's, compared per feature on level, scope, note and limits TestCapabilitiesAreNeitherTheUnionNorTheIntersection eight features that are native on JetStream and absent on Core, and two that are the reverse TestCommonIsTheLiveIntersection Common() against the intersection of two live tables, so a claim added to or removed from either driver fails here TestCommonSharesFeaturesAtDifferentLevels the BatchPublish and PublisherConfirm traps, including the RequireAtLeast that passes on one profile and fails on the other TestConfirmDurableIsRefusedAtConstructionOnCore no publisher comes back at all, which is what distinguishes a construction-time refusal from a publish-time one TestRequireRefusesAtOpenOnTheWrongProfile both directions: refused on Core, met on JetStream TestRequireClosesTheClientItRefuses the server's own connection count returns to zero after five refused opens TestFacadeNamesAStreamItDoesNotCreate CodeNotFound, the stream named, and the stream still absent afterwards TestOpenWithClientServesBothProfilesOnOneConnection one borrowed *nats.Conn, two profiles, and the connection still usable afterwards TestSharedConfigurationFields the 19/2/22 configuration partition, recomputed by reflection TestConformanceHarnessOpensThroughTheFacade the conformance run really goes through the facade's Open and not the driver's TestInfoAndNativeAfterClose the kit's client/info-and-native scenario, which the kit cannot run here (below) FuzzUnifiedDSN the two parsing passes agree, the unselected half stays zero, the rendering never carries a credential, the input's scheme is the one the grammar reads (case-insensitively), and the rendering parses back to every setting the input filled, compared field by field

docs.title: nsq
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 3 · Owner: @qoke

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's nsq image (make bench-native CLIENTS="nsq"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary nsq github.com/nsqio/go-nsq github.com/nsqio/go-nsq@v1.1.0 nsqd OK response to PUB/MPUB (memory-backed until mem-queue-size)

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • size limits. nsqd's defaults cap a single message at 1 MiB (--max-msg-size) and a whole command body at 5 MiB (--max-body-size), so an MPUB of 100 64 KiB messages (6.4 MiB) must be split into smaller chunks. Verified against: nsqd v1.3.0 flag defaults; verified by the MPUB chunking in the nsq baseline.
  • deferred publish and discovery. go-nsq exposes per-message delays through Producer.DeferredPublish (DPUB) and discovers nsqd instances through nsqlookupd, which requires nsqd to broadcast an address the client can reach. Verified against: go-nsq v1.1.0 producer.go:233; conformance/harness/brokers.go NSQ.
  • output buffering. nsqd buffers writes to each client and flushes them on a timeout the client sets in IDENTIFY: go-nsq defaults to output_buffer_size 16 KiB and output_buffer_timeout 250 ms, so a single small message can take a quarter of a second to arrive on an otherwise idle connection while a 64 KiB message fills the buffer and leaves at once. A latency-sensitive consumer must lower the timeout, and the client warns that going below 25 ms costs nsqd noticeable CPU. Verified against: go-nsq v1.1.0 config.go:165-172; visible in BenchmarkNative/nsq/EndToEnd, where 64 B and 1 KiB round trips take ~250 ms and 64 KiB takes ~380 us.
  • channels. A topic with no channel discards what is published to it, so a channel must exist (SUB, or the /channel/create HTTP endpoint) before the first publish or messages are lost. Verified against: nsqd v1.3.0 behaviour; verified by the nsq baseline's provisioning step.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq NSQ topic an nsqd topic, Config.TopicPrefix prepended verbatim subscription an nsqd channel Message.Key nothing native — see Headers & limits Message.Headers nothing native — see Headers & limits DeliveryInfo.Attempt nsqd's Attempts, 1 on the first delivery DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires the receipt time plus the negotiated msg_timeout DeliveryInfo.Partition, Offset, Sequence never set: nsqd has none of them

A channel is both the fan-out and the consumer group: every channel of a topic receives a copy of every message, and every consumer of one channel competes for its messages. A subscription therefore cannot be empty — there is no such thing as an unnamed channel — which is the opposite of the SQS profile, where the subscription is empty because a queue has no fan-out.

The mapping is a pure prepend and never an escape. nsqd's grammar is ^[.a-zA-Z0-9_-]+(#ephemeral)?$, one to sixty-four bytes, and a portable topic outside it is refused rather than transformed: a mapper that replaced the illegal bytes would map a/b and a-b onto one NSQ topic, and a caller would then find one subscription receiving another's messages. nsq.CheckTopic is checked against go-nsq's own validator by FuzzNSQTopicName, because this driver validates by hand — one regular-expression match per publication is not free — and two spellings of one grammar drift the day somebody edits either.

A topic carrying a pattern metacharacter (*, ?, #, >) is refused with ErrUnsupported and not with "invalid topic": NSQ has no pattern subscription at all, and the feature being missing is the more useful thing to tell a caller who wrote a pattern on purpose. A trailing #ephemeral is not a pattern.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
nsqd creates a topic on the first publication to it whatever any client asks, which is a property of the broker rather than a choice this driver makes. The channel is not created that way, and that matters: a topic holds its messages until it has at least one channel and then hands the backlog to the channel that appears — a second channel created afterwards starts empty. So a consumer that subscribes after the publications it wants has missed them.

Config.EnsureTopology is the deliberate creation, through nsqd's HTTP API, and it is off by default. The specification's "no hidden topology creation" is about a driver that could provision and chooses not to; the conformance harness turns it on, because there the kit is the operator.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
Publish is PUB, PublishBatch is MPUB, and a publication carrying a delay is DPUB. All three are answered by nsqd with OK, and this driver waits for that answer.

The boundary is: nsqd has taken the message into the topic it names. That queue is in memory up to nsqd's --mem-queue-size and on disk beyond it, so OK survives a consumer crash and does not survive an nsqd crash with an in-memory queue.

mode Honoured as ConfirmNone the same round trip: go-nsq has no publish this driver could use without giving up the answer ConfirmDefault, ConfirmAccepted nsqd's OK ConfirmDurable refused when the sink is opened, with ErrUnsupported

A caller's context bounds the wait and not the work: the frame is written by go-nsq's asynchronous form and the driver selects on the answer and on the context. A context that expires after the frame is on the wire makes the outcome ambiguous — IsAmbiguous is true and Retryable is false — because nsqd may well have taken the publication, and reporting "did not publish" would make a duplicate look like a loss.

There is no AsyncSink and no FlushSink: a publication is a completed round trip by the time Publish returns, so there is nothing admitted to flush.

With several nsqd addresses configured, publications go round-robin and there is no failover: the specification gives retry policy to the core, and a driver that tried the next endpoint would turn one publication into two attempts with the core's own count blind to the second. The core's next attempt lands on the next endpoint anyway, because the cursor has moved.

docs.title: Batch splitting
docs.text:
MPUB is one command carrying many bodies and one answer, so a partial outcome is not something nsqd reports. A batch larger than Config.MaxBodyBytes (nsqd's --max-body-size) is split into as many MPUBs as it needs, counting the command's own framing, and each piece is its own command with its own outcome. A batch can therefore half succeed, and the *BatchError's Errs are index-aligned with the messages — every index a failed command carried gets that command's error, and no index gets another message's outcome.

A batch carrying a delay cannot use MPUB at all, because DPUB takes one body; such a batch is published one message at a time.

FeatureAtomicBatchPublish is not claimed.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
nsq.Consumer.AddConcurrentHandlers delivers by calling the driver and the SPI asks the driver to be called, so driverkit.PushAdapter sits between them:

  • MaxInFlight is the core's resolved prefetch, so nsqd's own RDY accounting is the primary bound and the ring is sized to hold everything it can send;
  • the ring's capacity is that prefetch, and Push blocks when it is full, which is the backpressure a broker that delivers by callback understands;
  • the handler pool is min(prefetch, 8). It does not need to be the prefetch: a handler goroutine only moves a delivery into the ring, and what the pool size bounds is how many deliveries sit in a blocked push — each of them a message whose nsqd timeout is running down while nothing works on it, so fewer is safer rather than slower.

DisableAutoResponse is set on every delivery, before anything else can return, and the handler always returns nil. Both halves are load-bearing: without the first, go-nsq's handler loop would FIN the message the moment the callback returned — before the application had seen it — and with an error return it would requeue the message with a backoff of its own.

A delivery whose body this driver cannot decode is requeued with a delay and counted, because nsqd's verbs are finish, requeue and touch and none of them says "this is not my message". Backend.Undecodable() is the count. The health state does not change: the connection that carried the record is healthy, and a degraded state would make the next successful Ping report a reconnection.

Fetch drops a delivery that went dead while it sat in the ring — one whose lease expired, or which a later delivery of the same message superseded. Handing it out would make the handler's work certainly wasted and its acknowledgement certainly refused. Backend.Stale() counts them.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Config.LookupdAddrs is preferred over Config.Addrs whenever it is set, and the preference is not a tie-break: a consumer connected straight to the nsqd addresses never learns about an nsqd that joins the cluster later, so on a cluster a direct connection silently consumes a subset of the topic. With one nsqd the two are equivalent and the direct form is one fewer moving part. Publication always goes to Config.Addrs: nsqlookupd is a discovery service for consumers and cannot be published through.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
iqmq NSQ Notes Ack FIN Nack (requeue) REQ(delay) nsqd's own delayed redelivery Nack (drop) FIN the specification calls it destructive and it is: finishing is nsqd's only way to make a message go away Nack (dead letter) — ErrUnsupported; see Dead-letter queue Extend TOUCH not a settlement batch settlement — nsqd has no batched verb, so no BatchSettler

nsqd answers none of the three. It replies to PUB, MPUB and DPUB and to nothing else, so the settlement boundary here is the frame was handed to the connection. Every correctness question a broker would otherwise answer is therefore answered locally, before the frame is written, and this is the part of the driver worth reading twice.

docs.title: The local lease check
docs.text:
nsqd will accept a FIN for a message whose timeout has already expired, and after a redelivery that FIN finishes another consumer's work. There is no verb that asks "do I still hold this?". The specification makes "lets a stale ack settle a later redelivery" a disqualifier rather than a rough edge, so the driver keeps:

  • a local view of each delivery's deadline, moved by TOUCH and read before every settlement, with Config.LeaseGuard of slack;
  • a map from nsqd message identifier to the delivery it currently vouches for, so a redelivery supersedes its predecessor the moment it arrives;
  • a delivery generation, so a settlement carrying a stale one is refused.

A settlement for a delivery that fails any of these is refused with ErrLeaseLost and nothing is written at that moment. A delivery that failed only the deadline is given back with REQ(0) shortly afterwards, for the reason under The lease sweeper. A second settlement of a delivery that is still ours is ErrAlreadySettled, which is a different answer for a different reason: one says the work was accounted for once, the other says it was never accounted for and the message is coming back.

docs.title: The lease sweeper
docs.text:
The driver gives a delivery back one LeaseGuard before its deadline, with REQ(0), if nothing has settled or extended it. It costs nothing that expiry would not have cost — nsqd would have requeued the message a moment later — and it turns the local check from a diagnosis into a prevention: with it, a delivery is superseded only by a redelivery the driver did not see coming.

Config.LeaseGuard is therefore two things at once, and a caller using the core's lease extension has to keep them in step: it is how much slack the settlement check demands, and it is how early the delivery is given back. A caller that opts into mq.WithLeaseExtension(lead) must choose a lead LONGER than LeaseGuard, or the driver requeues the delivery before the core gets round to extending it and a long handler never keeps its lease at all. The default lead is zero — extension is opt-in — so the default configuration has nothing to trip over.

Once a deadline has passed, nsqd may already have redelivered the message, so the driver never writes a FIN or TOUCH for that delivery. It still owes nsqd an answer, and that matters more than it sounds: go-nsq counts one response per delivery on each connection, does not finish closing a connection until that count is zero, and does not reconnect to that nsqd until the close has finished. An unanswered delivery on a connection that drops therefore stops the subscription receiving from that nsqd at all. go-nsq does not tell the driver when a connection is closing, so the driver cannot wait for the moment a frame is harmless.

When a redelivery arrives and supersedes the old delivery, the old one's debt is chained onto the delivery that superseded it and paid once that one has been answered, when nsqd no longer holds the identifier in flight and the frame is refused harmlessly. When none arrives, the lease sweeper answers the old delivery with REQ(0) on its next pass but one, one to two sweep intervals (half a LeaseGuard each) after a settlement or a Fetch found the lease gone. The wait gives a redelivery that is already on its way time to arrive and take the debt over, which is the common case shortly after a deadline.

nsqd accepts a REQ only from the client holding the message, so the sweeper's frame never touches another consumer's delivery, and on a dropped connection it goes nowhere but still settles go-nsq's count, so the consumer reconnects. The one case where it changes anything is a redelivery to this same connection that nsqd sent and the driver has still not received when the sweep comes round. nsqd requeues that redelivery, the driver hands it out as live, and its Ack later finds nothing in flight at nsqd, so the message is delivered once more. That is a duplicate and never a loss, and it is why the frame is a REQ: a FIN in the same place would finish a message whether or not anyone had done its work.

docs.title: TOUCH is not an addition
docs.text:
nsqd's TOUCH resets a message's timeout to the channel's negotiated msg_timeout, measured from now, and caps a message's total in-flight time at --max-msg-timeout from its first delivery. So:

  • Extend(by) is refused for by past Config.MaxAckDeadline, which mirrors that cap;
  • anything shorter is granted, and what it buys is the channel's timeout rather than the amount asked for. Capabilities().Limit(LimitMaxLease) is that timeout, and it is the number a caller plans against, because the SPI has no way for an extension to report what it actually bought ;
  • Extend(0) or less is CodeInvalidArgument: nsqd would reset the timeout to the channel's default, which for a short remaining lease is an extension nobody asked for and for a long one is a shortening.

An extension leaves the delivery settleable. The settler has a peek beside its claim for exactly that: a driver whose Extend took the delivery's state would make the acknowledgement that follows it fail, and the message would be processed twice for no reason but the extension meant to prevent it.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
No ordering is claimed, in any scope. the specification's "ordering never claimed" is literal here: nsqd makes no promise about the order in which a channel's messages are delivered, not even for one producer, one consumer and no failures — an in-memory queue and a disk-backed queue are drained independently, and a requeue puts a message back wherever there is room.

A Conditional claim with a note would be the wrong answer, because there is no condition under which it holds. A caller that needs ordering needs the core's hash lanes over a broker that has it, or another broker.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
Native, in both directions:

  • a publication delay is DPUB, bounded by Config.MaxRequeueDelay (nsqd's --max-req-timeout, default one hour) and advertised as the specification's MaxDelay. PublishOptions.DeliverAt is converted to a delay against the injected clock, and an instant already past is "deliver now" rather than an error;
  • a redelivery delay is REQ(delay), bounded the same way.

RequeueWithoutBackoff and not Requeue: go-nsq's Requeue sets the consumer's RDY to zero for the whole subscription while a backoff of its own runs, so one message's failure would stop every other message. The delay is the core's and the client library does not get a second one.

Scheduled publication is nsqd's own and needs no emulation, so nothing here is EmulatedVolatile and no Emulation policy is consulted.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
No native route. FeatureDeadLetter means the driver knows where a dead letter goes and can get it there in one native settlement, and nsqd has no verb for it — so Nack(NackDeadLetter()) is refused with ErrUnsupported rather than emulated inside the driver.

the specification's "ED" for this broker is the core's emulation: mq.WithDeadLetter publishes the message to a topic and then acknowledges the original, which classes as semantics-preserving and which needs nothing from this driver. It carries the duplicate risk the specification requires to be disclosed: the publication and the acknowledgement are two operations and a failure between them means the message exists in both places.

mq.WithNativeDeadLetter() is refused by the core against this driver, which is the rule that a capability the driver does not have is refused rather than emulated in silence.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
NSQ has no headers at all — not a limited set, not string-only values. The protocol carries a body and nothing else. So the promise of ordered, duplicate-preserving, binary-capable headers is kept here by the portable envelope of github.com/iqhive/iqmq/wire and by nothing else, and the same goes for the message key, the message identifier and the typed properties.

the four modes therefore reduce to three behaviours:

Mode Behaviour MetadataNativeStrict (default) a message carrying any header, identifier, typed property or key — including an empty key, because the specification makes nil and empty different — is refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O, naming the field MetadataPortableEnvelope every message is enveloped; a non-iqmq consumer reads the envelope rather than the body MetadataAdaptive the messages that carry metadata are enveloped and a bare body is left alone MetadataLenientDrop the metadata is discarded and the body is published; Backend.DroppedMetadata() counts what went

Config.Metadata is the deployment's one-time "yes, envelope on this broker". The specification makes the header-less envelope an interop-affecting emulation, available under EmulationAll or an explicit metadata mode, and the SPI carries no emulation policy at all — so there is nowhere else to say it once rather than on every publisher and consumer. A handle that names a mode keeps it: the field replaces the zero value and nothing else, so an explicit MetadataPortableEnvelope is never downgraded and an explicit MetadataLenientDrop is never upgraded. A handle that names MetadataNativeStrict explicitly is indistinguishable from one that named nothing, which is why the conformance run documents metadata/native-strict-rejection as inapplicable.

With the envelope configured, the three header features are advertised as EmulatedDurable with the emulation stated, because the headers really do travel and are as durable as the message. Without it they are Unsupported.

Two of this driver's reasons to envelope are invisible to driverkit.Envelope.Needed, which reads the capability table :

  • a message key. The inventory has no native-key feature, so a keyed message with no other metadata answers "nothing to do" and would go out with its key discarded, silently.
  • an empty body. nsqd answers a zero-length PUB with E_BAD_MESSAGE, so the nil-versus-empty distinction survives here only inside an envelope, which is never empty. In the two non-enveloping modes an empty message cannot be published at all, and that is refused before the round trip.

Under MetadataAdaptive a body that begins with the envelope's magic is enveloped too, even though nsqd could carry it natively. With no headers there is nowhere to record which records are enveloped, so the body is the only evidence there is — and a driver that published such a body natively would decode a payload as metadata on the way back, or leave a record it could neither deliver nor settle. wire.Detector.DetectFull is the read side of the same rule: it claims a body only when the body is, exactly and entirely, a canonical envelope. A producer that deliberately publishes a valid envelope as a payload is still indistinguishable from one that enveloped it; that is a property of a broker with nothing out of band, and drivers/sqs avoids it with a message attribute because it has one.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Every limit this driver advertises mirrors an nsqd flag rather than a value nsqd reports: nsqd publishes none of its limits over either the TCP protocol or its HTTP API, so an operator who moves a flag must move the configuration with it.

limit Config field nsqd flag Default MaxMessageBytes MaxMessageBytes --max-msg-size 1 MiB MaxBatchBytes MaxBodyBytes --max-body-size 5 MiB MaxDelay MaxRequeueDelay --max-req-timeout 1 h MaxLease MaxAckDeadline --max-msg-timeout 15 min MaxBatchMessages, MaxHeaderCount, MaxHeaderBytes — — not advertised: nsqd bounds no such thing and the specification forbids guessing

Two more flags are mirrored as refusals rather than as limits, because nsqd enforces them in the IDENTIFY handshake and a client that asks for less has its whole connection refused: Config.OutputBufferTimeout must be at least --min-output-buffer-timeout (25 ms) and an ack deadline at least --min-msg-timeout (1 s). Both are checked by Config.Validate, which is the specification's "validate config before starting background work" — the alternative is every operation on the client failing with an error about a handshake.

The size check is applied to what will be written, which for an enveloped message is the envelope: a 1 MiB body plus its headers is over nsqd's default even though the body alone is not, and finding that out from nsqd costs a round trip and an E_BAD_MESSAGE.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
go-nsq owns the reconnection, in both halves: a producer redials on the next publication, and a consumer either re-polls nsqlookupd or retries the direct address every Config.LookupdPollInterval. This driver adds no loop of its own, which is why there is no driverkit.Reconnector here.

The consequence is stated rather than hidden: go-nsq offers no reconnection callback, so the specification's OnReconnect has only one source on this driver — a Ping that succeeds after a failure. It is coarse, and a caller that never calls Ping never sees one. Backend.Health() is what carries the state, and Backend.Reconnects() and Backend.DegradedTransitions() are the numbers.

A lost connection makes nsqd requeue everything that connection was holding, at once. Every delivery from it is therefore superseded when its message comes back and every settlement for it is refused with ErrLeaseLost — which is the same machinery as an expired lease and is tested the same way.

Config.HeartbeatInterval must be less than Config.ReadTimeout or go-nsq reads with a deadline nsqd's heartbeat cannot beat, and every idle connection looks dead. Validate refuses it.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
The window is between nsqd accepting a message and the driver's FIN reaching it, and a message is delivered again whenever that window is interrupted:

  • the per-message timeout expires — or the lease sweeper hands the message back one guard earlier, deliberately;
  • the connection holding it goes away, in which case nsqd makes every message on it available at once;
  • the source is closed, which requeues everything it has handed out and never settled;
  • the lease sweeper gives back a delivery whose lease has passed, and its REQ lands on a redelivery still on its way to the same connection (see The lease sweeper);
  • a REQ for any reason, including the core's retry schedule.

A duplicate is normal and an ordering change is normal with it. There is no de-duplication and no idempotent publish: FeatureDeduplication, FeatureIdempotentPublish and FeatureExactlyOnceDelivery are all unsupported, and a handler has to be idempotent.

Two narrower windows are worth naming. A publication whose context expires while the frame is in flight is ambiguous, so a core retry of it may produce a second message. And a FIN is a frame nsqd does not answer, so a FIN lost with the connection produces a redelivery of a message the application had finished.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
client, err := nsq.Open(ctx, nsq.Config{
    Addrs:        []string{"nsqd-a:4150", "nsqd-b:4150"},
    LookupdAddrs: []string{"http://lookupd-a:4161", "http://lookupd-b:4161"},
    AdminAddrs:   []string{"nsqd-a:4151", "nsqd-b:4151"},
    Metadata:     mq.MetadataAdaptive,
    AckDeadline:  30 * time.Second,
})

The DSN form is the same configuration as a connection string (nsq.ParseDSN). The authority is the nsqd TCP endpoints, a host with no port takes 4150, and the path is Config.TopicPrefix:

nsq://nsqd-a:4150,nsqd-b:4150/acme.?lookupd=http://lookupd:4161&metadata=adaptive&ackdeadline=30s

The parameters are listed on ParseDSN, and an unknown one is a construction error naming it. Three decisions in the DSN are not obvious:

  • lookupd= and admin= are comma-separated lists, because the shared parser refuses a repeated key outright and that refusal is right for every scalar it was written for ;
  • max_in_flight is not a parameter, though the example DSN shows one. Prefetch is the core's: it is resolved from the consumer configuration and handed to the driver, and a DSN that set it would be a second owner of one number that the driver would then have to choose between, silently ;
  • Config.AdminAddrs, when empty, is derived from the TCP addresses by adding one to each port — nsqd's own default layout, and a guess rather than a discovery, which is why the field is explicit.

Config.AuthSecret is a dsn.Secret: neither Config.String(), nor Config.LogValue(), nor Config.DSN(), nor any error this driver builds can carry it.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text:
Client.Admin() is nsqd's HTTP API — /topic/create, /topic/delete, /channel/create, /channel/delete, /channel/empty, /stats — because that is where nsqd puts topology; the TCP protocol has none.

Every one of those endpoints is answered by one nsqd about itself. nsqlookupd knows which nsqd holds a topic but cannot create, delete or purge anything, so an administrative call has to reach every nsqd the deployment has: this driver sends each one to every address in Config.AdminAddrs and reports the first failure, and Stats sums what they answer. A deployment whose AdminAddrs name a subset of its nsqd instances gets a partial answer.

QueueStats.Lag is never known: a channel holds what has not been finished and keeps nothing else, so there is no position in a log to be behind. The specification makes that an unknown rather than a zero.

The HTTP requests go over a transport of the backend's own, cloned from http.DefaultTransport when the backend opens: a proxy or dialer an application set there still applies, nothing else in the process can close its connections under a request in flight, and Close releases them. An admin call after Close returns ErrClosed. With Config.TLS set the requests are HTTPS and verify each nsqd with Config.TLS against that nsqd's own host name, exactly as the protocol connection does -- a ServerName in Config.TLS is ignored by both.

nsqlookupd discovery is the third HTTP surface, and its scheme is the operator's to choose. Config.TLS is nsqd's TLS, on the protocol connection; what discovery does is decided by the scheme in each LookupdAddrs entry, and go-nsq prepends http:// when there is none. So a scheme-less or http:// lookupd address is cleartext discovery even with Config.TLS set, and that is not refused: nsqlookupd is a different service from nsqd, a TLS nsqd behind a plain-HTTP nsqlookupd on a private network is a real layout, and the traffic carries no credential, though only because this driver turns go-nsq's LookupdAuthorization off: that field defaults to true, and with an AuthSecret configured the discovery poll carried Authorization: Bearer <secret> in the clear. Measured, and the opposite of what was first recorded. The secret now goes to nsqd's AUTH handshake and nowhere else. What it discloses is the topic name in the query and the nsqd host names in the answer. Write https:// and Config.TLS is what the poller uses — its roots, its client certificate and its InsecureSkipVerify. That last part was not true before: go-nsq builds its own lookupd transport with TLSClientConfig unset, so an https:// lookupd verified against the system roots and a private CA failed as an unknown authority. Both halves are measured on the wire.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
1. A channel must exist before the publication you want it to see. A topic hands its backlog to the first channel that appears; a channel created later starts empty. Use Config.EnsureTopology or Admin.EnsureSubscription.
  2. OK is not durable. nsqd's queue is in memory up to --mem-queue-size, so a publication acknowledged by an nsqd that then dies uncleanly is gone. ConfirmDurable is refused rather than silently weakened.
  3. An empty message cannot be published in a mode that does not envelope: nsqd answers a zero-length body with E_BAD_MESSAGE.
  4. go-nsq's defaults would break the core's retry accounting, and this driver turns two of them off. MaxAttempts defaults to five and what go-nsq does when a message passes it is call FINISH — a message discarded by the client library while the core was still retrying it, which the specification makes a disqualifier. MaxBackoffDuration defaults to two minutes and its backoff sets RDY to zero for the whole subscription. Both are zero here, and TestCriticalGoNSQRetriesAreOff is what keeps them there.
  5. output_buffer_timeout has a floor of 25 ms and a default of 250 ms. go-nsq's default adds a quarter of a second to the latency of every otherwise-idle delivery; this driver's default is nsqd's floor, and nsqd refuses anything below it in the IDENTIFY handshake.
  6. A #ephemeral topic or channel is deleted when its last client goes away, taking whatever it held. The name is legal here and the consequence is nsqd's.
  7. Two nsqd instances are two independent brokers. There is no replication, no partitioning and no cross-instance ordering; a topic exists separately on each nsqd that has seen a publication for it, and a consumer without nsqlookupd sees only the ones it was told about.
  8. Attempts is nsqd's and counts deliveries, including the ones this driver refused to hand out because their lease had gone. A retry budget keyed on it is therefore slightly conservative, which is the safe direction.
  9. Config.LeaseGuard must be shorter than the core's lease-extension lead. It is how early the driver gives a delivery back as well as how much slack a settlement demands, so a mq.WithLeaseExtension(lead) with lead below it means the driver requeues the delivery first and the extension never happens. Extension is opt-in and the default lead is zero, so a default configuration has nothing to trip over.
  10. The conformance run lowers the fidelity figure from 100,000 to 10,000. Every publication here is a PUB answered by nsqd, and the scenario publishes them one at a time; the specification asks a driver that lowers the figure to say so, and this is saying so.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
The specification names "NSQ deferred requeue, backoff, lookupd changes" for this driver. They are TestCritical* in drivers/nsq, run by make critical DRIVER=nsq and by make ci, against nsqfake — an in-process model of a channel's message lifecycle, because every one of them is a decision the broker makes and a real nsqd cannot be asked to make any of them on demand.

Test What it holds TestCriticalDeferredRequeue three requeues with rising delays: each comes back only after its own delay, with its attempt count one higher, and never through a client-library backoff TestCriticalGoNSQRetriesAreOff twelve negative settlements, past go-nsq's default MaxAttempts twice over, and the broker finishes nothing: a message the client library gave up on would have been finished and never delivered again TestCriticalLookupdIsPreferredOverDirectAddresses a configuration with a lookupd discovers through it, and one without connects directly TestCriticalARedeliveryAfterAConnectionLossIsNotSettledTwice eight messages made available again at once: every settlement from the first round is refused and none of them reaches the broker

The model reproduces nsqd's exact laxity — a FIN, REQ or TOUCH names a message identifier and lands on whatever is under it — and counts every settlement that landed on the wrong delivery attempt. A model that refused a stale settlement would make the driver's defence untestable, because the test would pass with the defence removed.

Beside them, TestCloseRacesTheHandlerForThousandsOfRounds is this repository's recurring defect class in the shape it takes here: a delivery placed in the ring while the source is closing. Three thousand rounds, every other delivery deliberately left unsettled, and the conservation law it asserts is that after Close every message the broker took is either finished or back in the channel and none is still in flight.

docs.title: pulsar
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
drivers/pulsar is over github.com/apache/pulsar-client-go, pinned at v0.21.0. The transaction helper is a separate module, x/pulsartx, so a program that does not use transactions does not carry the coordinator client.

The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's pulsar image (make bench-native CLIENTS="pulsar"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary pulsar github.com/apache/pulsar-client-go github.com/apache/pulsar-client-go@v0.21.0 broker send receipt (Producer.Send), persistent topic

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the driver and the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves. The first four are the facts benchmarks/native-baselines records, quoted verbatim — nativebench.TestFactsRecorded holds this page to them — and the rest are this increment's.

  • producer batching. The Go client batches by default — 10 ms BatchingMaxPublishDelay, 1000 messages, 128 KiB — so a synchronous Send measures the batch delay unless batching is disabled; the baseline disables it for the per-message benchmarks and keeps it for the batched ones. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/producer.go:141-165. One broker entry therefore holds several messages, which is what makes the batch-index acknowledgement rules below matter.
  • message size. The broker advertises its maximum message size during the connection handshake and the client falls back to the 5 MiB default when it does not, so payload limits are negotiated per connection rather than fixed by the client. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/internal/connection.go:337-342. The client surfaces the negotiated figure nowhere, so this driver reads maxMessageSize from the administrative API at open instead.
  • retry topics and transactions. Dead-letter and retry topics are a client-side policy (ConsumerOptions.DLQ, DLQPolicy), not a broker feature, and transactions are supported by the Go client but must be enabled on both the client and the broker. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/consumer.go:69-101,183-185; pulsar/client.go ClientOptions.EnableTransaction. A consumer with RetryEnable subscribes to two topics, and pulsar-client-go refuses Seek and SeekByTime on a multi-topic consumer. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/consumer_impl.go:139-199,745-786.
  • ordering. Key_Shared subscriptions keep per-key order only while the consumer set is stable: a new consumer takes over hash ranges, and messages already delivered to the previous owner may be redelivered out of order relative to the new owner's, so ordering claims must be scoped to a stable subscription. Verified against: Pulsar Key_Shared documentation. AllowOutOfOrderDelivery=false makes Pulsar BLOCK a reassigned range instead, which is what this driver sets. Adding partitions rehashes every key onto a different partition, which ends the promise whatever the subscription type. Verified against: TestCriticalPartitionExpansion.
  • no client acknowledgement timeout. v0.21.0 has no AckTimeout option — the field the Java client still has was removed — and Pulsar's broker redelivers an unacknowledged message only when the consumer disconnects. An unsettled delivery therefore never comes back while the consumer holds its connection. It is why Config.AckTimeout is this driver's own deadline and why FeatureExtendLease is EmulatedVolatile. Verified against: grep -r AckTimeout over pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 finds nothing.
  • batch-index acknowledgement. ConsumerOptions.EnableBatchIndexAcknowledgment makes the client put an acknowledgement set in the frame; the broker honours one only when its own acknowledgmentAtBatchIndexLevelEnabled is true, and Apache Pulsar's default is false. Without the option, the client holds an individual acknowledgement back until every index of the entry has been acknowledged. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/consumer_partition.go:549-595, pulsar/ack_grouping_tracker.go:148-183.
  • nil and empty bodies are distinguishable. pulsar-client-go sets the message metadata's null-value flag for a nil payload and the consumer reports it, so the distinction survives without an envelope. It is the only broker in this repository where that is true. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/producer_partition.go:727-729,778-780; pulsar/consumer_partition.go:1373-1395.
  • delayed delivery is the dispatcher's. Pulsar's delayed-delivery tracker belongs to the Shared and Key_Shared dispatchers; an Exclusive or Failover subscription receives a delayed message as soon as it reaches the topic. Verified against: Apache Pulsar's delayed-message documentation.
  • partitionProducer.failTimeoutMessages outlives a closed producer. It is started when SendTimeout > 0 and exits only when its one-shot timer next fires AND the producer is closing, so a closed producer leaks one goroutine for up to one SendTimeout. goleak in this repository ignores it by name. Verified against: pulsar-client-go v0.21.0 pulsar/producer_partition.go:238-240,940-952.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
A portable topic is the local name of a Pulsar topic:

persistent://<Config.Tenant>/<Config.Namespace>/<Config.TopicPrefix><topic>

Config.Domain chooses persistent (the default) or non-persistent.

Two forms are accepted and the difference is deliberate:

  • a topic carrying :// is taken as a fully qualified Pulsar topic and validated as one. It is how a caller reaches another tenant or another namespace, and the only way to name a non-persistent topic from a persistent client;
  • anything else is the local name inside the configured namespace.

A short name containing a slash is refused rather than read as tenant/namespace/topic, which Pulsar itself would accept. A deployment that configured a tenant and a namespace has said where its topics live, and a name that silently escaped that would put one tenant's messages in another's. An empty topic is refused too: with a prefix configured it composes to the prefix alone, which is a legal topic every caller who forgot to name one would share (found by FuzzPulsarNaming).

There is no escaping and no rewriting. A name segment holds letters, digits and -, _, =, :, .; anything else is refused, because a mapper that transformed an illegal character would fold two portable topics onto one Pulsar topic and one subscription would receive another's messages. Pulsar's -partition-N suffix is refused for the same class of reason: a handle opened on it sees a fraction of the topic with no indication that it has.

A portable subscription is a Pulsar subscription: a named, durable cursor every consumer of that name shares. It takes the topic grammar, because Pulsar builds the retry and dead-letter topic names out of it (<topic>-<subscription>-RETRY).

A topic carrying a regular-expression metacharacter — `* ? [ ] ( ) | ^ $ + \ { }

docs.title: >— is a **pattern** and opens a regex subscription;.` is deliberately not
docs.text: one of them, because it is an ordinary character in a Pulsar topic name and orders.eu is a name. A pattern is qualified with the configured namespace before it reaches the client, because Pulsar matches the pattern against the whole topic name.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
One producer per topic, cached on the backend and reference-counted, so two publishers on one topic share it and the last one to close closes it.

mode What it waits for ConfirmNone the client has admitted the publication (SendAsync returned). The outcome still reaches the driver's health state and counters, because a publication whose failure nobody can see is a lost message with no evidence ConfirmAccepted Producer.Send has returned the broker's send receipt ConfirmDurable the same round trip. On a persistent topic the send receipt is given after the entry has been written to the configured write quorum of bookies, so the two modes are the same boundary here and both are durable. On a non-persistent topic there is no durable boundary at all and ConfirmDurable fails at construction

PublishAsync is Producer.SendAsync, and its native callback is the specification's done: there is no goroutine per message and no completion pool of this driver's. PublishBatch is one SendAsync per message and one wait for every callback, which is what lets the producer's own batching put them in one entry — Pulsar has no "publish these together" verb, and the *BatchError is index-aligned with the input. Flush is Producer.FlushWithCtx.

ProducerQueueIsFull is backpressure, not a failure. The driver sets DisableBlockIfQueueFull, so a full producer queue is answered rather than waited on, and the answer is CodeBackpressure: the message was never admitted, so the outcome is certain and the specification gives the core a mode for exactly this. Mapping it to CodeUnavailable would make a caller's retry policy hammer a broker that is keeping up. ClientMemoryBufferIsFull is the same thing measured in bytes.
