Refused before any I/O, naming the reason: a per-message TTL (Pulsar's is a namespace policy), a priority (Pulsar's PriorityLevel is a consumer's), a de-duplication key (Pulsar de-duplicates by (producer name, sequence number)), an explicit partition (a Pulsar partition is the producer router's choice), a delay longer than pulsar.MaxDelay, and a message larger than the advertised maximum.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
ConsumerOptions.MessageChannel is the fetch seam, and its capacity is the resolved prefetch. There is no driverkit.PushAdapter: the kit's adapter turns a native callback into a bounded ring, and pulsar-client-go does not call back — it writes into a channel the caller supplies, which already is the bounded hand-off, and behind it sit the per-partition receiver queue and the protocol's own flow-control permits. A ring in front of that would be a second buffer of the same messages: twice the memory a prefetch asks for, and a delivery whose lease is running down in a queue the broker cannot see.

Fetch is one blocking wait for the first delivery and then a non-blocking drain, which is what makes FeatureBatchReceive a batch. Close selects on the source's own channel, because pulsar-client-go's Close does not close the message channel the caller supplied.

DeliveryInfo carries the concrete topic (never the pattern a wildcard subscription named, and never the retry topic a redelivered message came back through), the partition with its Has flag, the received time, the emulated lease's expiry, Redelivered, and the attempt count.

The attempt count adds two of Pulsar's counters. RedeliveryCount is the broker's and counts how many times this message was pushed again; RECONSUMETIMES is pulsar-client-go's and counts hops through the retry topic, which are republications, so the broker's counter starts again at zero for each of them. A driver that read only the broker's counter would report attempt 1 on every delivery of a message that had been round the retry topic five times, and a MaxAttempts policy above it would never fire. pulsar-client-go's own system properties are stripped on decode, so a message that came back through the retry topic carries the headers its publisher set and no others.

A delivery that cannot be decoded is negatively acknowledged rather than acknowledged — there is no settlement that means "this is not a message I can read", and acknowledging it would discard somebody's message — and the failure surfaces as Backend.Undecodable() and a health transition.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
Portable Pulsar Ack Consumer.AckID, grouped by the client's acknowledgement-grouping tracker AckBatch a loop over Consumer.AckID. pulsar-client-go v0.21's AckIDList discards every per-partition error that is not an AckError, so a failed batch would read as settled; the grouping tracker still coalesces the frames Nack (requeue, no delay) Consumer.NackID; the client asks the broker to redeliver after Config.NackRedeliveryDelay Nack (requeue, delay) Consumer.ReconsumeLater when Config.RetryEnable is on — a republication to the retry topic with the delay as a DeliverAfter — and an in-process hold when it is not Nack (drop) AckID. The specification calls it destructive and it is: Pulsar's only way to make a message go away without a destination is to mark it consumed Reject (dead letter) the client's dead-letter router, reached by pushing the message's reconsume count past Config.MaxAttempts — the same route a message exhausted by redelivery takes. Refused with ErrUnsupported when no destination is configured Extend a store to the driver's deadline. There is no frame: see the lease below NackBatch a loop. Pulsar has no batched negative acknowledgement, and the driver says so rather than presenting a loop as a round trip

The settlement boundary depends on Config.AckWithResponse. With it off — the default, and pulsar-client-go's — an acknowledgement is handed to the client's grouping tracker and sent within AckGroupingMaxTime, and Ack returns once the client has taken it. With it on, every acknowledgement is a round trip the broker answers and Ack returns when the answer arrives.

Every local check happens before anything is written. Pulsar redelivers a message under the same (ledger, entry, batch index), and the broker accepts an acknowledgement for it from any consumer of the subscription that holds it — so an acknowledgement written for a delivery a later one has superseded would settle the work that replaced it, which is the specification's "lets a stale ack settle a later redelivery". There is no verb that asks "do I still hold this?", so the driver refuses: a delivery a redelivery superseded, or one past its lease guard, answers ErrLeaseLost and writes nothing. Backend.Stale() counts the refusals, and a driver whose Stale is zero under a workload that overruns its deadlines is not checking the lease.

docs.title: Batched entries
docs.text:
One Pulsar entry usually holds several messages and an acknowledgement names an entry. AckRules is the truth table, and two of its five rows lose messages:

identifier carries the client's bitmap client sends an acknowledgement set broker honours one what an acknowledgement settles — (entry holds one message) — — that message yes no — nothing, until every index is acknowledged; then the entry yes yes yes the named index yes yes no the whole entry, siblings included no — — the whole entry, siblings included

Both bad rows are guarded. The driver keeps the identifier the consumer handed it for the delivery's whole life and never rebuilds one — an identifier put through Serialize and DeserializeMessageID is indistinguishable through the MessageID interface and settles the entry — and Config.EnableBatchIndexAck requires Config.AdminURL, with Open refusing it against a broker whose acknowledgmentAtBatchIndexLevelEnabled is false. A settlement the rules cannot make safely is answered ErrNotSettleable, which leaves the message to be redelivered rather than destroying its siblings.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Config.SubscriptionType decides every claim, and nothing else does. It is why the subscription type is the conformance report's profile: two subscription types are two capability tables.

OrderedByKey OrderedByPartition OrderedGlobally ConsumerGroups ScheduledPublish Shared (default) unsupported unsupported unsupported native native Key_Shared (AllowOutOfOrderDelivery=false) conditional unsupported unsupported native native Exclusive conditional native conditional unsupported unsupported Failover conditional native conditional conditional unsupported
  • Shared promises nothing. Pulsar hands a Shared subscription's messages to whichever consumer has permits, so there is no order of any kind — not per key, not per partition, and not even with one consumer, because a negative acknowledgement puts a message back behind the ones that followed it.
  • Key_Shared sends every message of one key to one consumer and delivers them in publication order, and AllowOutOfOrderDelivery is false so Pulsar blocks a reassigned hash range rather than handing it over early. Two things still end the promise and neither is under the driver's control: a consumer joining or leaving moves hash ranges, and adding partitions rehashes every key onto a different partition, after which a key's older and newer messages are in two partitions with no order between them. A client configured for Key_Shared also gives its producer the key-based batcher, and that is a correctness requirement rather than tuning: Pulsar dispatches an entry to one consumer, and with the default batcher one entry holds several keys — so the subscription would have to send one consumer an entry holding another's keys and the per-key claim would be false for every key that shared an entry.
  • Exclusive and Failover deliver each partition's entries to the single active consumer in the order they were written. On a non-partitioned topic that is the whole topic's order, which is why OrderedGlobally is conditional rather than unsupported; on a partitioned one it is per partition, and adding partitions rehashes every key. Failover's second consumer is a standby that receives nothing until the active one goes away, which is why its ConsumerGroups claim is conditional rather than native; Exclusive refuses a second consumer outright with ConsumerBusy.

A negative settlement reorders by construction on every type: the message comes back after the ones behind it.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
Two different delays, and they are not the same mechanism.

  • A delayed publication (mq.Delay, mq.PublishOptions.DeliverAt) is ProducerMessage.DeliverAfter / DeliverAt, held by the broker's delayed-delivery tracker. FeatureScheduledPublish is native — except on a client configured for Exclusive or Failover, where Pulsar's tracker does not apply and the message would arrive at once. The driver refuses the schedule there rather than making one that does not happen , and the capability table says unsupported.
  • A delayed negative settlement (mq.NackDelay) is either Pulsar's retry topic or an in-process hold:
  • with Config.RetryEnable, Consumer.ReconsumeLater republishes the message to the retry topic with the delay as a DeliverAfter and acknowledges the original only once the republication is stored, so a failed republication never loses the message. FeatureDelayedRedelivery is native, and the attempt count survives the hop in RECONSUMETIMES. The cost is that the consumer is then multi-topic, and pulsar-client-go refuses a seek on one: FeatureSeekByTime becomes unsupported.
  • without it, the driver holds the unsettled delivery in this process for the delay and then negatively acknowledges it. FeatureDelayedRedelivery is EmulatedVolatile: the hold is lost with the process, after which the message comes back at the next disconnection rather than at the time asked for. Backend.HeldDelayedNacks() is how many are waiting.

The hold is the source's one scheduler — one timer per source over a list bounded by the prefetch, never a timer per delivery — and it is the same scheduler that sweeps the lease.

pulsar.MaxDelay (30 days) bounds both. Pulsar's delayed-delivery tracker holds an in-memory index entry per delayed message, so a very distant delivery time is a broker-side leak rather than a schedule.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Config.DeadLetterTopic and Config.MaxAttempts are pulsar-client-go's DLQPolicy. The client publishes the message to the dead-letter topic and acknowledges the original only once that publication succeeded, so the specification's "a failed dead-letter publish never acknowledges" is the library's own rule here.

It fires on its own once a message has had MaxAttempts deliveries — that path happens inside the client and never reaches this driver — and an explicit Reject reaches the same router at once, by pushing the message's reconsume count past MaxAttempts. Backend.DeadLettered() counts only the explicit ones, because the other path is below this driver's view.

Without a destination there is no claim and no route. FeatureDeadLetter is advertised only when Config.DeadLetterTopic is set, and Reject is otherwise refused with ErrUnsupported: a driver that invented a destination would destroy a message the caller believed was routed. mq.WithDeadLetter — the core's publish-then-acknowledge emulation — needs one thing from this driver, and did not get it until the route's five provenance headers are under mq.ReservedHeaderPrefix, which Representable refused outright, so every dead-letter publication failed before any I/O. Those five keys are now admitted and nothing else under the prefix is.

Config.MaxAttempts without a destination is refused at construction, because Pulsar would route the message to a topic this driver never named and the caller would find neither the message nor the reason.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
A header is a Pulsar property. Properties are a map[string]string, which imposes five losses, and each of them is something iqmq's portable envelope can carry:

why a header value that is not valid UTF-8 a property is a protobuf string a header key that is not valid UTF-8 the same a repeated header key a map holds one value per key a message key that is not valid UTF-8 ProducerMessage.Key is a string a message key that is empty but not nil pulsar-client-go writes the partition key only when it is non-empty, so an empty key arrives as no key at all — and the specification makes nil and empty observably different

MetadataNativeStrict refuses all five before any I/O, naming the field. MetadataAdaptive wraps exactly the messages that need it, and MetadataPortableEnvelope wraps every message. The two key cases are the ones driverkit.Envelope.Needed cannot express — the inventory has no word for a message key at all — so the driver asks its own Representable and takes a second envelope in the portable mode for them.

Header order is the sixth loss and the one without a flag: a map has none, so two different keys come back in an arbitrary order. FeatureNativeHeaders is native with a note saying so, and MetadataPortableEnvelope is what keeps the order.

A nil body and an empty one survive natively: Pulsar has a null-value flag in its message metadata and pulsar-client-go sets it for a nil payload. It is the only broker in this repository where the distinction needs no envelope.

Message.ID and the typed properties travel as reserved properties under the specification's iqmq- prefix (iqmq-id, iqmq-content-type, …). A caller's own header under that prefix is refused rather than renamed. Properties.CreatedAt is Pulsar's EventTime plus an iqmq-created marker: a Pulsar message that carries no event time arrives with the Unix epoch rather than the zero time, so a decoder without the marker would invent a creation time of 1970 for every message that carried none. The time round-trips as an instant and not with its location — Pulsar's event time is milliseconds since the epoch and the envelope's is nanoseconds, so a CreatedAt comes back in UTC.

Limit Where it comes from MaxMessageBytes the broker's own maxMessageSize, read from the administrative API at open, falling back to Pulsar's documented 5 MiB default. The figure is negotiated per connection in the binary protocol and pulsar-client-go surfaces the negotiated value nowhere, so an administrative lookup is the only route MaxDelay pulsar.MaxDelay, this driver's own bound MaxBatchMessages, MaxBatchBytes Config.BatchingMaxMessages / BatchingMaxSize, when set MaxLease not advertised. The lease is this driver's own and has no maximum — an extension is a store to a deadline in this process — so Config.AckTimeout is a default rather than a bound, and the specification forbids reading an advertised limit as anything but a bound

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
pulsar-client-go owns the dial loop: the client reconnects inside its own connection pool, with its own backoff, and re-creates its producers and consumers. This driver therefore does not use driverkit.Reconnector — a second dial loop over a client that already has one would be two policies for one connection.

Ping itself is the cheap check and creates no topology. With Config.AdminURL it is the broker's own health endpoint, which touches no topic. Without one it is a partitioned-topic metadata lookup for a topic this backend already has a handle on, or Config.PingTopic; with neither it reports ErrUnsupported, because on a namespace with automatic creation a lookup for a topic nobody created is exactly the hidden topology creation forbids.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
Four windows, and each of them is a duplicate rather than a loss.

  1. Between a delivery and its acknowledgement. A consumer that disconnects makes every unacknowledged message of its subscription available again at once, which is also how this driver's Close gives work back: the specification's "requeues or abandons everything it has handed out" is the broker's here and not a loop of this driver's.
  2. Between an acknowledgement being grouped and being sent, when Config.AckWithResponse is off. A process that dies inside AckGroupingMaxTime loses the acknowledgement and not the message.
  3. A delayed negative settlement held in this process, when Config.RetryEnable is off. The hold is lost with the process.
  4. The emulated lease. Config.AckTimeout is the driver's deadline: it tracks each delivery's, hands the message back with a negative acknowledgement one LeaseGuard before it, and refuses a settlement that arrives afterwards. Config.DisableAckTimeout removes it and gives Pulsar's own behaviour — an unsettled delivery that never comes back while the consumer holds its connection.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
pulsar://broker:6650/tenant/namespace/prefix?admin=http://broker:8080&subscriptiontype=keyshared
pulsar+ssl://broker:6651/acme/billing?trustcerts=/etc/ssl/ca.pem

With pulsar+ssl:// the broker is verified against trustcerts when it is given and the system roots when not, insecureskipverify=true turns verification off, and authname=tls presents the provider's client certificate. A DSN sets no Config.TLS: pulsar-client-go uses a *tls.Config exactly as given and reads none of those beside it, which is why a programmatic Config.TLS is refused together with TLSTrustCertsFilePath, AuthName "tls" or an InsecureSkipVerify it does not carry itself.

authname=tls needs the pulsar+ssl:// scheme and is refused without it. A client certificate is presented during a TLS handshake, pulsar-client-go picks the transport from the scheme alone, and on pulsar:// there is no handshake at all: measured against a TLS port that requires a certificate, the port saw no handshake and zero certificates, so the authentication silently did nothing. The mechanisms that travel in the CONNECT frame instead — Token, and authname "oauth2", "basic" or "athenz" — are accepted on either scheme.

Both schemes are registered: pulsar+ssl:// is what Pulsar's own tooling and service URLs use, so a driver that accepted only pulsar://?tls=true would refuse the connection string an operator already has. The path is the tenant and namespace, with an optional third segment for the topic prefix — Pulsar's own service URLs put the namespace in the topic, so there is no established spelling to copy and this is the natural place.

Every parameter is listed on ParseDSN. A parameter this driver does not have is a construction error naming it, not a setting nobody notices was ignored. Prefetch is deliberately absent: it is the core's, resolved from the consumer configuration, and a DSN that set it would be a second owner of one number. receiverqueuesize is a different number — the per-partition buffer behind the prefetch, which defaults to the prefetch.

Credentials (Config.Token, Config.AuthParams) are dsn.Secret, so String(), LogValue() and DSN() render the redaction and never the plaintext. Config.DSN() deliberately does not round-trip: a rendering that round-tripped would be a rendering that carried the credential.

Config.Logger is where pulsar-client-go's own logging goes, and nil discards it. The library's default is logrus.StandardLogger(), which writes every reconnection and every lookup to the standard error of a process that never asked for it; a library does not own its host's log stream.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
• Batching means an entry holds several messages, and an acknowledgement names an entry. If you reach past this driver to Consumer.AckID with an identifier you serialised, you will acknowledge every sibling in the batch. See AckRules.
  • Config.EnableBatchIndexAck needs the broker to agree. Apache Pulsar's acknowledgmentAtBatchIndexLevelEnabled is false by default, and a client that sends an acknowledgement set to such a broker acknowledges the whole entry with no error anywhere. The driver refuses the option at open unless the administrative API says the broker honours it.
  • Config.RetryEnable costs you Seek. The consumer is then subscribed to two topics, and pulsar-client-go refuses a seek on a multi-topic consumer.
  • A delayed publication does nothing on an Exclusive or Failover subscription. The driver refuses it, which is the honest answer and may surprise a caller whose client is configured for those types but only publishes.
  • FeatureReplay is the namespace's, not the topic's. Pulsar's default retention is zero, under which an entry every subscription has acknowledged may be deleted at once. A deployment that wants to replay a topic sets a retention policy; Backend.SetNamespaceRetention is the typed extension that does it, and the conformance harness calls it.
  • StartAt is a seek, and a seek moves an existing subscription's cursor. The specification describes a start position as where a subscription with no committed position begins, and this driver cannot tell the two apart without the administrative API — so a StartAt on a subscription that already has a position rewinds it.
  • pulsar-client-go leaks one goroutine per closed producer for up to one SendTimeout. partitionProducer.failTimeoutMessages exits only when its one-shot timer next fires and the producer is closing, and the library offers no way to wake it. goleak in this repository ignores it by name.
  • A non-persistent topic has no durable boundary. ConfirmDurable fails at construction, and FeatureDurableStorage is not advertised.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text:
All four are in drivers/pulsar/critical_test.go, against the in-process model, and each was watched failing under a deliberate mutation before it was made to pass.

Test What it holds TestCriticalKeySharedOrdering one key goes to one consumer and arrives in publication order, and a Key_Shared client's producer asks for the key-based batcher — without which an entry holds several keys and the per-key claim is false for all of them TestCriticalPartitionExpansion after the partition count grows, the producer discovers it and publishes the same key to a different partition, the consumer receives from the new partitions, every delivery says which partition it came from, and the per-key ordering claim is not native TestCriticalSubscriptionModes the four types' ordering, consumer-group and scheduled-publish claims, what a second consumer of one subscription is, and the refusal of a delayed publication on the two types that would deliver it at once TestCriticalBatchIndexAckDoesNotSettleASibling the disqualifier in Pulsar's clothing, in four parts: the client holds a partial batch's frame back; an identifier with no batch bookkeeping is refused; a broker that ignores an acknowledgement set is refused at open; and a broker that honours one settles the named index alone

Beside them, race_test.go covers this repository's recurring defect class in the two routes this driver adds: a delayed negative settlement placed while the source is closing (three thousand rounds), and an asynchronous publication admitted while the sink is closing — which is a race the suite actually found.

docs.title: rabbitmq (AMQP 1.0 profile)
docs.text:
Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Owner: iqmq maintainers

This page is the AMQP 1.0 profile for RabbitMQ 4.0 and newer (drivers/rabbitmq/amqp10, the second arm). The AMQP 0-9-1 driver has its own page, rabbitmq.md, and the two are never silently substituted for one another — the specification says so, and the list under "Known gotchas" is why.

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The profile is built on drivers/amqp10, the shared AMQP 1.0 core, which wraps github.com/Azure/go-amqp. It has no native baseline of its own yet: the amqp091 baseline in benchmarks/native-baselines/ measures the other protocol's client against the harness's rabbitmq image, and a number taken from it is not comparable with this profile's, because the confirmation boundary is reached by a different mechanism.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary (none yet) github.com/Azure/go-amqp github.com/Azure/go-amqp@v1.7.0 would be: the peer's accepted disposition on a durable quorum queue

The version gate is this driver's headline behaviour. Open refuses a broker that reports anything below RabbitMQ 4.0 with mq.ErrUnsupported naming both versions, and nothing falls back to AMQP 0-9-1. RabbitMQ 4.0 is the first release that speaks AMQP 1.0 natively; on 3.13 it is a plugin whose feature set, address syntax and settlement behaviour differ, so a driver that accepted either would be claiming this profile's behaviour for something else. A peer that reports no version satisfies the gate no more than an old one does: the specification makes "the peer did not say" distinct from any claim, and a gate that read an unknown version as new enough would gate nothing.

A peer whose product connection property names something that is not RabbitMQ is refused before the version is read. That is the same rule pointed the other way: Apache Artemis reports version 2.44, which satisfies no RabbitMQ gate, and it also auto-creates an address from an attach — so a client pointed at the wrong endpoint would not fail, it would create an address literally called /exchanges/orders/orders and publish into it for ever. A peer that names no product at all is accepted, because an AMQP 1.0 proxy in front of RabbitMQ need not forward the broker's properties; it still has to satisfy the version gate.

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building this profile; re-verify when a pin moves. The unverified list is under "Known gotchas" and is longer than this one, because nothing in this increment ran against a broker.

  • native AMQP 1.0 from 4.0. RabbitMQ 4.0 is the first release with a native AMQP 1.0 endpoint; earlier releases need rabbitmq_amqp1_0, a plugin with different addressing and different settlement behaviour. Verified against: RabbitMQ 4 release notes; internal/rabbit/version.go's MinBrokerAMQP10.
  • the address form. A publication addresses an exchange and a routing key together as /exchanges/<exchange>/<routing-key>, and a consumer addresses a queue as /queues/<queue>, because an AMQP 1.0 link carries one address and has no second field for a routing key. Each segment is percent-encoded. Verified against: RabbitMQ AMQP 1.0 address-format (v2) documentation; internal/rabbit/protocol/amqp10.go.
  • no topology from an address. The endpoint creates no exchange, queue or binding: an attach to a queue that does not exist closes the link with amqp:not-found. Verified against: RabbitMQ AMQP 1.0 documentation ("queues and exchanges must be declared out of band"); asserted by TestProfileShape's AutoCreates row.
  • quorum queues. A quorum queue replicates to a majority and fsyncs before the broker answers a publication, so an accepted disposition from one is a much stronger boundary than one from a classic queue and must not be compared with it. Verified against: RabbitMQ quorum-queue documentation; the same fact docs/drivers/rabbitmq.md records for the confirm on the other protocol.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
The same topology as the AMQP 0-9-1 driver, derived by the same code (internal/rabbit), so that a caller who moves between the profiles finds one topology rather than two wearing one name. What differs is how a name becomes an address.

Portable RabbitMQ AMQP 1.0 address topic orders exchange <prefix>orders, routing key orders sink /exchanges/orders/orders topic orders + subscription workers durable quorum queue <prefix>orders.workers source /queues/orders.workers a rejected or expired message exchange <queue>.dlx, queue <queue>.dlq, fixed routing key dlq (the queue's own policy; this driver publishes no copy) a wildcard pattern a binding on a topic exchange not expressible — ErrUnsupported

Three things about it are load-bearing.

Every segment is percent-encoded, and that is not tidiness. The address format is path-shaped and a routing key is arbitrary caller-supplied text: the topic orders/eu is a legal RabbitMQ name, and an unescaped / in it would end a segment, so the link would attach to the exchange orders with the routing key eu — somebody else's traffic, with the publisher none the wiser. The escaping is internal/rabbit/protocol's, shared by both arms, and FuzzRabbitAMQP10Address holds it to being reversible: decoding each segment returns the name that went in, byte for byte, which is what makes two different names unable to reach one address.

Nothing is declared, and nothing can be. Config.Declare exists and is refused with a message naming the three things that can declare topology (drivers/rabbitmq, the management API, rabbitmqctl). The field is kept rather than omitted so that a caller who moves from the other driver finds it and is told why, instead of not finding it and assuming the topology appears. Config.Names is how a provisioner asks for the names it has to create.

A wildcard subscription is refused with ErrUnsupported, not with an invalid-name error. A wildcard is a binding pattern and a receiving link addresses a queue, so the pattern is not expressible in the portable Topic at all; the refusal has to be ErrUnsupported because that is what the specification's negative probe for FeatureWildcardSubscribe reads, and a refusal carrying CodeInvalidArgument would leave the claim unverified in both directions.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
A publication is one transfer on a sending link attached to the topic's exchange path.

Mode Boundary ConfirmNone the transfer is sent pre-settled: the frame leaves, no disposition is coming, the call costs no round trip. Local admission, which the specification says may be lossy ConfirmAccepted the peer's accepted disposition for this transfer. It is the AMQP 1.0 equivalent of basic.ack on a confirm channel, per transfer and with no mode to enable ConfirmDurable the same accepted disposition, on a durable quorum queue, where RabbitMQ returns it once the message has been written to a majority of the queue's replicas. A classic-queue configuration defines no durable boundary, so a publisher that asks for ConfirmDurable against one fails when its sink is opened

There is no confirm mode and therefore no. Every transfer on an unsettled link gets its own disposition, so the per-message, windowed and asynchronous strategies have no equivalent here: there is nothing to select. What a caller sizes instead is the link's credit (Config.Credit), which is also what basic.qos became. It is simpler and it is not free — there is no cumulative form to amortise a batch across, which is why this driver's conformance fidelity figure is lowered to 5,000 messages from the 100,000.

Two publication outcomes deserve naming because a caller acts on them differently from an ordinary failure.

  • Unroutable. RabbitMQ releases a transfer that an exchange routes nowhere. The shared core's generic table reads released as the peer declining to act — retryable, because another node might take it — and on RabbitMQ that is wrong in the way that costs the most: the message is gone, the topology is what is wrong, and retrying throws away another copy. So this profile adds one rule to the table and it is the only one it adds: on OpPublish, released is CodeNotFound, not retryable, not ambiguous. That is the same answer the specification's "Mandatory + NotifyReturn = Rejected" gives on the other protocol, reached by a different mechanism — and it is a rule the core could not have written, because only the profile knows that this broker's released means unroutable rather than "try another node".
  • Ambiguous. A transfer that has left the socket and whose disposition never arrived may have been accepted. The specification makes reporting that as a definite failure a disqualifier, so it is CodeAmbiguous with Ambiguous set. A peer's own rejected or released disposition stays definite, which is the half a driver that marked everything ambiguous would destroy.

A target address whose exchange does not exist is a third thing again: the broker closes the link with amqp:not-found, which maps to CodeNotFound.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
A source is a receiving link attached to /queues/<topic>.<subscription> with a credit window. No link is attached when the source is opened: the first fetch attaches one, so a broker that is down at that instant is a retryable fetch failure rather than a consumer that could not be constructed.

Credit is the AMQP 1.0 answer to basic.qos, and it is the only window this protocol has, because it grants no lease at all. An unsettled delivery is this receiver's for as long as the link lives, so DeliveryInfo.LeaseExpires is the zero time, FeatureExtendLease is unsupported, and there is no DeadlineExtender anywhere in the module. Config.Credit (default 100) caps what one source may hold whatever prefetch the core resolved.

DeliveryInfo.Attempt is the AMQP header's delivery-count plus one — the header counts redeliveries, so Attempt is 1 on a first delivery. That is a protocol field of the header section rather than RabbitMQ's x-delivery-count header extension, which means the count needs no queue argument and no header a publisher must be careful not to overwrite. Whether a classic queue's redeliveries reach it is not verified here; the capability note says so and the claim withdraws on one.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
Settlement is one disposition each, and the mapping is more direct than basic.ack/basic.nack/basic.reject: modified carries delivery-failed and undeliverable-here as separate flags, so a nack says what it means rather than leaving it to a broker's reading of a requeue.

action AMQP 1.0 outcome Notes Ack accepted final when the frame is written under the default receiversettle=first; confirmed by the broker under second, at a round trip each Nack (requeue) released does not count the attempt, which is the protocol's own distinction and not an emulation Nack (requeue, delay) — ErrUnsupported, and settles nothing. RabbitMQ has no AMQP 1.0 spelling for "hold this back" Nack (drop) rejected AMQP 1.0 has no destroy outcome, so on a queue with a dead-letter exchange a dropped message reaches <queue>.dlq rather than being destroyed. The safe direction, stated rather than hidden Nack (dead-letter) rejected needs Config.DeadLetter; without it the action is refused with ErrUnsupported and settles nothing, rather than rejecting the message into nowhere Extend — there is no lease and no frame; FeatureExtendLease is unsupported a delivery this driver could not decode modified{undeliverable-here} so that it goes back to the queue without this link being handed it again

A settlement the driver cannot perform is refused before the delivery's slot moves, which is the specification's "returns ErrUnsupported and settles nothing": a driver that took the slot first and then discovered it could not honour the action would leave the delivery unsettleable for ever.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
A queue is FIFO, so one queue's messages are delivered in the order the exchange routed them, and FeatureOrderedByPartition is claimed at group scope. Nothing above one queue is ordered, and FeatureOrderedGlobally is not claimed.

Ordering by key is not claimed on this profile, and the other one claims it conditionally. On AMQP 0-9-1 the routing key is a field of every basic.publish, so WithKeyAsRoutingKey makes one key's messages reach one queue. Here the routing key is part of the link's address, so it is fixed when the link attaches and cannot vary per message. Honouring the option would need the anonymous-terminus extension — a sender attached to a null target with each message's to property naming the address — which the shared core does not implement: a sink is bound to one address for its lifetime. Config.KeyAsRoutingKey is therefore refused rather than accepted and ignored.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
None, in either direction, and neither absence is a limitation of this module's code.

A delayed redelivery has nothing to express it: a modified disposition makes the message available again at once, and RabbitMQ has no annotation that holds one back. The other profile builds one from a TTL queue that dead-letters back or from the delayed-message plugin; the first needs topology this profile cannot create, and the second is unverified — see below. NackOptions.Delay is refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O and settles nothing.

A scheduled publication has nothing either. The rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange plugin reads an x-delay header on AMQP 0-9-1, and which AMQP 1.0 section and key that becomes — a message annotation, an application property, neither — is not verified here. forbids claiming a capability that cannot be proved, so the profile carries no delay rule at all and PublishOptions.Delay and DeliverAt are refused before any I/O. The alternative would be worse than a refusal: a message sent without its delay is delivered immediately to a publisher who asked for it in an hour.

Limits.MaxDelay is therefore left unknown rather than advertised as zero, which the specification makes a different answer.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
<queue>.dlx and <queue>.dlq, derived from the queue's own name by internal/rabbit, with a fixed dead-letter routing key: RabbitMQ dead-letters a message with its original routing key unless the queue names a replacement, so a fan-out-shaped DLX with one binding would route a message keyed orders.eu nowhere at all.

The route is the queue's own x-dead-letter-exchange policy and not something this driver publishes to. A rejected disposition is what reaches it. Config.DeadLetter records that whoever declared the queues set the policy, which is what makes FeatureDeadLetter claimable; without it the claim is withdrawn and a dead-letter Nack is refused.

The profile supplies no DeadLetterAddress to the shared core, deliberately. Supplying one would make the core publish a copy itself and then reject the original — one more copy, one more window, and a second dead-letter mechanism for a broker that already has one.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
A portable header is an AMQP application property, and that choice is interoperability rather than taste. RabbitMQ converts between its two protocols by mapping application properties to and from the AMQP 0-9-1 field table, so a header this driver put in the message-annotation section would be in a different place on the other protocol — and a message published through one RabbitMQ driver would read back without that header through the other. The profile's AnnotationPrefix is therefore empty, even though RabbitMQ's own controls live under x- annotations: a caller who needs an annotation reaches past the portable API.

An application-property value is typed, so a header value that is not valid UTF-8 travels as an AMQP binary and comes back byte for byte — FeatureBinaryHeaders at native level, as on the other profile, by a better mechanism. A repeated key cannot travel at all, because application-properties is a map: MetadataPortableEnvelope and MetadataAdaptive carry one in the envelope and MetadataNativeStrict refuses it.

Under MetadataAdaptive a message is also enveloped when its body begins with the envelope's own magic (IQMQ and a version byte), even if the native fields could carry everything else: the adaptive read side decides from the body, so a native body that looks like an envelope would be claimed as one and refused. A non-iqmq consumer therefore reads such a body wrapped.

No limit is advertised, and that is the rule rather than an omission:

Limit Advertised Why MaxMessageBytes unknown, unless the peer declares a maximum on the sender link RabbitMQ's max_message_size is a server setting rather than a connection property, so a number here would be a guess MaxHeaderBytes unknown see below MaxDelay, MaxLease unknown there is no delay and no lease; advertising zero would read as "every lease expires immediately"

The header ceiling is the one worth explaining. An AMQP 1.0 application-property key is a string with no 255-byte limit, while an AMQP 0-9-1 field-table key is a shortstr — so a key longer than 255 bytes published through this profile cannot be read through the other one. That is an interoperability ceiling rather than a limit this driver enforces, and makes an advertised limit something a caller may rely on, so it is stated here instead of advertised.

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
The driver owns its dial loop, which the specification requires: go-amqp does not reconnect, so the shared core's supervisor notices the connection's death, bumps the connection generation before anything else happens, invalidates every delivery token, and re-dials with jittered backoff (Config.Backoff, full jitter by default). Config.ReconnectAttempts of zero means "until the client is closed"; a positive value makes the backend go Degraded and stay there with every operation answering CodeUnavailable.

There is no topology to restore, which is the one way a reconnection here is simpler than on the other profile: this driver declared nothing, so a reconnection re-attaches links and nothing else. Config.Addrs is a failover set tried in order and re-tried from the first — AMQP 1.0 is one long-lived connection, and a client that spread its links over two nodes would have half its deliveries die with each.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
From the transfer that delivered the message until the disposition the broker acted on. A process that stops inside it — a crash, a link that detached, a connection that died — leaves the delivery unsettled, and detaching an AMQP 1.0 link returns everything unsettled on it to the queue, where RabbitMQ hands it to whichever consumer of that queue is next. So a handler may run twice for one message and the application has to absorb the duplicate; DeliveryInfo.Attempt is delivery-count plus one, so the second delivery says so.

Under the default receiversettle=first a settlement is final when the disposition frame is written, so an Ack costs no round trip and a link that died immediately afterwards leaves the message redeliverable — at-least-once behaving as advertised. Under second the peer confirms the settlement, at a round trip each, and a failed settlement changes class with it: first means the broker never got it (a lost lease, so the message is coming back), second means it may have (an unknown outcome, sticky for ever).

A settlement whose link belongs to an older connection is refused with ErrLeaseLost and never written to the wire. That is the disqualifier in AMQP 1.0's clothing: a peer that reuses delivery ids across an attach would otherwise apply the disposition to whatever took the delivery's place. The guard is the shared core's; this profile adds nothing that could defeat it, and "Driver-specific critical tests" below is what holds that.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
Config is RabbitMQ's vocabulary; the protocol's own knobs are the shared core's types rather than copies of them, because a translation table between two identical enumerations is a table that can drift. Config.CoreConfig and Config.Profile are the conversion and are this module's real API.

Field What it is Addrs amqp://host:port, amqps://host:port or bare host:port; a failover set Username, Password SASL credentials; Password is a dsn.Secret, so no rendering can carry it Vhost the virtual host, which reaches RabbitMQ as the OPEN frame's hostname under vhost: HostName that field outright, for a deployment that needs a particular one. Refused together with Vhost Prefix prepended to every exchange and queue name; internal/rabbit's, so both profiles agree ExchangeType, QueueType, DeadLetter, MaxPriority assertions about a topology this driver did not create. Each moves a capability claim Declare refused; see "Topic / subscription mapping" KeyAsRoutingKey refused; see "Ordering" Credit the link credit ceiling of one source: this protocol's basic.qos and its only window ReceiverSettle first (default) or second; see "At-least-once window" SenderSettle mixed (default) is the only mode under which one sink serves both ConfirmNone and ConfirmAccepted NonDurable publish with the AMQP durable flag clear. Inverted so that the zero Config publishes durable Backoff, Reconnect*, NoReconnect the dial loop Publisher, Consumer the AMQP 1.0 link controls — link name, properties, capabilities, source filters — which is this profile's escape hatch where the other has ConsumeArgs Clock, Hooks the injected clock and the callbacks

The DSN scheme is rabbitmq+amqp10, which is neither rabbitmq (the AMQP 0-9-1 driver's) nor amqp10 (the core's generic profile's). A registry in which one scheme could open either profile would make a connection string ambiguous about which capability table the caller gets, and the tables really differ. Registering both RabbitMQ modules with one registry is the supported arrangement.

rabbitmq+amqp10://user:password@host:5672,host2:5672?vhost=acme&queuetype=quorum&deadletter=true

This profile's parameters are vhost, prefix, exchangetype, queuetype, deadletter, maxpriority and credit; the shared core's — sasl, tls, insecureskipverify, insecureplainsasl, containerid, hostname, sendersettle, receiversettle, idletimeout, maxframesize, maxsessions, maxcredit, maxpending, nondurable, dialtimeout, operationtimeout, writetimeout, backoff, reconnectbase, reconnectmax, reconnectgrowth, reconnectattempts, noreconnect — pass through unchanged. Anything else is a construction error naming it, which is how a copied declare=true or confirm=windowed is caught rather than ignored.

A DSN has no path. On AMQP 0-9-1 the URL's path is the virtual host; AMQP 1.0 has no virtual-host field, so there is nothing for a path to mean and one is refused rather than ignored.

Config.DSN() renders the configuration with the credential replaced by the redaction marker and everything else intact, and the result parses back — which is what makes it usable for the thing it exists for, a log line a person then pastes.

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text: This section is the one that earns its place on this page, because moving between the two RabbitMQ profiles is a change of behaviour and the specification forbids doing it silently.

docs.title: What a caller who moves from drivers/rabbitmq loses
docs.text:
1. Native request/reply. amq.rabbitmq.reply-to is an AMQP 0-9-1 extension with no AMQP 1.0 form. A reply address still travels in the reply-to property, which is the portable emulation, not a native mechanism.
  2. A delayed redelivery and a scheduled publication. Both are refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O. A delayed Nack settles nothing, so the message stays the broker's — it is not dropped, and it is not requeued without the delay either.
  3. Ordering by key. Config.KeyAsRoutingKey is refused: the routing key lives in the link's address.
  4. A wildcard subscription. Refused with ErrUnsupported: the pattern is a binding, and a link addresses a queue.
  5. The confirm strategy. There is no confirm mode, so the specification's three strategies have no equivalent. What a caller tunes is Config.Credit.
  6. mandatory and basic.return. An unroutable message is released by the broker. The outcome a caller sees is the same as the other profile's — CodeNotFound, not retryable — but the mechanism is a disposition rather than a returned message, so there is no returned message to inspect.
  7. Declaring topology, and Client.Admin. Both are refused. The exchange, the quorum queue and the dead-letter route have to exist before a link attaches, or the attach is answered with amqp:not-found. RabbitMQ 4 does have an AMQP 1.0 management extension over a /management node; this profile does not implement it and does not claim FeatureAdmin.
  8. At-most-once delivery. Not claimed: every receiving link is attached unsettled and every delivery is settled explicitly. (The AMQP 0-9-1 arm's shared protocol table claims it natively; whether that driver really offers a no-ack consume path is its own page's question.)
  9. The virtual host moves. It is a vhost parameter, not the DSN's path, and it reaches the broker as the connection's hostname. A copied rabbitmq://host/acme string is refused rather than silently landing in the default virtual host.
  10. A header key over 255 bytes stops being portable between the two profiles. It is legal here and cannot become an AMQP 0-9-1 field-table key.

The specification marks this profile itself (verify) and marks x-delivery-count → Attempt (quorum queues) (verify). Nothing in this increment ran against a RabbitMQ broker — every test runs against a scripted AMQP 1.0 peer — so the honest split is:

Every unverified item above is either Unsupported in the capability table or a Conditional claim whose condition is stated. None of them is a capability this driver advertises.

docs.title: Smaller ones
docs.text:
• Stream queues are not addressed. RabbitMQ 4 exposes streams over AMQP 1.0, and their semantics — offsets, filters, a consumer that reads a log rather than competing for messages — are not this profile's. Config.QueueType has quorum and classic only.
  • SASL none is in the enumeration and RabbitMQ does not want it. It is the shared core's value for a peer that offers no SASL layer, which is what this module's own scripted test peer is.
  • Config.MaxPriority forces a classic queue. RabbitMQ refuses x-max-priority on a quorum queue, so a prioritised subscription gives up the quorum queue's durable confirmation boundary and its attempt count. The conformance harness makes that trade explicitly for the priority scenario.
  • The conformance suite needs the topology created first. This profile declares nothing, so a run against an empty broker fails at the first attach. ConformanceHarnessWithProvisioner takes the step that creates each scenario's Need; ConformanceHarness is that with no provisioner, for an endpoint an operator has already prepared.

docs.title: Maturity & tier
docs.text: See the pinned client version and the module tests when evaluating this driver.

docs.title: Driver-specific critical tests
docs.text: All of them run against the scripted peer and none needs a container.

docs.title: rabbitmq
docs.text: Maturity: Experimental · Tier: 2 · Driver: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/rabbitmq

docs.title: Client & version policy
docs.text:
The native baselines for this driver live in benchmarks/native-baselines/ and measure the clients below against the harness's rabbitmq image (make bench-native CLIENTS="amqp091"). A driver number is only comparable with a baseline taken from the same client version, broker version and confirmation boundary, so the pins move together; each baseline's package comment records the settlement boundary it measures as well.

Baseline Client Pinned version Confirmation boundary amqp091 github.com/rabbitmq/amqp091-go github.com/rabbitmq/amqp091-go@v1.15.0 publisher confirm (basic.ack) on a durable quorum queue

docs.title: Verified facts (the API contract)
docs.text:
Checked while building the native baselines; re-verify when a pin moves.

  • Client. github.com/rabbitmq/amqp091-go is the AMQP 0-9-1 client maintained by the RabbitMQ core team, and it is the client the baseline measures; RabbitMQ 4 also speaks AMQP 1.0 natively, for which github.com/Azure/go-amqp is the Go client. Verified against: amqp091-go v1.14.0 README.md; RabbitMQ 4 release notes.
  • Quorum queues. Quorum queues count redeliveries in the x-delivery-count header and fsync before returning a publisher confirm, so a confirmed publish to a quorum queue is a much stronger boundary than a memory-durability publish and must not be compared with one. Verified against: RabbitMQ quorum-queue documentation; verified by the amqp091 baseline's declaration.
  • Delayed messages. Delayed publishing needs the rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange plugin, which is not part of the official image: the harness builds hack/images/rabbitmq-delayed for it, and a driver must detect the exchange type rather than assume it. Verified against: hack/images/rabbitmq-delayed/Dockerfile; conformance/harness/brokers.go RabbitMQDelayed.

docs.title: Topic / subscription mapping
docs.text:
iqmq RabbitMQ topic a durable exchange, topic-typed by default (Config.ExchangeType), named <Prefix><topic> subscription a durable quorum queue named <Prefix><topic>.<subscription>, bound to the exchange with the topic as the routing key dead-letter destination the exchange <queue>.dlx and the queue <queue>.dlq, bound with the fixed routing key dlq — or, with Config.DeadLetterTopic, another topic's exchange, so that the destination is consumable through mq.Client delay bucket (ttldlx) the queue <queue>.delay.<milliseconds> delayed exchange (plugin) the exchange <exchange>.delayed, type x-delayed-message reply address amq.rabbitmq.reply-to, which is not a topic at all — see Known gotchas

The naming is derived once, in internal/rabbit, and is shared with drivers/rabbitmq/amqp10: a caller who moves between the two protocol profiles finds the same exchange, the same queue and the same dead-letter route, because two independent derivations would be two topologies wearing one name.

Three naming rules are narrower than the broker's, and each one exists because the alternative is a silent failure.

  • A topic may not contain * or #, and a wildcard SUBSCRIPTION is not supported either. The topic is both the exchange's name and the routing key a subscription's queue is bound with, and on a topic exchange those two characters are the binding pattern's wildcards — so a topic literally called orders.# would bind a subscription's queue to every routing key under orders, and one subscription would receive another topic's messages. A wildcard subscription is refused for a deeper reason: a topic maps to its OWN exchange, so orders.* would have to bind one queue to every exchange whose name matches, including exchanges created later, and a binding names one exchange. FeatureWildcardSubscribe is therefore unsupported and a pattern topic is answered with ErrUnsupported rather than with an invalid argument, which is what makes the negative claim provable. Mapping every topic onto one shared exchange WOULD make it work and was rejected: one exchange is one authorisation boundary, so every publisher would need write on every topic. The pattern power is still reachable inside one topic through Config.KeyAsRoutingKey and a binding of the operator's own.
  • A subscription may not contain ., because the queue is <topic>.<subscription> and a dotted subscription makes that name ambiguous to read and to parse back.
  • dlq, dlx and delay are reserved subscription names. <topic>.dlq is the dead-letter queue of every other subscription of that topic, so a consumer of the dlq subscription would be consuming somebody else's dead-letter queue with every name valid and nothing refused.

Nothing is declared unless Config.Declare says so, which is the rule. With declaration off, a publisher's open performs a passive exchange.declare and a consumer's a passive queue.declare, so a topology nobody created is an error at open rather than a client that succeeds and moves no messages.

docs.title: Publish path & confirmation boundary
docs.text:
A publication is a basic.publish on a channel in confirm mode. There is one channel per publisher, which is what makes each publisher's confirm window, its basic.return correlation and its channel exceptions its own.

ConfirmationMode what this driver waits for ConfirmNone the frame has been written to the socket. Nothing has confirmed anything. ConfirmAccepted (the default) basic.ack for this publication's delivery tag. On a quorum queue that means the message was written to a majority of the queue's replicas; on a classic non-durable queue it means the broker holds it in memory. ConfirmDurable the same basic.ack, and the sink REFUSES TO OPEN unless the queues are durable quorum queues, so that the boundary really is a durable one.

How the publisher waits is and is chosen by Config.ConfirmKind:

kind outstanding blocks basic.return needs a token a channel close leaves ambiguous permessage (the default) 1 yes no 1 publication windowed ConfirmWindow (64) yes yes the whole window async ConfirmWindow (64) no yes the whole window

FeatureBatchPublish is therefore claimed as an emulation and not as an absence: there is no batch frame and a batch still works, because the core loops and this driver confirms each publication. The level follows the confirm's durability — emulated-durable on a quorum queue, emulated-volatile on a classic one — and FeatureAtomicBatchPublish stays unsupported, because there is no frame that could be all-or-nothing.

Two publication outcomes deserve naming because a caller acts on them differently from an ordinary failure.

Rejected. With Config.Mandatory — off by default; see Known gotchas — a publication no queue is bound for comes back as basic.return and is then acked. The broker took the message and threw it away, which the specification makes a rejection: CodeNotFound, not retryable, because retrying will throw it away again. It almost always means the topology is wrong.

The default is the interesting decision and it is worth stating plainly. With mandatory ON, a publication to a topic nobody has subscribed to FAILS — a stricter contract than the portable one, and one on which a publisher has to know the subscription topology, which no other driver in this repository asks of a caller. iqmq's own conformance kit publishes to unsubscribed topics in four scenarios and requires every one to succeed. It is still worth turning on in a deployment that provisions its own topology, because the broker's behaviour without it — discard an unroutable message and ack it — is the most common way a RabbitMQ deployment loses messages.

Ambiguous. A channel that closes with confirms outstanding leaves every one of those publications unresolved: the broker may have taken them all and may have taken none. The driver reports CodeAmbiguous with Ambiguous set, which the specification requires and names a settlement disqualifier to get wrong.

docs.title: Consume path
docs.text:
A source is a basic.consume on its subscription's queue, on a channel of its own, with basic.qos(prefetch) sent BEFORE the consume — the broker applies a prefetch to the consumers started after it, so the other order would be an unbounded consumer for the channel's whole life.

The topology is declared when the source is opened and the basic.consume happens on the first Receive. RabbitMQ pushes: a consume makes the broker start sending, and every message it sends counts against the prefetch and starts its acknowledgement deadline whether or not anybody has asked for a delivery — a lease ticking against a caller who has not called Receive. Two broker behaviours fall out of the lateness and neither is recoverable inside an eagerly-attached consumer, because both belong to the broker's QUEUE rather than to the client's buffer:

  • a message expires by its own TTL while it is QUEUED, and not after it has been pushed to a consumer's buffer;
  • a priority queue serves the most urgent message it HOLDS, and no priority can overtake a message that has already left the queue.

Both were failing their conformance probes against the pinned container with the message already sitting in this driver's ring. The declaration stays eager, because a publication made between opening a consumer and its first Receive has to reach a queue that exists. The cost is one round trip on the first Receive, which a caller was going to spend waiting for a delivery anyway.

RabbitMQ pushes. The SPI asks for a pull Fetch, and driverkit.PushAdapter is what makes the two meet: a bounded ring whose capacity is the prefetch, so a broker delivering faster than the application consumes is answered by the library's delivery goroutine blocking rather than by unbounded memory.

The prefetch is the ring's capacity, the token table's size and the per-delivery storage's length, all three. The broker will not hold more than prefetch unsettled deliveries at one consumer, so anything larger would be storage nothing can fill and anything smaller a ring the broker can overrun. That bound is the BROKER's count, not the driver's, and the two differ for an instant: a settlement writes its frame before it frees its token slot, and the broker answers the frame by sending the next delivery at once, so a delivery can arrive while the table is still full. The driver waits for the slot rather than leaving that delivery unsettled — which, on a live channel, RabbitMQ would never give back.

A consumer the BROKER cancels — which is what a queue.delete under a live consumer produces — is reported as CodeNotFound and not ErrClosed: the caller closed nothing, and the queue is gone.

docs.title: Ack / nack / extend mapping
docs.text:
AMQP 0-9-1 Ack basic.ack{multiple=false} Nack, requeue, no delay basic.nack{requeue=true} — back to the HEAD of the queue, marked redelivered Nack, requeue, with a delay The message is re-published and the original acknowledged. See Delays. Nack, dead-letter basic.nack{requeue=false} onto the queue's x-dead-letter-exchange; ErrUnsupported when Config.DeadLetter is off, and NOTHING is settled Nack, drop basic.ack. See Known gotchas — this is the mapping that looks wrong. Extend not offered. A delivery's lease here is the channel's lifetime, so there is nothing to extend and nothing to expire.

Settlement is serialised per channel and INDIVIDUAL. basic.ack{multiple=true} would settle every delivery up to a tag, which is safe only when deliveries are settled in the order they arrived; the core makes no such promise, and the specification asks for "individual acks unless cumulative proven safe". It is not proven, so FeatureBatchSettle is Unsupported.

Two independent guards stand between a settlement and the wrong delivery, and both are necessary because a delivery tag is per CHANNEL and restarts at 1 on a new one.

  1. driverkit.TokenTable's generation, bumped at the moment a channel is lost, refuses every settlement for a delivery handed out before then with ErrLeaseLost.
  2. The delivery's own channel identity is compared with the source's current one.

The second is latent: every route by which this driver replaces a channel invalidates the token table first, so the generation catches every currently reachable case, and the guard is kept for the change that adds a fourth route and forgets the invalidation. FuzzRabbitTagSettlement and TestCriticalStaleTagNeverSettlesOnANewChannel are the evidence, and both check that a refused settlement sends NO FRAME: a driver that sent the ack and mapped the broker's refusal would, on a broker that did not refuse it, have acknowledged a delivery the caller never saw.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
A queue is FIFO, and that is the whole of what this broker guarantees.

  • FeatureOrderedByPartition is native: one queue's messages are delivered in the order they were enqueued, and one consumer settling them in order sees them in order.
  • FeatureOrderedByKey is Unsupported by default and Conditional with Config.KeyAsRoutingKey. With the key in a header the broker cannot read it, so two messages under one key can be interleaved by two publishers or spread across a consistent-hash exchange's queues. With the key AS the routing key one key's messages reach one queue, and the subscription's queue then binds with #.
  • FeatureOrderedGlobally is Unsupported. Nothing above one queue is ordered.

A nack with requeue=true puts the message back at the HEAD, so ordering survives a retry; a DELAYED redelivery does not, because the message is re-published and loses its position.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
The specification. AMQP 0-9-1 has no delayed redelivery, so the specification's NackDelay(d) is built out of what the broker has, and there are two ways:

ttldlx (the default). The message is re-published into a queue whose x-message-ttl is the delay and whose x-dead-letter-exchange routes back, and then the original is acknowledged. It works on every RabbitMQ and needs no plugin. It costs:

  • one queue per (target, bucket) pair. A queue's TTL is fixed at declaration, so one queue serves one delay. The delay is rounded UP to the first bucket of Config.DelayLadder, which defaults to twenty-one buckets doubling from 100 ms to a little over a day.
  • a rounding error. The specification makes a delay a MINIMUM, so rounding up is allowed and rounding down is not; with the doubling ladder the worst case is one tick short of twice the requested delay. A deployment whose delays are known exactly should name them in Config.DelayLadder and gets both an exact delay and one queue per delay it really uses.
  • two broker hops instead of one.

plugin. The message is re-published to <exchange>.delayed with an x-delay header and the broker holds it for exactly that long. One exchange serves every delay, the delay is exact and there is one hop. It needs rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange, which is not part of the official image: hack/images/rabbitmq-delayed/ builds one that has it, and the plugin only supports the RabbitMQ minor it was built for.

Two properties of the mechanism a caller has to know:

  • The order is publish, wait for the confirm, then ack. A crash between the publish and the ack leaves both copies, which is a duplicate and inside the at-least-once; a crash between an ack and a publish would lose the message entirely. Waiting for the confirm is what makes the first option safe, and it is why a CONSUME channel is in confirm mode in this driver.
  • A delayed redelivery restarts the BROKER's attempt count, and the driver carries its own across the hop. The redelivery counter belongs to the queue entry and a re-publication is a new entry, so without help every delayed redelivery would report attempt 1 for ever and a "dead-letter after three attempts" policy would retry a poison message without end. The driver writes the attempt it knows into the reserved header x-iqmq-attempt when it parks the copy and reads it back on the redelivery, taking the LARGER of what the broker counted and what it carried — a max and not a sum, because a requeue of the parked copy raises the broker's count too.

A delay queue dead-letters to the default exchange with the subscription's queue name as the routing key, and not to the topic's exchange. A delayed redelivery belongs to the one subscription that nacked the message; the topic exchange would fan it out as a duplicate to every other subscriber.

Scheduled PUBLICATION (mq.Delay on a publish) needs the plugin and is Unsupported without it. The TTL-and-dead-letter mechanism can delay a redelivery to one queue; a scheduled publication has to reach every subscription of a topic, which would need a delay queue per subscription and would deliver at a different moment to each.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text:
Config.DeadLetter declares the exchange <queue>.dlx and the queue <queue>.dlq and points each subscription's queue at them through x-dead-letter-exchange and x-dead-letter-routing-key. It needs Config.Declare.

A delivery the consumer cannot decode is the one message the driver settles on its own. With Config.DeadLetter on, it is rejected onto the dead-letter route. With it off, the driver re-publishes the message to the back of its own queue, waits for the confirm and then acknowledges the original, so nothing is destroyed and the messages behind it keep arriving. Leaving it unsettled would hold one basic.qos slot per message and stop the consumer once prefetch of them arrived, and a plain requeue would put it back at the head of a classic queue where the consumer would receive nothing else. The re-published copy is a new queue entry, so a quorum queue's delivery limit never catches it: it keeps going round until a dead-letter route or an operator takes it.

Config.DeadLetterTopic sends the dead letters to another TOPIC instead, and it exists because the derived destination is a QUEUE: an operator finds <queue>.dlq by name from the queue it belongs to, which is the right default, and nothing can consume it through mq.Client. The dead-letter destination is a place a caller reads from, so a deployment that wants to read its own failures names a topic and every subscription of that topic receives them. The derived queue is then not declared at all: the queues behind the named topic belong to that topic's own subscriptions, and declaring both would give a rejected message two destinations. The named topic has to exist — RabbitMQ drops a dead-lettered message whose dead-letter exchange is missing, silently — so the driver declares its exchange.

Three details, each of which is a way to lose a dead-lettered message:

  • The dead-letter exchange is declared BEFORE the queue that names it. RabbitMQ accepts a queue whose x-dead-letter-exchange does not exist and then drops every dead-lettered message silently.
  • x-dead-letter-routing-key is a fixed word (dlq) and not the message's own key. RabbitMQ dead-letters a message with its original routing key unless the queue names a replacement, so a dead-letter exchange with one binding would route a message keyed orders.eu nowhere at all.
  • The dead-letter queue has no dead-letter route of its own. A dead-letter queue that dead-lettered would send an unprocessable message round a cycle; a message there is meant to sit until somebody looks at it.

Without a dead-letter route, a nack asking for one returns ErrUnsupported and settles NOTHING, so the delivery stays settleable and the core's own policy takes over.

docs.title: Headers & limits
docs.text:
Headers map to the basic.properties field table. It carries a byte array natively, so a binary header value survives byte for byte; what it cannot do is carry a REPEATED key, because it is a map. The specification promises duplicate-preserving headers, so:

MetadataMode a repeated header key MetadataNativeStrict (the default) refused with ErrUnsupported before any I/O MetadataPortableEnvelope carried, inside iqmq's envelope in the body MetadataAdaptive carried, and only the messages that need it are enveloped MetadataLenientDrop dropped, and counted

the typed properties map to the fixed basic.properties fields — content type, content encoding, correlation id, reply-to, message id, timestamp — except CausationID, which has no slot and travels in the table under x-iqmq-causation.

Four table entries are this driver's own and are refused as caller headers. None of them ever reaches an application: a round trip through this driver adds no header the publisher did not set.

entry what it carries why the protocol has no slot x-iqmq-key the message key a key is bytes and a routing key is a shortstr, and using the key as the routing key changes the ROUTING (Config.KeyAsRoutingKey) x-iqmq-pub the publisher-confirm correlation token basic.return carries the returned message and not its delivery tag, so with more than one publication outstanding there is nothing else to match on x-iqmq-nil that the published body was NIL rather than empty a body is a sequence of content frames and a zero-length body is no frames, which is what a nil body is too; the specification makes the distinction observable x-iqmq-attempt the attempt count across a delayed redelivery the broker's counter belongs to the queue ENTRY and a parked copy is a new entry

An empty body comes back as a non-nil zero-length slice and a nil body comes back nil, in both directions, which is what the carrier is for. The reading is guarded on the body's length so that a native publisher cannot forge a body away.

Limits:

limit advertised MaxHeaderBytes 255 — the protocol's own, because a field-table key is a shortstr MaxMessageBytes not advertised. RabbitMQ's max_message_size is a server configuration readable through the HTTP management API, and the specification makes an unadvertised limit distinct from one advertised as zero. A driver that guessed would be advertising a guess. MaxHeaderCount, MaxBatchMessages, MaxBatchBytes, MaxLease not advertised: the protocol bounds none of them and the lease is the channel's lifetime MaxDelay the delay strategy's ceiling: the ladder's largest bucket, or a little under twenty-five days for the plugin

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text:
This driver owns its dial loop, which the specification requires and which the client library can also do itself since v1.14 (see Client & version policy). A reconnection is four things in this order, and a failure in any of them is answered by another attempt rather than by a half-restored client:

  1. Dial. Config.Addrs in order; the first that answers wins. The backoff is driverkit.Reconnector's under Config.BackoffPolicy, which defaults to full jitter and NOT to the specification's Auto — whose current winner is none, i.e. no delay at all, which the specification's "reconnect with backoff (never busy-spin)" forbids. Since driverkit.ReconnectConfig.Policy's own zero value is a jittered policy too, so this default agrees with the helper's rather than working around it. A caller who really wants no delay sets backoff.None and gets it; what they cannot get by accident is a busy dial loop.
  2. Watch. The connection's own close and its connection.blocked notifications are registered before anything is published.
  3. Replay the topology. Everything this client declared is declared again, in the order it was declared. The durable exchanges and quorum queues survive, and the DELAY queues may not — x-expires deletes an unused one — so a client that did not replay would come back unable to delay a redelivery.
  4. Re-attach the handles. Every sink gets a new confirm-mode channel and every source a new consumer with its prefetch. It happens inside the dial step, so Health.Ready means the client can work again.

Before any of that, and at the moment the loss is noticed: every sink resolves the publications it was holding as Ambiguous, and every source bumps its token generation and discards the deliveries it had buffered. A settlement carrying a token from before then reports ErrLeaseLost.

A CHANNEL exception is narrower and is repaired by the HANDLE itself, once and without a loop, on both sides: a consumer attaches a new channel and a new basic.consume, and since a publisher does the same. Once, because a channel exception that repeats is a topology problem the caller has to fix and a driver that re-attached for ever would hide it behind an empty Fetch or a publisher that never publishes. Whichever route notices the loss first CLAIMS it, so a channel the supervision loop has already taken responsibility for — every channel on a lost connection — is repaired by the dial loop and not twice.

connection.blocked — RabbitMQ under a memory or disk alarm — is reported through health and the reconnect hook, because it is the only explanation a stalled publisher has: the broker stops READING from a publishing connection, so a publication blocks in the socket with no error and no timeout of its own. Backend.Blocked reads it directly.

docs.title: At-least-once window
docs.text:
The window is from the broker's basic.deliver to this driver's basic.ack. A process that stops inside it — a crash, a channel close, a connection loss — leaves the delivery unacknowledged, and RabbitMQ redelivers it to whichever consumer of that queue is next. So a handler may run twice for one message, and the redelivery accounting is the core's rather than this driver's.

For a PUBLICATION the window is from the basic.publish to its basic.ack. A publication whose confirm never arrives is Ambiguous, and a caller that retries it may duplicate the message; one whose channel closed is the same.

A delayed redelivery adds a second window of its own: the parked copy is published and confirmed before the original is acknowledged, so a crash between them leaves both. That is the duplicate-over-loss choice and it is deliberate.

FeatureAtMostOnce is withdrawn. basic.consume has a no-ack mode and this driver never uses it — every consumer settles explicitly, which is what a Settler is for — so a claim of at-most-once delivery would be a claim about a code path that does not exist. The AMQP 1.0 profile withdraws it for the same reason.

docs.title: Config & DSN
docs.text:
rabbitmq://user:password@host:5672,host2:5672/vhost?declare=true&deadletter=true&deadlettertopic=parked&mandatory=true&confirm=windowed&confirmwindow=64

Config is the whole surface; the DSN is the same settings in a connection string, with strict unknown-parameter rejection — a parameter this driver does not have is a construction error naming it rather than a setting nobody notices was ignored. Config.DSN() renders a redacted round trip: everything but the password parses back.

The settings that change behaviour rather than tuning it:

field default what it decides Declare off whether this driver creates its own topology DeadLetter off whether a dead-letter route exists at all DeadLetterTopic empty, so the destination is the derived <queue>.dlq whether the dead letters land somewhere mq.Client can consume QueueType quorum replication, and whether x-delivery-count exists ExchangeType topic whether a wildcard subscription is expressible Mandatory off whether an unroutable publication is Rejected or discarded and acked KeyAsRoutingKey off whether ordering by key is expressible ConfirmKind auto → permessage DelayKind auto → ttldlx DetectDelayPlugin off whether the driver probes for the plugin and upgrades MaxPriority 0, so priority is Unsupported whether mq.Priority means anything, and it forces a CLASSIC queue BackoffPolicy full (jitter), explicitly and NOT the specification's auto how the dial loop waits between attempts

docs.title: Known gotchas
docs.text:
mandatory is OFF by default, and it is worth turning on. Without it the broker DISCARDS an unroutable message and acknowledges it, so a publisher with a misconfigured topology succeeds for ever while nothing arrives — the single most common way a RabbitMQ deployment loses messages. Config.Mandatory turns it on and it costs one returned frame on the failing path and nothing on the working one.

The default is off because ON is a stricter contract than the portable one: a publication to a topic nobody has subscribed to fails, so a publisher has to know the subscription topology, which no other driver in this repository asks of a caller. Set it in a deployment that provisions its own topology and publishes only to topics it created; leave it off in a library that does not know its caller's topology.

Nack(NackDrop()) is a basic.ack. Drop destroys the message, and basic.ack is the frame that removes a message from a queue without routing it anywhere; basic.nack{requeue=false} would DEAD-LETTER it whenever the queue has a route, which is the opposite of destroying it.

A reply address is not a topic. amq.rabbitmq.reply-to is a routing key the broker minted, on the default exchange, under the reserved amq. prefix that the shared naming refuses to derive from. A responder publishes a reply to Delivery.Properties.ReplyTo, which reaches this driver as a topic — so the sink recognises a reply address (rabbitmq.IsReplyAddress) and routes around the naming layer entirely. It is the one special case in the publish path.
