if err := chacha.Register(suites); err != nil { … }
ring, err := encrypt.NewRotatingKeyring(suites, encrypt.SuiteChaCha20Poly1305, key32, "2026-09")

The primitive is in golang.org/x/crypto, which the root module may not import, so it lives in its own module, x/encrypt/chacha. The root defines the suite — its envelope byte, its 32-byte key, 12-byte nonce and 16-byte tag, its name — and the module supplies the construction by registering it in an encrypt.Suites you build and pass to the keyrings that name the suite. Nothing is registered process-wide, so the code that builds a keyring decides which primitive a suite byte means. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • A consumer whose keyrings were built without chacha.Register still parses an envelope naming the suite, and reports ErrNoKey for it — a deployment problem, and the same answer a consumer missing a rotated key gets — rather than calling it a corrupt message.
  • SuiteOf never picks it. A 32-byte key is AES-256-GCM unless you name SuiteChaCha20Poly1305.

It is held to exactly what the AES suites are held to: the package x/encrypt/encrypttest holds the envelope, tamper, key-id, wrong-key, additional-data, rotation and header-binding cases, and all three suites run that one function — including rotation onto ChaCha20-Poly1305 from AES-GCM, which is how a deployment adopts it. The contract itself has been watched failing: x/encrypt runs it against deliberately broken AEADs (one that skips the tag check, one that ignores the additional data, one that ignores the nonce) and requires the right case to fail for each. A known-answer test pins the suite to RFC 8439 §2.8.2's vector.

Its nonce is 12 bytes, like GCM's, so the birthday bound below applies unchanged. XChaCha20-Poly1305's 24-byte nonce would lift it and is not offered: it is not an RFC, and an envelope suite byte is a promise to every other implementation that reads one.

docs.title: Nonces are random, never counters
docs.text:
Two messages sealed under one key with one nonce leak the exclusive-or of their plaintexts and let an attacker forge tags. A counter is unsafe the moment two processes or two restarts share a key, which is the normal case for a message queue, so every nonce comes from crypto/rand.

The cost is the birthday bound: at a 12-byte random nonce a single key should seal fewer than roughly 2³² messages before rotation. RotatingKeyring is what makes that possible without a restart — a key's safe message count is a property of throughput, not of your deploy cadence — and it keeps every previous key for opening, because a keyring that forgets an old key makes every message still inside the topic's retention permanently unopenable.

docs.title: What this does not protect
docs.text:
The specification requires this list and it is the most useful section on this page.

  • Headers and properties. Only the body is sealed. Topic, partition key, message id, correlation id, reply-to, content type, timestamps and every application header travel in clear. A schema-id or a user-email header is as public as it was.
  • Size. The ciphertext is the plaintext's length plus a constant, so the length is disclosed exactly. Where the length is the secret, padding is needed and this package does none.
  • Timing, rate and volume. When a message was published, how many there were, and to which topic, are visible to anyone who can see the broker.
  • Replay. An envelope has no sequence number and no expiry. A sealed body captured and re-published opens perfectly, because it is authentic. Replay is a delivery-semantics problem: see x/inbox.
  • Ordering and deletion. An attacker who can write to the broker can drop, delay or reorder sealed messages. Each one that arrives is authentic, and nothing here says any arrived.
  • Forward secrecy. A leaked key opens every message it ever sealed, including those already in retention. Rotation bounds the blast radius going forward and does nothing for the past.
  • The key itself. Keyring is an interface so the key can live in a KMS or an HSM. StaticKeyring holds it in process memory, where a core dump or a debugger finds it.

docs.title: A precise note on tamper detection
docs.text:
No tampered envelope opens — the test flips every bit of every byte and truncates at every length. But that is true without the header-in-AAD binding as well, and the tamper test was found passing with the binding removed.

The reason is structural: every field in this header either selects the key (suite, key id) or moves an offset (the key-id length), and GCM's tag is computed under the key over the nonce and ciphertext. A tampered header therefore yields the wrong key or a shifted nonce, and the tag catches it either way.

So the binding is defence in depth today and load-bearing tomorrow. An envelope's additional data is frozen the moment the format ships, and the first future header field that neither selects the key nor shifts an offset — a flag describing how to interpret the plaintext, an algorithm parameter — would be forgeable for ever if the header were not already covered. TestTheHeaderIsInTheAuthenticatedData asserts the binding directly and is the check that fails when it is removed.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
RequireSealed is off by default so a topic can be migrated without dropping the messages already in it. Switch it on once the migration is done: a consumer that accepts unsealed bodies accepts anything a publisher without the key can write, which makes the encryption an integrity control an attacker can opt out of.

Config.AdditionalData is empty by default. Binding it to the topic would be stronger and is a footgun: a dead-lettered or forwarded message arrives on a different topic, and the dead-letter consumer — the reader that most needs to see it — would then be unable to open anything.

docs.title: Order with compression
docs.text: Compress first, then encrypt. Encrypted bytes do not compress, so the other order simply does not compress. See x/compress for what that leaks.

docs.title: x/idempotency
docs.text:
Reduce the duplicate rate with a two-phase claim in a store beside the work.

mw, err := idempotency.New(idempotency.Config{
    Store:  redisStore,                       // or idempotency.NewMemoryStore
    Key:    idempotency.KeyFromHeader("operation-id"),
    Window: 24 * time.Hour,
})

docs.title: What it is, and what it is not
docs.text:
The claim goes in a separate store, so the claim and the work are two systems with no transaction across them. It therefore reduces a duplicate rate that was never zero. It does not remove duplicates, and no amount of configuration makes it do so — which is the honest description of every idempotency cache and is why x/inbox exists for the case where your handler writes to a database you control.

Status has three values and the middle one is the one people forget:

Status Meaning The caller StatusFirst no record; you hold an open claim must Commit or Abort StatusDuplicate a claim was committed in the window holds nothing; skip StatusInFlight somebody else holds an open, unexpired claim holds nothing; come back later

StatusInFlight is not a duplicate. The work may never have been done, and skipping it loses the message.

StatusUnknown is the zero value on purpose: a caller who forgets to look at the status gets the answer that assumes nothing.

docs.title: The window is the only real engineering choice
docs.text: Config.Window must outlast the longest redelivery the substrate can produce — a lease that expires, a rebalance, a consumer restart, an operator replaying a day — because a duplicate that arrives after the window is a duplicate that is processed. It must also be short enough that the store holds the resulting number of keys.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
When the store cannot answer, the default is to process — fail open — because the substrate underneath is at-least-once already, so processing during an outage returns the system to the guarantee it advertises rather than to a new one. The alternative turns a cache outage into a consumer that makes no progress, and a consumer that makes no progress on a broker with a max-attempts policy dead-letters everything it is sent.

An unkeyed message is processed, unguarded, and counted: a topic that mixes keyed and unkeyed messages is ordinary, and refusing them would make adding this middleware a breaking change to a running service.

Both defaults are the opposite of x/inbox's, and that page explains why.

docs.title: The in-process store is lossy by design, and counts it
docs.text:
MemoryStore is a bounded LRU: DefaultMaxEntries is 100,000 and an entry evicted to stay inside the bound is a claim that will read as StatusFirst before its window lapsed. Stats.Evicted is how many. A non-zero Evicted with a duplicate rate that matters means MaxEntries is too small, and nothing raises it for you.

It is also per process: two replicas have two stores and two independent windows, so a duplicate delivered to the other replica is StatusFirst there. x/idempotency/redisstore is the store that crosses replicas.

docs.title: x/inbox
docs.text:
Record that you processed a message in the same transaction as the side effect. This is the one way at-least-once delivery becomes effectively-once processing on every broker.

mw, err := inbox.New(inbox.Config{
    Store: myPostgresInbox,               // your database
    Key:   inbox.KeyFromHeader("operation-id"),
})
err = consumer.Run(ctx, handler, mq.WithMiddleware(mw.Wrap()))

The idea is one sentence: the record that you handled a message and the effect of handling it commit or roll back together, so there is no window in which one exists without the other.

BEGIN
  INSERT INTO inbox (message_id) VALUES ($1);   -- fails on a duplicate
  -- …the side effect…
COMMIT

See inbox and outbox for the pattern, and the extensions index for the comparison with x/idempotency.

docs.title: The condition, which the interface cannot enforce
docs.text:
Store.Once hands your function a context and runs it inside the store's transaction. If your function's side effect goes anywhere other than that database — a different database, an HTTP API, another broker — then the record and the effect are two systems again, with no transaction across them, and you have bought a slower x/idempotency.

Nothing in the type system says so. This paragraph is the only thing standing in the way, which is why it is here and in the package documentation.

docs.title: fn must not insert its own key again
docs.text:
Store.Once holds the transaction across your function. A re-entrant Once for the same key asks to insert a record that has not committed yet, which a real SQL store answers by blocking the caller on itself and MemoryStore answers by making the call wait for itself.

This is inherent to the pattern rather than an implementation limit: the point of the transaction is that nobody else sees the record until it commits, and "nobody else" includes your own second call. Reading the store, or a Once for a different key, is fine.

A function that panics has not committed. The store rolls the record back and lets the panic continue, so a runner that recovers it and redelivers the message runs your handler again rather than acking a duplicate of work that never finished.

docs.title: Both defaults are the opposite of x/idempotency's
docs.text:
That is deliberate, and it is the most useful thing to understand about this package.

When the store cannot answer, the default is to retry (OnUnavailableRetry). An idempotency store is a cache beside the work and fails open, because the substrate underneath is at-least-once already — processing during an outage returns the system to the guarantee it advertises. An inbox store is the database the work happens in: if it cannot be reached the side effect cannot happen either, so there is nothing to fail open to. Processing anyway is not "a duplicate for the duration of the outage"; it is a handler that will fail a moment later for the same reason.

OnUnavailableProcess exists for the deployment whose handler writes elsewhere — which is the case this pattern does not cover anyway.

An unkeyed message is refused (MissingKeyFail). An idempotency middleware that refused them would make adoption a breaking change to a running service, and its cost for letting one through is a duplicate. Here the cost is a side effect that is never recorded and is therefore repeated on every redelivery for ever — the failure the pattern was adopted to remove.

docs.title: The key
docs.text:
Config.Key has no default. The one failure in this package that can lose work is two distinct messages deriving one key: the second reads as a duplicate and is acked without being handled.

KeyFromHeader is right when the publisher owns the key, which is the usual case — the business operation's identifier, the same on every retry of that operation. KeyFromID is right only where Delivery.ID is the publisher's and is stable across its retries; a driver-assigned or broker-assigned id is not, and a publisher configured with the specification's IDGenerator is exactly the case it must not be used for.

Both come from x/idempotency rather than being declared again here: the problem is identical, and two copies that could drift apart would be worse than the coupling.

docs.title: Counts
docs.text: Middleware.Counts() returns Processed, Duplicate, Failed, NoKey and Unavailable. A deployment that adopts this pattern wants to know its actual duplicate rate, and Duplicate is that number.

docs.title: The memory store
docs.text:
NewMemoryStore is per process, and its "transaction" is a per-key wait — the part of a database it models. A second delivery of a key whose handler is still running waits for that handler's transaction to commit (and is then a duplicate) or roll back (and then runs); deliveries of different keys run concurrently, exactly as two transactions inserting different rows into a table with a unique index do. A waiter whose context ends stops waiting and is treated as a store that could not answer, so the delivery is retried.

It used to hold one mutex across every handler, which serialised the whole process behind its slowest handler and meant a test written against it never saw two handlers interleave — the one thing production is guaranteed to do.

It models none of the SQL, the isolation level or the durability. It refuses at its bound (ErrFull) rather than evicting, because an evicted key is a message that will be processed twice and silently turning a memory bound into a duplicate is the opposite of what this package is for.

Using it in anger — for more than tests, examples and a single process whose side effects are also in process — is the wrong store. A restart forgets every key and the record is not in the same transaction as anything, so for in-process duplicate suppression without a database x/idempotency's memory store is the right choice: a bounded LRU with a window per claim, which evicts — and counts what it evicted — rather than refusing at its bound. The inbox pattern proper wants a Store over the database your handler writes to: Once opens a transaction, inserts the key, runs your function with a context carrying that transaction, and commits. A unique violation on the insert is the duplicate.

A real inbox table is pruned by a job that deletes rows older than the broker's retention — a deletion you can reason about.

docs.title: x/outbox
docs.text:
Publish the messages your database transaction committed, and nothing else.

// In your transaction — your SQL, your handle:
//   INSERT INTO orders  …
//   INSERT INTO outbox (topic, key, headers, body) VALUES …

relay, err := outbox.New(outbox.Config{
    Store:   myPostgresOutbox,
    Publish: publishThroughYourMiddlewareChain,
    Batch:   100,
})
go relay.Run(ctx)

See inbox and outbox for why there is no ordering of a database write and a broker call that is correct, and examples/outbox-postgres for the worked Postgres version with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED against a real container.

docs.title: There is no Append on the Store interface
docs.text:
That is the design, not a gap. The append happens inside your transaction, with your own handle — a *sql.Tx, a pgx transaction, a GORM session — and an interface that took one of those would bind this package to that library.

So Store is the relay's half only: Claim, MarkSent, Release, Fail. The append is an INSERT you write, and Row plus EncodeHeaders and DecodeHeaders define the column shape so the round trip is specified rather than improvised.

docs.title: The two rules the relay must not break
docs.text:
Both are about the same thing — a row must never be marked sent unless it was really published — and both have a test named after them.

An ambiguous publication does not mark the row sent. the specification's ambiguous outcome is a publication whose acceptance is unknown. Marking it sent turns "we do not know" into "we are done", which is the only way this pattern can lose a message. Leaving it unsent produces a duplicate, which at-least-once already promised, and Stats.Ambiguous is its own counter precisely because it is the number that explains a duplicate a consumer saw.

Both halves of the surface are checked — an error carrying CodeAmbiguous, and one whose *OpError sets the Ambiguous flag — because a relay reading only one would mark half of them sent.

Only rows that were published are marked. A batch whose third row fails marks the first two and releases the rest. Marking the whole claim because the call returned is how a partial failure loses everything after the failure point.

docs.title: What the store must guarantee
docs.text:
Claim has two requirements the relay's correctness rests on, and both are SQL rather than Go:

  • Two relays must get disjoint rows, which on Postgres is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside the UPDATE that sets the lock. A store that let both claim the same row would publish it twice per pass, giving a duplicate rate set by the number of relays.
  • The lock must lapse. A relay that dies holding a claim must not strand its rows for ever, and the lapse is what turns a crashed relay into a duplicate rather than a loss. Set it to rather more than the longest publish timeout: a lock that lapses mid-flight is a duplicate, which is survivable; a lock that never lapses is a row nobody will ever send, which is not.

docs.title: Poison rows
docs.text:
A row whose body exceeds the broker's limit, or that the broker refuses as malformed or as something it cannot carry (a header NSQ has no field for, a binary attribute value on Pub/Sub), fails identically on every attempt. MaxAttempts (default 10) is compared with Row.Attempts, and a row past it that fails for one of those reasons is recorded via Store.Fail with ErrPoisonRow. Without the bound the relay spends every claim on the same unpublishable row, and with Concurrency of 1 nothing behind it is published.

A failure that is not the row's fault never makes it poison, however many claims it costs: the broker down or busy, an ambiguous publication, revoked credentials, a missing topic, or an error with no code at all. The row stays in rotation and Run backs off until the broker is back.

A store has to take that row out of rotation when Fail names ErrPoisonRow. The relay does not release a poison row, so a store that kept it claimable would hand it back each time its lock lapsed, and a claim's worth of them at the head of the table would stall the relay. Any other reason is a record of one failed attempt, and the row stays in rotation.

There is deliberately no "unbounded" setting.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Concurrency of 1 — the default — publishes in row order. Anything above 1 reorders, and this package does not pretend otherwise: two workers claiming disjoint rows finish in whatever order the broker acknowledges them. A deployment that needs per-key order and throughput partitions the claim by key hash, which is a Store concern because it is a WHERE clause.

docs.title: The message id should be the business operation's
docs.text: Row.MessageID is what the consumer's x/inbox will key on, so it must be the business operation's identifier and not a per-publication one. A row republished after a relay died carries the same id, which is exactly what lets the consumer recognise it as the same operation.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
EncodeHeaders renders headers as one opaque blob for a BYTEA or BLOB column: a count-prefixed sequence of length-prefixed key/value pairs.

It is deliberately not JSON. Headers are ordered and duplicate-preserving and a JSON object is neither, so round-tripping them through one would silently drop a repeated header and reorder the rest — which for traceparent and a multi-valued application header is a real loss.

DecodeHeaders reads a column something else wrote, so every length in the blob is a claim: the declared pair count is compared with what the blob can possibly hold before anything is allocated, each field's length is checked against what remains, and trailing bytes are ErrBadHeaders rather than ignored.

docs.title: Run reports a broken store rather than looping
docs.text:
A pass that published something does not wait before the next one — sleeping between full batches is how a relay falls behind a burst. A pass that found nothing waits Interval.

A store or publish failure is returned to the caller, who decides whether to keep going. A relay that swallowed them and looped would hide a permanently broken database behind a process that looks healthy. A cancelled context and a Close are both clean stops and return nil.

Marking rows sent, releasing them and recording a failure run on your context's values but not its cancellation, bounded at 10 seconds. A shutdown in the middle of a pass still marks the rows it already published, so they are not published again when their lock lapses. If that mark or release fails, Run returns the store's error even though your context has ended.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Three pages, in order:

  1. Quick start — publish and consume one message against the in-process engine, with no broker and no container. About ten lines.
  2. Installation — which module you need for which broker, and why there is one per broker.
  3. Then either Concepts, if you want to know what the words mean before you rely on them, or your driver page, if you already know your broker and want to know what it does about acks, ordering, delays and dead letters.

Pre-alpha

Nothing here is ready for production use. The repository is being built increment by increment against the specification, and Status is the honest list of what works, what is measured and what is open. No performance, delivery-guarantee or compatibility claim is made here without the evidence behind it.

docs.title: The shape of the API, in one paragraph
docs.text: You open a *mq.Client — from a driver's Open, or from a DSN. You ask it for a *mq.PublisherHandle bound to one topic, or publish ad hoc with client.Publish. You ask it for a *mq.ConsumerHandle bound to a topic and a subscription, and then either run a handler with consumer.Run(ctx, handler) and let the runner settle for you, or call consumer.Receive and settle each *mq.Delivery yourself. Everything else — batching, ordering, retries, dead-lettering, lease extension, middleware, typed codecs, request/reply — is an option or a wrapper over those five things.

docs.title: The four things to read before you ship
docs.text:
• Delivery guarantees — what an ack means, and why exactly-once processing is not on offer.
  • Capability negotiation — how to find out what your broker can do, at construction, instead of at three in the morning.
  • Confirmation boundaries — what nil from Publish does and does not tell you, per broker.
  • Your driver page's Known gotchas and At-least-once window sections. Every driver has both, and they are where the surprises are written down.

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
One module per driver: importing the core never pulls a broker SDK.

go get github.com/iqhive/iqmq                       # the core, standard library only
go get github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/kafka         # and one module per broker

The core module depends on the standard library and nothing else, and make stdlib-check holds it to that. Each driver brings its own client library and only its own; a program that talks to Kafka never compiles the AWS SDK.

Broker Module DSN scheme In-memory (testing, and the reference driver) github.com/iqhive/iqmq (package memory) memory://, mem:// Kafka (franz-go) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/kafka kafka:// Kafka (kafka-go) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/kafka/kafkago kafkago:// NATS Core github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/nats nats:// NATS JetStream github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/jetstream natsjs:// NATS (both profiles behind one facade) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/natsunified nats://, natsjs:// NSQ github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/nsq nsq:// Google Cloud Pub/Sub github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/gcppubsub gcppubsub:// Amazon SQS github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/sqs sqs:// SNS fan-out to SQS github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/snssqs snssqs:// RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/rabbitmq rabbitmq:// RabbitMQ (AMQP 1.0) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/rabbitmq/amqp10 rabbitmq+amqp10:// ActiveMQ Artemis and Classic (AMQP 1.0) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/activemq activemq:// ActiveMQ (STOMP) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/activemq/stomp activemq+stomp:// Redis Streams (rueidis) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/redis redis:// Redis Streams (go-redis) github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/redis/goredis opened in Go, no scheme Pulsar github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/pulsar pulsar://, pulsar+ssl:// Generic AMQP 1.0 core github.com/iqhive/iqmq/drivers/amqp10 a profile the caller supplies

A driver never reaches for a global registry. It exposes Register(dsn.Registrar) and nothing else, so a program that composes two brokers owns the registry both are registered with; see the driver selection guide.

Two rows above have no DSN scheme, and that is deliberate rather than missing. drivers/redis/goredis is the second client library behind one capability table, so a connection string cannot choose between it and drivers/redis; drivers/amqp10 is a core rather than a driver and has no capability table of its own until a caller supplies a profile. The two NATS rows overlap for the same kind of reason: the facade answers to both profile schemes, so a program registers either the facade or the two profile drivers, never both.

docs.title: The command-line tool
docs.text:
go install github.com/iqhive/iqmq/cmd/iqmq@latest

The iqmq binary links every shipped driver, so one binary talks to every broker above — the opposite trade from the library, and the right one for a tool nobody can be asked to rebuild before debugging a deployment. Start with iqmq doctor <dsn>; the CLI page documents every command, and the exit-code contract.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
No broker, no container, no Docker. The in-process engine is a real driver — the same Backend, the same runner, the same settlement state machine as Kafka — so this program exercises the actual code path and not a mock.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "sync"

    mq "github.com/iqhive/iqmq"
    "github.com/iqhive/iqmq/memory" // swap for kafka.Open / dsn.Open(ctx, "kafka://…")
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    client, err := memory.Open(ctx, memory.Config{AutoCreate: true})
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer func() { _ = client.Shutdown(ctx) }()

    consumer, err := client.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{
        Topic:        "orders",
        Subscription: "billing",
    })
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    runCtx, stop := context.WithCancel(ctx)
    defer stop()
    handled := make(chan struct{})
    var once sync.Once
    go func() {
        _ = consumer.Run(runCtx, mq.HandlerFunc(func(_ context.Context, d *mq.Delivery) error {
            fmt.Printf("order %s: %s\n", d.Key, d.Body)
            once.Do(func() { close(handled) })
            return nil // ack
        }), mq.WithConcurrency(8), mq.WithOrderingByKey())
    }()

    if err := client.Publish(ctx, "orders", &mq.Message{
        Key:  []byte("cust-42"),
        Body: []byte(`{"id":1}`),
    }); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    <-handled
}

order cust-42: {"id":1}

That program is examples/quickstart-memory, in a module of its own outside this repository's, so it is compiled and run by make examples in every make ci against the published API and nothing else. The version here is the same code with the example's test scaffolding removed.

docs.title: Five things in it worth noticing
docs.text:
d.Key and d.Body, not d.Message().Key. mq.Delivery embeds its Message by value, so the fields are reached directly and a received message is not a second allocation.

once.Do is not defensive decoration. The runner redelivers a message whose handler failed, so a handler that closes a channel has to be written as though it may be called again. That is the specification showing up in ten lines of example code, and it is the single most common thing to get wrong.

return nil is the ack. Returning an error is the nack, and what happens next is the runner's retry policy — see acks and leases. Under the default mq.SettlementAuto the handler may also settle for itself and is not overruled.

mq.WithConcurrency(8) with mq.WithOrderingByKey() does not reorder a key. Routing every delivery of one key to one lane, one lane at a time, is the runner's default routing with or without the option; what the option adds is mq.OrderingStrict, which decides what a failure does to the deliveries behind it.

memory.Open is the only line that names a driver. Swapping it for dsn.Open(ctx, "kafka://…") is the whole of what the specification promises about changing brokers — with the caveat that the capabilities change too, which is what capability negotiation is for.

docs.title: In a test, use NewForTest
docs.text:
func TestBilling(t *testing.T) {
    client, broker := memory.NewForTest(t)   // AutoCreate on, fake clock, leak check on cleanup
    _ = broker.Advance(30 * time.Second)     // drive the scheduler instead of sleeping
    …
}

memory.NewForTest turns on AutoCreate, installs a fake clock, and registers a goroutine-leak check on t.Cleanup. Broker.Advance moves that clock, so a test of a 30-second backoff takes microseconds and is deterministic rather than flaky. See testing and synctest.
