docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
Three guides, one per starting point. Each is written the same way: what maps directly, what does not map at all, the traps, and what a reader loses — because the honest limits are the reason anything else on the page can be trusted.

  • From Watermill — the closest neighbour. The port is mostly mechanical; the two things that are not are metadata (a map[string]string against ordered, duplicate-preserving, binary-capable headers) and acknowledgement (bool against an error with portable codes, including mq.ErrNotSettleable for a transport that has no ack). What you lose: message.Router's process-wide handler graph, a <-chan *Message subscription in the primary API, and the freedom not to notice that a backend cannot do what you asked.
  • From gocloud.dev/pubsub — the one where a behaviour changes silently if you do not read the page. gocloud transforms metadata a backend cannot carry (awssnssqs hex-escapes keys and URL-escapes values); iqmq refuses it in the default metadata mode. A mixed fleet of gocloud and iqmq readers on one topic needs a decision before the port. What you lose: URL-string-first configuration, implicit topology creation, and gocloud's other five packages, which iqmq has no counterpart for at all.
  • From a raw client — the expensive one, and the page that starts with the measurement rather than the mapping. The batched overhead budget is breached on 4 of 12 measured rows today and undecided on 8 (10 of 12 on the point estimates, before), worst +46 %, so a high-volume batched publish path gives up throughput; the page says so first and lists what you get for it second.

docs.title: Two things common to all three
docs.text:
iqmq makes you name the confirmation boundary. Every one of these libraries has a publish call whose boundary is its own default, and every port that leaves PublisherConfig.Confirmation unset gets mq.ConfirmAccepted — which is stronger than what several of them offered and therefore slower. That is not a regression; it is a question you were not being asked before. The specification has the modes.

iqmq refuses instead of emulating, by default. The capability table (client.Capabilities()) is generated from conformance runs, and the strict metadata mode fails a publication that would have lost something. The other three modes — envelope, adaptive, lenient-drop — exist, and each one's cost is documented where it is defined. Choosing one is part of the migration.

The measured comparison of iqmq, Watermill, gocloud and a raw client at equivalent semantics, with everything that could not be made equivalent excluded by name, is the competitor benchmark.

docs.title: From gocloud.dev/pubsub
docs.text:
gocloud.dev/pubsub and iqmq answer the same question — one API over several brokers — and disagree about what to do when the brokers differ. gocloud normalises: one Message shape, one Send, one Receive, and where a backend cannot represent something, gocloud transforms it so that it can. iqmq declares: the capability table says what a driver cannot do, and the portable API refuses rather than transforms unless you configure otherwise.

Almost everything on this page follows from that.

The measured comparison at equivalent semantics is in the competitor benchmark, with its exclusions.

docs.title: What maps directly
docs.text: gocloud.dev/pubsub iqmq Note pubsub.OpenTopic(ctx, "nats://orders") dsn.Open(ctx, "nats://host/orders") or natsdriver.Open(ctx, cfg) iqmq prefers the typed Config in production and String()/LogValue() redact credentials URL openers, blank import per backend dsn.NewRegistry() + driver.Register(reg) iqmq's registry is always an instance the program builds and passes, so a library cannot change a program's driver set Topic.Send(ctx, m) pub.Publish(ctx, m) (no batch API) pub.PublishBatch(ctx, ms) gocloud's batcher merges concurrent sends; it has no caller-visible batch Subscription.Receive(ctx) con.Receive(ctx, dst []mq.Delivery) (int, error) iqmq fills a caller-owned slice; one call can return many msg.Ack() d.Ack() error gocloud's panics if called twice msg.Nack(), msg.Nackable() d.Nack(opts...) error, client.Capabilities().Has(mq.FeatureNack) gocloud's Nack panics on a driver that cannot nack; iqmq returns mq.ErrUnsupported pubsub.Message.Body mq.Message.Body pubsub.Message.Metadata (map[string]string) mq.Message.Headers not the same thing — see below Topic.Shutdown(ctx) / Subscription.Shutdown(ctx) client.Shutdown(ctx) one call for the client: publishers flush, then consumers drain, then the backend topic.As(&native), msg.As(&native) client.Native(), d.Native(), mq.NativeAs[T](d) same escape hatch, typed ErrorAs, gcerrors.Code(err) errors.As, mq.CodeOf(err) and the sentinels in errors.go (mq.ErrUnsupported, mq.ErrLeaseLost, mq.ErrSettlementUnknown, …) iqmq's codes are the and include the settlement-specific ones gocloud has no room for Message.BeforeSend / AfterSend mq.PublishMiddleware, hooks

docs.title: Metadata: gocloud rewrites it, iqmq refuses it
docs.text:
This is the single biggest behavioural difference and it is easy to miss, because gocloud's transformation is invisible and lossless within gocloud.

gocloud.dev/pubsub/awssnssqs hex-escapes every metadata key that is not ASCII-alphanumeric and URL-escapes every value on the way out, and un-escapes them on the way in. A key of x-trace-id does not arrive at SQS as x-trace-id. A non-gocloud consumer reading the same queue sees the escaped form; a gocloud consumer sees the original. The same pattern appears in other gocloud drivers for the same reason: the backend cannot carry the value, so gocloud encodes it.

iqmq does not do this. In the default mq.MetadataNativeStrict mode a header the driver cannot carry natively is mq.ErrUnsupported at publish. Your choices are explicit:

Mode What happens to a header the broker cannot carry mq.MetadataNativeStrict (default) the publication fails with mq.ErrUnsupported mq.MetadataPortableEnvelope an envelope is always used; portable binary and duplicate headers work, and the body on the wire changes, which is documented and breaks non-iqmq consumers mq.MetadataAdaptive native where possible, envelope where required (SQS over ten attributes, say) mq.MetadataLenientDrop dropped, with a hook and a metric; cannot satisfy a metadata requirement

What you lose: gocloud's escaping means a gocloud-written message is readable by gocloud and awkward for anything else, and a port to iqmq's strict mode will fail on headers gocloud used to accept. That is the point, and it is still work. If you want the old behaviour, mq.MetadataPortableEnvelope is the mode that says "the body is not the payload any more" out loud, and it is not compatible with gocloud's escaping either — an iqmq envelope and a gocloud escape are different wire formats. A mixed fleet of gocloud and iqmq readers on one topic needs a decision before the port, not during it.

docs.title: Panics become errors
docs.text:
Two gocloud behaviours are panics and their iqmq equivalents are not:

// gocloud: panics if the driver is at-most-once.
if m.Nackable() { m.Nack() }
// gocloud: panics on the second call.
m.Ack()

// iqmq: both are errors with portable codes.
if err := d.Nack(); errors.Is(err, mq.ErrUnsupported) { /* at-most-once transport */ }
if err := d.Ack();  errors.Is(err, mq.ErrAlreadySettled) { /* settled twice */ }

What you gain: a settlement bug is a log line instead of a crashed process, and mq.ErrSettlementUnknown names the case gocloud has no way to report at all — an ack whose result is ambiguous. What you lose: nothing, except that code relying on the panic to find double-acks in tests needs the error checked instead.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees are declared rather than documented
docs.text:
gocloud documents at-most-once and at-least-once per driver in prose and makes Nackable() the only programmatic signal. iqmq's capability table is generated from conformance runs (client.Capabilities(), capabilities.json), and every driver scenario results are published. mq.Requirement lets a consumer refuse to open at all:

con, err := client.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{
    Topic: "orders", Subscription: "billing",
    Requirements: []mq.Requirement{
        mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureExplicitAck, mq.Native),
        mq.RequireAtLeast(mq.FeatureOrderedByKey, mq.Native),
    },
})
// err is mq.ErrUnsupported here on a transport that cannot do both.

There is no gocloud equivalent; the nearest thing is reading the driver's documentation and hoping.

docs.title: Receive: the shapes are different on purpose
docs.text:
Subscription.Receive(ctx) returns one message and hides its prefetch inside a batcher whose parameters are the driver's. That is a genuine convenience and it is also why the competitor benchmark excludes every Receive row: four libraries have four prefetch models and comparing them compares the configurations rather than the libraries.

iqmq's Receive(ctx, dst) fills a caller-owned []mq.Delivery and returns how many it filled, with Prefetch and MaxInFlight on the consumer config. The port is mechanical:

// gocloud
for {
    m, err := sub.Receive(ctx)
    if err != nil { return err }
    handle(m); m.Ack()
}

// iqmq
dst := make([]mq.Delivery, 64)   // allocated once, reused
for {
    n, err := con.Receive(ctx, dst)
    for i := range n {
        handle(&dst[i])
        if err := dst[i].Ack(); err != nil { log(err) }
    }
    if err != nil { return err }
}

Note the shape of the error handling: Receive may return a non-nil error together with deliveries, and those deliveries are valid and must be settled before the error is returned. gocloud's one-message signature cannot express that case and so never has to.

Or skip the loop entirely and use con.Run(ctx, handler, opts...), which is what most gocloud receive loops are reimplementing: concurrency, lane routing by key, retry, dead-lettering, lease extension and a graceful drain.

docs.title: What does not map at all
docs.text:
• gocloud's blob, docstore, runtimevar, secrets and mysql packages. iqmq is messaging only. If your use of gocloud is really "the Go Cloud Development Kit", only the pubsub part has an iqmq counterpart.
  • URL-string configuration as the primary path. iqmq parses DSNs (a pure, fuzzed function) but the typed Config is the production path, and unknown DSN parameters are an error rather than ignored.
  • pubsub.Message.LoggableID. iqmq logs no body and no header by default; there is no redacted-id field because there is nothing logging it for you.
  • gocloud's implicit topic and subscription creation. iqmq's auto-provision is off by default; client.Admin() creates topology explicitly, or returns mq.ErrUnsupported on a backend with no admin surface.
  • The driver package as an extension point with five methods. iqmq's driver SPI (the specification) is larger, because a driver also declares its capabilities, its settlement semantics and its limits. examples/custom-driver is a complete one written from outside the repository.
  • gocloud's ordering-key support via BeforeSend. iqmq's Message.Key is a first-class field and mq.WithOrderingByKey() is a runner option, but the driver must advertise mq.FeatureOrderedByKey — there is no per-send hook that makes an unordered transport ordered.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
A gocloud Topic is one topic; an iqmq Client is a connection. Porting OpenTopic per topic to client.Publisher per topic is right; porting it to Open per topic gives you a connection per topic.

Send on gocloud's NATS driver does not flush. natspubsub's SendBatch says so in its own source. If your port sets Confirmation to its default, iqmq's mq.ConfirmAccepted adds a PING/PONG round trip per publication and your throughput drops — not because iqmq is slower, but because you asked for a stronger boundary. Set mq.ConfirmNone to keep the old semantics, and know what you are keeping.

gocloud's Ack is asynchronous and returns before the ack is sent. iqmq's returns when the settlement has been attempted and tells you the outcome. A port that measures handler latency will see it move.

mq.ErrPartial on a batch. PublishBatch reports per-item failures with index-aligned results. gocloud has no batch and therefore no partial-failure case; code ported from a for … Send loop needs to decide what a partially failed batch means for it.

docs.title: A worked port
docs.text:
Before:

topic, err := pubsub.OpenTopic(ctx, "awssqs://"+queueURL)
defer topic.Shutdown(ctx)
sub, err := pubsub.OpenSubscription(ctx, "awssqs://"+queueURL)
defer sub.Shutdown(ctx)

if err := topic.Send(ctx, &pubsub.Message{
    Body:     body,
    Metadata: map[string]string{"x-trace-id": traceID},
}); err != nil { return err }

m, err := sub.Receive(ctx)
if err != nil { return err }
process(m.Body, m.Metadata["x-trace-id"])
m.Ack()

After:

client, err := sqs.Open(ctx, sqs.Config{QueueURL: queueURL})
defer client.Shutdown(ctx)

pub, _ := client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{Topic: queueURL})
con, _ := client.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{Topic: queueURL, Subscription: "workers"})

m := &mq.Message{Body: body}
m.Headers.Set("x-trace-id", []byte(traceID))
if err := pub.Publish(ctx, m); err != nil { return err }

dst := make([]mq.Delivery, 1)
n, err := con.Receive(ctx, dst)
for i := range n {
    v, _ := dst[i].Headers.Get("x-trace-id") // Delivery embeds Message by value
    process(dst[i].Body, string(v))
    if aerr := dst[i].Ack(); aerr != nil { log(aerr) }
}
if err != nil { return err }

The header survives this port because x-trace-id is ASCII-alphanumeric plus hyphens and SQS carries it natively. A key gocloud used to escape will not: it becomes mq.ErrUnsupported in the default metadata mode, and the queue you are reading may still contain gocloud-escaped keys from before the port. Deciding what to do about those is the migration, and it is the part a mechanical rewrite will not do for you.

docs.title: From a raw client
docs.text: This is the migration that costs the most and gains the most, and it is the one this project's second design principle is about: measured overhead budgets against raw clients. Before you read the mapping, read what the measurement says, because it is not a flattering number.

docs.title: What the overhead actually is, measured
docs.text:
Driver overhead against the raw client is the page, and its summary is:

  • the batched budget is ≤ 5 % throughput loss. It is breached on 4 of the 12 measured batched rows -- all three jetstream rows and redis/streams/PublishBatch/64B -- and on the other eight this host's own spread is wider than the excess, so they are undecided rather than met. The worst row is jetstream/PublishBatch/64KiB at +46 %, an effect ten times its own measurement spread. It read as ten of twelve until each row's verdict was read on its confidence interval.
  • the single-message budget is ≤ 10 %. It is breached on 1 of 12 rows, jetstream/Publish/64KiB at +31.9 %, which is the one of the three the point estimate flagged that is clear of its spread.
  • Of the twenty-four gated ratio rows, five are red, two are met and seventeen are undecided: since a row's verdict is read on both medians' confidence intervals rather than on the two medians alone, and on this host seventeen rows' intervals straddle their ceiling. Nothing has been widened or waived to make any row green -- eight rows moved from breach to undecided and nine moved from met to undecided, and none moved from breach to met.

So: if you are replacing a raw client with iqmq for a high-volume batched publish path, today, expect to give up throughput, and measure it. The figures are per broker and per operation, so read the table rather than a single number. The cause is unmeasured and is a profile away; the honest state of it is on that page.

The competitor comparison in the competitor benchmark puts the same question differently: how do iqmq, Watermill and gocloud each compare with the raw client at the same semantics.

docs.title: What you get for it
docs.text:
Every item here is something a raw-client codebase writes for itself, usually once per broker, usually differently each time:

  • A capability table (client.Capabilities()), generated from conformance runs, and a portable API that refuses what a transport cannot do instead of silently dropping it.
  • Settlement with a stated boundary. mq.ErrSettlementUnknown, mq.ErrLeaseLost and mq.ErrAlreadySettled name three cases raw-client code usually conflates into "err != nil".
  • A runner — bounded prefetch, an in-flight semaphore, lane routing by key, a fixed worker pool, one centralised lease-extension scheduler, retry with backoff, dead-lettering that never acks a failed DLQ publish, and a drain that stops receiving before it waits on workers.
  • A conformance kit. testkit.RunConformance puts your own driver, or the one you chose, through 155 scenarios.
  • The memory driver and synctest, so the tests of your message handlers need no container and no sleep.
  • One error model across brokers, with errors.As reaching the native error underneath.

docs.title: What maps, per client
docs.text: The mapping is mechanical; the boundaries are not. Confirmation is the field to get right, because a raw-client call's boundary is whatever that client's default is and iqmq makes you name it.

docs.title: nats.go
docs.text: nats.go iqmq Boundary nc.Publish(subj, b) pub.Publish with mq.ConfirmNone in the client's write buffer nc.Publish + nc.Flush() pub.Publish with mq.ConfirmAccepted the server has parsed it; nothing is stored js.Publish(subj, b) (JetStream) jetstream driver, mq.ConfirmDurable a PubAck nc.SubscribeSync + NextMsg con.Receive(ctx, dst) nc.QueueSubscribe ConsumerConfig.Subscription a queue group msg.Ack() (JetStream) d.Ack() on Core, d.Ack() is mq.ErrNotSettleable — correctly, there is no ack nats.Header mq.Message.Headers NATS headers are a text line: a control byte, a leading space, a colon in a name and the reserved prefix are refused

docs.title: franz-go / kafka-go
docs.text: Raw iqmq Boundary cl.Produce with a callback pub.PublishAsync(ctx, m, done) acks maps to ConfirmationMode cl.ProduceSync pub.Publish cl.PollFetches con.Receive(ctx, dst) cl.CommitRecords d.Ack() iqmq's offset tracker turns per-record acks into a watermark manual partition assignment mq.Ordering, mq.WithOrderingByKey kgo.RecordPartitioner mq.Message.Key the driver's partitioner

docs.title: rueidis / go-redis
docs.text: Raw iqmq Boundary XADD pub.Publish with mq.ConfirmAccepted the XADD reply XADD + WAITAOF mq.ConfirmDurable needs an append-only file on the server XREADGROUP con.Receive XACK d.Ack() XAUTOCLAIM the driver's reclaim loop

docs.title: AWS SDK (SQS/SNS)
docs.text: Raw iqmq Boundary SendMessage pub.Publish the API response SendMessageBatch (10 max) pub.PublishBatch the driver splits and reports index-aligned results ReceiveMessage (10 max, long poll) con.Receive(ctx, dst) DeleteMessage d.Ack() ChangeMessageVisibility d.Extend(by) see the trap below message attributes (10 max) Headers + mq.MetadataAdaptive the envelope appears above ten attributes

docs.title: What does not map at all
docs.text:
• Every broker-specific knob. Linger, prefetch, pipelining depth, poller count, partitioner, compression: these are typed options in the driver package (kafka.WithLinger(2*time.Millisecond)), not in the portable API, so they fail at compile time on the wrong driver rather than being ignored. Anything without a driver option is reachable through client.Native(), which hands you the raw client back.
  • Broker-specific administration. client.Admin() covers the portable subset (EnsureTopic, EnsureSubscription); a Kafka partition reassignment or a JetStream stream update is client.Native().
  • Anything that needs the raw client's own concurrency model. franz-go's PollFetches is designed to be called from one goroutine and hands you a whole fetch; iqmq's runner owns that loop. Mixing the two on one client is possible through OpenWithClient(ctx, cl, driverkit.ClientBorrowed, cfg) and is your problem to keep coherent.
  • Exactly-once claims. iqmq does not make one, and neither does the raw client. Kafka transactions are in x/kafkatx; the semantics you get are the broker's.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
ChangeMessageVisibility on SQS sets the visibility window from the CALL, so raw code that passes the extension it wants shortens the lease of any message with more than that left. Your raw code has this hazard and usually has a comment about it; iqmq's SQS driver does not, because Delivery.Extend(by) moves the deadline at least by further and the driver sends the remaining window plus by to achieve it. What the portable API still cannot tell you is the new deadline: DeliveryInfo is the snapshot the receive handed over, so assume the documented minimum.

Publishing a []byte you then mutate. iqmq's Raw codec and the owned publication path (PublishOwned) hand your slice to the driver without a copy, which is the zero-copy path the specification is about. The contract is that you do not touch it until the publication completes. A raw client generally copies, so code that reused a buffer safely before may not now — or use mq.Message.Body with the default safe mode, which clones caller-owned mutable data exactly once.

d.Ack() takes no context. Settlement is not a cancellable operation in this API; it is bounded by the driver's own timeouts. Raw code that passed a per-ack context has nowhere to put it.

A non-nil error from Receive can accompany valid deliveries. Settle them before you return the error, or you strand a lease per delivery on the last fetch of every loop. Raw clients differ on this and most do not have the case.

The portable Prefetch default is 128 and the driver may override it. Raw code tuned to a specific fetch size should set ConsumerConfig.Prefetch and check the driver's note rather than assume.

docs.title: How to decide
docs.text:
1. Read the overhead page for your broker and your operation. If your hot path is a large batched publish on JetStream, the measured cost today is tens of per cent and you should know that before you port.
  2. Port one consumer first, not one publisher. The runner is where most of the code you delete lives, and the receive path's measured overhead is not what the breached budgets are about.
  3. Keep the raw client reachable. OpenWithClient(ctx, native, driverkit.ClientBorrowed, cfg) lets one connection serve both, so a hot path can stay raw while the rest moves.
  4. Run the conformance kit against your chosen driver before you rely on a capability. conformance/reports has the stored runs; your broker version may differ from the one they were taken against.

docs.title: From Watermill
docs.text:
Watermill is the closest thing to iqmq in the Go ecosystem, and the two make opposite bets in one place: Watermill's Publisher/Subscriber pair is deliberately tiny and every backend fits behind it, while iqmq's surface is larger and every backend has to declare what it cannot do. Most of this page is the consequence of that one difference.

The comparison of the two at equivalent semantics is in the competitor benchmark, with its exclusions.

docs.title: What maps directly
docs.text: Watermill iqmq Note message.Publisher.Publish(topic, msgs...) client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{Topic: …}) then pub.Publish(ctx, m) / pub.PublishBatch(ctx, ms) iqmq binds the topic at the publisher, not per call; client.Publish(ctx, topic, m) is the ad-hoc form message.Subscriber.Subscribe(ctx, topic) returning <-chan *Message client.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{Topic: …, Subscription: …}) then con.Receive(ctx, dst) or con.Run(ctx, handler) a channel adapter is not in the primary API; see "What does not map" message.Message.Payload mq.Message.Body both []byte message.Message.UUID mq.Message.ID Watermill's is for debugging and may be empty; iqmq's is an application identifier and is empty unless you set it or configure AutoID message.Message.Metadata (map[string]string) mq.Message.Headers not the same thing — see below msg.Ack() / msg.Nack() d.Ack() / d.Nack() Watermill's return bool (false when the other was already sent); iqmq's return error and tell you why message.Router + AddHandler con.Run(ctx, handler, opts...) the runner is per consumer rather than a process-wide router message.HandlerMiddleware mq.Middleware (iqmq/middleware) same shape: func(Handler) Handler Watermill's Retry middleware mq.WithMaxAttempts, mq.WithRetryBackoff a runner option rather than a middleware, because the retry decision interacts with settlement Watermill's CorrelationID middleware middleware.CorrelationID Watermill's Poison middleware mq.WithDeadLetter(topic) / mq.WithNativeDeadLetter() iqmq refuses to ack a delivery whose dead-letter publish failed or was ambiguous Watermill's Recoverer middleware on by default; mq.WithoutRecovery() turns it off gochannel.GoChannel memory.Open both in-process; the memory engine has topology profiles, retention, delay and leases

docs.title: Metadata is the first real difference
docs.text:
Watermill's Metadata is map[string]string. iqmq's Headers are ordered, duplicate-preserving, binary-capable and deterministically encoded, and a Watermill-shaped map[string]string goes in with a two-line loop over Headers.Set, whose value is a []byte.

Going the other way is where you lose something:

  • Order. A map[string]string has none. If a consumer of yours depends on header order — a trace context stack, a signature over the header block — it cannot depend on it in Watermill and can in iqmq.
  • Duplicates. Watermill cannot represent two values for one key. iqmq can, behind mq.FeatureDuplicateHeaders, and rejects the publication at the client on a driver that cannot carry them rather than silently keeping one.
  • Binary values. Watermill's values are string, so a binary value has to be encoded by you. iqmq carries []byte where the driver advertises mq.FeatureBinaryHeaders, and refuses or envelopes it (your choice of metadata mode) where it does not.
  • Limits. iqmq enforces MaxHeaderCount and MaxHeaderBytes before the publication reaches the socket, and reports them in the capability table. Watermill's backends fail at the broker, later and less specifically.

What you lose: every Watermill subscriber in the wild reads msg.Metadata["key"]. Nothing in iqmq gives you a map[string]string view for free, and there is no map[string]string view to read back. A port of a large Watermill codebase touches every metadata read.

docs.title: Acknowledgement is the second
docs.text:
Watermill's Ack() returns bool: false means "a nack was already sent". Nothing tells you whether the backend can nack, whether your lease has expired, or whether the ack reached the broker. iqmq's Ack() error answers all three, with the portable codes:

if err := d.Ack(); err != nil {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, mq.ErrAlreadySettled):   // a second terminal settlement
    case errors.Is(err, mq.ErrLeaseLost):        // the lease expired; somebody else has it
    case errors.Is(err, mq.ErrNotSettleable):    // this transport has no ack (NATS Core)
    case errors.Is(err, mq.ErrSettlementUnknown): // ambiguous: it may or may not have landed
    }
}

mq.ErrNotSettleable is the one that changes a port. On NATS Core, Watermill's msg.Ack() returns true — it is a client-side signal that releases the subscriber's slot — and iqmq's d.Ack() returns mq.ErrNotSettleable, because NATS Core has no acknowledgement to send. Neither is wrong; iqmq is telling you something Watermill does not, and code that ignores the error will look like it broke.

docs.title: Capabilities: what you gain and what it costs you
docs.text:
Watermill has no capability model. Every Publisher satisfies the same interface, so a feature a backend cannot provide is either silently absent or a runtime surprise in the backend package. iqmq publishes a capability table per driver and profile (client.Capabilities()), generated from conformance runs, and the portable API refuses rather than emulates unless you ask:

if !client.Capabilities().Has(mq.FeatureScheduledPublish) {
    // mq.Delay(d) would be mq.ErrUnsupported here.
}

What you gain: a publication that would have quietly lost its delay, its ordering key or its duplicate header fails at the call site, in the strict metadata mode that is the default.

What you lose: code that worked against three Watermill backends may now need a branch, an explicit mq.MetadataLenientDrop or an emulation policy, for each capability one of them lacks. iqmq makes you decide; Watermill let you not notice. If what you want is "it works everywhere and I accept the loss", mq.MetadataLenientDrop with the drop hook wired to a metric is the mode that says so out loud.

docs.title: Confirmation boundaries
docs.text:
Watermill's Publish returns when the backend's publish call returns, and what that means is the backend's business. iqmq makes it a configured value:

pub, _ := client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{
    Topic:        "orders",
    Confirmation: mq.ConfirmDurable, // None | Accepted | Durable
})

This is not cosmetic. On NATS Core, watermill-nats' Publish calls PublishMsg and returns — the message is in the client's write buffer and nothing has acknowledged it. mq.ConfirmNone is that same boundary named; mq.ConfirmAccepted costs a PING/PONG round trip; mq.ConfirmDurable is mq.ErrUnsupported, because NATS Core stores nothing. A port that leaves Confirmation at its default gets ConfirmAccepted, which is slower than the Watermill code it replaced and stronger, and the comparison in the competitor benchmark is measured at ConfirmNone for exactly that reason.

docs.title: What does not map at all
docs.text:
• message.Router's process-wide graph. Watermill's router owns handlers across topics, with AddNoPublisherHandler, plugins and a single Run. iqmq's runner is per consumer: con.Run(ctx, h, opts...). A router with twelve handlers becomes twelve consumers and your own supervision, or one errgroup. Nothing in iqmq replaces the router's plugin surface.
  • A <-chan *Message subscription. iqmq's primary receive surfaces are Receive(ctx, dst []Delivery) (int, error), Messages(ctx) (an iter.Seq2) and Run. A channel adapter is deliberately outside the primary API: a bounded channel per subscription is a goroutine and a buffer per subscription, and the specification forbids that on the receive path. If you want one, build it over Receive — it is ten lines and it is then your buffer policy.
  • msg.Acked() / msg.Nacked() channels. iqmq settlement is synchronous and returns an error. There is no channel to select on.
  • msg.Context() and msg.SetContext(). A Watermill message carries a context. An iqmq Message is data; the context is the handler's argument.
  • Watermill's SQL, io, firestore and other backends. iqmq has no equivalent for several of them. Check the driver matrix before planning a port.
  • Watermill's Subscriber as a plugin point for your own backend. iqmq's extension point is the driver SPI, which is a larger interface because it also has to declare capabilities and settlement semantics. Writing one is examples/custom-driver; it is not two methods.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
Watermill's Ack() is idempotent-ish and iqmq's is not. A second Ack() in Watermill returns true and does nothing. In iqmq it is mq.ErrAlreadySettled. Handler code that acks defensively at two exit points will start reporting errors.

A Watermill handler that returns an error nacks; an iqmq handler that returns an error nacks and counts an attempt. iqmq's runner owns the retry policy (WithMaxAttempts, WithRetryBackoff, WithDeadLetter), so a handler that retried internally and then returned an error will now be retried twice over. Port the retry out of the handler.

mq.WithSettlement(mq.SettlementManual) is what a Watermill handler that acks by hand actually wants. The default is Auto: nil error acks, non-nil nacks. If your handler calls Ack() itself and returns nil, the runner's ack is the second one.

Watermill's gochannel Publish can block for ever on a full buffer, and so can iqmq's memory engine. Both are correct; the configuration is in different places (OutputChannelBuffer against memory.Config's capacity and overflow policy, which also offers reject, dropnew and dropold).

The iqmq- header prefix is reserved. A Watermill codebase that puts its own keys in metadata is fine, unless one of them starts with iqmq-, which is rejected at publish.

docs.title: A worked port
docs.text:
Before:

pub, _ := nats.NewPublisher(nats.PublisherConfig{URL: url, Marshaler: &nats.NATSMarshaler{}}, logger)
sub, _ := nats.NewSubscriber(nats.SubscriberConfig{URL: url, Unmarshaler: &nats.NATSMarshaler{}}, logger)

router.AddHandler("orders", "orders", sub, "billed", pub,
    func(m *message.Message) ([]*message.Message, error) {
        defer m.Ack()
        return []*message.Message{message.NewMessage(watermill.NewUUID(), out)}, nil
    })

After:

client, _ := natsdriver.Open(ctx, natsdriver.Config{Addrs: []string{url}})
defer client.Shutdown(ctx)

billed, _ := client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{Topic: "billed"})
orders, _ := client.Consumer(ctx, mq.ConsumerConfig{Topic: "orders", Subscription: "billing"})

err := orders.Run(ctx, mq.HandlerFunc(func(ctx context.Context, d *mq.Delivery) error {
    // No Ack(): the runner acks on a nil return (mq.WithSettlement(mq.SettlementAuto)).
    return billed.Publish(ctx, &mq.Message{Body: out})
}), mq.WithConcurrency(8), mq.WithMaxAttempts(3))

Three things changed that are worth naming. The defer m.Ack() is gone, because acking before the downstream publish is what turns a broker outage into lost messages and the runner's automatic settlement waits for the handler to return. The retry is a runner option instead of a middleware. And on NATS Core the Run above will report mq.ErrNotSettleable from its settlement step unless the driver is one that acks — which is the capability model telling you that the defer m.Ack() you just deleted never did anything either.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
What an operator needs from this library, and what it deliberately does not provide.

Page Metrics the canonical metric names, through integrations/prometheus Tracing the four spans and W3C trace context, through integrations/otel Logging what the library logs, what it never logs, and where your handler's logs come from Health five client states, and the difference between "connected" and "working" Capacity the four bounds that decide memory, and how to size them Troubleshooting symptom to cause, with the error codes Upgrades broker upgrades, client-library upgrades, and the release train Credential rotation rotating a secret under a live client

docs.title: Three things that are true of all of them
docs.text:
Observation is opt-in and costs nothing when it is off. mq.Hooks is a struct of function fields; an unset field is a nil check on a path that is already compiled to booleans. There is no global registry, no init()-time side effect, and no instrumentation you did not install.

Nothing in the library logs by itself. There is no package-level logger and no default handler. What the library gives you instead is hooks, stats snapshots and errors; turning those into log lines is middleware.Metrics, integrations/otel, or four lines of your own. That is deliberate — a library that logs has opinions about your log format that it should not have.

The error is the interface. Every failure carries one of the specification's twenty-six mq.ErrorCode values, reachable with mq.CodeOf(err) and matchable with errors.Is against the sentinel of the same name. An operations runbook written against those codes keeps working when the message text changes, which is the point of having them.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
There is no built-in admin UI, no metrics endpoint, and no "iqmq agent". The iqmq command-line tool is a diagnostic — doctor, pub, sub, tail, bench — and not a control plane.

Topology management is mq.Admin and is deliberately small: ensure a topic, ensure a subscription, delete either, list, purge, stats. It is Conditional or absent on several drivers, because several brokers have no portable way to do it and inventing one would mean guessing. The matrix's Admin row says which.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text: How much memory a client holds, and which four numbers decide it.

docs.title: The consumer side
docs.text:
ConsumerConfig.Prefetch is the ceiling on unsettled deliveries the runner will hold. It is the dominant term in a consumer's footprint and in its duplicate rate after a crash: every unsettled delivery is a message that comes back.

mq.WithMaxInFlight(n) bounds the same thing from the runner's side, and mq.WithConcurrency(n) bounds how many handlers run at once. A prefetch far above the concurrency buys latency at the cost of duplicates; a prefetch equal to the concurrency is the conservative setting and costs a round trip per batch of work.

ConsumerConfig.BufferReuse is the allocation lever: with it on, a delivery's storage returns to the consumer the moment it is settled. That makes the receive path allocation-free and makes Delivery.Body borrowed — see The specification and Delivery.CloneMessage. A handler that keeps the body past the settlement without cloning it is a data race, and the reason the mode is off by default.

A rough figure, and it is rough on purpose: Prefetch × (envelope + body). The envelope is small — the memory engine's is about 96 bytes — and the body is yours. If your messages are 64 KiB and your prefetch is 1024, you have asked for 64 MiB per consumer before anything else.

docs.title: The publisher side
docs.text:
PublisherConfig.MaxPendingMessages and MaxPendingBytes bound the publisher's own buffer: the asynchronous publications outstanding at the driver plus the messages waiting in the batching buffer. Zero for the first selects mq.DefaultMaxPendingMessages (1024) rather than "unbounded" — the specification requires the buffer to be bounded by default, so there is no value that turns the bound off.

PublisherConfig.Backpressure is what happens at the bound, and the two drop modes are the only way a publication is lost without the caller being told; see backpressure.

Then there is the client library's own buffer, which is not this library's and which the driver page states.

docs.title: The memory engine
docs.text:
Different question, because here the engine is the broker and the messages are yours to hold.

Bound What it limits Config.MaxTotalMessages, MaxTotalBytes the whole broker TopologyConfig.CapacityMessages per subscription-partition; default 65,536 TopologyConfig.CapacityBytes the same, by size TopologyConfig.MaxInFlight, MaxDelayed unsettled and scheduled records per lane TopologyConfig.Retention the retained log, for TopologyStream

the last invariant is the one to hold onto: fixed limits imply a memory plateau. A broker configured with bounds does not grow without limit under any load — the model fuzzer asserts it after every step, and a run that grew would be a failure rather than a tuning note.

CapacityMessages: 0 selects an unbounded chunked queue, and it is explicit for that reason.

docs.title: Sizing, in the order the questions actually arrive
docs.text:
1. How large is a message? caps.Limit(mq.LimitMaxMessageBytes) is what the broker will take, and Known == false means the driver has not said.
  2. How many can be in flight? Prefetch × concurrency, and then ask whether you can afford to reprocess all of them after a crash.
  3. How long can a handler take? If it is close to the lease, you need mq.WithLeaseExtension — and a driver that has a DeadlineExtender. The matrix's ExtendLease row says which do.
  4. What happens when the broker slows down? That is the backpressure mode, and it is the question most people answer last and should answer first.

docs.title: Measured numbers
docs.text:
Per-operation costs, allocation budgets and the throughput figures live in the performance section. Two things to carry over here:

  • the allocation budgets in benchmarks/budgets.yaml are gated — a change that allocates on a path the specification requires to be allocation-free fails make gate;
  • the overhead budgets against the raw clients are breached on 10 of the 12 batched rows measured, by up to 46 %. Driver overhead has the figures.

docs.title: Credential rotation
docs.text: Rotating a secret under a client that is serving traffic. Two facts decide how this goes, and both are about this library rather than about your secret store.

docs.title: Fact one: a credential reaches a driver once
docs.text:
A driver's Config — or its DSN — is read at Open and is not re-read. There is no SetCredentials, and there is no callback the core will invoke to ask for a fresh one. That is deliberate: a configuration that can change under a running client is a configuration whose state nothing can reason about, and the capability model depends on a client's answers being constant for its life.

So the portable rotation is open a new client and drain the old one:

next, err := kafka.Open(ctx, newConfig)   // new credential
if err != nil {
    return err                            // keep serving on the old one
}
swapIn(next)                              // your own pointer swap
if err := prev.Shutdown(drainCtx); err != nil {
    slog.Error("drain after rotation", "err", err)
}

The ordering matters. Open first, and only swap when the open succeeded — otherwise a bad credential takes down a client that was working. Shutdown flushes publishers and drains consumers, bounded by its context, so in-flight handlers finish rather than being cancelled mid-transaction. See graceful shutdown.

Some client libraries take a credential provider rather than a value — the AWS SDK's credential chain refreshes itself, and a Pub/Sub service-account key is renewed by the metadata server. Where that is true, rotation is the SDK's and this page does not apply; the driver page says which.

docs.title: Fact two: the credential is never rendered
docs.text:
Every driver's Config implements slog.LogValuer and renders itself with the credential redacted, and the same is true of String, GoString and DSN. Each driver has a test — TestConfigNeverRendersACredential or its local name — that pushes the config through all four and through a real log/slog handler and asserts that the secret appears in none of them.

the rule completes it: an error never carries a credential or an address, so a failed open does not leak the thing that failed. A log line from this library is safe to ship to a log aggregator you do not own.

The CLI holds the same line: iqmq doctor prints capabilities and limits and not the DSN it dialled with, and it takes a password from the environment rather than from a flag so that it does not reach the process table or a shell history.

docs.title: What to watch while rotating
docs.text: Signal Means the new Open returns an error whose mq.CodeOf is mq.CodeUnauthorized or mq.CodeForbidden the new credential is wrong, or has not propagated. Nothing was swapped. mq.CodeOf(err) on the new Open is mq.CodeUnauthorized or mq.CodeForbidden the new credential is wrong, or has not propagated. Nothing was swapped. the new Open fails with mq.CodeUnauthorized or mq.CodeForbidden the new credential is wrong, or has not propagated. Nothing was swapped. the old client's Health() goes mq.HealthDegraded during the drain the old credential was revoked before the drain finished. Shorten the overlap next time, or lengthen the drain. Shutdown returns non-nil the drain hit its deadline and handlers were cancelled. Whatever they were doing is unfinished and unsettled, so it comes back.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: There is no shutdown hook, so a drain that exceeded its timeout during a rotation is not a metric — only the Shutdown error and your own log line. It is recorded with as its owner; see logging.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
snap := client.Health()
switch snap.State {
case mq.HealthReady:      // serving
case mq.HealthDegraded:   // snap.Err says why
case mq.HealthClosed:     // Shutdown or Close has run
}

mq.HealthSnapshot is two fields: a State and an Err which is non-nil exactly when the state is not ready. The error never carries a payload, a credential or an address, so the snapshot is safe to serve from an unprotected endpoint.

docs.title: Five states
docs.text: State Means mq.HealthConfigured the client exists and has not connected mq.HealthConnecting a connection is being established mq.HealthReady serving mq.HealthDegraded something is wrong and Err says what mq.HealthClosed Shutdown or Close has run

docs.title: It is a snapshot, not a subscription
docs.text:
Health answers with what is true now, cheaply, with no I/O. It does not block, does not dial, and does not tell you when something changes.

For changes, use mq.Hooks.OnReconnect, which the driver fires when it observes one. The two together are the whole story: poll Health from your readiness probe, and hook OnReconnect if you want to alert on flapping.

docs.title: Readiness and liveness are different questions
docs.text:
Liveness — is the process wedged? client.Health().State != mq.HealthClosed is a weak answer and a process that is deadlocked inside a handler will still pass it. A better liveness signal is your own: a handler that has not completed anything in n seconds while ConsumerStats.InFlight > 0 is stuck, and ConsumerStats.Received not advancing while the topic has lag is stuck differently.

Readiness — should traffic come here? mq.HealthReady plus your own dependencies. Note that a client is ready before it has consumed anything: Consumer.Run starting is not part of the client's health, because a client with no consumers is a perfectly healthy publisher.

client.Ping(ctx) is the deeper check, and it costs a round trip. requires it to never consume a message and never create topology, so it is safe to call on a schedule — but it is a broker check, not a client one, and on some drivers it is the only thing that will notice a silently dead connection. That is also how OnReconnect gets fired at all on such drivers, which is worth knowing before you decide not to ping.

docs.title: HealthReporter is what a driver adds
docs.text: A driver that can say more than the core can infer implements mq.HealthReporter, and the client uses it. A driver that does not gets the core's own view: configured, ready once open succeeded, degraded once an operation failed with a connection error, closed after shutdown.

docs.title: Draining is a health event and has a timeout
docs.text:
client.Shutdown(ctx) flushes publishers, drains consumers and then closes the backend, bounded by ctx. The runner's own wait for handlers already in flight is mq.DefaultDrainTimeout — 30 seconds — or whatever mq.WithDrainTimeout(d) says; past it their contexts are cancelled.

A drain that exceeds its timeout is the production event this library currently cannot report as a metric, because the specification has no shutdown hook. It is recorded with as its owner. In the meantime: the Shutdown error is the signal, and it is worth logging at Error.

See graceful shutdown for the ordering guarantees the drain gives you.

docs.title: iqmq doctor
docs.text: For the "is this configuration going to work at all" question, the CLI has iqmq doctor, which dials, reports the driver's capabilities and limits, and exits 3 when the driver lacks a capability the command needs. It is the thing to run before a deployment, not during one.

docs.title: The library has no logger
docs.text:
There is no package-level logger, no SetLogger, and no default output. This is not an omission: a library that logs decides your format, your level mapping and your sink, and gets all three wrong for somebody.

What you get instead:

  • mq.Hooks — OnPublishStart, OnPublishDone, OnReceive, OnSettle, OnReconnect. Five function fields on a struct; set the ones you want.
  • ConsumerStats and PublisherStats — snapshots you poll on your own schedule.
  • errors — every one carrying an mq.ErrorCode.
  • middleware.Metrics and the two integration packages, for when you want the standard thing rather than your own.

A minimal log/slog bridge is about eight lines:

client := mq.NewClient(backend, mq.WithHooks(mq.Hooks{
    OnSettle: func(e mq.SettleEvent) {
        if e.Err != nil {
            slog.Error("settle failed",
                "topic", e.Topic, "subscription", e.Subscription,
                "code", mq.CodeOf(e.Err).String(), "err", e.Err)
        }
    },
    OnReconnect: func(e mq.ReconnectEvent) {
        slog.Warn("reconnected", "driver", e.Driver, "attempt", e.Attempt, "err", e.Err)
    },
}))

docs.title: What the library never puts in an error
docs.text:
The specification is a rule about content, not about wording: an error never carries a message body, a key, a header value, a credential or an address. So an error is safe to log at any level, and safe to put in an alert, and safe to return to a caller you do not trust with the payload.

This is checked rather than promised. Every driver has a test that renders its configuration through String, GoString, LogValue, DSN and a real log/slog handler and asserts that no credential appears in any of them — the Config types implement slog.LogValuer for exactly that reason.

It also means an error will not tell you which message failed. SettleEvent and the delivery carry the identity (Delivery.ID, topic, subscription, partition, offset); the error carries the reason. Log both if you need to correlate them, which is what the middleware does.

docs.title: Levels, if you want the convention
docs.text:
The library does not enforce these; they are what the integrations use and what the troubleshooting page assumes.

Event Level Why a settled delivery not logged one line per message is a bill, not a log a handler error that will be retried Warn expected, bounded, and visible in ConsumerStats.Nacked a dead-lettered message Error you have lost the ability to process it in band a Discard(err) Error the specification requires it to be logged and counted, never silent a FailureSkip ack Error the one destructive policy; it acked a message nobody handled a reconnect Warn with the attempt count, because a flapping connection is a pattern rather than an event a poison halt Error the runner has stopped; something has to page

docs.title: Where the gaps are
docs.text:
There is no shutdown hook. the five fields do not include one, so nothing observes a client, publisher or consumer closing, and neither integration has anything to say about a drain that exceeded its timeout — which is exactly the production event an operator wants a metric for. Recorded with as its owner: either the list is complete and the plan's reading of it was wrong, or a sixth field is owed.

iqmq_dropped_total{policy} has no source in the core for the policy label. PublisherStats carries Drops and not the mode, so prometheus.AddPublisher takes the mq.BackpressureMode from you.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
integrations/prometheus exposes iqmq's observation points as Prometheus metrics under the canonical names the API fixes.

import (
    mq "github.com/iqhive/iqmq"
    "github.com/iqhive/iqmq/middleware"
    iqmqprom "github.com/iqhive/iqmq/integrations/prometheus"
    "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"
)

reg := prometheus.NewRegistry()
m, err := iqmqprom.New(iqmqprom.Config{Registerer: reg})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

client := mq.NewClient(backend, mq.WithHooks(m.Hooks()))

Several families come from somewhere other than the hooks, because the core has no hook for them:

// The handler families, through the middleware chain.
consumer.Run(ctx, handler, mq.WithMiddleware(middleware.Metrics(m.Recorder(), nil)))

// The gauges and the counters the core keeps in its stats snapshots.
m.AddConsumer("orders", "billing", consumer.Stats)
m.AddPublisher("orders", mq.BackpressureBlock, publisher.Stats)

// The broker's own view, polled on your schedule rather than on a scrape.
if st, err := admin.Stats(ctx, "orders", "billing"); err == nil {
    m.ObserveQueueStats("orders", "billing", st)
}

// The memory engine's per-lane gauges.
m.AddMemory("orders", "billing", broker)

docs.title: The names are the API
docs.text:
A dashboard, an alert rule and a recording rule are all written against a metric name and its label names, and renaming either breaks every one of them with nothing at compile time to notice. So there is no namespace or subsystem option: the names are the specification, and the whole exposed surface — name, type, label names and help text — is pinned by a golden file (integrations/prometheus/testdata/metrics.golden) that go test compares byte for byte.

Metric Type Labels Source iqmq_publish_messages_total counter topic, outcome Hooks.OnPublishDone iqmq_publish_bytes_total counter topic Hooks.OnPublishDone iqmq_publish_duration_seconds histogram topic, outcome Hooks.OnPublishDone iqmq_publish_batch_size histogram topic Hooks.OnPublishDone iqmq_consume_messages_total counter topic, subscription Hooks.OnReceive iqmq_handler_duration_seconds histogram topic, subscription, outcome Metrics.Recorder iqmq_settle_duration_seconds histogram topic, subscription, kind Hooks.OnSettle iqmq_settle_failures_total counter topic, subscription, kind Hooks.OnSettle iqmq_lease_extensions_total counter topic, subscription, outcome Hooks.OnSettle iqmq_reconnects_total counter driver, outcome Hooks.OnReconnect (see below) iqmq_redeliveries_total counter topic, subscription ConsumerStats.Redelivered iqmq_in_flight gauge topic, subscription ConsumerStats.InFlight iqmq_pending_publishes gauge topic PublisherStats.Pending iqmq_backpressure_events_total counter topic PublisherStats.BackpressureEvents iqmq_dropped_total counter topic, policy PublisherStats.Drops iqmq_queue_depth gauge topic, subscription Admin.Stats iqmq_lag gauge topic, subscription Admin.Stats iqmq_memory_ready gauge topic, subscription memory.Broker.Inspect iqmq_memory_delayed gauge topic, subscription memory.Broker.Inspect iqmq_memory_inflight gauge topic, subscription memory.Broker.Inspect iqmq_memory_retained_bytes gauge topic, subscription memory.Broker.Inspect

Each quantity has exactly one source. Where a hook and a stats snapshot both carry a number — deliveries received, settlements failed, lease extensions — the hook wins and the snapshot is not read, because a quantity with two sources is a quantity that double-counts.

iqmq_settle_failures_total has no kind="extend" series: an extension is not a settlement, and its outcome is iqmq_lease_extensions_total.

docs.title: What is not exposed, and why
docs.text:
A metric that is always zero is worse than none: "no option was ignored" and "nobody wired up ignored options" look identical on a graph. Unsourced() returns the list in code, and the test that checks it against the registry runs in make ci.

  • iqmq_option_ignored_total is not registered. An option a driver cannot honour is a construction error naming the option, not a silently ignored setting, so nothing in the core or in any driver has an ignored option to count.
  • iqmq_reconnects_total is registered and the core never fires it. A Backend is built before the Client that holds mq.Hooks, and no part of the SPI carries them, so at v0 the reconnect event reaches a driver's own Config. Pass m.Hooks() to the driver that offers it. Passing it to both the driver and mq.WithHooks counts every reconnection twice.
  • iqmq_dropped_total's policy label has no source. PublisherStats does not carry the backpressure mode and PublisherHandle has no accessor for it, so AddPublisher takes the mq.BackpressureMode you configured.
  • iqmq_queue_depth and iqmq_lag are pushed, not pulled. The answer is a broker round trip, and a collector that called Admin.Stats on every scrape would put an RPC — with its own timeout, failure and rate limit — inside /metrics. A value the driver reports as unknown produces no series at all, so a broker that cannot measure a queue is never graphed as an empty one.
  • ConsumerStats.Lag is always unknown at v0, because no SPI carries lag. iqmq_lag therefore only has series for the subscriptions whose Admin.Stats you polled. iqmq_lag is not in the canonical list, and it is the name integrations/otel uses for the lag gauge that sentence does ask for; one quantity is better named once than twice.
  • iqmq_memory_retained_bytes is memory.Snapshot.Bytes, the accounted payload bytes of every record the lane holds. The engine has no separate retention-log byte count.

docs.title: Cardinality
docs.text:
topic and subscription are label values, and both normally come from your own configuration — except that a wildcard subscription resolves to whatever concrete topic the broker delivered, which your program did not choose.

iqmqprom.Config{
    Registerer: reg,
    Cardinality: iqmqprom.Cardinality{
        MaxSeries: 256,      // 0 = 128; negative = unbounded, explicitly
        Overflow:  "other",  // everything past the limit folds onto this value
        OmitTopic: false,    // true replaces the value with "", which PromQL reads as absent
    },
}

The fold is a relabelling and not a discard: the observation is still counted, on the overflow series. A message identifier is never a label.

A topic name is also not necessarily yours: the specification makes a delivery's topic the concrete one the broker reported, so a wildcard subscription, a NATS subject or a queue somebody else created decides what goes into the label. client_golang panics on a label value that is not valid UTF-8 — on the goroutine that published or settled, inside the hook — so invalid bytes are replaced with U+FFFD before the label is built, one replacement per run, and the readable part of the name survives. FuzzMetricLabels is what found that and what holds it.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
With no hooks installed, nothing: the core builds no event and reads no clock (the specification's "disabled hooks/observer path: 0 allocs, ≤ 1 predictable branch").

With the hooks installed, zero allocations per event. The per-series children are resolved once, on the first event for a label combination, and found afterwards through one atomic load and one map lookup. TestAllocs pins both halves, and make allocs runs it.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
integrations/otel instruments iqmq with OpenTelemetry: the API's four spans, its histograms and gauges, and W3C trace context carried through a message's headers.

import (
    mq "github.com/iqhive/iqmq"
    "github.com/iqhive/iqmq/middleware"
    otelmq "github.com/iqhive/iqmq/integrations/otel"
)

i, err := otelmq.New(otelmq.Config{
    TracerProvider: tp,          // nil disables every span
    MeterProvider:  mp,          // nil disables every instrument
    System:         "kafka",     // messaging.system; required
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

client := mq.NewClient(backend, mq.WithHooks(i.Hooks()))

// Publishing: the span and the injected trace context.
pub, _ := client.Publisher(ctx, mq.PublisherConfig{Topic: "orders"})
out, err := middleware.WrapPublisher(pub, i.PublishMiddlewareFor("orders"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}

// Consuming: the process span, parented to the publisher's.
consumer.Run(ctx, handler, mq.WithMiddleware(i.Middleware()))

// The gauges.
i.AddConsumer("orders", "billing", consumer.Stats)
if st, err := admin.Stats(ctx, "orders", "billing"); err == nil {
    i.ObserveQueueStats("orders", "billing", st)
}

Use PublishMiddlewareFor("orders") for a publisher bound to a topic. mq.PublishFunc's topic argument is read from Message.Topic, and the specification says a bound publisher ignores Message.Topic — so the chain sees an empty one, and a span built from it would have no messaging.destination.name.

docs.title: The four spans
docs.text:
Span Comes from Parent publish <topic> PublishMiddleware the caller's span process <topic> Middleware the publisher's span, read out of the delivery's headers receive <topic> Hooks.OnReceive none ack/nack/extend <topic> Hooks.OnSettle none

The first two are proper children, and together they are what makes one trace span the broker. The last two cannot be: mq.Hooks carries no context.Context, so there is nothing to parent them to and nothing to put them in. They are recorded with explicit start and end timestamps derived from the event's own duration, so their position in time is right even though their position in the trace is nowhere.

If you would rather have no span than an unparented one — or if one settle span per message is more than you will pay for — turn them off:

otelmq.Config{Spans: otelmq.Spans{NoReceive: true, NoSettle: true}}

A suppressed span's hook is not installed at all, so the core does not build its event either.

docs.title: Pinned semantic conventions
docs.text:
The attribute names come from one pinned convention version, otelmq.SemconvVersion, and nothing derives an attribute name from the OTel module's own release. Changing the semantic-convention version changes the exported attribute names.

The messaging conventions have renamed attributes between releases — messaging.destination became messaging.destination.name, messaging.operation became messaging.operation.type with a narrowed value set, messaging.kafka.consumer.group became the system-independent messaging.consumer.group.name. A dashboard built on the old name shows an empty graph after the upgrade that renamed it, and nothing at compile time notices. So the whole span surface — every name, kind, attribute key and attribute value — is pinned by a golden file (integrations/otel/testdata/spans.golden).

The specification names the four spans publish, receive, process and settle, and those are the messaging.operation.name values. messaging.operation.type carries the convention's own enumeration, which has no "publish" and calls it send; a settlement's operation name is ack, nack or extend under operation type settle.

A message identifier is never an attribute: one attribute value per message is how a tracing backend's index falls over.

docs.title: W3C trace context, and the envelope
docs.text:
Inject and Extract render and parse through middleware.TraceContext, which is the root module's own W3C implementation — the one the correlation middleware uses and FuzzTraceContext fuzzes. There is deliberately no second W3C parser in the repository.

A malformed traceparent never fails a delivery and never becomes a parent: The specification makes broker-delivered metadata untrusted, and a consumer a publisher can stop by writing nonsense into a header is a denial of service. tracestate is bounded at 512 bytes and dropped if it carries control characters.

There is nothing special for a broker with no headers, and that is the design: a backend whose body is an opaque blob carries the whole header table in iqmq's own envelope (the specification's MetadataPortableEnvelope, the wire package), so a traceparent written into Headers travels inside the envelope on exactly the brokers that have no header field and as a native header everywhere else. FuzzTraceContext proves it through wire itself.

For baggage as well as trace context, hand in an OpenTelemetry propagator:

otelmq.Config{Propagator: otelmq.W3CPropagator()}

That replaces Inject/Extract on every path with upstream's implementation, including its own W3C parser, which is why it is not the default.

docs.title: The instruments
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry sentence asks for three histograms and two gauges. The instrument names carry no unit suffix, because an OpenTelemetry instrument names its unit in a field and a Prometheus exporter appends the suffix from it — so what reaches a Prometheus server is the canonical name.

Instrument Unit Exported as iqmq_publish_duration s iqmq_publish_duration_seconds iqmq_handler_duration s iqmq_handler_duration_seconds iqmq_end_to_end_duration s iqmq_end_to_end_duration_seconds iqmq_in_flight {message} iqmq_in_flight iqmq_lag {message} iqmq_lag

Two of them are honest about what they cannot know:

  • End-to-end latency needs a creation timestamp. The specification says the publish path never reads the clock on its own, so a message carries Properties.CreatedAt only when the publisher was configured to stamp one (middleware.Timestamp). A message without one contributes no observation rather than a latency measured from the zero time.
  • Lag has no source in the SPI. ConsumerStats.Lag is always unknown at v0, so the gauge is observable and reports a series only for a subscription whose Admin.Stats you polled through ObserveQueueStats. A subscription nobody has measured has no data point, rather than a zero that reads as "caught up".

docs.title: Cardinality and cost
docs.text:
Cardinality bounds how many (operation, topic, subscription) attribute sets are cached and folds the rest onto one overflow destination, keeping the operation so that a publication never appears in a span called process other.

A destination name is not necessarily yours either: the specification makes a delivery's topic the concrete one the broker reported. Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are replaced with U+FFFD before they become a span name or an attribute value, because an OTLP exporter encodes both into protobuf string fields and proto3 requires valid UTF-8 — one odd topic would otherwise fail the export of a whole batch and lose every span in it.

With neither provider set, the middlewares are the identity and Hooks() is the zero mq.Hooks: zero allocations, and no code on the message path at all. With a non-recording tracer — the state a sampled-out span is in — a publish or process span costs three allocations and an unparented receive or settle span five, every one of them the OpenTelemetry API's own (a span's context value, an injected header's bytes, the boxed timestamp options). Not one of them is an attribute slice or a formatted span name: those are built once per destination. A recording SDK adds whatever it charges for a span. TestAllocs states all four columns.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom to cause. Every row names the error code or the counter that distinguishes it, because the codes are the stable interface and the messages are not.

Drivers do not use a global registry.

docs.title: Asking the system
docs.text:
iqmq doctor 'kafka://localhost:9092'      # dial, then print capabilities and limits; exit 3 on a missing one
iqmq tail 'kafka://localhost:9092' orders # watch messages without settling anything

Exit 3 from doctor means the driver lacks a capability the command needed — the honest answer rather than a crash. The CLI page has the rest, including what it deliberately cannot express.

docs.title: When it is the library
docs.text:
Two things to check before writing an issue, because both have caught real bugs and both are cheap:

  • run under -race. The engine's recurring defect class is a record placed in a lane while the subscription is closing, and it appears as five to twenty failures per two or three thousand rounds — which means a hundred rounds proves nothing either way.
  • reproduce on the memory driver. memory.NewForTest gives you a fake clock and a leak check, and a failure that reproduces there is a core failure rather than a broker one. That halves the search.

A driver bug report wants the iqmq doctor dump, which is what the issue form asks for.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: Three different upgrades with three different risks: the library, the client library underneath it, and the broker.

docs.title: Upgrading iqmq
docs.text:
v0.x while the API settles. Breaking changes are announced with migration notes, and make apidiff holds the public surface against hack/api/root.export so that a change to it is deliberate rather than noticed by a user.

From v1.0 the root package and the SPI are stable: growth happens through optional interfaces and concrete handles, because adding a method to a public interface is a breaking change for everyone who implemented it. The SPI is Backend plus nine optional interfaces rather than one large one.

Core minors ship as a release train: every official module is tagged together, so iqmq v1.4.0 and iqmq/drivers/kafka v1.4.0 are a matched pair. Patches are independent. A generated compatibility manifest lists which driver ranges work with which core.

Deprecations are kept for at least two minor releases with Deprecated: markers. Go version bumps happen only on minors, and are announced.

docs.title: Upgrading the client library under a driver
docs.text:
This is the one that bites, because it is a transitive dependency of your module: drivers/kafka requires franz-go, and go get -u will move it.

Each driver's go.mod records its client dependency. Check that version and the driver page's Client & version policy when upgrading.

This checkout contains no generated conformance reports or capability matrix to establish tested compatibility. Run the relevant conformance suite against your chosen source revision, client and broker versions before relying on a compatibility claim.

docs.title: Upgrading the broker
docs.text:
The risk here is a capability changing under you, in either direction, and three examples show the shapes:

  • a feature arrives. JetStream's Nats-TTL needs 2.11 and scheduled messages need 2.12. A driver that advertises them unconditionally against a 2.10 server would be lying, so the claim is conditional and the condition is the server version.
  • a feature becomes available a different way. RabbitMQ ≥ 4 speaks AMQP 1.0, which is why drivers/rabbitmq/amqp10 exists as a separate profile — and it is never silently substituted for the 0-9-1 driver, because the two have different settlement and ordering behaviour.
  • a default changes. This is the dangerous one, and the only defence is the broker-version matrix: make matrix runs the conformance suite against the broker versions conformance/harness/images.lock pins, nightly, and a claim that stops holding on a newer image is a failed scenario rather than a surprise in production.

docs.title: The order to do it in
docs.text:
1. Run iqmq doctor against the new broker with the old driver. It dials, reports capabilities and limits, and exits 3 when something a command needs is missing.
  2. Compare that against the capability table for your profile. A level that dropped from Native to Conditional, or a limit that shrank, is the thing to find now rather than at peak.
  3. Upgrade the driver, then the broker, on a topic you can afford to replay.
  4. Watch ConsumerStats.Redelivered, SettleFailures and DeadLetterFailures. Those three move first when a settlement contract has changed.

docs.title: Preparing a release
docs.text: Run the release checks, API compatibility checks and relevant test suites against the intended source revision. Record fresh results when making conformance or performance claims. Local release tags are lightweight references and provide no signature verification.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Benchmark the workloads and broker settings your application uses. The repository includes core microbenchmarks, native-client comparisons and driver overhead tools.

  • Methodology
  • Native client comparisons
  • Driver overhead
  • Tuning

docs.title: Benchmark methodology
docs.text:
No benchmark results are tracked in this checkout. The commands below generate new measurements; their presence does not establish a performance result.

Use a quiet host and the same Go version, CPU allocation, payloads, broker configuration and client settings for each comparison. Repeat measurements and compare their distributions.

Run core benchmarks with go test -run=^$ -bench=. -benchmem ./.... Use make bench-overhead for driver comparisons and make bench-compare for comparisons with other libraries. These targets write local output under benchmarks/reports/.

Use make benchguard-test and make benchgate-test to check the measurement tools. Results from emulators describe those emulators; use the intended managed service when assessing production behaviour.

docs.title: Native client comparisons
docs.text:
The benchmarks/native-baselines module runs broker clients without the iqmq API. Match its payload, batch size, acknowledgements and concurrency to the driver workload when comparing overhead.

Run make native-baselines on a quiet host with the required brokers available. Keep results local and compare repeated samples under the same configuration.

docs.title: Driver overhead
docs.text:
A driver that adds a millisecond to every publish costs you more than the broker does, so each measured driver is timed against the client library it wraps. Both arms send the same payloads to the same broker container, on the same pinned CPUs, and the gap between them is the driver's overhead.

The figures here are a fresh baseline taken on 19 October 2026 from the v1.0.0 release tree. Earlier overhead figures, and some of the benchmarks behind them, stayed in the private Bitbucket repository when the project moved to GitHub, because they held internal, project-specific information. Compare future runs against this page, not against anything older.

docs.title: The run
docs.text:
Run benchmarks/reports/results/20261019T024052Z-overhead (kept locally, not committed) Host AMD EPYC 9474F, 16 CPUs held by the benchmark (GOMAXPROCS 16), performance governor Go go1.27.2 Samples 10 rounds of 50ms per benchmark, both arms interleaved Brokers Redis and NATS containers pinned in conformance/harness/images.lock Guard clean for every broker

The budgets are on throughput lost, not time added. An arm that is 10% slower per operation moves 9.09% fewer messages a second. A single-message publish may lose up to 10%, and a batched publish up to 5%.

EndToEnd contains a receive, so it carries the same asymmetry. Both medians are in the table above; what is compared is a batched publication and a single-message publication, which is what the two budgets are written about.

docs.title: What this baseline shows
docs.text:
Single-message publishing is within its budget, or too close to call, on every arm. Batched publishing is where the overhead sits. The table marks 13 rows as breaches on their medians alone. make overhead-gate, which allows for the noise in both arms, fails this run on two rows, JetStream PublishBatch at 1KiB (+15.7%) and 64KiB (+27.7%), whose confidence intervals sit wholly above the 5% budget. The other 20 compared rows are undecided, because the noise on a shared host is wider than the gap being judged. Redis Streams batching (+10.7% to +16.5%) is the likeliest to become a confirmed breach on a quieter run.

make overhead-gate runs locally only. Neither CI nor the release workflow runs it, so these breaches are open work, not a release blocker.

docs.title: Reproduce it
docs.text:
make bench-overhead
make overhead-report RESULTS=benchmarks/reports/results/<run>/raw.txt
make overhead-gate RESULTS=benchmarks/reports/results/<run>/raw.txt.gz

A container benchmark on a shared host is evidence, not a verdict. Before you quote a figure, check that the run's guard verdict is clean, and repeat any run marked contended.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text: The knobs, in the order they matter, with what each one costs. The specification rule 10 requires every driver to document its own with the measured effect; this page is the portable layer.

docs.title: The four that matter most
docs.text:
ConsumerConfig.Prefetch. How many unsettled deliveries the runner will hold. Raising it buys throughput by hiding the fetch round trip, and costs memory (Prefetch × message size) and duplicates after a crash (every unsettled delivery comes back). Start at your concurrency and raise it while watching ConsumerStats.InFlight.

mq.WithConcurrency(n). How many handlers run at once. The default is one serial worker per assigned lane, which preserves order. If you have asked for mq.OrderingStrict, raise this: a strict retry parks a worker for the whole backoff, so at concurrency 1 the first failure stops the runner for up to 30 seconds.

ConsumerConfig.BufferReuse. Returns a delivery's storage to the consumer the moment it is settled, which makes the receive path allocation-free. The price is Delivery.Body and the headers are borrowed until settlement, so a handler that keeps them must CloneMessage first. Off by default for that reason.

The publisher's batching. PublisherConfig.Batching groups asynchronous publications. It is the single largest throughput lever on every broker — and it is also where the batched overhead budget is breached by 7 % to 46 %, so it is the path where this library currently costs you the most against the raw client. Driver overhead has the figures.

docs.title: The ones that change semantics, not speed
docs.text:
Worth separating, because they look like tuning and are not:

Knob Looks like Actually is mq.ConfirmNone "faster publishes" a different durability contract: may be lossy mq.BackpressureDropNewest / DropOldest "never block" a publication lost without the caller being told mq.FailureSkip "stop the queue filling up" an ack for a message nobody handled mq.OrderingRelaxed "higher throughput on failure" order abandoned for that key from the failure onwards mq.MetadataPortableEnvelope "portable headers" a wire-format change every other reader of that topic sees

Each of those is the right answer sometimes. None is a tuning knob.

docs.title: Per-driver knobs
docs.text:
Every driver page has a Tuning section with its own — linger, prefetch, poller count, pipelining depth, batch size, credit window — and rule 10 requires the measured effect rather than an assertion. The shapes that recur:

  • linger versus latency. Every batching producer trades one for the other. The knob is the client library's and the driver exposes it in typed config.
  • poller count. SQS's long poll is 20 seconds × 10 messages per poller, so throughput is pollers × 10 / poll duration and the only way up is more pollers.
  • pipelining depth. Redis: how many commands are in flight. Both Redis drivers pipeline batches, and it is the lever the batched overhead breach lives on.
  • credit window. AMQP 1.0: ReceiverOptions.Credit, which is the prefetch under another name.
  • the ack batching strategy. SQS coalesces DeleteMessageBatch, and which strategy — immediate, count, time, hybrid — was a bake-off of its own. Ack waits for the configured delete boundary, so the strategy is visible in your ack latency.

docs.title: The memory engine
docs.text:
memory.EngineConfig selects the variant implementations, and every field's Auto value is the bake-off winner recorded in an ADR:

memory.EngineConfig{
    Queue:     memory.QueueAuto,   // lane queue
    Wait:      memory.WaitAuto,    // empty-lane strategy
    Timer:     memory.TimerAuto,   // scheduler
    // …Arch, Hash, Pool, Registry, RetryLane
}

Leave them on Auto. The whole point of the bake-off is that Auto moves when the evidence moves and your code does not. Naming a kind explicitly is for a differential test, or for a workload you have measured yourself and found the default wrong for — and if you have, that is a benchmark worth contributing, because it is a row the campaign is missing.

memory.SafeEngine() forces the mutex reference implementations. It is for differential testing, not for production.

docs.title: How to tell whether a change helped
docs.text:
make bench-quick                         # smoke: seconds, never a decision
make gate BASE=main GATE=pr              # the regression gate, two interleaved runs
