make allocs                              # allocation counts; load-insensitive, always trustworthy

Three rules from this repository's own history:

Allocation tests are always trustworthy; timing on a shared host is not. testing.AllocsPerRun is deterministic. Run make allocs freely; treat a timing delta on a loaded machine as noise until the guard says otherwise.

A verdict of clean is not a verdict of quiet. clean means no foreign benchmark ran. Read foreign_runnable_p95 beside it.

Suspect the instrument. A number that is implausibly bad is as likely to be the harness as the code — and in this repository it has more often been the harness.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
The failure modes this library has an opinion about, and what that opinion is.

Page The failure Inbox and outbox your database and the broker disagree about whether something happened Poison messages a message that will never succeed, blocking one that would Graceful shutdown a deploy in the middle of a handler Rebalance the broker moves your partition to somebody else Chaos testing proving any of the above, deliberately

docs.title: The three rules underneath them
docs.text:
Never lose a message to make an operation succeed. Every branch in the runner that could drop a message instead requeues it and stops. The dead-letter route confirms before it acks; an exhausted message halts rather than being skipped; mq.FailureSkip exists and is never a default. The one place the library chooses a duplicate is the ambiguous dead-letter publication, and it counts the choice.

Never report an unknown as a known. An ambiguous publish outcome, an ambiguous settlement and an unadvertised limit are three different unknowns, and each has a representation of its own — mq.IsAmbiguous, mq.CodeSettlementUnknown, Limit[T].Known == false. The specification calls misclassifying ambiguity a disqualifying correctness defect.

Exactly one layer owns redelivery accounting. The specification. Two retry loops produce a message tried 25 times when you asked for 5, and a message the driver dead-lettered and the runner requeued. Where the broker has native retry and dead-letter policy the driver maps it and the runner stands down.

docs.title: What is proved, and how
docs.text: Property Held by the record lifecycle's invariants, after every step the memory engine's model fuzzer: one logical state per record, terminal release exactly once, stale tokens cannot settle a newer delivery, conservation per subscription, memory plateau under fixed limits acks equal successes, one settlement per delivery FuzzDispatcher the shutdown ordering, including DLQ-publish-before-ack models/tla/Shutdown and internal/model/shutdown — a TLA+ spec and a Go reference model, checked in make ci a capability claim, in both directions the conformance kit, per driver, against a containerised broker linearizability of the memory engine's history testkit/linear, over the histories internal/engine's TestEngineLinearizable, TestEngineLinearizableKeys and FuzzEngineLinearizable record — as tests in make ci, and weekly as make linearize-campaign, which gives the fuzzer hours instead of seconds and whose own negative control is make linearize-selftest an allocation budget on a path that must not allocate make allocs and the gated budgets

docs.title: Checking a deployment
docs.text: Chaos, soak and differential test packages are available. make suites-modes lists their commands; conformance/suites.json declares which modes each driver supports. Run the relevant modes and retain their source revision and results before making a claim about your deployment.

docs.title: Chaos, soak and differential testing
docs.text:
Proving the reliability claims by breaking things on purpose, and by running the same operation script against two implementations and comparing what they settled.

Everything on this page is a make target, and make suites-modes prints the state of every run mode, which is the generated answer to "what actually runs?":

chaos         implemented  conformance/chaos TestChaos_*
soak          implemented  conformance/soak TestSoak_*
differential  implemented  conformance/differential FuzzDifferential_*
matrix        implemented  conformance/matrix TestMatrix_*

A suite may only declare a run mode this repository implements, so conformance/suites.json and the mode registry are checked against each other in make ci (make suites-check). A mode declared and not implemented used to turn a skipped job into one that failed at a step that could not pass.

docs.title: What each mode is for
docs.text: Mode Question Cost When make chaos DRIVER=x does the driver keep and the promises while the network is broken? a broker and a Toxiproxy nightly subset, weekly EXTENDED=1 make soak DRIVER=x TIME=4h does anything grow without bound? one broker for TIME weekly make differential DRIVER=x is what the broker did a legal reading of what the memory engine did? a broker per seed nightly make matrix DRIVER=x do the claims that depend on the broker's VERSION actually change with it? one broker per image nightly

docs.title: Chaos: the L3 fault scenarios
docs.text:
conformance/chaos holds six scenarios, each naming the specification it is evidence for:

Scenario Fault What must hold reset-mid-burst reset_peer 200 ms into every connection no loss, and the client recovers within 30 s latency-over-timeout-during-ack 4 s downstream latency during settlement at least one ErrSettlementUnknown, then duplicates and no loss session-timeout-invalidates-the-generation the proxy is disabled: the socket answers nothing no loss across the rebalance bandwidth-bounds-backpressure 8 kbps upstream the publisher buffer stays inside its bound container-stop-start-reconnects (weekly) the broker container is stopped the workload resumes within 90 s topology-deletion-is-refused-or-degrades (weekly) the topic is deleted through Client.Admin an operation is refused, or Health reports degraded

Three things about the design are worth copying if you write your own.

A chaos run in which nothing failed has tested nothing. Every scenario's first check is FaultBit, which requires the injected fault to have made at least one operation fail. A Toxiproxy toxic silently does nothing more often than it does anything — the wrong stream, a proxy name that does not match, a workload whose own timeouts outlast the toxic — and each of those produces a run in which every property holds trivially. Two of the four nightly scenarios reported exactly that against a live broker with a live toxic in place, because the fault was being injected after the consumer's prefetch buffer was already full: the remaining work was local and could not fail. The workload now runs in two halves with the fault injected between them.

A message that was never fetched is not a message that was lost. The ledger's "missing" column counts accepted publishes with no delivery, and it only means loss once the final drain has converged — three consecutive empty receives that did not error. A run whose client never reconnected reported eight messages as lost that the drain had never had a chance to fetch. Run records Drained, NoLoss declines to claim loss without it, and DrainConverged is the check that says so.

A settlement you cannot fail is a settlement whose loss you cannot detect. latency-over-timeout-during-ack needs an acknowledgement whose fate is genuinely unknown, and on JetStream an Ack without Config.DoubleAck returns as soon as the frame is in the write buffer — there is no round trip for a latency toxic to straddle. The chaos arm therefore sets DoubleAck, and the scenario then reports 23 ambiguous settlements, 9 duplicates and no loss, which is the contract exactly.

The verdicts are pure functions of a Run struct, and verdict_test.go hands every one of them a run it must accept and a run it must reject. That half runs in make ci, with no container.

docs.title: Soak: three grades, never two
docs.text:
make soak DRIVER=x TIME=4h runs the L4 workload — publish, consume, settle, a reconnect storm every TIME/20 and a lease left to expire every TIME/40 — and samples the live heap, the live object count and the goroutine count throughout.

The verdict has three grades, and that is the whole point:

  • fail — a fitted growth rate above a ceiling and a material absolute increase over the fitted window.
  • pass — no such growth, over a run long enough to say so.
  • inconclusive — the run was shorter than ten minutes, took fewer than eight samples, or its workload made no progress.

A ten-minute soak that reports "no leak" has not tested a leak slower than ten minutes, so a short run cannot grade pass however flat its samples are. The grade is printed beside the duration every time, and a run's JSON artefact carries both.

Two details that were wrong on the first attempt and are worth knowing:

  • the slope is fitted to the tail of the series, not to the first and last samples. A process that allocates its buffers in the first thirty seconds and then holds them steady has a large first-to-last difference and no leak.
  • a slope alone cannot fail a run. A per-hour rate extrapolated from a two-second window multiplies by eighteen hundred, and a healthy two-second run graded fail on "+51946 objects/h" of ordinary allocation noise. A failure needs the fitted window to span at least a minute and a material absolute increase — four megabytes of live heap, ten thousand live objects, two goroutines.

docs.title: Differential: the relation, written down first
docs.text:
make differential DRIVER=x runs one operation script against the in-process memory engine and against the broker, and compares.

It cannot compare the two for equality. A broker may interleave two keys differently, redeliver a message whose settlement it did not see, and answer a publish ambiguously — so an equality check either fails on every run or is weakened until it passes, and after that it is a check that cannot fail. What is compared instead is a relation:

  • every id both arms accepted is delivered at least once by both;
  • no id the subject refused is delivered, and no delivery carries an id nobody published;
  • the settled multisets agree: an id the oracle acked is acked by the subject too, and an id the oracle dropped is not;
  • per key, the order in which ids are first delivered is the same on both arms — a redelivery cannot move a first delivery, which is what makes the ordering half insensitive to exactly the behaviour brokers differ on;
  • a message the script nacked comes back and one it dropped does not.

Every one of those is conditional on what the driver claims. PermissionsFor(caps) reads the permissions off the capability table, so a driver that advertises FeatureOrderedByKey is held to per-key order and one that advertises nothing is held to loss and settlement only. The only way to make a failing ordering run pass is to change the claim — at which point the conformance suite's negative probes require the driver to refuse what it no longer claims. Each run logs which half of the relation actually bound it (held to [...], not checked [...]) and how many ids it compared, because "no divergence" over zero compared ids is not a result: KindVacuous is a divergence.

The relation is a pure function of two observations, so it is held to a table of nineteen transformations — six a conforming broker may make, which it must accept, and thirteen injected defects, which it must reject under their own kind. The same table is then applied to the observation a real broker produced, because a relation that only ever saw a hand-written fixture could depend on something the fixture has and a run does not.

docs.title: Recording a run
docs.text: Record the source revision, broker image, command and outcome when running a campaign. A scenario being implemented does not establish that it passes for a particular driver or deployment.

docs.title: Doing it yourself
docs.text:
make broker-up NAME=toxiproxy starts the proxy, and the compose files under hack/compose start each broker from the digests conformance/harness/images.lock pins.

Three rules if you do, all learned here. Start one broker at a time and remove your own containers by id — a filtered docker rm has taken out other people's work on a shared machine. Read a fault-injection result with the same suspicion as a benchmark: a number that is implausibly bad is as likely to be the instrument as the code, and three of the defects on this page were in the instrument. And when a chaos run is green, read what it says it did — faulted=, unknown=, drained=, compared= — rather than the word "PASS".

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text: What happens between SIGTERM and the process exiting, and what the library guarantees about it. Specification the ordering is modelled in models/tla/Shutdown and internal/model/shutdown, both checked in every make ci.

docs.title: The two calls
docs.text:
client.Shutdown(ctx)   // graceful, bounded by ctx: flush, drain, close
client.Close()         // prompt: stop now

Shutdown flushes publishers, drains consumers and then closes the backend. It is idempotent, and closing a child handle afterwards is also idempotent — which matters, because a defer consumer.Close() inside a function whose caller already called Shutdown is the normal shape of Go code and must not be an error.

Close is the prompt version, for when the deadline has passed and you would rather lose the in-flight work than the process.

The API provides a prompt Close and a graceful Shutdown, rather than one method with a flag.

docs.title: The order, and why each step is where it is
docs.text:
1. stop accepting. New publications and new fetches are refused with mq.ErrClosed. Nothing new enters the system, so the set to drain is finite.
  2. flush publishers. Asynchronous and batched publications that were admitted are sent and confirmed. A publication the publisher accepted is a publication it owes you, so this is not optional.
  3. drain consumers. Handlers already in flight run to completion and settle. The wait is mq.DefaultDrainTimeout — 30 seconds — or mq.WithDrainTimeout(d); past it their contexts are cancelled.
  4. requeue what was not settled. Whatever the runner held and did not settle goes back to the broker, so it is redeliverable rather than sitting on a lease nobody will settle. ConsumerStats.InFlight returns to zero.
  5. close the backend. The client library's connections go last, because steps 2 and 4 need them.

Step 4 is the one that is easy to get wrong and is the reason this ordering is in a TLA+ spec rather than in a comment. A runner that closed its source before requeueing would strand every unsettled delivery on an expiring lease: no loss, but a redelivery storm one lease-timeout later, on a broker that has just lost a consumer.

docs.title: What a handler sees
docs.text:
Its context is cancelled when the drain timeout expires — or earlier, if you passed Shutdown a context with a nearer deadline. A handler that respects its context stops; a handler that does not is abandoned, its delivery is unsettled, and the message comes back.

So the handler contract during shutdown is exactly the handler contract at any other time: return promptly when your context is done, and do not settle after you have returned. A handler that ignores its context turns a graceful shutdown into a hard one.

mq.WithLeaseDeadline() helps here for a different reason: it ends the handler's context with the lease, so a handler cannot keep working past the point at which its work no longer counts — which during a shutdown is usually sooner than the drain timeout.

docs.title: Ordering during a drain
docs.text: Under mq.OrderingStrict, a delivery in a backoff wait when the shutdown starts is requeued rather than retried. The runner does not sit out the remaining backoff during a drain and it does not skip the message either: it gives it back, and the next process gets it. That is the branch that makes a shutdown in the middle of a retry loop lose nothing.

docs.title: The recurring defect this is the fix for
docs.text:
The engine's most-repeated bug in this repository has been a record put into a lane, a store or a retained log while its subscription or the engine is closing: the placing goroutine checks the closed flag, Close drains, and the placement lands after the drain — so the payload's release callback never runs and the engine-wide reservation is consumed for ever, breaking the specification's terminal-release invariant.

It has been publish-versus-close, nack-versus-close twice, and Seek-versus-close. The established fix is to re-read the closed flags after placing and re-drain, or to place under the same mutex the drain takes; and the established test is thousands of rounds under -race, because the known instances appeared at five to twenty failures per two or three thousand rounds. A hundred rounds proves nothing, which is why this paragraph is in the documentation and not only in the playbook.

docs.title: A caveat about goroutines
docs.text: Shutdown returning does not always mean every goroutine is gone, and the reason is not in this library: some client libraries hold a goroutine past a close — up to one of their own timeouts — and there is nothing the driver can do about it. The driver pages record the known instances with the upstream cause, and the drivers' own tests use goleak so that a new one is a test failure rather than a slow leak in production.

docs.title: Inbox and outbox
docs.text: The pattern for when your database and the broker must not disagree. Both halves are in this library as extensions — x/outbox and x/inbox — and neither ships a SQL store: the part that has to live in your database is yours, and those pages say exactly what it must guarantee. The shapes are here because the pattern is what people reach for first and because the half-measures are worse than the pattern.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
tx.Exec("INSERT INTO orders …")   // (1)
tx.Commit()                       // (2)
pub.Publish(ctx, msg)             // (3)

Three failure points, and each of them produces a different wrong answer:

  • fail after (2) and before (3): the order exists and nobody was told.
  • fail during (3) with an ambiguous outcome: nobody knows whether anybody was told.
  • publish before committing instead: somebody is told about an order that was rolled back.

There is no ordering of those two operations that is correct, because they are two systems and there is no transaction across them. That is not a limitation of this library; it is the shape of the problem.

docs.title: The outbox
docs.text:
Write the message into your own database, in the transaction that produced it. A separate process reads the unpublished rows, publishes them, and marks them sent.

BEGIN
  INSERT INTO orders  …
  INSERT INTO outbox (topic, key, headers, body) VALUES …
COMMIT
-- then, separately:
--   SELECT … FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
--   publish, then UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = now()

What it buys: the order and the intent-to-publish commit or roll back together, so the first and third failures above disappear. An ambiguous publication is now resolvable — the row is still unsent, so it is retried, and the duplicate that produces is a duplicate rather than a loss.

What it costs: at-least-once publication, which you had anyway; a relay to run; and ordering that is the relay's rather than your application's, so a relay with concurrency reorders unless it partitions by key.

x/outbox is the relay half: outbox.New runs the claim, publish and mark loop over a Store whose four loop methods — Claim, MarkSent, Release, Fail — you implement against your own table, and Row with EncodeHeaders/DecodeHeaders fixes the column shape. The append is an INSERT in your own transaction, so the interface deliberately has no Append. The worked Postgres version, with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED against a real container, is examples/outbox-postgres; it predates the package and still declares its own store types rather than implementing outbox.Store. Status is the current state of every module.

docs.title: The inbox
docs.text:
The consumer half: record that you processed a message, keyed on its identity, in the same transaction as the side effect.

BEGIN
  INSERT INTO inbox (message_id) VALUES ($1)   -- fails on a duplicate
  …the side effect…
COMMIT

A unique-constraint violation means you have seen it: ack and move on. This is how at-least-once delivery becomes effectively-once processing, and it is the only way that works on every broker — which is the argument the duplicates page makes at more length.

The identity is Delivery.ID where the broker provides one, or your own DedupKey carried in a header where it does not.

x/inbox is this half: its middleware hands each delivery to Store.Once, which records the key and runs your handler in one transaction. Its MemoryStore is for tests; in production the Store is your database. x/idempotency is the cheaper, weaker sibling — a claim in a separate store, in process or in Redis (x/idempotency/redisstore), which reduces the duplicate rate rather than closing the window — and the extensions index compares the two.

docs.title: What not to do instead
docs.text:
Do not publish inside the database transaction. A broker call inside a transaction holds the transaction open for a network round trip, and on a timeout you have both problems at once.

Do not use a broker transaction as a substitute. Kafka transactions and Pulsar transactions are real and this library exposes them — x/kafkatx, x/pulsartx — and they make a set of broker operations atomic with respect to a broker read. They do not make your database write atomic with them. The specification says so and it is worth repeating: a broker dedup or transaction feature does not make an arbitrary side effect exactly-once.

Do not use mq.FailureSkip to make the numbers look better. It acks a message nobody handled. It is the only destructive failure policy, it is never a default, and reaching for it here means the outbox row was never written and nobody will ever know.

docs.title: The claim-check variant
docs.text: When the message is too large for the broker — mq.ErrMessageTooLarge, refused before any I/O against the driver's advertised MaxMessageBytes — the pattern is to store the payload somewhere addressable and publish the address. That is x/claimcheck, which stores the body and publishes a reference to it. The relevant part here is that the refusal is local and cheap, so discovering the limit costs no round trip.

docs.title: Poison messages
docs.text: A poison message is one that will never succeed. The library's whole job here is to stop it from also preventing the messages behind it from succeeding — without destroying it, because a destroyed poison message is a bug report nobody can answer.

docs.title: What happens by default
docs.text:
Five attempts with bounded exponential jittered backoff. Then, if a dead-letter destination is configured, the message is dead-lettered; otherwise the runner halts with a *mq.PoisonError carrying mq.CodePoisonMessage, having first requeued the message.

The halt is the part worth defending. The three alternatives are: skip it (silent data loss — forbidden as a default), retry it for ever (the queue never drains and nobody is told), or auto-create a dead-letter topic (a production topology change nobody asked for). Halting is loud, loses nothing, and puts the decision where it belongs.

docs.title: Configuring it
docs.text:
err := consumer.Run(ctx, handler,
    mq.WithMaxAttempts(5),
    mq.WithRetryBackoff(mq.ExponentialBackoff{
        Base:   200 * time.Millisecond,
        Max:    30 * time.Second,
        Jitter: mq.FullJitter,
    }),
    mq.WithDeadLetter("orders.dlq"),
    mq.WithFailurePolicy(mq.FailureDeadLetter))
Policy On exhaustion mq.FailureDeadLetter publish to the destination, confirm, then ack. The default when a destination exists. mq.FailureHalt *mq.PoisonError, requeue, stop. The default when none does. mq.FailureSkip ack a message nobody handled. Destructive; never a default; logged and counted. mq.FailureInfiniteRequeue give it back with the backoff, for ever

There is no FailureCustom policy. The API exposes typed failure-policy choices through RunOption rather than a custom policy closure.

docs.title: Short-circuiting the attempts
docs.text:
A handler that already knows the message is poison should not wait for five attempts:

if errors.Is(err, ErrSchemaUnknown) {
    return mq.DeadLetter(err)   // now, without exhausting the attempts
}

mq.DeadLetter(err) dead-letters immediately. With no dead-letter destination it halts — dropping instead is the one answer the specification forbids, so the directive cannot be used to discard by accident.

mq.Discard(err) is the deliberate discard: ack without success, logged and counted, never silent. It is the handler's decision and never the runner's, and it is the honest way to say "this message is garbage and I accept the loss".

mq.Halt(err) stops the runner. It stops the fetch first and requeues after — in that order, so the runner cannot hand itself the same message on its way out.

docs.title: The bound that may never be reached
docs.text:
mq.WithMaxAttempts(5) bounds Delivery.Attempt, which is the broker's count and is 0 on a broker that keeps none. Under the default mq.OrderingRelaxed a message the runner gave back carries nothing else, so on such a broker the exhaustion branch is never reached and the message is retried for as long as it fails.

If your broker does not count attempts and you need the bound, use mq.OrderingStrict: the runner holds the message in the process, so the count is exact. The matrix says which drivers count; the driver pages state it under Attempt counting.

docs.title: Consuming the dead-letter topic
docs.text:
It is a topic. Consume it like any other — and read the five provenance headers, which are the reason the dead-letter topic is useful rather than a graveyard:

iqmq-origin-topic, iqmq-origin-subscription, iqmq-attempts, iqmq-failure, iqmq-first-delivered-at. The names are exported as mq.HeaderOriginTopic and friends, deliberately: a name you have to copy out of a specification is a name that goes wrong.

iqmq-first-delivered-at is present only when the dead-lettered delivery was the first one. A missing header means "not known", because a redelivery may reach a different process and nothing in the SPI carries a first-delivery time back.

On mq.WithNativeDeadLetter() — the broker's own dead-letter route — there are no provenance headers at all, because nothing on that path writes a message. That is the trade: the native route has no publish-then-ack window and no duplicate risk, and it also tells you nothing about why.

docs.title: Where this is limited today
docs.text: mq.WithDeadLetter works on all twelve drivers. It did not until six of them refused any header under mq.ReservedHeaderPrefix on publish, which is the rule about a caller's headers applied to the core's own five, so the publication failed before any I/O, the runner requeued the message and counted a DeadLetterFailures, and the message was redelivered for ever.

docs.title: Rebalance
docs.text:
A rebalance is the broker taking a partition away from this process and giving it to another one, usually because a consumer joined or left. Everything in-flight on that partition is suddenly somebody else's problem, and the question is whether it is processed twice, processed once, or lost.

This page is mostly about Kafka, because Kafka is where the portable API has to do the most work.

docs.title: The offset tracker
docs.text:
Kafka commits a single offset per partition and means "everything before this is done". A consumer that processes messages concurrently completes them out of order, so the naive commit — the highest offset seen — would skip the ones still in flight.

driverkit/offset is the tracker that makes this correct:

  • it marks delivered offsets as in-flight;
  • it commits only the highest contiguous completed offset plus one;
  • a failed or unresolved offset therefore blocks later commits rather than being skipped over;
  • it pauses the partition when the gap or the in-flight count exceeds its bounds, so an unbounded gap cannot become unbounded memory.

The offset-tracker implementations and their benchmarks are under driverkit/offset. Compare them on your workload before changing the binding.

The consequence to plan around: one stuck message stops the commit for its whole partition. The messages behind it are still processed — they are marked in-flight and completed — but the committed position does not advance past the gap, so a rebalance re-delivers them. That is the trade the specification asks for: duplicates rather than a silent skip.

docs.title: What the driver does on revocation
docs.text:
In OnPartitionsRevoked, in this order:

  1. stop dispatching for the revoked partitions. No new handler starts on work that is about to belong to someone else.
  2. wait, bounded. Handlers already running get a chance to finish.
  3. commit the safe boundary synchronously. Still inside the callback, because after it returns the partition is gone and a commit is refused.
  4. invalidate the old generations. Every outstanding delivery for those partitions has its generation bumped, so a late settlement from a handler that finished after step 2 returns mq.ErrLeaseLost instead of settling an offset that now belongs to another consumer.

Step 4 is what the generation token is for, and it is why a stale *mq.Delivery is safe to hold: it cannot settle the new owner's work.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
Signal Meaning mq.ErrLeaseLost from a settlement the partition moved while your handler ran. Expected during a rebalance; the message will be redelivered. ConsumerStats.Redelivered jumping the new owner started from the last committed position the handler's context cancelled the bounded wait in step 2 expired

None of the three is an error to alert on individually. A rate of them that does not settle down after a deploy is: that is a consumer group that cannot stop rebalancing, usually because a handler is slower than the session timeout.

docs.title: Ordering across a rebalance
docs.text:
Order within a key survives only if the key's partition does not move, and a rebalance moves partitions. The cooperative-sticky balancer minimises the movement — it is the driver's default for exactly this reason — but it does not eliminate it.

If your requirement is that a key is never processed out of order even across a rebalance, the ordering has to come from the broker rather than from the consumer: a FIFO group (SQS FIFO), a Key_Shared subscription (Pulsar), or a partition you never move.

docs.title: The other brokers
docs.text:
• SQS has no rebalance: every consumer takes from the same queue, and a visibility timeout is the only thing that transfers a message.
  • JetStream and Pub/Sub redistribute by lease expiry rather than by a group protocol, so the "rebalance" is just the redelivery path and mq.WithLeaseExtension is the lever.
  • Redis Streams reassigns through the pending-entries list: the mandatory XAUTOCLAIM reclaim loop takes over entries idle past the ack deadline, and the delivery count it returns becomes Delivery.Attempt.
  • RabbitMQ moves a consumer rather than a partition; the driver owns bounded reconnection and topology restoration.

Each driver page's Reconnect and At-least-once window sections state its own version.

docs.title: What is not tested yet
docs.text: What is tested: TestCriticalReconnectRestoresTheTopology and the drivers' own critical tests, in-process, in every make ci. One of them is rare-flaky under host load and is recorded as such rather than retried until green.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Specification. This page is what the library does, what it refuses to do, and what is not in place yet.

Vulnerability reports go through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting — never a public issue.

docs.title: Broker-delivered payloads are untrusted
docs.text:
A message that arrives from a broker is input from the network, and this library treats it as such:

  • limits are enforced before allocation. A decoder reads the declared size and count and refuses, rather than allocating what a malicious header claims it needs. That is an allocation bound, and the review found that it is not by itself a cost bound — see what the review found. mq.ErrMessageTooLarge is the refusal a size or count limit gives, and mq.CodeCorruptMessage is the code a malformed payload's error carries. wire's decoder has its own refusals for a bad magic, a bad version, a truncated frame, a varint that does not terminate and trailing bytes — five named errors rather than one, because a corrupt frame's shape is diagnostic.
  • the wire envelope is never auto-detected unless you configured it. mq.MetadataNativeStrict is the default precisely so that a payload cannot become a header set because it happened to begin with the right bytes. That is a parsing decision with a security consequence, which is why it is a mode rather than a heuristic — and the one time adaptive mode got that sniff wrong, the regression input is committed and runs under -race in every CI build.
  • asynchronous and retry storage is bounded. Every buffer has a default bound; there is no value of MaxPendingMessages that turns it off. An unbounded retry queue is a remote memory-exhaustion primitive.
  • compression middleware caps decompressed output. A decompression bomb is a size limit's problem, not the decompressor's.
  • a reserved iqmq- header on an INBOUND delivery is producer-controlled data. Headers.Validate refuses that prefix to a caller of this library and that is the whole of the enforcement: a producer using the broker's own client can set any header it likes. So an arriving iqmq-attempts or iqmq-origin-topic is a claim by whoever published, not provenance from the core — and nothing in the core reads one back as authority. Delivery.Attempt comes from the driver's own delivery count, and the five provenance headers are written on the dead-letter copy for an operator to read. The prefix reads as an authenticity claim; it is not one.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
TLS is on by default for remote and cloud profiles. Any option that disables transport security has Insecure in its name — that is a naming rule, so grep -r Insecure over your own configuration finds every place you turned it off.

Contradictory TLS settings are rejected at construction, not ignored with the safer one winning. A configuration that says both things is a configuration whose author is wrong about something, and guessing which half they meant is how a deployment ends up in plaintext.

There is no custom cryptography anywhere in this repository, and that is an inventory rather than an assurance. The only primitives any module uses are the standard library's: crypto/tls (36 files), crypto/rand (9), crypto/aes + crypto/cipher for the AES-GCM in middleware.Encrypt, crypto/sha256 for deriving a queue name in the two SQS drivers, and crypto/sha1 in internal/streams — which is Redis's own EVALSHA script digest, a protocol identifier and not a security primitive.

docs.title: unsafe
docs.text:
None in the core package. Avoided in the memory engine. Any use requires: an ADR, a safe pure-Go fallback behind a build tag, a material measured benefit, race and multi-architecture testing, a security review, and isolation in its own package.

The bake-off scoring adds 1000 lines of notional complexity per use of unsafe when breaking a tie, so an unsafe implementation has to win on merit by more than a margin to be selected at all.

Two packages import it, and the review corrected this paragraph, which used to name internal/queue and wire — wire has never imported it:

  • internal/queue/slot_unsafe.go, behind the iqmq_unsafe build tag, with a pure-Go file taking its place by default. That is the shape exactly.
  • internal/payload/alias.go, unconditionally and with no fallback, for unsafe.SliceData in Overlaps: it compares two slices' addresses to decide whether writing through one can be observed through the other, and it never dereferences either. There is no safe way to ask that question in Go, and a build-tagged fallback would have to answer it wrongly in one direction — always-true costs a copy on every borrowed payload, always-false misses real aliasing, which is a correctness bug in the memory-ownership contract. So it is a deliberate deviation from "isolated package or build tag" rather than an oversight, and it is recorded here because a policy with an unrecorded exception is a policy nobody can check.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
licence Apache-2.0, with NOTICE. make license scans dependencies. vulnerabilities govulncheck in every module per PR, on main and daily (vuln.yml → make vuln), on the latest Go patch release, judged against owned waivers — see below static analysis CodeQL weekly (codeql.yml) Actions pinned by full commit SHA, least-privilege permissions:, held by make workflows-lint Scorecard scorecard.yml weekly; the target is ≥ 8, and ≥ 7 at v1.0 dependency hygiene the root module depends on the standard library only, held by make stdlib-check. Each driver brings one client library and only its own.

That last row is a security property as much as a performance one: your program's attack surface is one broker SDK, not eleven.

docs.title: What the review found
docs.text: The review that asks for has happened. It read every decoder for the allocation rule, every Config for both renderings, every place a credential can reach an output, every TLS refusal and every crypto/ import, and ran govulncheck over all 48 modules. Each finding below has a test that failed before the fix.

docs.title: A decoder whose cost was the square of its input
docs.text:
internal/wire's own documentation says "a hostile envelope can cost at most its own size". The TLV layout broke it in time: the commit pass asked for the i-th header by restarting the walk from the first field of the metadata section, so it was quadratic in a header count bounded only by the envelope's length. A legal one-mebibyte envelope carrying 262,144 empty headers took 3m1s to decode; the fixed-width layout, which carries its cursor forward, took 4.8ms for the same byte budget.

The reachability is the part that matters. The default limit is 1024 headers, so a consumer's own limit refuses that envelope in 16.85µs — and then adaptive metadata mode calls wire.Detector.DetectFull to tell a refused envelope from a native body, and DetectFull removes every limit deliberately, so that "is this an envelope" cannot depend on one consumer's configuration. The escalation happened precisely on the input the limit exists to refuse, whatever was configured, and the attacker picks the layout by writing it into the envelope's version byte. Fixed; the test states the claim as a five-second budget for a one-mebibyte body, which is a five-hundredfold margin over the linear cost.

docs.title: Two renderings that were not safe
docs.text: dsn.Config.String is documented as "safe to put in a log line or an error" and wrote every query parameter verbatim. Four shipped drivers read a credential from one — token (NATS, JetStream, Pulsar), authsecret (NSQ), authparams (Pulsar), sessiontoken (SQS, SNS+SQS) — so the one rendering documented as safe printed ?token=… in full. Worse, it had a pointer receiver, so a Config value implemented neither fmt.Stringer nor slog.LogValuer and %v of one printed the struct with the parameter slices in it. Both are fixed, the predicate that decides which parameter is a credential now has one home, and memory.Config — which implemented neither rendering — has both.

docs.title: A static analysis that covered one module of 48
docs.text: codeql.yml ran go build ./... in the repository root. A Go pattern does not cross into a nested module, and the root module is stdlib-only by policy, so CodeQL extracted the one package set with no dependencies and none of the code that links a broker client. It runs make build now. (It has still never run at all — see below.)

docs.title: Three defects in the gate itself
docs.text: Found while wiring make security-check in, and all three live on main: a merge had put docs-check after the ## in the Makefile's ci: line, where make does not see it; the same line's trailing backslash continued the comment and swallowed work-sync's rule, so make work-sync exited 0 having done nothing — a check in this repository's own gate that could not fail; and the line's indentation made hack/ci-parity.sh, whose job is to notice exactly that drift, exit 2 instead. All three are fixed and ci-parity now owns the shape of that line.

docs.title: Dependency advisories, as govulncheck reports them
docs.text:
make vuln runs govulncheck in every module and judges what it finds against a table of waivers in tools/securitycheck/vuln.go, each with an owner. It exits 0 on go1.27.1 with the database of 2026-09-16: 48 modules scanned, six affected, sixteen findings, every one waived.

Advisory Module Fixed in Reaches State GO-2026-5046 (CPU exhaustion, Avro decoder) hamba/avro/v2 none codec/avro, cmd/iqmq, drivers/pulsar, x/pulsartx waived: no fix exists; codec/avro refuses the input before the decoder sees it GO-2026-5047 (integer overflow, Avro decoder) hamba/avro/v2 none as above as above GO-2026-5048 (unbounded map allocations) hamba/avro/v2 none as above as above GO-2026-6061 (gRPC xDS RBAC / HTTP-2) google.golang.org/grpc v1.82.1 benchmarks, benchmarks/competitors fixed at v1.84.0 GO-2026-6348 (gRPC HTTP-2 DATA fragmentation OOM) google.golang.org/grpc v1.83.1 as above fixed at v1.84.0 GO-2026-4945 (go-jose JWE panic) go-jose/v4 v4.1.4 drivers/pulsar, x/pulsartx fixed in both GO-2026-6253 (tar path traversal) moby/go-archive v0.3.0 conformance (testcontainers) fixed GO-2026-6354, GO-2026-6355 (SSH channel DoS) golang.org/x/crypto v0.56.0 conformance (testcontainers) fixed

Four things a reader should take from that table:

make vuln is deliberately not part of make ci: its verdict depends on a database published after the commit, and a make ci that turned red overnight with no change would stop meaning "this commit is green".

docs.title: Release verification
docs.text:
Local release tags span v0.5.0 through v1.0.0 and are lightweight references to commits. They carry no tag messages, tagger identities, dates or signatures. The commits are unsigned. GitHub publication and release-artefact signatures have not been verified.

Tags before v0.9.0 use the bitbucket.org/iqhive/iqmq module path. The v0.9.0 and later release trains use github.com/iqhive/iqmq.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Testing code that uses a message broker, and testing this library itself.

Page Memory driver the in-process engine as a test double that is also a real driver synctest deterministic tests of backoff, leases and scheduled delivery, with no sleeping testkit the conformance kit: prove a driver's capability claims in both directions Conformance running the suite, its run modes and generating fresh reports Fuzzing 130 fuzz targets, the differential shape, and the ratchet

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Use memory.NewForTest(t). It is not a mock. It is the same Backend, the same runner and the same settlement state machine your production driver uses, with AutoCreate on, a fake clock installed, and a goroutine-leak check registered on t.Cleanup.

func TestBilling(t *testing.T) {
    client, broker := memory.NewForTest(t)
    // …publish, run a handler, assert…
    _ = broker.Advance(30 * time.Second)   // drive the scheduler; do not sleep
}

Never sleep in a test of a backoff. Broker.Advance(d) moves the fake clock, so a test of a 30-second retry takes microseconds and gives the same answer every time. Under testing/synctest you can go further and assert the schedule — see synctest.

Inject faults rather than arranging them. broker.Faults() is the specification's injector: reject the nth publication, delay or fail a settlement, force a duplicate delivery, expire leases, close consumers, simulate reconnect generations, fail a dead-letter publication. Every counted fault carries a counter, and a fault that fired zero times is how you discover that your test did not reach the path it was written for.

Assert on error codes, not on messages. mq.CodeOf(err) and errors.Is(err, mq.ErrLeaseLost). The codes are the stable interface.

docs.title: What testing this library looks like
docs.text:
Because it is worth knowing which of these an ordinary contribution has to satisfy:

Check What it is make test-race every module, under -race make allocs testing.AllocsPerRun with exact counts on the hot paths the specification names make fuzz-seeds every committed corpus input, under -race, in every CI run make ratchet the fuzz-target count only rises, and parsing or stateful packages must have one make modelcheck the Go reference models, including the record lifecycle's invariants after every step make tla the TLA+ specifications, models/tla/Shutdown among them make conformance-memory the kit against the memory driver, no container make critical every driver critical tests, in-process against fakes make docs-check this documentation's own shape: the specification sections, links, anchors, nav reachability

The rule underneath all of them, from the contributor notes and earned the hard way: watch a new check fail before you make it pass. The single most-repeated defect in this repository has been a check that could not fail — nine instances — and every one of them was green.

docs.title: Running the conformance suite
docs.text:
No generated conformance reports or capability matrix are tracked in this checkout. The suite definitions and test code describe checks that can be run; they do not establish that any particular broker configuration passed.

Generate reports from the source revision you intend to assess. A report without an available source revision cannot establish conformance of the current checkout.

testkit is the kit. This page is the machinery around it: how CI drives it, which reports it writes, what those reports are evidence for, and how to select one of the seven run modes.

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text: conformance/suites.json is the list CI drives from — 22 suites today. Each entry names the test, the run modes it declares, its broker images and its reports.

docs.title: The seven run modes
docs.text:
make suites-modes prints this, and it is the authority rather than this page:

Mode State What it is integration implemented the whole kit against the suite's containerised broker. Writes the reports the capability matrix is generated from. inprocess implemented the kit against a driver that needs no broker, in the driver's own package. make conformance-memory is this, and make ci runs it. critical implemented the driver-specific critical tests, against an in-process fake. Needs no container, so make ci runs every driver's set. matrix implemented the broker-version matrix from the pinned images. Nightly. chaos implemented fault-injection scenarios against the selected broker soak implemented long runs with heap, goroutine and settlement observations differential implemented compare an operation script against memory and a broker

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
make conformance-memory                      # the memory driver, in-process, no container
make critical DRIVER=nats                    # one driver's critical tests
make integration DRIVER=nats                 # the full kit against a container
make integration                             # every suite (starts brokers, one at a time)
make matrix DRIVER=kafka                     # the broker-version matrix
make suites-modes                            # what each mode is and what it is missing

make integration starts containers. On a shared machine start one broker at a time, from the digests conformance/harness/images.lock pins, and remove only the containers you started, by id.

docs.title: The reports
docs.text:
Reports record the driver and profile, broker and client versions, Go version, run date, source revision and scenario outcomes. The testkit writes these fields when a suite runs. Generate fresh reports with make conformance-memory-report or make integration DRIVER=<driver>.

For each scenario, these fields carry most of the meaning:

  • positive — whether this scenario checks that the feature works or that the unsupported path is refused. Both halves of a claim have a row, which is what "proved in both directions" means concretely.
  • outcome — pass, fail or skip.
  • note — why it was skipped. A skip with no reason would be indistinguishable from a claim nobody checked, so the reason is required and is what the matrix renders when it explains a missing verification.
  • feature and claimed — the capability a scenario is about, and the level the driver advertises for it, read from the capability table of the client the scenario opened. A scenario that returned before it had a client — a documented skip, a topology the driver refused, an Open that failed — says "claimed": "unread": no level was read, and neither an empty field nor a level borrowed from another scenario's client may stand in for one, because a driver's level can depend on the topology it was opened for. confgen refuses a result that names a feature and carries no level at all, and renders a claim that no scenario could read as ∅.
  • kind — absent for a behaviour, guarantee for a claim one run cannot settle. It is what tells a reader whether the evidence is two-sided: a pass on a guarantee's positive direction means "this run saw no counter-example", and a denied guarantee nothing contradicted renders as unrefuted rather than unverified. A behaviour probe that found the driver accepted the feature's call and did something else carries it too — for that driver there was no call to refuse. The kit's page has the whole table.

evidence is the one to read first: inprocess, container, emulator or managed. An emulator report's cells are marked ◐ in the matrix and are never presented as the managed service's answer. A report must describe the environment its suite actually used.

docs.title: From reports to the matrix
docs.text: When reports are present, make generate-check fails when generated artifacts are stale and validates the reports before it renders them: an image images.lock does not pin, a commit that is not a commit, a report no suite publishes, a suite whose report is missing, a report far behind the newest in the corpus, or one recording a FAILED scenario is a failure there rather than a capability claim nobody can support. It also fails on a generated page no report produces — which is the gap -check had, where deleting a driver's report left its capability page stating capabilities from evidence that no longer existed.

docs.title: Using the kit on your own driver
docs.text:
That is the point of it being a published module rather than an internal test helper. The driver author guide has the whole path; the short version is a conformance_test.go in package <driver>_test that calls testkit.RunConformance with your Harness.

Model it on drivers/nats/conformance_test.go. Do not model it on memory/conformance_test.go, which reaches unexported engine helpers — legitimate for that driver's own package and useless as an example, and recorded as such.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text: 130 fuzz-target functions across the repository, with a ratchet that stops the count going down. Specification.

docs.title: What is fuzzed, and in what shape
docs.text:
Parsers and encoders, for crashes and round-trips. wire's envelope encode/decode, header packing, DSN parsing, the drivers' own native mappings (record mapping, attribute encoding, tag settlement, error mapping). The property is usually "decode(encode(x)) == x, and decode never panics on anything".

State machines, differentially. This is the shape that finds the interesting bugs: the fuzzer writes an op script — publish, receive, ack, nack, expire, close, advance the clock — and the script is run against both the implementation and a reference oracle, step by step, with the states compared after every step. internal/fuzzutil is the script machinery, and Script.WriteStep is how a seed corpus is authored in code so it stays readable.

FuzzDispatcher is the runner's: it asserts that acks equal successes and that there is exactly one settlement per delivery.

Message-shaped data, steered. testkit/fuzzkit generates the awkward shapes from fuzz input — nil versus empty bodies, duplicate header keys, hot keys, hierarchical topic names, maximum-length values — while guaranteeing the structural properties the system under test relies on: a generated topic is always a valid portable name, a generated payload never aliases the fuzz input, sizes respect the limits. The generators have exact mirrors (Put…) so a seed can be written by hand.

It depends on the standard library and internal/ only, never on the root package, so the lowest-layer targets can use it.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
make fuzz-seeds                    # every committed input, under -race. In every make ci.
make fuzz-smoke                    # a few seconds per target
make fuzz FUZZTIME=30s             # a real campaign, locally
make fuzz-nightly                  # the 10 minutes per target, sharded eight ways
make fuzz-targets                  # what the campaign would run (SHARDS=8 SHARD=3 for one shard)
make ratchet                       # the count only rises; parsing/stateful packages need a target
make ratchet-update                # after adding targets

Do not set -parallel by hand. A fuzz worker is a separate PROCESS with its own GOMAXPROCS, and the shell starts several of those at once (xargs -P for make fuzz, one child per shard for the nightly), so the real cost is jobs x workers x GOMAXPROCS. All three come from hack/cpucap.sh fuzz via JOBS, SHARDS and FUZZ_WORKERS, so the product stays inside IQMQ_MAX_CPUS — 2 x 2 x 4 = 16 on this host. Keep -parallel 8 is what this page used to say, and at the current width that would have been 128 threads against a 16-core ceiling. The scheduled campaign job takes FUZZTIME_NIGHTLY (10 minutes), SHARDS and SHARD, and ends with fuzzmanifest -require-runs — so a shard that died is a failure rather than a manifest with a hole in it.

The campaign also records the crashers and exports the corpus before the manifest step.

Cadence, and why it is not nightly. The full campaign runs weekly (Wednesday 01:00 UTC), not nightly. Eight shards at ten minutes a target is about 2,000 runner-minutes per campaign, which as a nightly job was 87 % of this repository's entire CI bill — for a library that is not under active fuzz-driven development, that is a cost without a matching signal. Weekly is also better fuzzing for the same money: go test -fuzz builds its corpus over the length of a single run, so one ten-minute run a week finds more than seven ninety-second runs would, and the corpus cache carries between them either way.

What still runs on every pull request is seeds-and-changed, which fuzzes the targets your change actually touches — that is where a new crasher comes from. The race-instrumented campaign stays weekly on Sunday, and workflow_dispatch runs the full campaign on demand, which is what to use while preparing a release.

.github/workflows/fuzz.yml does the same across eight runners instead of eight background shells, and has to spell the campaign out because the pieces land on different machines:

step where why there hack/fuzz.sh shard 8 N 10m each shard job one eighth of the targets make fuzz-corpus each shard job the fuzz cache it reads is that runner's make fuzz-manifest-complete the nightly-manifest job -require-runs is a statement about the whole target set, so only the job that has collected every shard's results can make it

-require-runs asks for a run of every target the default build includes. conformance/differential's three FuzzDifferential_* targets are //go:build integration and need a live broker, so they are in the manifest with their corpus hashes and a build_constraint field rather than counted as holes: the campaign enumerates 192 targets where the manifest walk finds 195, and those three are the difference.

The weekly race campaign is sharded the same way (hack/fuzz.sh race-shard), because one job over 195 targets at two minutes each never finished: it was cancelled at its 340-minute timeout every week and reported nothing.

docs.title: Replaying a failing input
docs.text:
Fuzzing writes failing inputs under testdata/fuzz/<target>/. CI uploads these files when a shard fails. Replay an input from its module directory:

go test -run='FuzzTarget/input-hash' ./path/to/package

Use -race when replaying an input found by a race shard. Inspect the failure output before treating an input as a code defect: build failures and worker termination can also interrupt a fuzz run. File issues manually with the input, replay command and output.

docs.title: The race shards keep the race report
docs.text:
hack/fuzz.sh sets GORACE=log_path=… for any -race run. Without it a race found by a shard reaches the log as

testing.go:1712: race detected during execution of test

Not halt_on_error=1: it also saves a crasher, but it kills the worker mid-report and the report text is lost again, which is the one thing this is for.

docs.title: make fuzz-seeds is the one that matters most
docs.text:
It runs every committed corpus input under -race, in every CI run. So a crash that was found once is a crash that is checked for ever after, at the cost of a few seconds.

Which is why committing an input is the important step after a crash, and why tools/fuzzcorpus export adds inputs and deletes nothing: deciding which of the thousands of interesting inputs earn a commit is a person's judgement, and throwing one away is not a tool's decision to make.

Two committed inputs in this repository are worth knowing about because they pin real, fixed defects:

  • a native body that begins with the envelope's magic prefix, which MetadataAdaptive once mis-decoded as an envelope. See metadata modes.
  • a RabbitMQ delivery-tag settlement ordering that raced. It made main intermittently red from its own committed seed, which is exactly what a seed corpus is for.

docs.title: The ratchet
docs.text:
hack/fuzz-ratchet.yaml holds a baseline_count that only ever increases, and a list of packages that must have a fuzz target. make ratchet (in make ci) fails when the count drops or when a parsing or stateful package has none.

It is a blunt instrument and deliberately so: the failure mode it prevents is a refactor that quietly deletes a target, which is invisible in a diff and removes coverage that took a machine-week to earn.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text:
func FuzzMyMapping(f *testing.F) {
    // A seed corpus authored in code, so it is readable in review: the Put
    // functions are the exact mirrors of the Gen functions.
    var w fuzzutil.Writer
    if err := fuzzkit.PutTopic(&w, fuzzkit.Default, "orders.eu"); err != nil {
        f.Fatal(err)
    }
    fuzzkit.PutPayload(&w, fuzzkit.Default, somePayload)
    f.Add(w.Bytes())

    f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, in []byte) {
        r := fuzzutil.NewReader(in)
        topic := fuzzkit.GenTopic(r, fuzzkit.Default)   // always a valid portable name
        p := fuzzkit.GenPayload(r, fuzzkit.Default)     // never aliases `in`
        // …encode, decode, compare. Never accept a partial round trip.
        _ = topic
        _ = p
    })
}

fuzzkit.GenTopicUnchecked is the deliberate exception, for a target whose subject is the validator.

For a state machine, fuzzutil.Script[S] is the op-script interpreter: Steps are the available operations over your state S, MaxSteps bounds the run, and Check runs after every step — which is where a differential comparison or an invariant assertion belongs, because a violation found three steps later is a violation you have to bisect by hand.

One caveat: internal/fuzzutil is internal to this repository, so a driver written outside it has testkit/fuzzkit (which is published) and its own script machinery. That asymmetry is recorded rather than hidden.

Three rules from this repository's own corpus:

Assert the property, not the absence of a panic. A fuzz target that only checks for crashes finds crashes. One that checks decode(encode(x)) == x finds wrong answers, which are more common and worse.

Compare against an oracle where one exists. For the engine that is the reference model; for a codec it is the standard library; for a driver's mapping it is the client library's own round trip. A differential target is the strongest shape available.

Never let the generated data alias the fuzz input. fuzzkit guarantees this for you. A target that hands the fuzzer's own slice to something that retains it produces failures that do not reproduce.

docs.title: Where a crash goes
docs.text: A crash writes an input under testdata/fuzz/<Target>/. Commit it with a testdata/fuzz/<Target>.README line saying what it reaches — the existing ones do, and a corpus input whose purpose nobody recorded is an input the next person deletes during a cleanup.

docs.title: The memory driver as a test double
docs.text:
github.com/iqhive/iqmq/memory is in the root module, depends on the standard library only, and implements the same mq.Backend as Kafka does. That last part is the whole argument for using it in tests: a test written against it exercises the real runner, the real settlement state machine and the real capability guards.

It is also the reference target for this repository's own state-machine, linearizability and differential testing, which means its conformance is held tighter than any network driver's.

docs.title: NewForTest
docs.text:
client, broker := memory.NewForTest(t, opts...)

Three things it does that memory.Open does not:

  • AutoCreate on. Topics appear when you publish to them. Open defaults it off, to be consistent with network drivers where creating a topic is a privileged operation.
  • a fake clock. Nothing advances until you say so.
  • a goroutine-leak check on t.Cleanup. A consumer you forgot to close fails the test rather than slowing down the next one.

memory.TestRealClock() hands time back to the wall clock — or, inside a synctest bubble, to the bubble. That is the option the synctest page is about.

docs.title: Driving time
docs.text:
broker.Advance(30 * time.Second)   // lease expiry, delayed delivery, TTL, backoff

Advance moves the fake clock and lets the scheduler fire everything that is now due: delayed publications, delayed requeues, TTL expiry and lease expiry all run off the same per-broker scheduler, so one call exercises all four.

It returns an error, and the error is informative rather than decorative: on a broker left on the real clock there is no fake clock to move, and Advance says so instead of silently doing nothing.

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
f := broker.Faults()
f.RejectPublish(1)         // the next publication is refused
f.FailSettlement(-1)       // every settlement fails until disarmed with 0
f.DuplicateDelivery(2)
f.FailDeadLetter(1)        // the runner must requeue, not ack
f.DelaySettlement(3)
f.Reorder(4)               // only where no order is promised

n := f.ExpireLeases()      // the sweeps happen NOW rather than when due
_ = f.CloseConsumers()
_ = f.Reconnect()

// and the counters that say the path was taken
_ = f.PublishRejections()
_ = f.SettlementFailures()
_ = f.DeadLetterFailures()
_ = f.Duplicates()

the list, and the counters are the point. Each armed fault reports how often it fired, so a test asserts that the path it wanted was taken rather than that nothing crashed — and a fault that fired zero times tells you the test did not reach the branch. That has caught more broken tests here than broken code.

A positive count fires that many times; a negative count fires until disarmed with 0. The sweep methods — ExpireLeases, ExpireRecords, TrimRetention, CloseConsumers, Reconnect — are not armed faults but immediate actions returning how many records or consumers they touched: the scheduler does them on its own, and the fault makes them happen now rather than being the only way they happen.

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text:
snap, err := broker.Inspect("orders", "billing")   // per-lane state
msgs, bytes, discarded := broker.Totals()

Inspect is what the engine's model tests assert on, and it is available to you for the same reason: when a test fails, "there are three records ready and one in flight" is the fact that explains it.

docs.title: The three topologies
docs.text:
memory.TopologyConfig.Kind — and they are genuinely different code paths rather than one with flags, because the specification requires the queue fast path not to pay for stream bookkeeping:

Kind Behaviour memory.TopologyQueue competing consumers; the record is removed after a terminal ack memory.TopologyTopic fan-out to independent subscriptions, each with its own backpressure and settlement state memory.TopologyStream a bounded retained log with replayable cursors and consumer groups

Pick the one that matches the broker you are standing in for. A test against TopologyQueue will not catch a bug that only appears when a second subscription is slow, and a test against TopologyTopic will not catch one that depends on replay.

memory.TopologyForTest is the shorthand for a topology in a test.

docs.title: What it is honest about
docs.text:
It is never persistent, and never advertises durable storage. So it cannot stand in for a durability test, mq.ConfirmDurable fails at construction on it, and FeatureDurableSubscriptions renders as emulated-volatile rather than as support. Those are the right answers and they are why you cannot use the memory driver to prove a durability claim.

Its capability table is generated from a real conformance run, like every other driver's: docs/drivers/memory.capabilities.md. The engine is held to the same evidence standard as a network broker.

docs.title: Choosing the engine's internals
docs.text:
memory.EngineConfig selects the variant implementations, and every Auto is a recorded bake-off winner. Leave them on Auto — except for one case:

cfg.Engine = memory.SafeEngine()   // every family forced to its mutex reference kind

That is the differential-testing configuration. If a test passes under SafeEngine() and fails under the defaults, you have found a bug in a variant implementation, and that is a report worth making.

docs.title: Testing with testing/synctest
docs.text:
testing/synctest runs a test inside a bubble: a goroutine group with its own fake clock, where time advances only when every goroutine in the group is blocked. A test of an hour's backoff finishes in microseconds and — the part that matters — you can assert how much time passed.

This library is built to work in one. internal/clock is injected everywhere, nothing in a hot path calls time.Now unless an observer is active, and the memory engine's scheduler is a single goroutine that sleeps until the next non-empty slot rather than ticking.

docs.title: The two clocks, and which one you want
docs.text:
memory.NewForTest(t) memory.NewForTest(t, memory.TestRealClock()) clock the engine's own fake clock whatever time does — the bubble's clock inside synctest advance broker.Advance(d) the bubble advances it when everything blocks use it for a plain unit test with no bubble a synctest test

TestRealClock is the option that hands time to the bubble. Inside a bubble the "real" clock is fake, so this is not a contradiction: the bubble owns time, and the engine must not own a second clock that the bubble cannot move.

broker.Advance on such a broker returns an error, because there is no clock of its own to move, and the error says exactly that rather than silently succeeding.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
func TestChargeWorkflowInABubble(t *testing.T) {
    const base = time.Hour
    synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) {
        client, broker := memory.NewForTest(t, memory.TestRealClock())
        if err := broker.Advance(time.Second); err == nil {
            t.Fatal("Advance succeeded on a broker left on the wall clock")
        }

        start := time.Now()
        if err := chargeWorkflow(t.Context(), &out, client, base); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        // Two failures and a doubling backoff based at an hour is one hour
        // then two: exactly three hours of bubble time.
        if got, want := time.Since(start), base+2*base; got != want {
            t.Errorf("took %v of bubble time, want exactly %v", got, want)
        }
    })
}

That is examples/testing-with-synctest, which is compiled and run by make examples in every make ci.

docs.title: Why the assertion is the point
docs.text:
Anybody can run a retrying consumer under synctest and watch it finish quickly. What a deterministic test buys is that the schedule is checkable: if the runner stopped waiting between attempts, or capped the delay, or drew it out of a jitter envelope when the test asked for none, that time.Since would change and nothing else in the test would.

A test that only asserts "it eventually succeeded" passes against a runner with no backoff at all. This one does not.

docs.title: What to assert, by feature
docs.text: Feature The assertion retry backoff elapsed bubble time equals the sum of the intervals your policy defines. Use mq.NoJitter — mq.FullJitter is the default and is deliberately not deterministic. a lease expiring mid-handler the settlement returns mq.ErrLeaseLost, and ConsumerStats.Redelivered advanced delayed publication nothing is delivered before the due time, and exactly one thing is at it TTL the record is gone at the boundary and present just before it a drain timeout Shutdown returns non-nil after exactly mq.DefaultDrainTimeout

docs.title: Two rules
docs.text:
Do not time.Sleep in a bubble to "let things settle". The bubble advances time when everything is blocked, so a sleep is an assertion about ordering dressed up as a delay. Block on the thing you are waiting for.

Use mq.NoJitter when you assert a schedule. The default is mq.FullJitter — it draws uniformly from [0, interval], because the default is bounded exponential jittered backoff and a caller who names a base and a cap should get the jitter rather than a retry storm. A schedule assertion against a jittered backoff is a flaky test, and the fix is to name the jitter rather than to widen the assertion.

docs.title: Outside a bubble
docs.text: broker.Advance(d) is the whole mechanism and it is enough for most tests. The bubble adds two things: your own goroutines are also on fake time, and the "everything is blocked" condition gives you a precise notion of quiescence. If your code under test has no timers of its own, Advance alone is simpler.

docs.title: testkit — the conformance kit
docs.text: github.com/iqhive/iqmq/testkit is the suite every driver has to pass, and the machine-readable report it produces. Specification.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
A driver's capability table is a set of claims, and the specification says they have to be true. The kit is what makes them checkable: every scenario is gated by a capability, and every claim is proved in both directions — the feature works when the driver says it does, and the unsupported path is refused when it says it cannot.

A claim proved in only one direction is not proved, and that is not a nicety. Two drivers are invisible to a happy-path suite: one that advertises delayed redelivery and silently redelivers immediately, and one that says it cannot dead-letter while its reject destroys the message.

docs.title: It uses only the portable API
docs.text:
Every scenario goes through mq.Client and the handles it opens. Nothing in the kit reaches for the SPI, for a driver's own types, or for Native. A conformance kit that used a driver's internals would pass a driver whose public behaviour was wrong, which is the one thing it exists to prevent.

That also makes it usable on your own driver, from outside this repository.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
func TestConformance(t *testing.T) {
    testkit.RunConformance(t, testkit.Harness{
        Driver:    "mydriver",
        Open:      open,
        TopicName: func(p string) string { return "conformance." + p },
        Timeout:   30 * time.Second,
        Evidence:  testkit.EvidenceInProcess,
    })
}

RunConformance is the *testing.T entry point. Run is the same suite without one, and it exists for a specific reason: it is what lets the kit's own tests check that it rejects a driver it should reject. A conformance kit nobody has watched fail is assumed not to work.

Write the test in package <driver>_test, not in the driver's own package. drivers/nats/conformance_test.go is the model. A harness that reaches unexported helpers works for its own driver and is useless as an example for anybody else's — which is exactly the state memory/conformance_test.go is in, and it is recorded as such.

docs.title: Evidence is part of the report
docs.text:
Value Means testkit.EvidenceInProcess no broker; the memory driver testkit.EvidenceContainer a real broker in a container testkit.EvidenceEmulator a vendor emulator — Pub/Sub's, LocalStack, ElasticMQ testkit.EvidenceManaged a real managed service

This is not bookkeeping. An emulator's evidence is never presented as the managed service's: the capability matrix renders such a cell with ◐, and The specification layer 4 is where a managed-service claim belongs. A report that claimed EvidenceContainer for ElasticMQ would be the specific dishonesty the whole generated-matrix machinery exists to prevent — and no run has ever carried EvidenceManaged.

docs.title: What a driver has to supply
docs.text:
Beyond Open: the things the kit cannot know.

  • TopicName — the driver's own naming, so the kit's topics do not collide with anything.
  • Wildcard — the subject syntax, where the driver has wildcards. The kit cannot guess orders.* versus orders.#.
  • Secrets — for the redaction scenario.
  • Faults — the injection hook, where the driver has a fake backend to inject into. testkit.Faults.LeakSecret already exists and is wired into the kit's own fake, and so do the three the negative probes are held to: ShareSubscriptions (two subscription names are one subscription, which is a queue broker's shape and what the SPI cannot declare), RefuseOpenSource (a refusal from a call that is not the feature's) and NackError (a driver that answers the feature's own call with something that is not a refusal).

docs.title: Guarantees, behaviours, and the driver that does something else
docs.text:
Every claim is checked in both directions, and the negative direction — the driver says it cannot do this; prove it refuses — has a question behind it that only sometimes has an answer.

A behaviour is a call the driver can refuse: a delay, a lease extension, a seek, a dead-letter route. One run settles it in both directions.

A guarantee is a promise about every run: an ordering, a delivery multiplicity, a durability. There is no call to refuse, so one run can observe it broken and no number of runs can observe it absent. testkit.Kind says which a result is evidence about, and the report carries it.

The third case is the one that took longest to name: a driver that accepts the feature's own call and does something else. A queue broker takes two subscription names and makes them one subscription; a broker that deletes a settled message takes a second reader at the earliest position and has nothing to give it; a driver with settlement and no at-least-once takes a Nack and correctly never redelivers. Nothing is refused, the call succeeds, and the difference shows up only in what arrives. A probe says so with testkit.Diverged, and the two directions read it oppositely:

the driver negative direction (.../refused) positive direction (.../works) refuses the feature's own call pass — the denial is proven, and the note names the call fail — it advertises the feature and refuses it does the feature fail — an unverified negative claim is how a caller comes to rely on behaviour the driver may remove pass accepts the call and does something else unrefuted — a skip that says what happened; the result's kind becomes guarantee, so the matrix renders unrefuted rather than unverified fail, naming what happened instead answers the call with something that is neither fail — the specification allows exactly one refusal, ErrUnsupported (or the specification's ErrNotSettleable) fail never reaches the feature's own call skip, naming the call that was not reached fail

The last row is why each probe names the one call that matters. A refusal from somewhere else in the probe — opening a consumer, publishing on the way past — is evidence about that call, and reading it as the refusal made a driver that could not open a consumer at all look like one whose every negative claim had been refuted by observation.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text: It also fails on a generated page no report produces, which is the gap -check used to have: remove a driver's report and its capability page stayed on disk, stating capabilities from evidence that was gone.

docs.title: Its own known weaknesses
docs.text:
Documented rather than glossed, because a kit's blind spots are the reader's business:

  • A driver that accepts a header and loses it cannot be told from a broker that has no such header. The three header claims are the one place where "the call was accepted and the value did not survive" is both a violation (a driver that cannot carry a header must refuse the publication) and the honest shape of a broker without native headers. The probe reports a divergence, so the negative direction stays unrefuted rather than failing a truthful denial — and an enveloping driver, whose headers do survive, therefore fails the negative direction because the header comes back. Recorded with an owner.
  • Nine of the features have no portable probe at all — a probe would need something the kit cannot do portably, such as restarting a broker for durability or knowing a filter expression's syntax. Fifteen more are probed by some runs and not others. Those claims render in parentheses, and the matrix derives the list from the reports rather than counting by hand.
  • There is no provisioning hook, so a fan-out driver must provision inside Harness.Open — SNS delivers only to subscriptions that exist when a message is published, and several scenarios publish before they open a consumer.
  • harness.Image returns the tag rather than the digest images.lock pins. Four drivers have recorded it. The report therefore names a tag where it should name a digest.
